1.ctx: Mark opens not with a birth story but with a statement of what the book is about, then goes straight to John in the Judean wilderness, around AD 28. The quotation blends Malachi 3:1 with Isaiah 40:3; Mark names only Isaiah, which was common practice with combined quotations.
1.mean: Mark says John's role is to prepare the way, and John himself points away from himself to one who is stronger and will baptise with the Holy Spirit. In verses 9 to 11 Jesus is baptised like any other Israelite — a real man going down into the river — and the Father's voice and the Spirit's descent identify him as the beloved Son. Christians have long seen here the first place in Mark where Jesus appears as fully human and fully divine at once: the church's doctrine of the two natures, explained further at 4:35.
1.big: From the first line, Mark tells the reader what the characters inside the story will struggle to see: Jesus is the Son of God.
1.diff: Some early manuscripts lack 'the Son of God' in verse 1. Both readings are ancient; the title appears at the centre and climax of the Gospel regardless.
1.h: The Mission of John the Baptist

1.ctx: Immediately after the baptism. Mark gives the temptation two verses where Matthew and Luke give fuller accounts, and adds the detail that Jesus was with the wild animals.
1.mean: Mark says the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness for forty days. The number recalls Israel's forty years in the wilderness, and many scholars read this as Jesus succeeding where Israel failed. His first recorded words, in verse 15, summarise his message: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom of God has come near, repent and believe.
1.big: Jesus arrives announcing that God's long-promised rule is now breaking in.
1.h: The Temptation and Preaching of Jesus

1.ctx: The Sea of Galilee, where fishing was a substantial trade. Simon, Andrew, James and John were not poor labourers: Zebedee employs hired men.
1.mean: Mark says Jesus called and they left immediately. He gives no explanation of their motives — only the call and the response. This suggests Mark's interest is in the authority of the one calling rather than the psychology of those called.
1.big: Jesus calls people with an authority that expects immediate, costly obedience.

1.ctx: Capernaum, Jesus' base in Galilee, in the synagogue on a Sabbath, where visiting teachers were often invited to speak.
1.mean: Mark says the people were astonished because he taught with authority, not as the scribes — who characteristically cited earlier teachers. A man with an unclean spirit is the first character in the Gospel to name Jesus correctly, and Jesus silences him. Compare 1:34 and 3:11: throughout Mark the spirit world recognises Jesus while people do not.
1.big: Jesus' authority is visible in both his teaching and his power over evil, yet his identity remains hidden from the people around him.

1.ctx: The same Sabbath, now in Simon's house. The crowds wait until sunset, when the Sabbath ended and carrying the sick became permissible.
1.mean: Mark says the healing is immediate and complete: Simon's mother-in-law gets up and serves them. By evening the whole town is at the door. Mark again notes that Jesus would not let the demons speak, because they knew him.
1.big: Jesus' power to restore is shown in ordinary homes as well as public places.

1.ctx: Very early the next morning, after a day of healing and growing popularity.
1.mean: Mark says Jesus got up while it was still dark to pray alone. When Simon finds him and says everyone is looking for him, Jesus moves on because preaching is why he came. The Son of God prays — a mark of real human dependence on the Father, which the church has always affirmed alongside his divinity (see 4:35).
1.big: Jesus is directed by his mission and his communion with the Father, not by the demands of the crowd.

1.ctx: Leprosy in Scripture covered several skin diseases and, under Leviticus 13 and 14, brought ritual uncleanness and exclusion from the community.
1.mean: Mark says Jesus touched the man before healing him. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean; here the direction is reversed and the man is made clean. Jesus sends him to the priest as the law required. The man's disobedience in spreading the news forces Jesus out of the towns.
1.big: Jesus' holiness is not endangered by contact with the unclean; instead it overcomes the uncleanness.
1.diff: Some manuscripts say Jesus was 'moved with anger' rather than 'compassion' in verse 41. If that reading is original, the anger is most likely directed at the disease and its effects, not at the man.

2.ctx: Back in Capernaum. This passage begins five conflict stories (2:1 to 3:6) that build toward the plot to kill Jesus in 3:6.
2.mean: Mark says Jesus forgave the paralysed man before healing him. The scribes reason that only God can forgive sins — and their reasoning is correct, which is why they call it blasphemy. Jesus proves his authority to do the invisible thing by doing the visible one. 'Son of Man', his preferred title for himself, draws on Daniel 7:13–14, where a human figure receives everlasting authority from God.
2.big: Jesus claims a right that belongs to God alone, and backs the claim with a healing anyone could see.

2.ctx: Tax collectors bought the right to collect for Rome and kept the excess, so they were regarded as collaborators and cheats.
2.mean: Mark says Jesus called Levi as directly as he called the fishermen, then ate with tax collectors and sinners — table fellowship that signalled acceptance. Jesus answers the objection by saying he came for the sick, not the healthy. The saying assumes they are genuinely sick: this suggests grace rather than approval of their conduct.
2.big: Jesus' mission is aimed deliberately at those the religious establishment had written off.

2.ctx: Devout Jews fasted regularly — the Pharisees twice a week — and John's disciples did too.
2.mean: Mark says Jesus compared his presence to a wedding, where fasting would be out of place. In the Old Testament God is described as the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2), so many scholars see an implied claim here. Jesus adds that the bridegroom will be taken away — the first hint in Mark of his death.
2.big: Jesus' arrival changes the character of religious life, because the one Israel waited for is present.

2.ctx: Still answering the question about fasting. His hearers knew the images well: unshrunk cloth was not used for patching, and wine was stored in skins that grew brittle with age.
2.mean: Mark records two short sayings: new cloth tears an old garment, new wine bursts old skins. Most scholars read these as saying that what Jesus brings cannot simply be absorbed into existing religious forms without changing them.
2.big: What Jesus brings is not an adjustment to existing religion but something that requires new forms.

2.ctx: Plucking grain as you walked was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25), but the Pharisees classed it as reaping, which was forbidden on the Sabbath.
2.mean: Mark says Jesus cited David eating the consecrated bread, then made two claims: the Sabbath was made for man, and the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. The second is the weightier: it claims authority over an institution God himself established.
2.big: Jesus claims authority over God's own law, not merely the right to interpret it.
2.diff: Mark names Abiathar as high priest, while 1 Samuel 21 names his father Ahimelech. Proposed explanations include that the phrase means 'in the passage about Abiathar', or that Abiathar was already serving alongside his father. It is a recognised difficulty.

3.ctx: The fifth conflict story, again on the Sabbath, in a synagogue, with opponents watching for grounds to accuse him.
3.mean: Mark says Jesus asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, and they were silent. Mark alone records that Jesus looked at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart. Real human emotion — anger and grief together — sits alongside divine authority to heal (see 4:35 on the two natures). The Pharisees then plot with the Herodians, normally their opponents, to destroy him.
3.big: Before a fifth of the Gospel is over, the decision to kill Jesus has already been made.

3.ctx: A summary passage. Jesus' fame now draws people from Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan and Tyre and Sidon — Jewish and Gentile regions alike.
3.mean: Mark says the crowds pressed to touch him and unclean spirits fell down crying 'You are the Son of God'. Jesus sternly ordered them not to make him known. This suggests Jesus did not want his identity proclaimed by demons or before its meaning could be understood.
3.big: Jesus' popularity grows, but recognition without understanding is not what he seeks.

3.ctx: On a mountain, a setting many scholars connect with Sinai, where Israel was constituted as a people.
3.mean: Mark says Jesus appointed twelve, first to be with him and then to be sent out. Twelve matches the tribes of Israel, and most scholars read the choice as Jesus forming a renewed Israel around himself. Judas is named in the list from the start, with his betrayal attached.
3.big: Jesus is forming a new community around himself, and its first calling is simply to be with him.

3.ctx: Mark begins one of his 'sandwich' structures, splitting the story of Jesus' family around the Beelzebul controversy so that each part interprets the other.
3.mean: Mark says Jesus' family set out to seize him because people said he was out of his mind, and scribes from Jerusalem claimed he was possessed. Jesus answers that Satan cannot cast out Satan, and describes himself as one who binds the strong man in order to plunder his house.
3.big: Jesus' power over demons shows he is not Satan's agent but the one overpowering him.

3.ctx: The centre of the sandwich, straight after the scribes' accusation. Mark's comment in verse 30 makes the link explicit.
3.mean: Mark records Jesus saying that every sin and blasphemy can be forgiven except blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The context shows what is meant: the scribes were looking at the Spirit's evident work and calling it Satan's.
3.big: The seriousness of rejecting Jesus lies in refusing to recognise God's work when it is plainly in front of you.
3.diff: Christians have often feared committing this sin. The consistent pastoral reading across traditions is that it describes a settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit's work, not a moment of doubt or a passing thought — and that a person anxious about having committed it has shown by that anxiety that they have not.

3.ctx: The sandwich closes: his mother and brothers arrive outside, having set out to take him home.
3.mean: Mark records Jesus saying that whoever does the will of God is his brother, sister and mother. This is not a rejection of his family but a statement about where the deepest belonging now lies.
3.big: Membership of Jesus' family is defined by doing God's will, not by natural relation.

4.ctx: Jesus teaches from a boat to a crowd on the shore. This is the longest block of teaching in Mark.
4.mean: Mark records a parable of seed falling on four kinds of ground with four outcomes. Most scholars read it as explaining why Jesus' ministry produced such mixed responses — and promising a harvest of thirty, sixty and a hundredfold, far beyond an ordinary yield.
4.big: Despite rejection and loss, God's word will produce a harvest far greater than its beginnings suggest.

4.ctx: Private teaching to the Twelve and those around him — a recurring pattern in Mark, where public teaching is followed by private explanation.
4.mean: Mark records Jesus quoting Isaiah 6:9–10: to outsiders everything comes in parables, so that they may see but not perceive. Mark says the secret of the kingdom has been 'given' to the disciples, which suggests understanding is received rather than achieved.
4.big: Understanding who Jesus is comes as a gift, not as an achievement.
4.diff: Readers divide over whether 'so that' expresses purpose (the parables intended to conceal) or result (concealment following rejection). Reformed interpreters stress that spiritual understanding is God's gift; all agree the disciples did not understand by their own ability, as the following chapters show.

4.ctx: Continuing the private explanation. Mark's first readers, facing persecution under Nero, would have recognised themselves in the ground that falls away 'when trouble or persecution comes'.
4.mean: Mark records Jesus explaining the parable himself. The seed is the word. It is snatched away by Satan, withers under pressure, is choked by worries, wealth and desires, or takes root and bears fruit.
4.big: Pressure from outside and distraction from within are presented as the two great threats to receiving God's word.
4.h: The Parable of the Sower Explained

4.ctx: Still part of the teaching by the lake. Oil lamps were set on stands to light a one-room house.
4.mean: Mark records two sayings. A lamp is brought in to be seen, so what is hidden will be disclosed. The measure you use will be measured to you — which most scholars read as how you listen determining what you receive.
4.big: What is now hidden about Jesus and his kingdom will not stay hidden.

4.ctx: The only parable found only in Mark. Galilean farmers sowed by scattering seed, and germination was genuinely mysterious to them.
4.mean: Mark records a farmer who sows and sleeps while the seed grows 'he knows not how'. Most scholars read it as saying that God's kingdom grows by God's power rather than human effort.
4.big: The growth of God's kingdom depends on God, not on those who sow.

4.ctx: The last parable in this block. The mustard seed was proverbial in Jewish sayings for smallness.
4.mean: Mark records the kingdom compared to the smallest seed becoming the largest garden plant, with birds nesting in its shade. Many scholars hear an echo of Ezekiel 17 and Daniel 4, where great trees shelter the nations.
4.big: The kingdom's small and unimpressive beginning is no measure of its final size.
4.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed

4.ctx: That evening, crossing to the eastern, largely Gentile shore. The Sea of Galilee lies in a basin surrounded by hills and is prone to sudden, violent storms.
4.mean: Mark says Jesus was asleep on a cushion in the stern — worn out from a day of teaching, and sleeping through a storm that frightened experienced fishermen. Woken, he rebuked the wind and the sea, and they obeyed. In the Old Testament, stilling the sea is something God does (Psalm 107:29, Psalm 89:9). The disciples' question — who then is this? — is Mark's question for the reader. The church has understood scenes like this through what it calls the hypostatic union: Jesus is one person with two complete natures, truly human and truly God, united without being mixed or divided, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451. Mark does not use that language, but he shows it: the same Jesus sleeps from exhaustion and commands the storm.
4.big: In a single scene Mark shows Jesus as truly human and as possessing the authority of God.
4.diff: Mark gives us the scene; the vocabulary of 'two natures' is the church's later formulation of what scenes like this show. It is accepted by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches alike.

5.ctx: The region of the Gerasenes, Gentile territory on the eastern shore — hence the herd of pigs, which Jews would not have kept.
5.mean: Mark says a man living among the tombs, unclean in every sense, was set free. The demons give their name as Legion, the word for a Roman military unit of several thousand soldiers. Once healed, he is the first person Jesus commissions to tell others rather than keep silent; many scholars suggest that in Gentile territory the misunderstanding the silence commands guarded against did not arise.
5.big: Jesus' authority reaches beyond Israel into Gentile lands, and restores someone beyond every human help.
5.diff: The death of the pigs troubles some readers. Commentators note that it demonstrated the reality and scale of the deliverance, and that the townspeople's response — asking Jesus to leave — reveals which loss they valued more.

5.ctx: Another Mark sandwich: the woman with bleeding placed inside Jairus's story, linked by the number twelve — twelve years of illness, a twelve-year-old girl.
5.mean: Mark says Jairus, a synagogue leader, fell at Jesus' feet. On the way, a woman bleeding for twelve years — and ritually unclean because of it — touched his cloak and was healed. Jesus insisted on finding her and called her 'daughter'. Meanwhile Jairus's daughter died, and Jesus raised her, speaking in Aramaic: 'Talitha koum'.
5.big: Jesus has power over lasting illness, ritual uncleanness and death itself — and delay is not defeat.

6.ctx: Nazareth, Jesus' home town, a small village where everyone knew his family by name.
6.mean: Mark says the townspeople were offended because they knew him: 'Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?' The question is a reminder that Jesus had lived an ordinary working life — a craftsman in a village, known to his neighbours (see 4:35 on his full humanity). Mark says Jesus could do no mighty work there apart from a few healings, and that he marvelled at their unbelief. Mark links miracles and faith elsewhere too (2:5, 5:34, 10:52), though not every miracle follows faith: the Gerasene man and Jairus's daughter had none to offer. Compare 8:11–12, where Jesus refuses to perform a sign on demand.
6.big: Familiarity with Jesus' ordinary humanity became, for his own town, a reason not to believe.
6.diff: Mark calls Jesus 'the son of Mary', unusual when men were named by their fathers; some see a slur on his birth, others simply that Joseph had died. The brothers named have been understood as later children of Mary, as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage, or as cousins, depending on the tradition.

6.ctx: The Twelve are sent out in pairs — Jewish law required two witnesses to establish testimony.
6.mean: Mark says they were to travel light and depend on hospitality, and that they preached repentance, cast out demons and anointed the sick. Shaking dust off their feet was a solemn sign of judgement, one Jews normally used when leaving Gentile territory.
6.big: Jesus' mission now extends through those he has called and sent.

6.ctx: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee — not the Herod of the nativity. The Jewish historian Josephus independently records John's execution at the fortress of Machaerus.
6.mean: Mark tells the story of John's death in detail, the one extended scene in the Gospel in which Jesus does not appear. It sits between the sending out and the return of the Twelve. Many scholars read the placement as deliberate: this is what happens to those who speak for God to people in power.
6.big: The fate of the forerunner foreshadows the fate of Jesus and warns those who follow him.

6.ctx: The apostles return from the mission of 6:7. They try to withdraw to a quiet place near Bethsaida, but the crowds run ahead of them.
6.mean: Mark says Jesus had compassion on the crowd because they were like sheep without a shepherd — a phrase from Numbers 27:17 and the theme of Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's failed shepherds and promises to shepherd the flock himself. The compassion is genuinely human feeling (see 4:35). Mark says he had them sit on green grass, which many hear as echoing Psalm 23, and his actions — took, blessed, broke, gave — match those at the Last Supper in 14:22.
6.big: Jesus is the shepherd God promised, who feeds his people in the wilderness.
6.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand

6.ctx: Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up a mountain to pray. The fourth watch of the night was between 3 and 6 in the morning.
6.mean: Mark says Jesus prayed alone and then came to them walking on the sea, and that 'he meant to pass by them' — language used when God passed by Moses (Exodus 33–34) and Elijah (1 Kings 19). His words 'Take heart, it is I' are literally 'I am'. As at 4:35, the one who prays in dependence on the Father also does what only God does. Mark ends by saying their hearts were hardened, the same word he uses of the Pharisees in 3:5.
6.big: Jesus acts as God acts in the Old Testament, and even his closest followers fail to grasp it.

6.ctx: They land at Gennesaret, the fertile plain on the north-west shore, rather than Bethsaida where they were heading. The episode closes a long section of miracles around the lake.
6.mean: Mark says people brought the sick wherever he went, begging to touch even the fringe of his cloak, and all who touched it were healed. Mark reports the enormous popularity without enthusiasm.
6.big: Jesus' fame is immense, but crowds seeking healing are not the same as disciples who understand him.

7.ctx: Mark explains Jewish washing customs for his readers, which is evidence that he was writing for Gentiles.
7.mean: Mark says the Pharisees objected that the disciples ate with unwashed hands — a matter of ritual tradition, not hygiene. Jesus quotes Isaiah on honouring God with lips while hearts are far away, and exposes 'Corban', a vow dedicating property to God that let a man avoid supporting his parents. Human tradition was being used to cancel a command of God.
7.big: Jesus places God's command above human religious tradition, and exposes tradition used to evade it.

7.ctx: Following directly from the dispute over handwashing. The food laws of Leviticus 11 were a daily marker separating Jews from Gentiles.
7.mean: Mark records Jesus saying that nothing entering a person defiles them; what comes out of the heart does, followed by a list of twelve evils. In verse 19 Mark adds his own comment: in saying this, Jesus declared all foods clean.
7.big: Real defilement is a matter of the heart, which is why the old boundary markers are no longer needed.

7.ctx: Jesus has gone north to the region of Tyre, a Gentile city on the coast of what is now Lebanon, looking for privacy. Relations between Tyre and Galilean Jews were historically tense.
7.mean: Mark says a Syrophoenician woman asked Jesus to heal her daughter, and he replied that the children's bread should not be thrown to the dogs. She accepted the priority he stated and pressed for the crumbs. Mark records that Jesus granted her request because of what she said — the only person in Mark who wins an argument with Jesus.
7.big: The blessing of God's kingdom reaches the Gentiles through humble persistence.
7.diff: Readers differ on the tone of Jesus' reply: a real test of her faith, or Jesus voicing a common attitude in order to overturn it. All agree the outcome shows the gospel reaching Gentiles.
7.h: The Faith of the Gentile Woman

7.ctx: A roundabout route through Sidon and back to the Decapolis, the ten Greek cities east of the Jordan — still mainly Gentile territory.
7.mean: Mark says Jesus healed a deaf man with a speech impediment, using touch and spittle and the Aramaic word 'Ephphatha', be opened. The crowd's words — he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak — echo Isaiah 35:5–6, a prophecy of God's coming salvation.
7.big: Jesus fulfils the signs the prophets said would mark God's arrival to save.

8.ctx: Probably still in Gentile territory, with a crowd that had been with Jesus three days.
8.mean: Mark records a second feeding, of four thousand, with seven loaves and seven baskets left over. Many scholars read the two feedings as Jewish and Gentile counterparts: the same provision offered to both.
8.big: Jesus' provision for his people extends to the Gentiles as well.
8.h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand

8.ctx: Back on the western shore after the feeding of the four thousand. The Pharisees wanted a sign from heaven, the kind Moses or Elijah had given, to prove him.
8.mean: Mark says Jesus sighed deeply in his spirit — a human expression of weariness and distress (see 4:35) — and refused to give a sign to this generation. This suggests that signs had already been given; what was missing was willingness to read them.
8.big: Jesus will not perform on demand for those who have already refused the evidence.

8.ctx: In the boat, the disciples worry about having only one loaf.
8.mean: Mark records Jesus warning them against the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod, then asking a series of sharp questions: do you not yet understand? The language of eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, used of outsiders in chapter 4, is now applied to the Twelve.
8.big: Even Jesus' closest followers are still, at this point, largely blind to who he is.
8.h: The Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod

8.ctx: Bethsaida, on the northern shore, home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip. This healing and the one in 7:31 bracket the disciples' failure to understand in 8:14–21.
8.mean: Mark says Jesus healed a blind man in two stages: first he saw people like trees walking, then clearly. It is the only two-stage healing in the Gospels. Most scholars read its placement as deliberate: in the next scene Peter sees partly, naming Jesus correctly and then misunderstanding what that means.
8.big: Mark uses a gradual healing to picture the gradual opening of the disciples' eyes.

8.ctx: Caesarea Philippi, near a centre of pagan worship and a temple to Caesar. Most scholars treat this as the turning point of the Gospel.
8.mean: Mark says Jesus asked who people said he was, then asked the disciples, and Peter answered: you are the Christ. Jesus told them to tell no one. From this point the journey turns toward Jerusalem and the teaching turns toward the cross.
8.big: The hinge of the Gospel: the disciples recognise Jesus as Messiah, and the story now turns to what kind of Messiah he is.

8.ctx: Immediately after Peter's confession. Popular expectation was of a Messiah who would defeat Rome, not suffer at its hands.
8.mean: Mark records the first of three predictions of Jesus' death: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise after three days. 'Must' suggests divine purpose rather than tragic accident. Peter rebukes Jesus and is rebuked in turn — 'Get behind me, Satan' — for thinking in human terms about what the Messiah should do.
8.big: The Messiah must suffer and die, and anyone who resists that has misunderstood him.

8.ctx: Still at Caesarea Philippi; Jesus now calls the crowd as well as the disciples. Crucifixion was common in Roman Judea, and condemned men carried their own crossbeam.
8.mean: Mark records Jesus saying that anyone who would follow him must deny himself, take up his cross and follow; that saving one's life means losing it; and that whoever is ashamed of him, the Son of Man will be ashamed of when he comes in glory.
8.big: The way of the Messiah through the cross becomes the way for everyone who follows him.

9.ctx: Six days after Peter's confession, on a high mountain, traditionally identified as Tabor or Hermon.
9.mean: Mark says Jesus was transfigured before Peter, James and John, and that Moses and Elijah — representing the law and the prophets — talked with him. The Father's voice says 'listen to him', which many scholars hear as echoing Deuteronomy 18:15, the promise of a prophet like Moses. Then they saw no one but Jesus.
9.big: The glory of the one who must suffer is briefly revealed, confirming who he is as the road to the cross begins.
9.diff: Verse 1, about some seeing the kingdom come with power, has been read of the transfiguration, the resurrection, Pentecost, the fall of Jerusalem, or the final coming. Its placement immediately before the transfiguration makes that the most natural reading.

9.ctx: Coming down from the mountain, they find the other disciples have failed to heal a boy, and scribes are arguing with them.
9.mean: Mark records a father saying 'I believe; help my unbelief', and Jesus healing his son. Jesus tells the disciples this kind comes out only by prayer. The father's prayer is honest about faith and doubt existing together, and Jesus answers it rather than demanding more certainty first. (Many Christians have found it one of the most honest prayers in Scripture; that is a devotional judgement rather than something Mark says.)
9.big: Jesus answers faith even when it is mixed with doubt, and his power is not dependent on his followers' ability.
9.h: The Boy with an Evil Spirit

9.ctx: Travelling secretly through Galilee to teach the disciples privately, as the final journey toward Jerusalem begins.
9.mean: Mark records the second prediction of the passion, now including betrayal: the Son of Man is to be delivered into human hands. Mark says they did not understand and were afraid to ask.
9.big: Jesus keeps telling them plainly where the road leads, and they keep failing to hear it.
9.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion

9.ctx: Back in Capernaum, probably in Peter's house. Rank and precedence mattered greatly in Jewish and Roman society.
9.mean: Mark says that after the passion prediction, the disciples had been arguing about who was greatest. Jesus set a child among them — someone of no status in that culture — and said that receiving such a child in his name is receiving him.
9.big: Greatness in Jesus' kingdom is measured by service to the least, not by rank.

9.ctx: Continuing in Capernaum. 'Little ones' covers both children and humble believers.
9.mean: Mark records strong warnings: causing a little one to stumble is worse than being drowned; it is better to lose a hand, foot or eye than to enter Gehenna whole. Most scholars read the language as deliberate exaggeration urging decisive action against sin. Gehenna was a valley outside Jerusalem associated with idolatry and burning, used by Jesus for final judgement.
9.big: Sin is to be dealt with drastically, because the stakes are final.
9.diff: The language is plainly hyperbolic and not a call to literal self-harm. Christians differ over the nature of the judgement described, but all take its seriousness at face value.

9.ctx: The end of the discourse. Salt preserved food, was added to sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13), and was a common image of wisdom and of covenant.
9.mean: Mark records short sayings linked by 'salt': everyone will be salted with fire, which many read as refining trial; salt that has lost its saltiness is useless; have salt among yourselves and be at peace with one another.
9.big: Disciples are to be distinct and at peace with each other — a pointed word after their argument about rank.

10.ctx: Judea and beyond the Jordan. Pharisees test Jesus on divorce, a subject rabbis of the day disputed vigorously.
10.mean: Mark says Jesus went behind the permission in Deuteronomy 24 to Genesis 1 and 2: the concession was given because of hardness of heart, but God's design from creation was lifelong union. In private he says that divorce and remarriage amount to adultery.
10.big: Jesus grounds marriage in God's creation design rather than in the concessions of the law.
10.diff: Matthew records an exception for sexual immorality, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 addresses desertion. Churches differ over what, if any, grounds permit remarriage. This is a question to work through with your own church leadership.

10.ctx: People bring children for Jesus to bless, and the disciples rebuke them.
10.mean: Mark alone says Jesus was indignant — real human anger (see 4:35). He says the kingdom belongs to such as these, and that whoever does not receive it like a child will not enter it. Children bring nothing but their need.
10.big: The kingdom is received as a gift by those who come empty-handed.

10.ctx: As Jesus sets out on the road. Matthew calls the man young and Luke a ruler. Wealth was widely seen as a sign of God's favour.
10.mean: Mark alone says Jesus looked at him and loved him — a detail of personal human affection (see 4:35). The command to sell everything targets this man's particular hold on wealth. The disciples are astonished; Jesus says salvation is impossible with man but possible with God.
10.big: Entry into the kingdom is humanly impossible and possible only as God's gift.

10.ctx: On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus walking ahead and the disciples afraid.
10.mean: Mark records the third and most detailed prediction: condemned, handed to the Gentiles, mocked, spat upon, flogged, killed, and after three days raised. Each detail is fulfilled in chapters 14 and 15.
10.big: Jesus goes to his death knowingly, not as a victim of events.
10.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion

10.ctx: On the road, straight after the third prediction. James and John were among Jesus' three closest disciples.
10.mean: Mark says they asked for the places of honour in his glory. Jesus speaks of his cup and baptism — his suffering — then says the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. 'Ransom' was the price paid to set someone free; 'many' echoes Isaiah 53:11–12. Christians have long seen in this verse the heart of Mark's account of why Jesus died.
10.big: Jesus states the purpose of his death: to give his life as a ransom, taking the place of many.
10.h: The Request of James and John

10.ctx: Jericho, the last town before the steep climb to Jerusalem, on the road Passover pilgrims were travelling.
10.mean: Mark says blind Bartimaeus called Jesus 'Son of David', a messianic title, and this time was not silenced. He is the only person healed in Mark whose name is given, and Mark says he followed Jesus 'on the way' — the road to the cross.
10.big: A blind beggar sees what the disciples struggle to see, and follows Jesus to Jerusalem.

11.ctx: Approaching Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives at Passover, when the city filled with pilgrims.
11.mean: Mark says Jesus arranged the entry deliberately, riding a young donkey. Most scholars see him enacting Zechariah 9:9, where Israel's king comes humble and riding a donkey rather than a warhorse. The crowd's words come from Psalm 118. They welcome a king, but this suggests they expected a different kind of king from the one arriving.
11.big: Jesus enters Jerusalem openly as its king, on his own terms rather than the crowd's.

11.ctx: The next morning, on the way into the city. Mark notes that it was not the season for figs.
11.mean: Mark says Jesus, being hungry — a plain human need (see 4:35) — found a fig tree in leaf but without fruit, and cursed it. Mark splits this story around the temple scene, and most scholars read the two as interpreting each other: the temple, busy with activity, was bearing no fruit.
11.big: The fig tree becomes an acted parable of judgement on a fruitless temple.

11.ctx: The outer court of the temple, the only area Gentiles could enter, used for selling sacrificial animals and changing money.
11.mean: Mark says Jesus drove out the traders, quoting Isaiah 56:7 — a house of prayer for all nations — and Jeremiah 7:11 — a den of robbers. The court meant for the nations had become a marketplace. Mark says the chief priests and scribes now sought a way to destroy him.
11.big: Jesus acts with authority over the temple itself, and the leaders resolve to kill him.
11.diff: John places a temple cleansing at the start of Jesus' ministry. Some hold that there were two; others that John arranged his material by theme rather than chronology.

11.ctx: The following morning, on the same road from Bethany, the fig tree is found withered from the roots.
11.mean: Mark records Jesus turning the moment into teaching: have faith in God. Whatever you ask in prayer, believe you have received it. Forgiveness is tied to prayer in verse 25 — praying while holding a grudge against someone does not fit the God being prayed to.
11.big: The judgement on the temple leads into teaching on a direct, forgiving trust in God.
11.diff: The promise about prayer is read within the rest of Scripture, where Jesus himself asked for the cup to pass and was not spared (14:36). Christians have understood it as a promise about God's willingness and power, not a formula guaranteeing any request.

11.ctx: In the temple courts. The chief priests, scribes and elders were the three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.
11.mean: Mark says they demanded to know his authority. Jesus asked in return whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men — a question that trapped them whichever way they answered. When they refused to answer, he declined to answer them.
11.big: The leaders who question Jesus' authority are unwilling to face the truth about God's messenger.

12.ctx: Still in the temple courts, addressed to the same leaders who had just challenged his authority.
12.mean: Mark records a parable of a vineyard, drawing on Isaiah 5, whose tenants reject servant after servant and finally kill the owner's beloved son. Mark says the leaders knew he had told it against them. Jesus quotes Psalm 118 on the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, placing himself at the end of the line of prophets and in a category of his own as the son.
12.big: Jesus presents himself as the beloved son whose rejection will lead to judgement — and vindication.
12.h: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants

12.ctx: Pharisees and Herodians together again, trying to trap him on paying the Roman poll tax.
12.mean: Mark says Jesus asked whose image was on the coin. Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. Many scholars note the implication: the coin bears Caesar's image, and people bear God's (Genesis 1:27).
12.big: Jesus escapes the trap and reframes the question: everything bearing God's image belongs to God.

12.ctx: The Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses as authoritative and denied the resurrection.
12.mean: Mark says they posed a case of a woman married to seven brothers in turn. Jesus answered that they knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, and argued from Exodus 3 — a text they accepted — that God is the God of the living.
12.big: Jesus affirms the resurrection from the very Scriptures his opponents claimed to rely on.

12.ctx: A scribe who had heard the debate and was impressed. Rabbis debated which of the law's many commands was greatest.
12.mean: Mark records Jesus joining Deuteronomy 6:4–5 — love God with all your heart — with Leviticus 19:18 — love your neighbour as yourself. The scribe agrees that this outweighs all sacrifices, and Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom.
12.big: Jesus sums up the whole law in love for God and neighbour.

12.ctx: Now Jesus takes the initiative, teaching in the temple after his opponents have run out of questions. 'Son of David' was a common title for the expected Messiah.
12.mean: Mark records Jesus asking how the Messiah can be David's son when David, in Psalm 110, calls him 'Lord'. Mark leaves the question unanswered in the text. It points beyond a merely human understanding of the Messiah, presenting him as David's son who is also David's Lord; Christians have read it as a key text for understanding Jesus' divine identity.
12.big: Jesus shows that the Messiah is greater than a human descendant of David.

12.ctx: Addressed to the large crowd in the temple. Scribes were experts in the law; some depended on the support of patrons, including widows.
12.mean: Mark records Jesus warning against scribes who love status, long robes and places of honour, and who devour widows' houses while making long prayers for show.
12.big: Jesus condemns religious performance that exploits the vulnerable.

12.ctx: Immediately after, in the court of the women, where trumpet-shaped offering boxes stood.
12.mean: Mark says a poor widow put in two tiny coins, everything she had, and Jesus said she had given more than all the others. Many scholars note the placement: straight after the condemnation of those who devour widows' houses, and straight before the prediction of the temple's destruction.
12.big: True devotion is measured by cost, not amount — even as the institution receiving it faces judgement.

13.ctx: Leaving the temple, a disciple admires its stones; some in Herod's temple weighed many tonnes. On the Mount of Olives, facing the temple, the disciples ask when it will be destroyed and what the sign will be. This opens the longest speech in Mark, often called the Olivet discourse. The temple was destroyed by Rome in AD 70.
13.mean: Mark records Jesus predicting that not one stone will be left on another, and warning against those who come claiming to be him, and against being alarmed by wars, earthquakes and famines — these are only the beginning. Reading the chapter well depends on seeing that it answers two things at once: the disciples' question about the temple, and the larger question of the end of the age and the return of the Son of Man.
13.big: Jesus prepares his followers for the fall of Jerusalem and for the longer wait for his return.
13.diff: Christians read this chapter in different ways. Many interpreters see verses 5–23 as mainly about the siege and destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and verses 24–27 as the final return of Christ. Others read the whole discourse as about AD 70, with the cosmic language as symbolic. Others again see a double reference throughout, with AD 70 as a pattern and foreshadowing of the end. All agree on the instructions the chapter repeats: do not be deceived, do not be alarmed, endure, and stay awake.

13.ctx: Warnings to the disciples themselves about what they will face.
13.mean: Mark records Jesus warning of arrest before councils, synagogues, governors and kings. The gospel must first be preached to all nations. When they are arrested, the Holy Spirit will give them words. Families will betray one another. The one who endures to the end will be saved. Much of this is seen in Acts.
13.big: Faithful witness under persecution is the calling of Jesus' followers before the end.

13.ctx: The 'abomination of desolation' comes from Daniel 9, 11 and 12, where it first referred to Antiochus IV setting up a pagan altar in the temple in 167 BC. Mark's aside — let the reader understand — signals a coded reference his first readers were expected to catch.
13.mean: Mark records Jesus saying that when this is seen standing where it should not, those in Judea must flee to the mountains immediately, without going back for belongings. The instructions are local and practical: Judea, housetops, fields, pregnant women, winter. That strongly suggests a historical event in Judea. The church historian Eusebius records that Jerusalem's Christians fled before the city fell in AD 70.
13.big: Jesus gives his followers practical warning to escape the coming destruction of Jerusalem.
13.diff: Proposed identifications include Roman military standards in the temple, the occupation and defilement of the temple by Zealot factions before the siege, and a future figure opposed to God. The first two fit the Judea-specific instructions most closely; some interpreters also see a further, final fulfilment.

13.ctx: After those days — a transition in the discourse. The language of the sun darkening and stars falling comes from the prophets (Isaiah 13:10, 34:4), and the Son of Man coming in clouds from Daniel 7:13.
13.mean: Mark records cosmic signs and then the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power, gathering his chosen people from the ends of the earth. In the prophets, language of the heavens shaking is regularly used for God's decisive acts in history, such as the fall of Babylon in Isaiah 13, not only for the end of the world. So interpreters divide over whether these verses describe Christ's final return, or use prophetic imagery for God's judgement in AD 70 and Christ's vindication, or both.
13.big: However the sequence is understood, the story ends with the Son of Man coming in power to gather his people.
13.diff: Most evangelical and Reformed interpreters read verses 24–27 as the second coming of Christ. A significant minority read them as prophetic imagery for the events of AD 70 and Christ's vindication. The chapter's central instruction — be watchful — applies on either reading.
13.h: The Return of the Son of Man

13.ctx: Still on the Mount of Olives. Fig trees in Judea lose their leaves in winter, and new leaves in spring were a reliable sign summer was near.
13.mean: Mark records the parable: when you see these things, know that he is near. 'This generation will not pass away until all these things take place.' Most scholars read 'these things' as the events leading to the fall of Jerusalem, which did take place within a generation of Jesus' words.
13.big: The destruction of the temple would come within a generation, confirming Jesus' words.
13.diff: Some interpreters take 'generation' to mean the Jewish people as a whole, or the generation alive when the final signs appear. The fulfilment in AD 70 is the simplest reading of the immediate context.
13.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree

13.ctx: The closing section of the discourse, moving from signs to the unknown timing of the end.
13.mean: Mark records Jesus saying that no one knows the day or hour — not the angels, nor the Son, but only the Father. Jesus then gives a short parable of servants told to keep watch because they do not know when the master will return. The same word — stay awake — is repeated three times.
13.big: Because no one knows when the end will come, the right response is watchfulness, not calculation.
13.diff: How the Son could not know the day has been discussed since the early church. The historic understanding, following the two-natures teaching explained at 4:35, is that Jesus spoke according to his human nature, having genuinely taken on human limitation. Every attempt to set a date contradicts this verse.

14.ctx: Two days before Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when Jerusalem's population may have tripled with pilgrims.
14.mean: Mark says the chief priests and scribes looked for a way to arrest Jesus quietly, not during the festival, for fear of the crowds. Mark places the story of the anointing between their plotting and Judas's offer.
14.big: The leaders' plot is set; the question is only when and how.

14.ctx: Bethany, about two miles from Jerusalem, at the house of Simon the leper.
14.mean: Mark says a woman broke a jar of nard worth about a year's wages and poured it on Jesus' head. Some objected that it could have been given to the poor. Jesus said she had anointed his body beforehand for burial, and that what she had done would be told wherever the gospel is preached.
14.big: Extravagant devotion to Jesus is honoured, and his death is acknowledged in advance.

14.ctx: In Bethany, two days before Passover, immediately after the anointing.
14.mean: Mark says Judas went to the chief priests to betray Jesus, and they promised him money. Mark gives no motive; many scholars note the contrast with the woman who had just given everything.
14.big: Devotion and betrayal are set side by side among Jesus' own followers.

14.ctx: The first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lambs were sacrificed.
14.mean: Mark says Jesus sent two disciples to follow a man carrying a water jar — unusual, since women normally carried water — to a furnished upper room. The detail of the arrangements suggests Jesus is directing events rather than being overtaken by them.
14.big: Jesus is in control of the events leading to his death.

14.ctx: Thursday evening in the upper room, at the Passover meal, which recalled the exodus through a set order of food, cups and readings.
14.mean: Mark says Jesus predicted that one of those eating with him would betray him. Then he took bread and said 'this is my body', and the cup: 'this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many'. The covenant language echoes Exodus 24, and 'for many' echoes Isaiah 53. Jesus himself interprets his coming death as a sacrifice that establishes a covenant.
14.big: Jesus explains his death in advance as a covenant sacrifice, and gives his followers a meal by which to remember it.
14.diff: Christian traditions differ over what happens in the Lord's Supper — from the bread and wine becoming Christ's body and blood, to Christ being spiritually present, to a memorial. All accept that Jesus interpreted his death as sacrificial and commanded the meal.

14.ctx: After the meal, walking out to the Mount of Olives across the Kidron valley, having sung the Passover psalms (Psalms 113–118).
14.mean: Mark records Jesus quoting Zechariah 13:7 — strike the shepherd and the sheep will scatter — and promising to go ahead of them to Galilee after he is raised. Peter insists he will never fall away; Jesus predicts three denials before the rooster crows twice.
14.big: Jesus foresees his followers' failure and promises to meet them again beyond it.

14.ctx: Gethsemane, meaning 'oil press', an olive grove on the Mount of Olives.
14.mean: Mark says Jesus was greatly distressed and troubled, and told the disciples his soul was sorrowful even to death. He prayed 'Abba, Father' — the intimate family word, preserved in Aramaic — asking for the cup to be removed, and then submitted: not what I will, but what you will. Here the human will of Jesus is seen struggling and yielding to the Father. It is one of the clearest windows in the Gospels onto his full humanity (see 4:35). The disciples sleep three times.
14.big: In his hour of greatest distress Jesus submits his own will to the Father's.

14.ctx: Still in the garden. The armed crowd is sent by the chief priests, scribes and elders.
14.mean: Mark says Judas identified Jesus with a kiss, the customary greeting of a disciple to a teacher. A bystander cut off the ear of the high priest's servant. Jesus said they could have arrested him any day in the temple, but the Scriptures must be fulfilled. All the disciples fled. A young man fled naked; some have suggested it was Mark himself, though that is speculation.
14.big: Jesus is abandoned by everyone, as Scripture foretold.

14.ctx: A night hearing before the Sanhedrin, which many scholars note was irregular under later Jewish law.
14.mean: Mark says the false witnesses did not agree. Jesus stayed silent until the high priest asked him directly whether he was the Christ, the Son of the Blessed. Jesus answered 'I am', then combined Psalm 110 and Daniel 7: they would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven. The high priest tore his clothes and the council condemned him for blasphemy. A bound prisoner claims the place beside God.
14.big: Jesus openly claims to be the Messiah and to share God's throne, and is condemned for it.

14.ctx: In the high priest's courtyard, below the room where Jesus was on trial. Mark sandwiches the denial around the trial so that both happen at once.
14.mean: Mark says Peter denied Jesus three times, the last time with curses, and the rooster crowed; Peter broke down and wept. If Mark's Gospel draws on Peter's preaching, as the early tradition held, this humiliating account came from Peter himself.
14.big: While Jesus confesses who he is, his leading disciple denies knowing him.

15.ctx: Early morning. Under Roman rule the Sanhedrin could not carry out a death sentence, so they brought Jesus to Pilate, governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.
15.mean: Mark says Pilate asked whether he was the King of the Jews — a political charge. Jesus answered briefly and then remained silent. Many see an echo of Isaiah 53:7, the servant silent before his accusers.
15.big: The religious charge becomes a political one, and Jesus does not defend himself.

15.ctx: Mark mentions a Passover custom of releasing one prisoner. It is not recorded in any source outside the Gospels.
15.mean: Mark says Barabbas, imprisoned for insurrection and murder, was set against Jesus, and the chief priests stirred up the crowd to ask for Barabbas. The guilty man goes free and the innocent one is condemned; Christians have long seen in this an illustration of substitution.
15.big: An innocent man is condemned in the place of a guilty one.

15.ctx: Friday morning at Pilate's residence. Pilate was known from other ancient sources for brutality and for clashes with the Jewish leadership.
15.mean: Mark says the crowd shouted 'Crucify him', and Pilate, wishing to satisfy them, released Barabbas and handed Jesus over to be flogged and crucified. Roman flogging was brutal and could itself be fatal.
15.big: Jesus is handed over to death by a governor who knew he was innocent.

15.ctx: Inside the governor's headquarters. A Roman cohort was nominally about six hundred men, stationed in Jerusalem to keep order at festivals.
15.mean: Mark says the soldiers dressed Jesus in purple, crowned him with thorns and mocked him as King of the Jews. Many scholars point to the irony: the mockery tells the truth.
15.big: In mocking Jesus as king, the soldiers unknowingly proclaim who he is.

15.ctx: The procession to Golgotha. Simon of Cyrene is forced to carry the cross; Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, which suggests they were known to his readers.
15.mean: Mark says Jesus refused wine mixed with myrrh, and was crucified between two rebels under the charge 'The King of the Jews'. Passers-by, the chief priests and those crucified with him all mocked him: he saved others; he cannot save himself.
15.big: The mockers speak more truly than they know: to save others, Jesus would not save himself.

15.ctx: Jesus had been on the cross since about nine in the morning. Crucifixion usually killed slowly, sometimes over days.
15.mean: Mark says darkness came over the land from noon to three. Jesus cried out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22 — My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? — and then breathed his last. It was a real human death (see 4:35). The temple curtain was torn from top to bottom, and a Roman centurion said: truly this man was the Son of God, closing the frame opened in 1:1. Psalm 22, which begins in abandonment, ends in vindication and worldwide worship.
15.big: At the moment of his death Jesus is recognised, by a Gentile soldier, as the Son of God.
15.diff: Mark records the cry and the death; how to understand Jesus' forsakenness is a theological question Christians have answered in different ways. Reformed and much evangelical theology holds that Jesus bore the judgement due to sinners, experiencing in his human nature the separation sin deserves, without any division within the Trinity. Others emphasise that in quoting Psalm 22 Jesus expressed both the depth of his suffering and his trust in its outcome.

15.ctx: Late Friday afternoon. Jewish law required bodies to be buried before nightfall (Deuteronomy 21:23), and the Sabbath began at sunset, adding urgency.
15.mean: Mark says Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member, boldly asked Pilate for the body. Pilate confirmed the death with the centurion. The body was wrapped and laid in a rock tomb, and a stone was rolled across the entrance. Two women saw where he was laid.
15.big: Mark records that Jesus' death was certified and his burial witnessed.

16.ctx: Sunday morning, after the Sabbath. The women come to anoint the body.
16.mean: Mark says the stone had been rolled away, and a young man in white told them: he has risen, he is not here. They were to tell the disciples — and Peter by name — that Jesus was going ahead of them to Galilee. The women fled in fear and said nothing to anyone. In the earliest manuscripts, the Gospel ends here.
16.big: The crucified Jesus has risen, and even Peter, who denied him, is named in the invitation to meet him.
16.diff: Whether Mark intended to end at verse 8, or an original ending was lost, is debated. Some scholars think an ending on fear and silence is deliberate, leaving the reader to respond where the women did not.

16.ctx: The longer ending (16:9–20), found in most later manuscripts but not in the earliest two complete manuscripts of Mark.
16.mean: The passage says Jesus appeared to Mary Magdalene and that her report was not believed. It summarises appearances recorded in the other Gospels.
16.diff: Most scholars conclude that verses 9–20 were added later: they are absent from the earliest manuscripts, and their vocabulary and style differ from the rest of Mark. Their content is consistent with the other Gospels, and no Christian doctrine depends on them.

16.ctx: Part of the longer ending, which appears to summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels.
16.mean: The passage says Jesus appeared to two disciples walking in the country, and that the others did not believe them. It closely parallels the Emmaus account in Luke 24.

16.ctx: Part of the longer ending. The scene parallels the commissions at the end of Matthew and Luke.
16.mean: The passage says Jesus rebuked the eleven for their unbelief and sent them to preach the gospel to all creation, promising signs to accompany believers. Verses 17–18, about handling snakes and drinking poison, have been taken literally by some groups with fatal results.
16.diff: Because these verses are very probably not original to Mark, practices should not be built on them. The commission itself matches Matthew 28 and Acts 1.

16.ctx: The final verses of the longer ending, summarising the ascension and the apostles' mission as described in Luke and Acts.
16.mean: The passage says Jesus was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God, fulfilling Psalm 110, and that the disciples went out and preached everywhere with the Lord working with them.

1.ctx: Paul writes to churches he founded in the Roman province of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey. Teachers have since arrived insisting that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Galatians is probably one of the earliest of Paul’s letters (see History & setting above).
1.mean: Paul opens by answering two charges before anyone has made them. First, his authority. He is an apostle ‘sent not from men nor by man’, sent directly by Jesus Christ and God the Father. His critics evidently said he was a second-hand apostle, dependent on Jerusalem. Second, his message. In one line he summarises the gospel: Christ ‘gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age’. That sentence already contains the argument of the letter. If Christ’s self-giving deals with our sins and rescues us, nothing needs to be added to it. ‘The present evil age’ is Jewish language for the world as it now is under sin, contrasted with the age to come; Paul says the rescue into that new age has already begun.
1.big: Both Paul’s authority and his gospel rest on what God has done in Christ, not on human credentials or human effort.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Galatians (Calvin Translation Society, 1854), CCEL
Michael Burer, Galatians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2024)

1.ctx: In every other letter Paul follows the greeting with thanks for his readers. Here he leaves the thanks out and goes straight to astonishment, which his first readers would have noticed at once.
1.mean: Paul is amazed ‘how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ’, for ‘a different gospel’. He immediately corrects himself: it is not another gospel at all, only a distortion of the one gospel. Then, twice, he pronounces a curse (Greek anathema, something handed over to God for judgment) on anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one they received. That includes Paul himself, or even an angel. The point is that the message has authority, not the messenger. The teachers in Galatia probably did not deny Christ. They added to him: faith in Christ plus circumcision and the law. Paul’s verdict is that the addition changes the whole thing.
1.big: Adding a requirement to Christ as the condition of being accepted by God does not improve the gospel; it replaces it.

src.l: D. Mangum & D. R. Brown, Galatians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham), surveying Betz, Bruce, Dunn, George, Hays, Longenecker, Martyn, Schreiner and others
Calvin, Commentary on Galatians (Calvin Translation Society, 1854), CCEL

1.ctx: Paul’s opponents seem to have claimed that he watered down the gospel to please Gentiles, and that he had learned it second-hand from the Jerusalem apostles.
1.mean: Paul says he is not a people-pleaser; if he were, he would not be Christ’s servant. He received his gospel ‘by revelation from Jesus Christ’, meaning the risen Christ’s appearance to him on the Damascus road (Acts 9). He then gives evidence. He was the most zealous of persecutors, so no human argument converted him; God did. After his call he went to Arabia, not Jerusalem, and only three years later spent fifteen days with Cephas (Peter) and met James, the Lord’s brother. The Judean churches knew him only by report, and they ‘glorified God because of me’. Paul is not claiming the Jerusalem apostles disagreed with him. His point is that he did not get his gospel from them.
1.big: Paul’s gospel was not borrowed from anyone; it came from the risen Christ, and his changed life is the proof.
1.diff: Verse 15 says God ‘set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace’. Reformed interpreters see here God’s sovereign choosing in Paul’s own conversion: God acted before Paul could do anything. Others, Arminian interpreters among them, agree that the initiative was God’s, but note that the language echoes the prophetic calls of Jeremiah (1:5) and the Servant (Isaiah 49:1), so Paul is describing his calling to a task (preaching to the Gentiles, verse 16) rather than teaching how individuals come to be saved. The two readings can overlap. Where Paul went in ‘Arabia’ and why is unknown: possibly to preach in the Nabataean kingdom (compare 2 Corinthians 11:32), possibly for a period of reflection.

Michael Burer, Galatians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2024)
D. Mangum & D. R. Brown, Galatians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham), surveying Betz, Bruce, Dunn, George, Hays, Longenecker, Martyn, Schreiner and others

2.ctx: Fourteen years later (after his conversion or after his first visit; Paul does not say which), Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. Titus is a Gentile believer who had not been circumcised, so he is a test case in person.
2.mean: Paul laid his gospel privately before the leaders. Some ‘false brothers’ tried to have Titus circumcised, but Paul did not give way ‘so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you’, and the leaders did not insist. James, Cephas and John, the recognised ‘pillars’, added nothing to Paul’s message. They saw that God had entrusted him with the gospel for the Gentiles as he had Peter for the Jews, and gave him the right hand of fellowship. Their one request, to remember the poor, was something Paul was already eager to do. So the very people the Galatian teachers appealed to had already accepted an uncircumcised Gentile believer as a full brother.
2.big: The leading apostles in Jerusalem recognised Paul’s gospel as the same gospel, with nothing added.
2.diff: Scholars differ over which visit in Acts this is. If it is the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30, the letter may come before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15, which would explain why Paul never quotes the council’s decision. If it is the council visit itself, Paul is describing the private meetings behind the public decision. Both views are held by careful scholars, and neither affects the teaching.

src.l: D. Mangum & D. R. Brown, Galatians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham), surveying Betz, Bruce, Dunn, George, Hays, Longenecker, Martyn, Schreiner and others
Michael Burer, Galatians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2024)

2.ctx: Antioch in Syria, the third city of the empire and home of the first mixed church of Jews and Gentiles (Acts 11:19–26). Sharing a meal there meant full acceptance, and many devout Jews avoided eating with Gentiles because of the food laws and purity rules.
2.mean: Peter had been eating with Gentile believers. When ‘certain men came from James’, he drew back and separated himself ‘for fear of those in the circumcision group’. The other Jewish believers followed, even Barnabas. Peter had not changed his theology; Paul calls it ‘hypocrisy’, acting against what he knew to be true. But the effect was to divide the church into two tables. The unspoken message to Gentile Christians was that to be fully accepted they must become Jews. So Paul opposed Peter publicly, ‘to his face’, because they were ‘not walking in line with the truth of the gospel’: ‘If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?’ Paul treats who eats with whom as a gospel question. If acceptance rests on Christ alone, no believer can be made a second-class member.
2.big: How believers treat one another at the table is a gospel issue, because it shows whether acceptance rests on Christ alone.
2.diff: It is unclear whether Paul’s words to Peter end at verse 14 or run on to verse 21. Many commentators think verses 15–21 restate what Paul said at Antioch in a form aimed at the Galatians. The note on 2:15 treats them separately. Some early Christian writers were uncomfortable with two apostles in conflict and suggested the quarrel was staged for teaching purposes; Jerome took this view. Augustine argued against it in his letters to Jerome: Peter really was in the wrong, and Scripture does not report pretence as truth.

Michael Burer, Galatians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2024)
Augustine, Letter 82 to Jerome (AD 405), NPNF 1st series vol. 1, New Advent

2.h: Justified by Faith, Not by Works of the Law
2.ctx: The heart of the letter, and one of the most important paragraphs Paul wrote. Here he states what was at stake at Antioch. Peter knew this, the Galatians had forgotten it, and the rest of the letter defends it. It closely parallels Romans 3:20–28.
2.mean:
The common ground (verse 15). Paul starts where Peter and every Jewish believer stood: ‘We who are Jews by birth and not Gentile “sinners”…’ The quotation marks matter. ‘Sinners’ was what Jews commonly called Gentiles, people outside God’s covenant and law. Paul is setting a trap.

The great reversal (verse 16). Even Jews with every advantage ‘know that a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ’. To be justified is a law-court word: to be declared in the right before God, the judge. If the people who had the law still had to come to God by faith in Christ, then the law was never the way in, for them or for anyone. Paul says it three times in one verse and ends with an echo of Psalm 143:2: ‘by works of the law no one will be justified’. The reason, which Paul spells out in 3:10–12 and Romans 3:19–20, is that everyone has broken the law. The law can show what righteousness is and expose our sin, but it cannot make a sinner righteous. Jew and Gentile are on the same footing after all: both are sinners, both justified the same way.

The objection (verses 17–18). If seeking to be justified in Christ means Jews end up classed with Gentile ‘sinners’, ‘does that make Christ a minister of sin? Certainly not!’ Christ did not create the sin; he revealed what was already true. The real lawbreaking would be to rebuild the law as the ground of acceptance after tearing it down. That is exactly what Peter did by withdrawing from the table.

Death and new life (verses 19–20). ‘Through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.’ The law itself, by condemning Paul, brought him to the end of himself. In Christ he has died to it as a way of standing before God. ‘I have been crucified with Christ.’ Paul is united to Christ so closely that Christ’s death counts as his, and Christ now lives in him. His ordinary life is lived ‘by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me’. This is personal faith in a person, not trust in a system.

The conclusion (verse 21). ‘If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.’ If our obedience could put us right with God, the cross would be unnecessary. So to add the law as a requirement is to say that Christ’s death was not enough.
2.big: No one is put right with God by keeping the law, because everyone has broken it; we are put right only through faith in Christ, who loved us and gave himself for us.
2.diff:
What are ‘works of the law’? The Reformers (Luther and Calvin) and many Reformed and evangelical scholars hold that the phrase means doing what the law of Moses requires, the moral law included, as a basis for acceptance. Calvin said the context ‘clearly proves that the moral law is also comprehended in these words’. He was answering earlier writers, including Origen and Jerome, who limited it to ceremonies such as circumcision and food laws. The ‘New Perspective on Paul’ (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright) stresses that the issue in Galatia was the law’s ‘boundary markers’ (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath), which separated Jews from Gentiles. Dunn himself says the phrase covers the whole law, viewed especially through those markers. Others, such as Thomas Schreiner, accept that circumcision and food laws were the issue in Galatia, but argue from 3:10, 5:3 and Romans 3:20 that the phrase means everything the law requires, so Paul’s reasoning applies to all the law’s demands.

‘Faith in Christ’ or ‘the faithfulness of Christ’? The Greek pistis Christou can mean either. Most translations, and scholars such as Bruce, Dunn and Schreiner, read ‘faith in Christ’, noting that the same verse says ‘we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus’. Richard Hays, J. Louis Martyn and Richard Longenecker argue for ‘the faithfulness of Christ’, meaning his obedience unto death. Both readings make Christ, not our law-keeping, the ground of justification.

What is justification? The Protestant traditions, Reformed, Lutheran and Arminian alike, agree that justification is God’s free verdict of acceptance received by faith, not earned. Reformed theology adds that Christ’s righteousness is counted (‘imputed’) to the believer (Westminster Confession 11.1). John Wesley described it as ‘pardon, the forgiveness of sins’. The Catholic Church teaches, from the Council of Trent, that justification is ‘not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man’, received first in baptism. Trent also teaches that nothing before justification, whether faith or works, earns it. The difference is over what justification is: a verdict, or a verdict together with an inner renewal.

hist.t: ‘Works of the law’ in the Dead Sea Scrolls
b: Until the 1990s, ‘works of the law’ was known almost only from Paul. Then a Dead Sea Scroll known as 4QMMT, preserved in six fragmentary copies from Qumran Cave 4 and probably composed in the mid-second century BC, became widely available. It is a letter from the community’s leaders listing more than twenty disputed points of law, mostly about temple purity, sacrifices and festivals. Its name comes from a phrase near the end, miqṣat ma‘aśe ha-Torah. Its editor, Elisha Qimron, translated it ‘some of the precepts of the Torah’; others, such as Martin Abegg, translate it ‘some of the works of the law’, Paul’s very phrase. The writers tell the reader that doing these things ‘will be reckoned to you as righteousness’.

This is the closest parallel to Paul’s phrase from his own century, and both sides of the modern debate use it. To some, it shows that ‘works of the law’ meant the specific rulings that marked out a group as faithful. To others, it shows that keeping the law’s requirements was linked with being counted righteous before God, which is exactly the link Paul denies. What is not disputed is that Paul’s phrase was real Jewish vocabulary in his day, not his own invention.

3.ctx: Paul turns from his own story to the Galatians’ experience. ‘Bewitched’ (Greek baskainō) is a word for casting the evil eye; it is as if someone has put a spell on them.
3.mean: Paul makes two arguments. The first is from experience. When Christ crucified was ‘clearly portrayed’ before them, did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? They received the Spirit before anyone told them about circumcision. So having begun by the Spirit, why try to be finished off by the flesh? The second is from Scripture. ‘Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness’ (Genesis 15:6). This was said of Abraham before he was circumcised (Genesis 17), and centuries before Sinai. So the true children of Abraham are those who believe, and Scripture ‘foresaw’ that God would justify Gentiles by faith. The promise ‘all nations will be blessed through you’ was the gospel announced in advance.
3.big: The Galatians’ own experience of the Spirit, and Abraham’s own story, both show that God accepts people through faith.

3.ctx: Paul now argues from the law itself, quoting Deuteronomy 27:26, Habakkuk 2:4, Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 21:23.
3.mean: This is where Paul makes plain why the law cannot save. ‘All who rely on works of the law are under a curse’, because the law itself says, ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law’. The unstated step is that no one does everything. The law demands complete obedience, and everyone falls short. Meanwhile Scripture names another way: ‘The righteous will live by faith’. The law works on a different principle, ‘The man who does these things will live by them’. Then comes the answer. ‘Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us’, since the law says, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree’. Crucifixion was the most shameful of deaths, and to a Jewish mind a crucified man looked cursed by God. Paul says that is exactly what happened, but the curse was ours. The result is that Abraham’s blessing reaches the Gentiles, and we receive the promised Spirit through faith.
3.big: Christ took the law’s curse on himself so that its blessing could reach those who believe.
3.diff: How does Christ ‘becoming a curse for us’? Reformed and many evangelical scholars, such as Schreiner, read it as substitution: Christ bore in our place the penalty our law-breaking deserved (the doctrine often called penal substitution). Longenecker speaks of an ‘exchange’: Christ takes our curse and we receive his blessing. Dunn reads it representatively: Christ took the place of the covenant-breaker outside the covenant, opening the blessing to Gentiles. Most Arminian theologians also hold that Christ died in our place, while some prefer to describe it in other ways, for example as Christ satisfying God’s moral government. All agree that Christ’s death is the means by which the curse is removed.

3.ctx: Paul answers the obvious question: if God’s promise to Abraham came first, what was the law for? He uses the picture of a will, which cannot be changed once it is ratified.
3.mean: The law came 430 years after the promise, so it cannot cancel or add conditions to it. The inheritance comes by promise, not by law. Paul notes that the promise was to Abraham’s ‘seed’, singular, which he applies to Christ, the one true offspring in whom all believers share. So why the law? ‘It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred.’ Is the law then against the promises? ‘Certainly not!’ But no law could give life. Instead ‘the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin’, so that the promise would be given through faith. The law was our paidagōgos, ‘guardian’: in Greek and Roman households, a trusted slave who escorted and disciplined a boy until he came of age. Now that faith has come, we are no longer under the guardian.
3.big: The law was never a rival way to God’s blessing; it was a temporary guardian that exposed sin and kept God’s people until Christ came.
3.diff: ‘Added because of transgressions’ may mean that the law was given to restrain sin, or to expose it as law-breaking (compare Romans 5:20; 7:7). Reformed and Lutheran theology has long taught that one use of the law is to convict of sin and drive people to Christ. The mention of angels and a mediator (verses 19–20) is among the most obscure lines in Paul. The mediator is almost certainly Moses, and the angels reflect a Jewish tradition also found in Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2. The point seems to be that the law came to Israel at one remove, while the promise came from God directly. The ‘430 years’ follows Exodus 12:40.

3.ctx: The conclusion of the argument begun in 3:1. Baptism, the public sign of entering the church, is used as shorthand for belonging to Christ.
3.mean: Everyone who is in Christ is a son of God through faith. ‘Sons’ here is legal language for heirs, and it includes daughters. All who were baptised into Christ have ‘clothed yourselves with Christ’. So ‘there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus’. These were the three great divisions of the ancient world. In Christ none of them decides who belongs or who inherits. And if you belong to Christ, the one Seed, you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise. Gentiles do not need circumcision to become Abraham’s children; they already are, in Christ.
3.big: In Christ every believer shares equally in God’s family and inheritance, whatever their background.
3.diff: Verse 28 is often cited in debates about men and women in church leadership. Complementarian scholars, such as Schreiner, read it as about equal standing and inheritance before God, not the removal of every distinction, since Paul elsewhere still addresses men and women, slaves and masters, separately. Egalitarian scholars see it as having wider implications for roles in church life. In context, the verse’s first point is that no one has a lesser place in God’s family. How baptism relates to faith here (verse 27) is read differently too. For Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians, baptism is a means through which God unites a person to Christ. For most Reformed and Baptist Christians it is the God-given sign and seal of a union received by faith.
