4.ctx: Paul continues the picture of an heir who, while still a child, is no better off than a slave. He is under guardians until the date his father has set.
4.mean: Before Christ, Paul says, ‘we were enslaved under the basic principles of the world’. ‘But when the time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.’ Each phrase counts. The Son was sent: he existed with the Father before he was born. He was born of a woman: truly human. He was born under the law: a real Jew who kept the law we broke. He came at the time God chose. Christians have long read verse 4 as holding together Christ’s divinity and his full humanity (see the note on Mark 4:35). Then God ‘sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out, “Abba, Father!”’ Abba is the Aramaic word Jesus himself used in prayer (Mark 14:36). The Father sends the Son and the Son’s Spirit, so believers share in Jesus’ own relationship with the Father. So ‘you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God’.
4.big: God sent both his Son and his Spirit so that believers would be not slaves but children, able to call God ‘Father’.
4.diff: ‘The Spirit of his Son’ (verse 6) is one of the texts Western churches, Catholic and Protestant alike, have cited for teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Father ‘and the Son’ (the filioque, added to the Western form of the Nicene Creed). The Eastern Orthodox churches hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and read this verse as describing the Spirit’s being sent to believers, not his eternal origin. Both sides confess the full deity of the Spirit. ‘Basic principles’ (Greek stoicheia; footnote: ‘elemental forces’) is debated. It may mean elementary religious rules, the physical elements, or spiritual powers. Paul applies it both to life under the law and to pagan religion (verse 9), which is part of his point.

4.ctx: Before they became Christians, the Galatians worshipped pagan gods. Paul now fears they are slipping back into a similar slavery by taking up the law’s calendar of special days.
4.mean: Once they did not know God and were slaves ‘to those who by nature are not gods’. Now they know God, ‘or rather are known by God’. Paul corrects himself, because their relationship began with God knowing them. So how can they turn back to ‘weak and worthless principles’, observing ‘days and months and seasons and years’? He fears his work among them has been wasted. Then Paul turns personal. He first preached to them because of an illness. They did not despise his condition but welcomed him ‘as if I were an angel of God’; they would have torn out their own eyes for him. Has he now become their enemy by telling the truth? The other teachers court them to win them over for themselves. Paul feels like a mother in labour again ‘until Christ is formed in you’.
4.big: Going back to rules as the way to stand before God is a return to slavery, not progress; the goal is Christ formed in us.
4.diff: Paul does not name his illness. Because of the eyes in verse 15 and the ‘large letters’ of 6:11, some have suggested an eye condition, but this is guesswork, and many scholars (Betz, Dunn) read 6:11 differently. Paul’s warning about ‘days and months’ concerns keeping them as a requirement for acceptance with God (compare Romans 14:5–6), not Christians marking special days in themselves.

4.ctx: Paul turns his opponents’ own ground, the law and the story of Abraham, against them. He invites those who want to be under the law to listen to what the law (here meaning the books of Moses) actually says.
4.mean: Abraham had two sons. Ishmael was born to the slave woman Hagar ‘according to the flesh’, by ordinary human means when Abraham and Sarah tried to bring about God’s promise themselves. Isaac was born to the free woman Sarah ‘through the promise’, by God’s miraculous action (Genesis 16–21). Paul says he is reading the story figuratively. The two women stand for two covenants. Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and ‘the present-day Jerusalem’, in slavery. Sarah stands for ‘the Jerusalem above’, which is free and is our mother. Isaiah 54:1 promised that the barren woman would have more children than the married one. Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise. And as Ishmael mocked Isaac, so now those born of the flesh pressure those born of the Spirit. Scripture’s answer is: ‘Expel the slave woman and her son.’ For the Galatians, that means sending away the teaching that would put them back into slavery.
4.big: Those who rely on the law for acceptance are children of slavery; those who trust God’s promise are children of freedom.
4.diff: Paul uses the verb allēgoreō, ‘to speak allegorically’ (verse 24). Scholars debate whether this is allegory in the later sense, where details stand for hidden ideas, or typology, a pattern repeated in history. Many, including Betz and Schreiner, see a mixture of the two. Philo of Alexandria also allegorised this story, but very differently. Some readers today worry about how the passage could be turned against Jewish people. In context, Paul’s target is teachers within the church who required Gentile believers to take on the law, not Jewish people as such (compare Romans 9:1–5; 11:1).

src.l: D. Mangum & D. R. Brown, Galatians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham), surveying Betz, Bruce, Dunn, George, Hays, Longenecker, Martyn, Schreiner and others

5.ctx: The turn from argument to practice. ‘Freedom’ is the key word of the rest of the letter.
5.mean: ‘It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.’ Paul spells out what accepting circumcision as a requirement would mean. Christ would be of no value to them. They would be obliged to keep the whole law. They would be ‘severed from Christ’ and ‘fallen away from grace’. You cannot rely on Christ and on your own law-keeping at the same time; one excludes the other. Instead, ‘by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness’. In Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, what matters is ‘faith, expressing itself through love’. Saving faith is never idle. It works itself out in love, though love is its fruit, not its foundation. Paul’s wish that the agitators would ‘emasculate themselves’ (verse 12) is deliberately coarse. If cutting the flesh saves, let them go all the way.
5.big: To rely on the law for acceptance is to let go of grace; the faith that saves shows itself in love.
5.diff: Christians differ over ‘you have fallen away from grace’ (verse 4). Reformed theology holds that those truly united to Christ will be kept by God to the end (Westminster Confession 17.1). It reads the verse as describing people who abandon the way of grace for the way of law, which shows they were never resting on Christ, or as a real warning God uses to keep his people. Arminian theology takes it as describing a real possibility that a true believer can turn away and be lost. John Wesley argued this in Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints. The original Arminian articles of 1610 left the question open. Catholic teaching holds that grace can be lost through grave sin and restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance (Trent, Session 6, ch. 14). All agree the verse is a serious warning against trusting anything besides Christ.

5.ctx: Having warned against the law, Paul now warns against the opposite mistake: treating freedom as permission to indulge the flesh (5:13).
5.mean: ‘Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.’ ‘Flesh’ here does not mean the body. It means human nature turned in on itself and away from God. Flesh and Spirit are at war, so that you do not do what you want. Paul lists ‘the acts of the flesh’: sexual sin, idolatry and sorcery, then a long run of community-wrecking sins (hatred, discord, jealousy, rage, rivalries, divisions, factions, envy), and finally drunkenness and carousing. He warns that those who live like this ‘will not inherit the kingdom of God’. Against these he sets the ‘fruit of the Spirit’: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. ‘Against such things there is no law.’ The law demanded this character but could not produce it; the Spirit grows it. Those who belong to Christ ‘have crucified the flesh’, so ‘let us walk in step with the Spirit’.
5.big: The Spirit produces in believers the character the law demanded but could not create.
5.diff: ‘Fruit’ is singular: one harvest with nine aspects, not a menu of separate gifts. Luther and others noted that Paul says ‘fruit’ rather than ‘works’ of the Spirit, because it is grown, not manufactured. How the struggle in verse 17 relates to Romans 7 is debated. Reformed interpreters generally see an ongoing tension in every Christian life, in which the Spirit is the stronger. Wesleyan theology also expects real, sometimes decisive, growth in holiness in this life (‘entire sanctification’), while agreeing that believers are never beyond the need of grace.

Calvin, Commentary on Galatians (Calvin Translation Society, 1854), CCEL

6.ctx: Practical instructions for church life. Galatians 6:1–2 is one of the passages Community of Brothers takes as a description of what brotherhood involves.
6.mean: If someone is caught in a sin, ‘you who are spiritual’ (those led by the Spirit, not a spiritual elite) should restore him gently, watching yourselves in case you are tempted too. ‘Restore’ is the word used for mending nets or setting a bone. ‘Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.’ The law of Christ is the life of self-giving love Christ himself lived (compare 5:14; John 13:34). No one should think himself something; each should test his own work, ‘for each one should carry his own load’. Those taught the word should share good things with their teachers. Then a solemn principle: ‘God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return.’ Sow to the flesh and reap decay; sow to the Spirit and reap eternal life. ‘Let us not grow weary in well-doing’, doing good to everyone, ‘especially to the family of faith’.
6.big: The freedom of the gospel is lived out in gentle restoration, shared burdens and persistent good.
6.diff: Verses 2 and 5 look contradictory: bear one another’s burdens, yet each carries his own load. Paul uses two different Greek words. The ‘burdens’ of verse 2 (barē) are heavy troubles we should share. The ‘load’ of verse 5 (phortion) is the ordinary responsibility each person answers to God for. ‘Sowing to the Spirit’ (verse 8) does not mean earning eternal life. Paul has spent the whole letter denying that. It describes the direction of a life that the Spirit is leading.

src.l: D. Mangum & D. R. Brown, Galatians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham), surveying Betz, Bruce, Dunn, George, Hays, Longenecker, Martyn, Schreiner and others

6.ctx: Letters were usually written by a secretary (compare Romans 16:22). Here Paul takes the pen to write the ending himself, as authors often did to authenticate a letter.
6.mean: ‘See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!’ Whatever the reason for the size, it underlines what follows. The agitators want to ‘make a good impression outwardly’. They push circumcision to avoid persecution for the cross, and they do not keep the law themselves; they want to boast about the Galatians’ flesh. Paul will boast only ‘in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is ‘a new creation’. Peace and mercy rest on all who walk by this rule. No one should trouble him further, because he bears on his body ‘the marks of Jesus’, almost certainly the scars of beatings and stoning (compare Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:23–25). Unlike the agitators, he has suffered for the cross.
6.big: The only thing worth boasting in is the cross, because through it God makes a new creation.
6.diff: Who is ‘the Israel of God’ (verse 16)? The Greek kai can mean ‘and’ or ‘even’, and the BSB’s ‘even’ reflects one view. Many interpreters, including most in the Reformed tradition, take Paul to mean the whole church of Jewish and Gentile believers: ‘peace on all who walk by this rule, that is, on the Israel of God’. Others read ‘and on the Israel of God’ as a second group: Jewish believers in particular, or the Jewish people whom God will yet show mercy to (compare Romans 11:26). Moo and Longenecker are among the commentators who set out the arguments in detail. The question affects how Christians understand the relationship between Israel and the church. Some suggest the large letters point to poor eyesight (compare 4:15); many commentators, such as Betz, Dunn and Martyn, take them simply as emphasis, like underlining.

1.ctx: Written from prison (3:1; 4:1; 6:20) and carried by Tychicus (6:21). See History & setting of Ephesians above for the questions of authorship and destination.
1.mean: Paul greets ‘the saints’, literally ‘holy ones’. In the New Testament that is a description of every Christian, set apart for God, not a title for the exceptionally good. They are also ‘the faithful in Christ Jesus’. ‘In Christ’ and its variations appear around thirty-five times in this letter. It is the key to everything Paul will say: every blessing believers have, they have because they are united to Christ. He wishes them grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, naming the Father and the Son together as the one source of blessing.
1.big: Every Christian is a ‘saint’, set apart for God, and every blessing comes ‘in Christ’.

src.l: D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others

1.ctx: Verses 3–14 are one long sentence in the Greek, a hymn of praise rather than an argument, moving from the Father (verses 3–6) to the Son (7–12) to the Spirit (13–14), each section ending ‘to the praise of his glory’.
1.mean: ‘Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms.’ Paul then lists them. The Father chose: ‘He chose us in him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in his presence. In love he predestined us for adoption as his sons through Jesus Christ.’ Salvation began in God’s heart before creation, and its aim is holiness and sonship. The Son redeemed: ‘In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.’ God has also made known ‘the mystery of his will’: his plan ‘to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ’. The Spirit sealed: when they heard and believed the gospel, they were ‘sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance’. A seal marked ownership and protected the contents; a pledge was a first instalment guaranteeing the rest. Paul’s response to all this is not argument but worship.
1.big: Every stage of salvation, from before creation to its final completion, is the work of Father, Son and Spirit, and it leads to praise.
1.diff: Election (verses 4–5, 11). Reformed: God chose particular individuals for salvation in Christ before creation, out of his own good pleasure, not because of anything foreseen in them. Calvin says ‘the counsel of his own will is the only and actual cause of their election’ (compare Westminster Confession 3.5). Arminian (Wesleyan): God chose to save all who would believe in Christ, and those he chose are those he foreknew as believers. Wesley wrote that God chose ‘whom he foreknew as believing in Christ’, and that God’s fixed purpose was to give the blessing of sonship ‘on all those who should believe in Christ’ (compare Remonstrance, art. 1). Corporate: God chose a people ‘in Christ’, the church, and individuals share in that election by being joined to Christ through faith. Many modern scholars across traditions stress this corporate side. All agree that Paul presents election as a reason for worship and holiness, not for pride or speculation, and that it is ‘in Christ’.

1.ctx: After the hymn of praise, Paul turns to prayer.
1.mean: Having heard of their faith in the Lord Jesus and their love for all the saints, Paul never stops giving thanks and praying for them. He does not ask for more blessings. He asks that they would understand the ones they have. He prays that God would give them ‘a spirit of wisdom and revelation’ in knowing him, and that the eyes of their hearts would be enlightened to know three things: the hope of God’s calling, the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, and ‘the surpassing greatness of his power to us who believe’. That power is the same power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him at God’s right hand, ‘far above all rule and authority, power and dominion’, and every name. God put everything under his feet and gave him as head over everything for the church, which is his body.
1.big: Paul prays not for more blessings but that believers would grasp the ones they already have, above all the power that raised Christ.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL
D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others

2.ctx: Paul now shows how the power that raised Christ (1:19–20) has been at work in his readers.
2.mean:
What we were (verses 1–3). ‘You were dead in your trespasses and sins.’ Paul does not say weak, or sick, but dead: unable to bring ourselves to life before God. Three things directed that life: ‘the ways of this world’, ‘the ruler of the power of the air’ (the devil), and ‘the cravings of our flesh’. And ‘like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath’. In plain words: by birth and by the way we lived, we stood under God’s just judgment like everyone else. Paul includes himself (‘we’); this is not Gentiles looked down on by Jews.

What God did (verses 4–7). ‘But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses.’ ‘But God’ is the turning point of the passage. He made us alive, raised us and seated us with Christ, so that in the ages to come he might display the riches of his grace.

How it happened (verses 8–10). ‘For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast.’ Grace is the source, faith is the means, and the whole is a gift. Then the purpose: ‘For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.’ Good works are not the root of salvation but its fruit.
2.big: God rescues people who were spiritually dead, by grace, through faith, as a gift, and they are remade for a life of good works.
2.diff:
What is ‘the gift of God’ in verse 8? In Greek, ‘this’ does not match the gender of ‘faith’ or ‘grace’, so most commentators take it to refer to the whole of salvation by grace through faith. Calvin himself wrote, ‘His meaning is, not that faith is the gift of God, but that salvation is given to us by God’. Wesley said the same: it ‘refers to the whole preceding clause’. Reformed theology still teaches, from other passages (Philippians 1:29; Acts 16:14), that faith itself is God’s gift worked by the Spirit (Westminster Confession 10.2; 14.1). Arminian theology holds that faith is made possible by grace, but is a response a person could refuse. All agree with Paul’s point: no part of salvation gives grounds for boasting.

‘Children of wrath’ (verse 3) is Paul’s own phrase. Reformed theology reads ‘by nature’ as pointing to original sin, sinfulness from birth (compare Psalm 51:5). Others read it as describing the life people actually lived, as verses 1–3 do. Either way, Paul’s point is that everyone needs rescue and no one is better than anyone else.

2.ctx: Gentiles were once outside Israel’s covenants. In the Jerusalem temple a stone barrier, carrying warning inscriptions, kept them out of the inner courts on pain of death (see the drop-down).
2.mean: Paul asks Gentile believers to remember what they were. They were separate from Christ, excluded from citizenship in Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, ‘without hope and without God in the world’. ‘But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.’ ‘For he himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility.’ He did this by abolishing in his flesh ‘the law of commandments and decrees’, the rules that kept Jew and Gentile apart, to create ‘one new man out of the two’. He reconciled both to God in one body through the cross. The cross does two things at once: it reconciles people to God, and in the same act to one another. Through Christ both have access to the Father by one Spirit.
2.big: The cross reconciles people to God and, in the same act, to each other, making one new humanity.
2.diff: What does ‘abolishing… the law of commandments and decrees’ (verse 15) mean? Most interpreters take it to mean the law as a system that divided Jew from Gentile, such as circumcision, food laws and purity rules, not God’s moral will. Paul goes on to quote the commandments as still guiding Christian life (6:2). Reformed theology has traditionally distinguished the ceremonial law, fulfilled and ended in Christ, from the moral law, which continues.

b: In Herod’s temple in Jerusalem, a stone barrier separated the outer Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts. Josephus says pillars set along it carried warnings in Greek and Latin, and that the inscription ‘forbade any foreigner to go in under pain of death’. One of these warnings, in Greek, was found near the Temple Mount in the late 19th century and survives complete. It says no foreigner may go inside the barrier around the sanctuary, and that anyone caught will have himself to blame for the death that follows.

Paul may or may not have this barrier in mind when he speaks of Christ tearing down ‘the dividing wall of hostility’. In Acts 21:28–29 Paul himself was accused of taking a Gentile past it, Trophimus, who came from Ephesus. The riot that followed led to Paul’s arrest and, in the end, to the imprisonment he writes from. Whether or not he alludes to it, it is a vivid picture of what the cross has done: Gentiles who were ‘far off’ have been ‘brought near’.

2.ctx: The picture shifts from citizenship to a family, and then to a building. Ephesus was dominated by the temple of Artemis, so a living temple would have struck home.
2.mean: ‘You are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.’ In a city like Ephesus, full citizenship was a privilege for a minority, and resident foreigners had limited rights. Gentile believers, slaves among them, are now full citizens of God’s people and members of his family. Then the image becomes a building: ‘built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone’. In him the whole building grows into a holy temple in the Lord, ‘a dwelling place for God in his Spirit’. God no longer lives in a building of stone in Jerusalem but in his people.
2.big: The church, Jewish and Gentile together, is now the temple where God lives by his Spirit.
2.diff: Most scholars read ‘prophets’ here as New Testament prophets alongside the apostles (compare 3:5; 4:11), both of whom had a foundational role. Whether prophecy continues today, and in what sense, is part of the wider debate about spiritual gifts: cessationists hold that foundational gifts ended with the apostles; continuationists that prophecy continues, subordinate to Scripture.

3.ctx: Paul begins a prayer (‘For this reason…’), breaks off to explain his ministry, and resumes the prayer in verse 14.
3.mean: Paul calls himself ‘the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles’. His imprisonment is not a defeat but part of his service to them. He explains ‘the mystery of Christ’. In the New Testament a mystery is not a puzzle but something once hidden and now revealed by God. Here it is that ‘through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus’. Paul, ‘less than the least of all the saints’, was given the grace to preach ‘the unsearchable riches of Christ’. And through the church, God’s many-sided wisdom is now made known even to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms. A multi-ethnic church is God’s exhibit to the universe.
3.big: God’s long-hidden plan was to unite Jews and Gentiles in one body, and the church itself displays his wisdom.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL
D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others

3.ctx: Paul resumes the prayer. Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling signals unusual earnestness.
3.mean: ‘I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name.’ Paul asks for four things that build on each other. First, that they would be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner being. Second, that Christ would dwell in their hearts through faith, at home there, not a visitor. Third, that being rooted and grounded in love, they would grasp with all the saints ‘the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge’. Fourth, that they would be filled with all the fullness of God. Then the doxology: to him who is able to do ‘immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine’, according to his power at work in us, be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations.
3.big: Paul prays that believers would know by experience a love too great to be fully understood.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL

4.ctx: The turning point of the letter. Chapters 1–3 describe what God has done; chapters 4–6 describe how to live in response.
4.mean: ‘I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received: with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.’ Unity is not something the church creates but something the Spirit has created, and believers must ‘keep’ it. Paul grounds it in seven ‘ones’: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Unity is not uniformity, though: ‘to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ’. The ascended Christ gave the church apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers. Their task is not to do all the ministry, but ‘to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ’. The goal is maturity, ‘the full measure of the stature of Christ’. Then believers are no longer infants tossed about by every wind of teaching. Instead, ‘speaking the truth in love’, they grow up into Christ, the head.
4.big: Christ gives leaders to equip every believer, so that the whole body grows up into him in unity and truth.
4.diff: Verse 8 quotes Psalm 68:18 with ‘gave gifts’ where the Hebrew has ‘received gifts’. Some Jewish interpretation of the psalm (in the Targum) also read ‘gave’. Others explain it as a conqueror receiving tribute in order to distribute it. ‘Descended to the lower parts of the earth’ (verse 9) is read as the incarnation (coming down to earth), as Christ’s descent to the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection, or as the Spirit’s descent at Pentecost. Whether apostles and prophets continue today is debated: most traditions agree that the foundational apostles (2:20) have no successors in that sense; some continuationists recognise apostolic and prophetic ministries today. ‘Pastors and teachers’ may be one role or two.

src.l: D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others
S. M. Baugh, Ephesians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham)

4.ctx: Ephesus was a centre of pagan worship, magic and the emperor cult.
4.mean: ‘You must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking.’ Paul describes life apart from God as darkened understanding, alienation from God’s life, and hardened hearts, leading to loss of all sensitivity and a craving for impurity. ‘But this is not the way you came to know Christ.’ They were taught to put off the old self, to be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness. Then Paul gets specific. Put off falsehood and speak truthfully. Be angry, yet do not sin; do not let the sun set on your anger. The thief must steal no longer but work, so as to have something to share. No unwholesome talk, only what builds up. Do not grieve the Holy Spirit. Get rid of bitterness, rage and slander. ‘Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.’
4.big: The new life in Christ is put on in the ordinary details of speech, work, anger and forgiveness.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL

5.ctx: Continuing the practical instruction. Sexual immorality was widely accepted in Greco-Roman society and bound up with some pagan worship, so Paul’s standard would have marked the church out sharply.
5.mean: ‘Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.’ The model of Christian love is the cross. Then the negative: sexual immorality, impurity and greed must not even be named among them, nor obscenity, foolish talk or crude joking, but rather thanksgiving. No immoral, impure or greedy person (‘that is, an idolater’) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Paul calls greed idolatry because it puts possessions in God’s place. Let no one deceive you with empty words.
5.big: Believers are to imitate God’s self-giving love and reject everything that contradicts it.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL

5.ctx: The contrast between darkness and light runs through the passage.
5.mean: ‘For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.’ Paul does not say they were in darkness, but that they were darkness; now they are light. Light produces goodness, righteousness and truth. It also exposes: have nothing to do with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them. ‘Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.’ ‘Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit.’ Paul describes what that looks like: speaking to one another with psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing to the Lord, always giving thanks to God the Father for everything, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
5.big: Being filled with the Spirit shows itself in worship, thanksgiving and mutual submission.
5.diff: Christians differ over what ‘be filled with the Spirit’ involves: a repeated experience, an ongoing state of yieldedness, or both. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians often link filling with spiritual gifts and a distinct experience after conversion; most Reformed and many other evangelicals see it as the ongoing control of the Spirit in every believer. The Greek is a present imperative, ‘keep being filled’, and Paul’s own description here is corporate and practical: singing, thanksgiving and submission to one another.

src.l: D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others

5.ctx: The ‘household code’ begins: a common form of moral teaching going back to Aristotle, which addressed husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and slaves. Paul uses the form but fills it with Christ.
5.mean: ‘Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.’ This verse links the Spirit-filled life (5:18) to the household instructions that follow. ‘Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Savior.’ Paul addresses wives as responsible people who choose to submit, not as property, which was unusual in ancient household codes. Then he spends three times as many words on husbands, and the demand is staggering: ‘Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.’ A husband’s model is the cross. Christ’s aim was his bride’s good: to make her holy, glorious and without blemish. Husbands are to love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them as Christ does the church. Then Paul quotes Genesis 2:24, the two becoming one flesh, and says: ‘This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church.’ Marriage was designed from the beginning as a picture of Christ and his people.
5.big: Christian marriage is meant to picture the self-giving love between Christ and his church.
5.diff: This passage is central to the debate between complementarians and egalitarians. Complementarians (including most Reformed and many other evangelical churches, and scholars such as Wayne Grudem and Clinton Arnold) read it as teaching a husband’s loving, sacrificial headship and a wife’s willing submission, both modelled on Christ and the church and rooted in creation. They read verse 21 as introducing submission within ordered relationships. Egalitarians stress verse 21’s mutual submission as governing the whole passage. Many read ‘head’ (kephalē) as ‘source’ rather than ‘authority’, and see the household code as Paul working within the structures of his culture, as he does with slavery, while sowing principles that transform them. The meaning of kephalē in ancient Greek is itself debated. Everyone agrees that Paul’s demand on husbands, to love as Christ loved and give himself up, rules out any selfish, harsh or controlling use of headship.

src.l: D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others
S. M. Baugh, Ephesians, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham)

6.ctx: The household code continues. In Roman law a father held near-absolute power over his children, so Paul’s instruction to fathers was a real restraint.
6.mean: ‘Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.’ Paul addresses children directly, as members of the church listening when the letter was read. He quotes the fifth commandment, ‘the first commandment with a promise’. Then: ‘Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.’ Christian fathers are to be neither harsh nor passive, but to take responsibility for raising their children to know the Lord.
6.big: The gospel reshapes family life in both directions: honour from children, patient discipling from fathers.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL

6.ctx: Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, though it was not based on race; slaves might be labourers, craftsmen, teachers or household managers. Many members of the early church were slaves.
6.mean: Paul tells slaves to obey their earthly masters with sincerity of heart, ‘just as you would obey Christ’, not only when watched, but doing God’s will from the heart, ‘because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free’. Then masters: ‘do the same for your slaves’, and give up threats, knowing that ‘He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him’. Master and slave stand as equals before the same Lord. That conviction, worked out over time, undermined the institution itself.
6.big: Master and slave stand as equals before the same Lord, and both serve him in their daily work.
6.diff: Paul regulates rather than abolishes slavery here, which troubles modern readers. He addressed a church with no political power. Elsewhere he encouraged slaves to gain freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21) and treated a slave as a ‘brother’ (Philemon 16). Christians campaigning against the slave trade drew on these very principles: one Master, no favouritism, and every person made in God’s image. The passage is now widely applied to employers and employees, though the situations are not the same.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL
D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others

6.ctx: The closing section of the letter. Roman soldiers would have been a familiar sight to a prisoner, and much of the imagery comes from Isaiah (11:5; 52:7; 59:17), where it describes God’s own armour.
6.mean: ‘Be strong in the Lord and in his mighty power. Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil’s schemes.’ The real enemy is not other people: ‘our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms’. The armour is God’s, and every piece is the gospel applied: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith to quench the flaming arrows of the evil one, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. The aim is to ‘stand’, repeated four times: to hold the ground Christ has won. And it is all done in prayer, praying ‘in the Spirit at all times’ for all the saints and for Paul, that he may boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, for which he is ‘an ambassador in chains’.
6.big: Believers face a real spiritual battle, and stand in it with God’s own armour and with prayer.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Ephesians (with Galatians), CCEL
D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others

6.ctx: Tychicus, a trusted companion from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4), carries the letter, as he also carries Colossians (Colossians 4:7).
6.mean: Paul sends Tychicus, ‘the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord’, to tell them how he is and to encourage their hearts. He closes with peace, love and faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ ‘with an undying love’.
6.big: The letter ends as it began, with grace and peace from the Father and the Son.

src.l: D. R. Brown & M. M. Whitehead, Ephesians, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Arnold, Best, Bruce, Hoehner, Lincoln, O’Brien, Snodgrass, Thielman, Grudem and others

1.ctx: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first place Paul planted a church in Europe (Acts 16). He writes from prison, probably in Rome in the early 60s, to a church that had supported him financially.
1.mean: Paul and Timothy greet the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons. The letter is warm and personal throughout.
1.big: Paul writes as a servant of Christ Jesus to a church he loves.
1.diff: The letter's place of writing is debated — Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have all been proposed. Rome is the traditional view. Nothing in its teaching depends on the answer.

1.ctx: A thanksgiving, as in most of Paul's letters. The Philippians had supported Paul financially from the start (4:15–16), which is the 'partnership in the gospel' he has in mind.
1.mean: Paul says he thanks God every time he remembers them because of their partnership in the gospel from the first day. He is sure that he who began a good work in them will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. He prays that their love may abound in knowledge and discernment, so that they may be pure and blameless, filled with the fruit of righteousness.
1.big: God finishes what he starts in his people.
1.diff: Reformed theology has often cited verse 6 in support of the perseverance of the saints — that God will keep those he has saved. Others read it primarily as Paul's confidence about this particular church. The verse's focus is on God's faithfulness rather than human endurance.

1.ctx: Paul is under guard, probably chained to a soldier in rented quarters, awaiting trial.
1.mean: Paul says his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel: the whole imperial guard knows he is in chains for Christ, and most believers have become bolder. Some preach Christ from rivalry, others from goodwill. Paul's response is that in every way Christ is proclaimed, and in that he rejoices.
1.big: Paul measures his circumstances by what they do for the gospel, not what they do for him.

1.ctx: Paul is awaiting a verdict that could mean release or execution. He writes knowing either outcome is possible, and weighs them openly.
1.mean: Paul says that to live is Christ and to die is gain. He is torn between departing to be with Christ, which is far better, and remaining in the flesh, which is more necessary for them. He is convinced he will remain for their progress and joy in the faith.
1.big: For Paul, Christ is the meaning of life and the gain of death.
1.diff: Verse 23, 'to depart and be with Christ', is one of the main texts Christians cite for believers being with Christ immediately after death, before the final resurrection.

1.ctx: 'Live worthy' uses a word connected with citizenship — pointed in a Roman colony proud of its status.
1.mean: Paul says to conduct themselves in a manner worthy of the gospel, standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side for the faith, not frightened by opponents. It has been granted to them not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for his sake.
1.big: Suffering for Christ is presented as a gift alongside faith, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

2.ctx: Paul appeals for unity, apparently because of tension in the church (see 4:2).
2.mean: Paul says that if there is any encouragement in Christ, comfort from love, or participation in the Spirit, they should complete his joy by being of the same mind. Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves, looking to their interests as well as your own.
2.big: Unity in the church depends on humility that puts others first.

2.ctx: Many scholars think verses 6–11 are an early Christian hymn, which Paul quotes or composed. It is one of the most important passages about Christ in the New Testament.
2.mean: Paul says to have the mind of Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, being born in human likeness. He humbled himself by becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Paul applies Isaiah 45:23 — where the LORD swears that every knee will bow to him — to Jesus. The passage holds together Christ's full deity and his full humanity, which the church has expressed as the two natures in one person (see the note on Mark 4:35).
2.big: The eternal Son took the lowest place, and God has given him the highest — and that pattern is the one believers are to follow.
2.diff: What 'emptied himself' means has been debated. The historic understanding is that the Son did not give up his divine nature but took on human nature and the status of a servant — adding rather than subtracting. Some modern 'kenotic' theories propose that he set aside certain divine attributes; most Reformed and evangelical theologians reject this, since the text says he was 'in the form of God' and the emptying consists in 'taking the form of a servant'.

2.ctx: 'Therefore' ties this to the example of Christ just described.
2.mean: Paul says to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in them, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Do everything without grumbling, so that they may shine as lights in a crooked generation, holding fast to the word of life. Even if Paul is poured out as a drink offering, he rejoices.
2.big: Believers work hard at living out their salvation precisely because God is already at work within them.
2.diff: Verses 12–13 are a classic text on how God's work and human effort relate. Reformed theology stresses that God's working is prior and effective, and human effort its result; other traditions place more weight on cooperation. All agree Paul is not telling them to earn salvation, which he denies in 3:9.

2.ctx: Two companions whose examples illustrate the self-giving Paul has described.
2.mean: Paul hopes to send Timothy, who is genuinely concerned for their welfare and has served with Paul like a son with a father. He sends back Epaphroditus, their messenger, who nearly died in the work of Christ, and asks them to honour such men.
2.big: The mind of Christ is seen in ordinary people who put others' needs above their own.

3.ctx: Paul warns against teachers insisting on circumcision, as in Galatians. The abrupt change of tone leads some scholars to think the letter combines more than one of Paul's letters, though many see a single letter.
3.mean: Paul says to watch out for the 'dogs' and 'mutilators of the flesh'. He could boast more than anyone in his Jewish credentials — circumcised on the eighth day, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless under the law. But whatever gain he had he now counts as loss, even as rubbish, compared to knowing Christ Jesus and being found in him, not having a righteousness of his own from the law, but the righteousness from God that depends on faith.
3.big: The best religious record in the world is worthless compared with the righteousness God gives through faith in Christ.
3.diff: As in Galatians 2:16, 'faith in Christ' in verse 9 can also be translated 'the faithfulness of Christ'. Reformed theology reads verse 9 as a clear statement of imputed righteousness — a righteousness from God credited to the believer. Some New Perspective scholars emphasise Paul's ethnic credentials as the 'righteousness of my own'. Both agree Paul rejects any righteousness grounded in the law.

3.ctx: Having renounced his own righteousness, Paul guards against the opposite error of thinking he has arrived.
3.mean: Paul says he has not already obtained this or been made perfect, but presses on to make it his own, because Christ Jesus has made him his own. Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward, he presses on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
3.big: The Christian life is lived between being grasped by Christ and finally grasping him.

3.ctx: Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens held Roman citizenship though they had never seen Rome.
3.mean: Paul says to imitate him and those who walk as he does, because many walk as enemies of the cross, whose god is their belly and whose minds are set on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body.
3.big: Believers are citizens of heaven now, awaiting a Saviour who will transform even their bodies.

4.ctx: Two women in the church, Euodia and Syntyche, who had worked alongside Paul, were in disagreement.
4.mean: Paul urges them to agree in the Lord and asks a companion to help them. He then says to rejoice in the Lord always, let their gentleness be known to all, and not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let their requests be made known to God. The peace of God, which surpasses understanding, will guard their hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. Whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely and commendable — think about these things.
4.big: The answer to anxiety is thankful prayer, and God's promise in response is his peace.

4.ctx: The Philippians had sent Paul a gift through Epaphroditus (2:25), and prisoners in the Roman system depended on friends for food and necessities.
4.mean: Paul thanks them, while saying he has learned to be content in whatever situation — in plenty and in hunger. He can do all things through him who strengthens him. He rejoices in their gift not for his own sake but for the fruit it credits to them, calling it a fragrant offering pleasing to God. And his God will supply every need of theirs according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
4.big: Contentment comes from Christ's strength, not from circumstances.
4.diff: Verse 13 is often quoted as a promise of success in any endeavour. In context it is about enduring every circumstance — plenty or want — through Christ's strength.

4.ctx: The closing greetings. 'Caesar's household' meant the large imperial staff of slaves and freedmen, not necessarily the emperor's family.
4.mean: Paul greets every saint in Christ Jesus, passes on greetings from those with him — especially those of Caesar's household — and closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
4.big: The gospel has reached even into the emperor's household.

1.ctx: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had not visited it; the church was founded by Epaphras (1:7). Paul writes from prison, most likely in Rome.
1.mean: Paul and Timothy greet the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae with grace and peace from God the Father.
1.big: Paul writes to a church he has never met, as one family in Christ.
1.diff: As with Ephesians, some scholars question whether Paul wrote Colossians, noting differences of style. The letter claims Paul as author, and many scholars, including most evangelicals, accept it; its close links with Philemon support that.

1.ctx: A thanksgiving and prayer, as usual in Paul's letters, for a church he knows only through Epaphras.
1.mean: Paul says he thanks God for their faith in Christ and love for all the saints, springing from the hope laid up for them in heaven, which they heard in the gospel now bearing fruit in the whole world. He prays that they may be filled with the knowledge of God's will, walk worthy of the Lord, and give thanks to the Father who has transferred them from the domain of darkness to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom they have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
1.big: Believers have already been rescued from darkness and brought into the kingdom of God's Son.

1.ctx: Many scholars think verses 15–20 are an early Christian hymn. It is one of the highest statements about Christ in the New Testament, and a key passage in discussions with Jehovah's Witnesses.
1.mean: Paul says the Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation, because by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible — all things were created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. He is the head of the body, the church; the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in everything he might be preeminent. In him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him God reconciled all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross.
1.big: The one who made and sustains all things is the same one who reconciled all things through his cross.
1.diff: 'Firstborn' has been read by some groups, including Jehovah's Witnesses, to mean Christ was the first thing created. The historic Christian reading is that 'firstborn' means rank and supremacy, as in Psalm 89:27 where David, the youngest son, is called firstborn — and verse 16 says all things were created through him, which would include any created thing. The New World Translation's insertion of 'other' ('all other things') is not in the Greek.

1.ctx: Paul turns to his own ministry, written from prison for a church that had not seen him.
1.mean: Paul says he rejoices in his sufferings for their sake, and in his flesh fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, the church. God made known to him the mystery hidden for ages: Christ in you, the hope of glory. Him we proclaim, warning and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
1.big: The heart of the gospel mystery is Christ living in his people and their future glory with him.
1.diff: Verse 24 does not mean Christ's saving suffering was incomplete, which Paul denies elsewhere. Most interpreters read it as the sufferings the church, Christ's body, must still endure in spreading the gospel, which Paul shares.

2.ctx: Paul addresses the particular danger facing the Colossians: teaching that added philosophy, special knowledge, rituals and angel-worship to Christ.
2.mean: Paul says he struggles for them and for those at Laodicea, that they may reach all the riches of full assurance and the knowledge of God's mystery, Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. He says this so no one deludes them with plausible arguments.
2.big: Every treasure of wisdom is found in Christ, so nothing needs to be added to him.
2.h: Absent in Body, Present in Spirit

2.ctx: The heart of the letter's warning. The exact nature of the 'Colossian heresy' is debated, but it seems to have mixed Jewish ritual, mystical visions and ascetic rules.
2.mean: Paul says to walk in Christ as they received him, rooted and built up in him. Do not be taken captive by philosophy and empty deceit according to human tradition, for in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and they have been filled in him. They were buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith. God forgave all their trespasses, cancelling the record of debt against them by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the rulers and authorities. So let no one pass judgement on them over food, drink, festivals or Sabbaths, which were a shadow of things to come; the substance belongs to Christ. Rules like 'do not handle, do not taste' have an appearance of wisdom but no value against the indulgence of the flesh.
2.big: Because all God's fullness dwells bodily in Christ, believers are complete in him and need no additions.
2.diff: Verse 9, 'the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily', is among the clearest New Testament statements that Christ is fully God and fully human — the two natures in one person (see Mark 4:35). Christians differ over whether the Sabbath commandment still binds believers in some form; Reformed churches have historically kept the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath, while others read verse 16 as ending any Sabbath obligation.

3.ctx: The practical section begins. As in Ephesians, what believers are in Christ comes first, then how they should live.
3.mean: Paul says that since they have been raised with Christ, they should seek the things above, where Christ is seated at God's right hand. Their life is hidden with Christ in God. So put to death what is earthly: sexual immorality, impurity, covetousness, which is idolatry, and anger, slander and lying. They have put off the old self and put on the new, in which there is not Greek and Jew, slave and free, but Christ is all and in all. Put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forgiveness as the Lord forgave, and above all love. Let the peace of Christ rule and the word of Christ dwell richly, singing with thankfulness, and doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.
3.big: Because believers' true life is now hidden with Christ, they are to put off the old self and put on the character of Christ.

3.ctx: The household code, parallel to Ephesians 5:21–6:9 but shorter.
3.mean: Paul tells wives to submit to their husbands as fitting in the Lord, and husbands to love their wives and not be harsh with them. Children are to obey their parents in everything, and fathers not to provoke their children, lest they become discouraged.
3.big: Christ's lordship reshapes every relationship in the home.
3.diff: As at Ephesians 5, Christians differ over how the call for wives to submit applies today. Complementarian and egalitarian readings are both held by evangelicals; all agree the husband's call to love rules out harshness.

3.ctx: Slavery was common in the Roman world. Onesimus, a runaway slave from Colossae, carries this letter with Tychicus (4:9), which makes the passage pointed.
3.mean: Paul tells slaves to obey their earthly masters sincerely, working heartily as for the Lord rather than for people, knowing that from the Lord they will receive the inheritance as their reward. Whoever does wrong will be paid back, and there is no partiality.
3.big: All work, even under an unjust system, can be done for the Lord who sees and rewards.

4.ctx: The instruction to masters completes the household code, then Paul turns to prayer and speech toward outsiders.
4.mean: Paul tells masters to treat their slaves justly and fairly, knowing they too have a Master in heaven. He urges steadfast, watchful prayer with thanksgiving, and prayer for an open door for the gospel. Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time; let speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so they know how to answer each person.
4.big: Believers are to pray for gospel opportunities and speak graciously to those outside the church.
4.diff: Verse 1's reminder that masters have a Master in heaven is one of the principles later Christians drew on in opposing slavery.

4.ctx: A list of Paul's companions, many of whom appear in Philemon and Acts.
4.mean: Paul commends Tychicus and Onesimus, who will bring news. He sends greetings from Aristarchus, Mark the cousin of Barnabas, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras who struggles in prayer for them, Luke the beloved physician, and Demas.
4.big: The gospel advances through a network of ordinary, named co-workers.
4.diff: The Mark named here is widely identified with John Mark, who deserted Paul on his first journey and whom Paul now commends — the same Mark traditionally linked with the Gospel of Mark.

4.ctx: The letter closes with greetings to the neighbouring church at Laodicea, about ten miles away.
4.mean: Paul greets Nympha and the church in her house, and asks that this letter be read also at Laodicea, and that they read the letter from Laodicea. He tells Archippus to fulfil his ministry, and signs the greeting in his own hand: remember my chains. Grace be with you.
4.big: Paul's letters were meant to be shared and read aloud across the churches.
4.diff: The 'letter from Laodicea' has not survived. Some scholars suggest it may be our Ephesians, if that was a circular letter.

1.ctx: From James, leader of the church in Jerusalem, to Jewish believers scattered beyond Israel. See History & setting of James above.
1.mean: James introduces himself not as Jesus’ brother but as ‘a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ’. The man who once did not believe in Jesus now calls his brother ‘Lord’. He writes ‘To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion’. ‘Dispersion’ (Greek diaspora) was the word for Jewish people living outside the land of Israel. Here it means Jewish Christians scattered abroad, though many also see a picture of the whole church as God’s people living as exiles in this world (compare 1 Peter 1:1).
1.big: James, once a sceptic, writes as the servant of his brother and Lord.

src.l: P. H. Davids, ‘James’ and ‘James, Epistle of’; R. V. G. Tasker, ‘Brethren of the Lord’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

1.ctx: The readers were facing pressure, including poverty and oppression by the rich (2:6; 5:1–6).
1.mean: ‘Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds.’ James is not saying trials are pleasant, but that they have a purpose: ‘the testing of your faith develops perseverance’, and perseverance makes a person ‘mature and complete, not lacking anything’. For that, believers need wisdom, which God gives ‘generously to all without finding fault’. But they must ask in faith. Someone who doubts, wavering between trusting God and not, is ‘a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways’. James then applies this to money. The poor believer should rejoice in his high position in God’s eyes; the rich believer in his low position, because wealth fades like a flower in the scorching sun. ‘Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial, because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.’
1.big: Trials, met with faith and God’s wisdom, produce mature, steady believers.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL
J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

1.ctx: The same Greek word can mean ‘trial’ or ‘temptation’. James now turns from outward trials to the inner pull towards sin.
1.mean: ‘When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.’ God may test his people, but he never tries to make them fall. The source of temptation is inside us: ‘each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.’ James traces it like a life cycle: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin, full-grown, gives birth to death. God gives the opposite: ‘Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.’ Unlike the sun and stars, which move and cast changing shadows, God never changes. His greatest gift is new life: ‘He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation.’ The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as the pledge of the rest.
1.big: Sin comes from our own desires; every good thing, above all new birth, comes from the unchanging God.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL
J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

1.ctx: One of James’s central themes: hearing God’s word is not enough.
1.mean: ‘Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.’ Instead, get rid of moral filth and ‘humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls’. Then the key command: ‘Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves.’ Someone who hears but does not act is like a man who looks in a mirror and immediately forgets what he saw. But whoever looks intently into ‘the perfect law of freedom’ and keeps doing it will be blessed. For James, God’s law, as fulfilled and taught by Jesus, is not a burden but the pattern of a free life. Real religion is tested in three areas: the tongue, care for the vulnerable (‘orphans and widows in their distress’, who had no one to provide for them), and keeping ‘from being polluted by the world’.
1.big: God’s word must be acted on, not just heard, and real religion shows in speech, compassion and purity.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL
J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

2.ctx: The word translated ‘meeting’ in verse 2 is literally ‘synagogue’, one sign of how early and Jewish this letter is.
2.mean: ‘My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism.’ James paints a scene. A rich man with a gold ring and fine clothes walks into the meeting and is shown a seat of honour; a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand or sit on the floor. That makes them ‘judges with evil thoughts’. It is also upside down: ‘Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him?’ And it is the rich who are oppressing them and dragging them to court. Favouritism breaks ‘the royal law’: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ James insists that the law is one whole. Whoever stumbles at one point is guilty of breaking all of it, because the same God gave every command. So believers should speak and act as people who will be judged ‘by the law that gives freedom’. ‘Judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.’
2.big: Treating people by their wealth or status contradicts faith in the glorious Lord and breaks the law of love.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL
J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

2.ctx: The most debated passage in the letter. It is about people who claim to have faith but whose lives show nothing of it.
2.mean: ‘What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him?’ Note the word ‘claims’: James is examining a faith that is only professed. His first example: to tell a hungry, ill-clothed brother ‘Go in peace; stay warm and well fed’ and give him nothing is worthless. ‘So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.’ His second example: ‘You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder.’ Agreeing with true statements about God is not saving faith; demons do that. His third example is Abraham. When Abraham offered Isaac (Genesis 22), ‘his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did’. That fulfilled the Scripture written decades earlier: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness’ (Genesis 15:6). Rahab too showed her faith by hiding the spies. James concludes: ‘As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.’ ‘As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.’
2.big: Faith that produces no change in a person’s life is not living, saving faith.
2.diff:
Does James contradict Paul? Paul says ‘a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law’ (Romans 3:28) and uses Abraham as his example. James says ‘a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone’ and also uses Abraham.

Protestant readings (Reformed and Arminian alike). The two are answering different questions. Paul asks how a sinner is put right with God, and answers: by faith, not by earning it. James asks what real faith looks like, and answers: it works. Calvin explains that Paul uses ‘justify’ for ‘the gratuitous imputation of righteousness before the tribunal of God’, while James means ‘the manifestation of righteousness by the conduct’: proof that someone is righteous. Wesley explains it through faith and works instead: ‘They do not speak of the same faith: St. Paul speaking of living faith; St. James here, of dead faith.’ Paul means works done before faith in order to earn salvation; James means works that follow faith. So, Wesley says, ‘St. James’s justification by works is the fruit of St. Paul’s justification by faith.’ Many modern scholars add that James may be using ‘justified’ for God’s final verdict at the judgment, which takes a person’s whole life into account. A well-known Protestant saying sums up the view: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

Catholic. The Council of Trent quotes James 2:24 to teach that, through good works done by God’s grace, the justified ‘increase in that justice which they have received through the grace of Christ’. In Catholic teaching, justification includes inner renewal and grows through a life of faith working in love.

Lutheran. Luther himself struggled with this passage (see James in church history above), but the Lutheran churches accept James and read it, like other Protestants, as describing the fruit of faith.

src.l: Calvin on James 2:20–26, CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on James 2
Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547), ch. 10, in Schaff vol. 2
Martin Foord, ‘The “Epistle of Straw”: Reflections on Luther and the Epistle of James’, Themelios 45.2 (2020)

3.ctx: In the early church, teaching was done largely by speaking, and many wanted the honour of being a teacher.
3.mean: ‘Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.’ James includes himself. Then he widens the point: ‘We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.’ Small things steer big things, as a bit steers a horse and a rudder steers a ship. Small things also destroy big things: ‘Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.’ The tongue ‘is a fire, a world of wickedness’, and ‘is itself set on fire by hell’. Every kind of animal has been tamed, ‘but no man can tame the tongue’. Worst of all is the inconsistency: ‘With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness.’ ‘My brothers, this should not be!’ A spring does not give both fresh and salt water.
3.big: Speech reveals and steers the whole person, and no one can control it without God’s help.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL
J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

3.ctx: ‘Wisdom’ in James means practical, godly skill for living, as in Proverbs.
3.mean: ‘Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom.’ Wisdom is proved by how someone lives, not by how much they know. There is a false wisdom, marked by ‘bitter jealousy and selfish ambition’. It is ‘earthly, unspiritual, demonic’ and produces ‘disorder and every evil practice’. True wisdom is different: ‘the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere.’ ‘Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness.’ This list reads like a portrait of Jesus.
3.big: God’s wisdom shows itself in a pure, peaceable, merciful character, not in clever words or ambition.

src.l: J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

4.ctx: James now confronts quarrels in the churches.
4.mean: ‘What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you?’ Fights in the church begin with desires in the heart. ‘You crave what you do not have’. ‘You do not have, because you do not ask. And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives.’ James then uses the Old Testament prophets’ language for unfaithfulness: ‘You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?’ ‘The world’ here means human life organised without God. Yet God does not give up: ‘But He gives us more grace.’ ‘God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’
4.big: Quarrels come from selfish desires, but God gives more grace to those who humble themselves.
4.diff: Verse 5 is one of the hardest verses in the New Testament to translate. No Old Testament verse says exactly these words, so James may be summarising a theme of Scripture. Readings include: (1) God jealously longs for the spirit he made to live in us (God, like a husband, wants his people wholly for himself); (2) the Holy Spirit whom God made to live in us yearns jealously over us; (3) the human spirit God placed in us tends towards envy. The BSB footnote shows the choice between ‘Spirit’ and ‘spirit’. The first two fit the context of spiritual adultery best, and most recent commentators prefer one of them.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL
J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

4.ctx: A string of commands, like a prophet calling God’s people to return.
4.mean: ‘Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.’ Coming back to God means real repentance: ‘Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.’ ‘Grieve, mourn, and weep.’ This is not a call to permanent gloom, but to take sin seriously instead of laughing it off. The promise: ‘Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.’ James then forbids slander: whoever judges a brother sets himself above God’s law, but ‘There is only one Lawgiver and Judge’.
4.big: Humble repentance brings people near to God, and he lifts them up.

src.l: J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

4.ctx: Addressed to travelling merchants, a familiar part of life in the Jewish diaspora.
4.mean: ‘Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.”’ James does not condemn business or planning. He condemns planning as though God did not exist. ‘You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.’ ‘Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.”’ And a sharp closing principle: ‘Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin.’
4.big: Make plans, but hold them humbly, under God’s will.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL

5.ctx: Written in the style of Old Testament prophets such as Amos. Withholding a labourer’s wages was expressly forbidden in the law (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Day labourers lived hand to mouth.
5.mean: ‘Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you.’ Their hoarded wealth is already rotting: clothes moth-eaten, gold and silver corroded, and the corrosion will testify against them. ‘Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.’ They have lived in luxury and ‘fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter’, like cattle feeding on the day they are killed. They have even condemned and murdered the righteous. This is aimed mainly at rich oppressors outside the church, but it is a warning to everyone about how money is gained and used.
5.big: God hears the cry of exploited workers, and wealth gained by injustice will testify against its owners.

src.l: Calvin, Commentaries on the Catholic Epistles (trans. Owen), CCEL
J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)

5.ctx: In Palestine, the autumn rains soften the ground for sowing and the spring rains ripen the crop. A farmer can do nothing but wait for them.
5.mean: ‘Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming.’ Like a farmer waiting for ‘the fall and spring rains’, believers wait for Christ’s return. ‘The Lord’s coming is near.’ ‘Look, the Judge is standing at the door!’ So they should not grumble against one another. James gives examples of patience: the prophets, and Job, whose perseverance ended in the Lord’s good outcome, because ‘The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.’ Then: ‘Above all, my brothers, do not swear’. Simply ‘let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no’, echoing Jesus (Matthew 5:34–37).
5.big: Believers wait patiently for Christ’s return, trusting the compassion of God.
5.diff: Oaths (verse 12). Some Christians, especially in the Anabaptist tradition (Mennonites, and also Quakers), take this as forbidding all oaths. The Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession of 1527 says Christ ‘prohibits all swearing to his people, whether true or false’. Most churches read James and Jesus as forbidding the casual, careless or evasive oaths common at the time, and allow solemn oaths, such as in court. The Westminster Confession says a lawful oath ‘is warranted by the Word of God, under the new testament as well as under the old’. All agree on James’s point: a Christian’s plain word should be completely reliable.

src.l: J. A. Motyer, The Message of James, Bible Speaks Today (IVP)
‘Schleitheim Confession’, Global Anabaptist Mennonite Encyclopedia Online
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text), ch. 22 and 17

5.ctx: ‘Elders’ were the recognised leaders of each congregation. Oil was used both as medicine (Luke 10:34) and as a sign of being set apart for God.
5.mean: James covers every situation with prayer: ‘Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises. Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.’ The power is in the Lord, not the oil: ‘the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.’ Not all sickness comes from sin, but where it does, there is forgiveness. ‘Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.’ Elijah proves it: he was ‘a man just like us’, yet his prayers stopped the rain and brought it back.
5.big: In sickness and in sin, the church turns to God together in faith-filled prayer.
5.diff: The anointing. Some take the oil as medicine, used with prayer. Most see it as a sign, setting the sick person before the Lord. Calvin thought the gift of healing was temporary: ‘the sign of it ought not to be deemed perpetual.’ Wesley, by contrast, thought this gift ‘seems to have been designed to remain always’. Many churches today, including Pentecostal and charismatic churches and some Reformed churches, practise anointing with prayer for healing. Catholic teaching sees here the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, quoting this passage (Catechism 1510), given by a priest to those who are seriously ill or elderly. Orthodox churches likewise anoint the sick in the sacrament called Holy Unction (in Greek euchelaion, ‘prayer-oil’). Many Protestant commentators, such as Motyer, argue that James describes elders praying for healing and restoration to life, not a preparation for death and not a means of forgiveness through the oil. Promise or principle? Christians also differ on whether verse 15 promises healing whenever there is faith, or describes what God normally does in answer to prayer, while healing ultimately belongs to his will (compare 2 Corinthians 12:7–9). The final ‘raising up’ of every believer is the resurrection. Confession (verse 16) is ‘to each other’. Wesley noted that James does not say ‘to the elders’. Catholic and Orthodox churches also practise confession to a priest.
