4.ctx: Jewish tradition often linked Abraham’s blessing to his faithfulness in keeping God’s commands. Paul points out that the promise came long before the law was given.
4.mean: The promise that Abraham would inherit the world came ‘through the righteousness that comes by faith’, not through the law. If it depended on law, faith would be pointless, because the law brings wrath. ‘Therefore the promise comes by faith, so that it may rest on grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring.’ Grace makes the promise secure, because it rests on God’s faithfulness, not ours. Abraham’s faith is a model. Against all hope, he believed. He faced the fact that his body was as good as dead, at about a hundred years old, and that Sarah’s womb was dead too. Yet he did not waver, ‘being fully persuaded that God was able to do what he had promised’. His faith was not in his own faith, but in the God ‘who gives life to the dead’. And it was written for us, who believe in the God who raised Jesus, who ‘was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification’.
4.big: Believers share Abraham’s faith in the God who gives life to the dead, and so share his blessing.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

5.ctx: Having shown how believers are justified (chapters 3–4), Paul turns in chapters 5–8 to what justification brings and how secure it is.
5.mean: ‘Since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.’ This is not first a feeling of peace but a changed relationship: the war between God and the sinner is over. Through Christ we have gained access into this grace in which we now stand, and we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. More than that, we rejoice in our sufferings. Suffering produces perseverance, perseverance produces character, and character produces hope. This hope will not disappoint us. The reason is not that we are strong, but ‘because God has poured out his love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit’.
5.big: Justification brings peace with God and a hope that suffering cannot destroy, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts.
5.diff: Some early manuscripts read ‘let us have peace’ (a call) rather than ‘we have peace’ (a fact). The two Greek words differed by one letter and sounded alike. Most translations and commentators prefer ‘we have’, which fits Paul’s argument that peace is the result of justification.

5.ctx: Paul explains the depth of God’s love shown at the cross.
5.mean: ‘At just the right time, while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly.’ Paul draws the contrast with human love. Rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die. ‘But God proves his love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.’ Then comes an argument from the greater to the lesser. If God reconciled us while we were his enemies, by the death of his Son, ‘how much more’, now that we are reconciled, will we be saved through his life. The hardest part, dealing with our guilt, is already done; our final salvation is safe in the hands of a living Saviour.
5.big: God loved his enemies enough to send his Son to die for them, which is why believers can be sure of their final salvation.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

5.h: Death in Adam, Life in Christ
5.ctx: One of the most theologically significant passages in the New Testament. Paul steps back to the beginning of the human story to show that what Christ has done is as wide as what Adam did, and wider.
5.mean: ‘Just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.’ Paul breaks off his sentence (verses 13–14) to note that death reigned even before the law of Moses: from Adam to Moses people died, though there was no written law to break. Adam, he says, was ‘a pattern of the one to come’. Then the comparison runs, again and again, ‘just as… so also’, but always with the gift exceeding the trespass. One trespass brought condemnation to all people; one act of righteousness brings justification and life to all people. ‘Through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners’; through the obedience of the one, the many will be made righteous. Two men stand at the head of two humanities, and every person belongs to one or the other. The law came in to increase the trespass, ‘but where sin increased, grace increased all the more’. Sin reigned in death; now grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ.
5.big: Christ undoes, and far more than undoes, what Adam’s sin brought on the human race.
5.diff:
‘Because all sinned’ (verse 12) translates a disputed Greek phrase, eph’ hō. The Latin Bible that Augustine read rendered it ‘in whom all sinned’, meaning all sinned in Adam, and that reading shaped Western teaching on original sin. Most modern scholars read it as ‘because all sinned’. Many, such as Byrne and Cranfield, see both Adam’s sin and each person’s own sin as causes of death; Fitzmyer and Schreiner read it as ‘with the result that all sinned’.

How does Adam’s sin affect us? Reformed: Adam acted as the representative head of humanity, so his guilt is counted to all his descendants and his corrupted nature is passed on, just as Christ’s righteousness is counted to his people (Westminster Confession 6.3). Catholic: original sin is ‘contracted’, not ‘committed’; it is the loss of original holiness and a wounded nature, and it is taken away in baptism (Catechism 404–405). Orthodox: humanity inherits death and a corrupted nature from Adam (‘ancestral sin’), but not Adam’s personal guilt. Arminian: fallen nature is corrupted so that no one can turn to God without grace (Remonstrance, art. 3); Arminians differ over whether Adam’s guilt is counted to his descendants. On the historical Adam, most evangelical scholars hold that Paul’s exact parallel with Christ treats Adam as a real individual.

6.h: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
6.ctx: Paul answers the objection his teaching on grace invites (compare 3:8): if grace increases where sin increases, why not sin more?
6.mean: ‘Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?’ Paul’s answer is union with Christ. Everyone baptised into Christ Jesus was baptised into his death. We were buried with him, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead, we too may walk in newness of life. ‘Our old self was crucified with him’: the person we were in Adam has died with Christ, so that the body ruled by sin might be done away with, and we are no longer slaves to sin. So ‘count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus’. This is not pretending, but believing what God says is true and acting on it. Do not offer the parts of your body to sin, but to God. ‘For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace.’ Grace is not a licence to sin; it is the end of sin’s right to rule.
6.big: Grace does not encourage sin; union with Christ in his death and resurrection breaks sin’s rule.
6.diff: Christians differ over what baptism does. For Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians it is a means through which God actually unites a person to Christ and gives new life. For most Reformed, Anglican and other Protestant Christians it is the God-given sign and seal of that union, received by faith. Baptists and others hold that it is for believers only, by immersion, and some see a picture of burial and resurrection in that mode. Paul’s point here, which all affirm, is that belonging to Christ means sharing his death and new life.

6.ctx: Paul uses the image of slavery, familiar in a city where a large proportion of the population were slaves or former slaves.
6.mean: ‘Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not!’ Everyone serves someone: ‘you are slaves to the one you obey’, either sin, which leads to death, or obedience, which leads to righteousness. Paul apologises for the human analogy, but it makes the point. They once offered their bodies to impurity; now they have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, and the fruit is holiness, ending in eternal life. The chapter ends with one of the best-known verses in the Bible: ‘For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.’ Death is a wage, earned. Life is a gift, given.
6.big: Everyone serves a master; sin pays wages of death, but God gives eternal life as a free gift in Christ.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

7.ctx: Paul explains how believers now relate to the law of Moses, using marriage law as an illustration.
7.mean: The law has authority over a person only as long as he lives. A married woman is bound to her husband while he lives, but if he dies she is free to marry another. In the same way, ‘you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another’, the risen Christ, and bear fruit for God. When we lived in the flesh, the law actually aroused sinful passions. Now, released, we serve ‘in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code’.
7.big: Believers are released from the law’s authority to belong to the risen Christ and serve by the Spirit.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

7.ctx: Paul guards against the conclusion that, since the law aroused sin, the law itself is sinful.
7.mean: ‘Is the law sin? Certainly not!’ Paul would not have known what sin was except through the law. He would not have known what coveting was if the law had not said, ‘Do not covet.’ Sin seized the opportunity and produced every kind of covetous desire. The commandment that was meant to bring life brought death, because sin used it to deceive and kill. The problem is not the law but the sin that hijacks it. ‘So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.’
7.big: The law is good; the problem is sin, which uses the law to provoke and expose itself.
7.diff: Who is the ‘I’ in verses 7–13? Some take it as Paul’s own experience as a boy coming under the law. Others take it as Adam (the one command in Eden, and sin deceiving), or Israel at Sinai (Moo), with Paul speaking for the group.

src.l: D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

7.ctx: Paul explains how the good law became an instrument of death. He switches to the present tense and the first person, which is why this passage has been read so differently.
7.mean: ‘We know that the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin.’ What follows is one of the most honest descriptions of moral struggle ever written. ‘I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do.’ The ‘I’ agrees that the law is good and wants to do right, but finds ‘another law’ at work, waging war against the law of his mind and taking him captive. Paul does not excuse himself: it is ‘sin living in me’, but it is still in me. The cry breaks out: ‘What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?’ And at once the answer: ‘Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!’ Chapter 8 will unfold that answer.
7.big: Knowing what is right is not the same as having power to do it; deliverance comes only through Christ.
7.diff: Christians have long divided over who is speaking. (1) A mature Christian, still fighting indwelling sin: Augustine (in his later writings), Luther, Calvin, and many Reformed interpreters. They point to the present tense, the delight in God’s law (verse 22), and the honest experience of believers. (2) A person without the Spirit, under the law: many early Greek fathers, Wesley, and many modern scholars. They point to ‘sold as a slave to sin’ (verse 14), which contradicts 6:17–18, and to the absence of the Spirit, who fills chapter 8. (3) Israel, or humanity, under the law, with Paul speaking representatively (Moo, Dunn and others in varied forms). Schreiner concludes there is truth in more than one view. The first reading has comforted many Christians who find sin still at war in them. The second guards against settling for defeat when the Spirit gives real victory.

8.ctx: The high point of the letter, and one of the most loved chapters in the Bible. The Holy Spirit, barely mentioned in chapter 7, appears around twenty times here.
8.mean: ‘Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.’ The reason follows: ‘the law of the Spirit of life’ has set us free from the law of sin and death. Then Paul explains how. ‘What the law was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin. He thus condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us.’ Sin was condemned in Christ’s flesh, so there is no condemnation left for us. Now two ways of life are set side by side. The mind set on the flesh is death and hostile to God; the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. ‘If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.’ If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus lives in you, he will give life to your mortal bodies too.
8.big: Because sin was condemned in Christ, those in him face no condemnation, and the Spirit gives them new life.
8.diff: ‘The likeness of sinful man’ (verse 3): Paul chooses his words carefully. Christ took real human flesh, but not sinful flesh, so ‘likeness’ guards against saying he sinned without denying that he was fully human. This is part of the church’s teaching on the two natures (see Mark 4:35). In verse 9 the Spirit is called both ‘the Spirit of God’ and ‘the Spirit of Christ’, one of the texts behind the doctrine of the Trinity.

8.ctx: In Roman law an adopted son had full legal rights as heir. Adoption was often used by families without natural sons to secure an inheritance.
8.mean: We owe the flesh nothing. ‘If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.’ Holiness is not passive. ‘For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.’ You did not receive a spirit of slavery that leads you back into fear, but ‘the Spirit of adoption’, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’ Abba is the word Jesus used. The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. If children, then heirs, ‘heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ’, if indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him.
8.big: The Spirit assures believers they are God’s adopted children and heirs with Christ, sharing his sufferings now and his glory later.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

8.ctx: Paul sets present suffering in the light of future glory. Genesis 3:17 describes the ground cursed because of human sin; Paul pictures creation waiting to share in humanity’s redemption.
8.mean: ‘I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us.’ Creation itself waits eagerly. It was subjected to futility, not by its own choice, but in hope that it will be set free from its bondage to decay. The whole creation groans as in childbirth: pain, but pain that will give way to new life. We groan too, as we wait for our adoption, ‘the redemption of our bodies’. Christian hope is not escape from the body or the world, but their renewal. And the Spirit groans with us. ‘We do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words.’
8.big: Present suffering is real, but it is the groaning of a new creation being born, and the Spirit prays for us in it.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

8.ctx: One of the best known and most misused verses in Scripture, followed by what is often called ‘the golden chain’ of salvation.
8.mean: ‘We know that God works all things together for the good of those who love him, who are called according to his purpose.’ This is not a promise that everything is good, or that things will turn out as we would like. It is a promise that God is at work in every circumstance for a particular good, defined in the next verse: becoming like Christ. Then comes the chain: ‘For those God foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son… and those he predestined, he also called; those he called, he also justified; those he justified, he also glorified.’ Each link holds; no one drops out between them. Even ‘glorified’, still future, is in the past tense, so certain is it. ‘If God is for us, who can be against us?’ He did not spare his own Son, so he will give us all things with him. Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; Christ died, was raised, and intercedes for us.
8.big: God’s purpose for his people runs unbroken from before time to final glory, and he works everything toward it.
8.diff: ‘Foreknew’ (verse 29). Reformed theology reads it as God’s prior, loving choice of particular people. In the Bible to ‘know’ often means to set one’s love on someone (Amos 3:2), and Paul says God foreknew persons, not their faith. So predestination does not rest on anything foreseen in them (Westminster Confession 3.5), and all who are called and justified will be glorified. Arminian theology reads it as God’s knowledge beforehand of who would freely believe; he predestines those he foresees will believe to become like Christ (Remonstrance, art. 1). Some read the chain corporately, as God’s plan for his people as a whole. On perseverance, Arminians generally hold that the chain describes God’s purpose for those who continue in faith; Reformed theology sees in it God’s guarantee that they will.

8.ctx: The conclusion of the first eight chapters, in a series of rising questions and answers.
8.mean: ‘Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?’ These were not theoretical; Paul had faced most of them (2 Corinthians 11). He quotes Psalm 44:22: ‘For your sake we face death all day long.’ Suffering is not a sign that God’s love has failed; it has always been the lot of his people. ‘No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.’ Then the great conclusion: ‘neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.’
8.big: Nothing in all creation can separate God’s people from his love in Christ.
8.diff: Does ‘nothing’ include the believer’s own choices? Reformed interpreters say yes: the list is deliberately all-inclusive (‘anything else in all creation’), and God keeps his people from finally falling away. Arminian interpreters agree that no outside power can separate a believer from God’s love, but hold that the passage does not address whether a believer can freely turn away from Christ (compare 11:22). Both agree that it is a promise for those who are in Christ.

9.ctx: Paul turns to the question of Israel, which fills chapters 9–11. If God’s promises are sure (8:28–39), why have most of Israel not believed in their own Messiah? Has God’s word failed?
9.mean: Paul begins not with argument but with grief. ‘I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.’ He could wish himself cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his own people, an echo of Moses offering himself for Israel (Exodus 32:32). He lists their privileges: the adoption as sons, the divine glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the temple worship, the promises, and the patriarchs. And from them, according to his human descent, comes the Christ, ‘who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.’ The hard doctrine that follows is written by a man in tears.
9.big: Israel’s unbelief grieves Paul deeply, because to Israel belong all God’s privileges, including the Messiah himself.
9.diff: Verse 5 can be punctuated to call Christ ‘God over all’ (as the BSB does), or with a full stop after ‘Christ’, making the rest a separate praise of God the Father. The early church fathers, such as Origen, read it of Christ, and so do many modern scholars, such as Fitzmyer. Others, such as Dunn and Fee, prefer the separate praise of God the Father. Either way, Paul elsewhere gives Christ the honour and titles of God (for example Philippians 2:6–11).

src.l: D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

9.ctx: Paul’s first answer: God’s word has not failed, because God’s promises were never made to every physical descendant of Abraham.
9.mean: ‘It is not as though God’s word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.’ Paul proves it from Genesis. Abraham had two sons, but the promise ran through Isaac, not Ishmael. Isaac and Rebecca had twins, and before they were born, or had done anything good or bad, God said, ‘The older will serve the younger.’ That was ‘in order that God’s plan of election might stand, not by works but by him who calls’. Malachi sums it up: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’, a Hebrew way of expressing choice and preference rather than emotional hatred.
9.big: God’s word has not failed, because his promises always rested on his free choice, not on human descent or human merit.
9.diff: See the note on 9:14 for the main interpretations of Romans 9.

9.ctx: Paul anticipates the obvious objection to verses 6–13.
9.mean: ‘What then shall we say? Is God unjust? Certainly not!’ Paul answers from Scripture. To Moses God said, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.’ That was said after the golden calf, when Israel deserved nothing. ‘So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy.’ Mercy by definition cannot be demanded. To Pharaoh the Scripture says, ‘I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.’ ‘Therefore God has mercy on whom he wants to have mercy, and he hardens whom he wants to harden.’
9.big: God is not unjust: mercy is his to give freely, and no one has a claim on it.
9.diff:
Romans 9 is the passage Christians argue over most. There are three main readings.
1. Reformed: individual, unconditional election. Paul is explaining why some individuals believe and others do not. God chooses individuals for salvation according to his own purpose, not because of anything foreseen in them, and passes over others (Westminster Confession 3.5–7; Canons of Dort, 1). Scholars such as Schreiner, Moo and John Piper argue that the language of mercy and hardening, the ‘vessels’ of verses 22–23, and the link to individual Israelites in chapter 11 all point to individual salvation.
2. National or historical election. Paul is speaking of God’s choice of peoples and their roles in his plan, not the eternal destiny of individuals. Jacob and Esau stand for Israel and Edom (Genesis 25:23; Malachi 1:2–3), and Pharaoh is raised up for a role in the exodus. John Wesley read verses 11–13 this way: it ‘does not relate to the person of Jacob or Esau’, nor ‘to the eternal state either of them or their posterity’. Commentators such as Cranfield and Witherington also see God’s purposes in history in view more than individual salvation.
3. Corporate election in Christ. God chooses a people, now defined by faith in Christ rather than by descent, and individuals join that chosen people by faith. Many Arminian scholars hold this view, which links to 9:30–10:13, where faith decides who belongs.
On hardening: some (such as Schreiner) argue God’s hardening of Pharaoh comes first and underlies Pharaoh’s own; others (such as Morris) note that Pharaoh also hardened himself, and see God confirming a choice Pharaoh had made. Everyone agrees that Paul defends God’s freedom and justice, and that he does so in anguish, not coldness (9:1–3).

9.ctx: The next objection: if God hardens whom he wills, how can he still blame anyone?
9.mean: ‘Who can resist his will?’ Paul’s first reply is not an explanation but a rebuke of the attitude behind the question: ‘But who are you, O man, to talk back to God?’ He uses the Old Testament picture of the potter (Isaiah 29:16; 45:9; Jeremiah 18). Does the potter not have the right to make from the same lump one vessel for honour and another for common use? Then a carefully worded question: what if God, wanting to show his wrath and power, ‘bore with great patience the vessels of his wrath, prepared for destruction’, in order to make known the riches of his glory to the vessels of his mercy, ‘whom he prepared in advance for glory’? These include ‘us, whom he has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles’. Hosea and Isaiah are quoted. God calls ‘not my people’ his people, and saves a remnant of Israel.
9.big: God is the Creator, not one of the creatures who can be called to account; and he has shown great patience as well as justice.
9.diff: Notice the wording of verses 22–23. The vessels of mercy are ones God ‘prepared in advance’; the vessels of wrath are ‘prepared for destruction’, without saying who prepared them, and God ‘bore with great patience’ with them. Reformed interpreters see God’s sovereign purpose in both, while not making God the author of sin (Westminster Confession 3.1). Arminian interpreters, following Wesley, see people fitting themselves for destruction ‘by their own wilful and final impenitence’. The interpretations of 9:14 apply here too.

9.ctx: Having explained Israel’s unbelief from God’s side, Paul now looks at it from the human side, and holds Israel responsible.
9.mean: Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith. Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, has not attained it. Why? ‘Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works.’ They stumbled over the stumbling stone. Quoting Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16, Paul says God laid in Zion a stone that makes people stumble, ‘and the one who believes in him will never be put to shame’. The stone is Christ. Paul holds together, without resolving it for us, God’s sovereign choice (9:6–29) and human responsibility (9:30–10:21).
9.big: Israel stumbled by seeking righteousness through works instead of receiving it by faith in Christ.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

10.ctx: Paul continues to explain Israel’s unbelief, while still praying for their salvation.
10.mean: ‘My heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation.’ They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. Not knowing the righteousness that comes from God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s. ‘For Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes.’ Paul then turns Deuteronomy 30 on its head. You need not climb to heaven to bring Christ down, or go down into the abyss to bring him up; the word is near you. ‘If you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.’ This is one of the earliest Christian confessions. ‘Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’ That universal promise drives mission. How can they call on one they have not believed in, believe in one they have not heard of, or hear without someone preaching? ‘Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.’
10.big: Salvation comes to anyone, Jew or Gentile, who confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him, which is why the message must be preached.
10.diff: ‘Christ is the end of the law’ (verse 4): the Greek telos can mean ‘end’ (termination) or ‘goal’. Christ may be the end of the law as a way to righteousness, the goal to which the law always pointed, or both. Many commentators hold both. In verse 13 Paul applies Joel 2:32, where ‘the Lord’ is the LORD, Israel’s God, to Jesus, a striking sign of how the first Christians understood who Jesus is.

11.ctx: Paul answers the question his argument has raised: has God rejected his people? He answers first from his own life as a believing Jew.
11.mean: ‘Did God reject his people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself.’ As in Elijah’s day, when the prophet thought he alone was left and God had kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, ‘at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace’. ‘And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.’ What Israel sought it did not obtain, but the elect did; the rest were hardened, as the Scriptures foretold.
11.big: God has not abandoned Israel; a remnant remains, chosen by grace.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

11.ctx: Paul uses the image of an olive tree, a common picture of Israel in the Old Testament (Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6), with some natural branches broken off and wild branches grafted in.
11.mean: Did Israel stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not! Through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous. And if their loss means riches for the world, ‘how much greater riches will their fullness bring!’ Paul speaks directly to Gentile believers. Some of the natural branches were broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root. Do not boast: ‘you do not support the root, but the root supports you’. They were broken off because of unbelief; you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but afraid. ‘Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God.’ And God is able to graft the natural branches back in, much more easily than the wild ones.
11.big: Gentile believers share Israel’s root by grace alone and have no grounds for pride.
11.diff: ‘Otherwise you also will be cut off’ (verse 22) is discussed in relation to perseverance. Reformed interpreters generally read it as addressed to Gentiles as a group, or as a real warning that God uses to keep true believers faithful. Arminian interpreters see a real possibility of an individual believer falling away through unbelief. Both agree the warning is to be taken seriously and that standing is by faith alone. This passage has also been an important rebuke to Christian anti-Jewish attitudes through history: Gentile Christians are guests on Israel’s tree.

11.ctx: Paul reveals a ‘mystery’, in the New Testament something previously hidden and now made known by God, about Israel’s future. It is addressed especially to Gentile believers tempted to look down on Israel.
11.mean: ‘A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved.’ Isaiah and Jeremiah are quoted: the Deliverer will come from Zion and remove godlessness from Jacob, when God takes away their sins. Israel stands in a double relationship to God. ‘Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs. For God’s gifts and his call are irrevocable.’ God has consigned everyone to disobedience, Jew and Gentile alike, ‘so that he may have mercy on everyone’.
11.big: God’s purposes for Israel are not finished, because his gifts and his calling cannot be revoked.
11.diff: ‘All Israel will be saved’ has three main readings. (1) A large-scale future turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return. This was held by many Puritans and Reformed theologians such as Charles Hodge, by most premillennial interpreters, and by many modern scholars across traditions, including Cranfield, Moo and Schreiner. (2) The full number of elect Jews saved throughout history, alongside the Gentiles (Herman Bavinck, and others in the Reformed tradition). (3) The whole people of God, Jew and Gentile together (Calvin, and N. T. Wright). Many commentators think the contrast with ‘hardening in part’ and ‘the full number of the Gentiles’ makes the first the most natural. None of the readings suggests Jewish people are saved apart from Christ, who is ‘the Deliverer’.

11.ctx: Paul breaks into praise after the hardest chapters of the letter.
11.mean: ‘O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and untraceable his ways!’ Quoting Isaiah 40:13 and Job 41:11, Paul asks, ‘Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?’ ‘Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?’ No one. ‘For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever! Amen.’ The right response to God’s purposes is not a solved puzzle but worship.
11.big: The right response to God’s sovereign purposes is not a solved puzzle but worship.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

12.ctx: The turn to practical living. ‘Therefore’ connects everything that follows to the mercies of God set out in chapters 1–11.
12.mean: ‘I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.’ Under the old covenant, sacrifices died. Now the whole of a believer’s life, body included, is offered to God, and it stays alive. ‘Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.’ Change works from the inside out. Then Paul applies it to life in the church. Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought. We are one body with many members and different gifts, each given by grace. Use them: prophecy in proportion to faith, service, teaching, encouraging, giving generously, leading diligently, showing mercy cheerfully.
12.big: In response to God’s mercy, believers offer their whole lives as worship and serve one another with their different gifts.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

12.ctx: A series of short commands on life together. Verses 10–13 are among the passages Community of Brothers takes as a description of brotherhood.
12.mean: ‘Love must be sincere.’ Without pretence. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good. Paul then shows what sincere love looks like in the church. Be devoted to one another in brotherly love; outdo yourselves in honouring one another. Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervour, serving the Lord. Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer. Share with the saints who are in need. Practise hospitality: the Greek means to pursue it, not wait for it to happen.
12.big: Genuine love shows itself in honour, zeal, patience, prayer and open homes among believers.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

12.ctx: Paul turns to relationships with those outside the church, including enemies.
12.mean: ‘Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.’ This is an echo of Jesus’ own teaching (Luke 6:28). Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. Live in harmony, do not be proud, and associate with the lowly. Do not repay anyone evil for evil. ‘If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone.’ Paul admits it is not always possible, but make sure the failure is not yours. Do not avenge yourselves, but leave room for God’s wrath, since vengeance belongs to him. Instead, ‘if your enemy is hungry, feed him’. ‘Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.’
12.big: Believers overcome evil not by revenge but by doing good, leaving justice to God.
12.diff: ‘Heap burning coals on his head’ (verse 20, quoting Proverbs 25:22) is usually understood as producing shame and remorse that may lead to repentance, not as a refined form of revenge. Leaving vengeance to God (verse 19) does not rule out the state’s role in justice, which Paul turns to in 13:4.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

13.ctx: Paul writes under the emperor Nero, early in his reign, before the persecution of Christians began.
13.mean: ‘Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God.’ Even pagan rulers hold power because God has granted it. Rulers are ‘God’s servant for your good’. They hold the sword to punish wrongdoing and restrain evil, which is why Christians, who have just been told not to take revenge (12:19), should support legitimate justice. Submission is not only out of fear of punishment but ‘for the sake of conscience’. ‘This is also why you pay taxes… Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due.’
13.big: Civil government is ordained by God for the common good, and believers should respect and support it.
13.diff: Christians differ over the limits of this instruction. The New Testament itself shows that when authorities command what God forbids, ‘we must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29), and Revelation 13 portrays a state that has become beastly. Paul describes what government is for; he does not say every ruler fulfils it. How this applies to unjust governments, protest and resistance has been argued throughout church history. Positions range from Lutheran caution about resistance, to the Reformed tradition of resistance led by lesser magistrates, to Anabaptist non-resistance.

b: Romans was written early in Nero’s reign (AD 54–68), years before his persecution of Christians after the fire of Rome in AD 64. The historian Tacitus records that in AD 58 there were persistent public complaints in Rome about the abuses of the private companies that collected indirect taxes. Nero even considered abolishing those taxes, before his advisers talked him out of it and he published new rules instead.

Paul distinguishes ‘taxes’ and ‘revenue’ (13:7), the Greek terms for direct tribute and indirect dues. This background may help explain why he addresses tax-paying so specifically: resentment over taxes was in the air in Rome when the letter arrived.

13.ctx: After paying what is owed to governing authorities, Paul turns to the one debt that can never be paid off.
13.mean: ‘Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love, for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.’ The commandments against adultery, murder, theft and coveting are summed up in one: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’. Love does no wrong to a neighbour; therefore love is the fulfilment of the law. This does not set the commandments aside. It shows what they were always for.
13.big: Love for neighbour fulfils everything the law requires in our dealings with others.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

13.ctx: The early church lived in expectation of Christ’s return. Paul uses the picture of dawn approaching after a long night.
13.mean: ‘The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber, for our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed.’ ‘The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near.’ So lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armour of light. Live decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, sexual immorality and debauchery, quarrelling and jealousy. ‘Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh.’
13.big: Because Christ’s return draws nearer every day, believers should live as people of the day.
13.diff: These verses (13–14) are the passage Augustine read in a garden in Milan in AD 386 when he was converted (Confessions 8.12). See Romans in church history above.

src.l: Augustine, Confessions 8.12 (NPNF), New Advent

14.ctx: The Roman church had disagreements, probably between Jewish and Gentile believers, over food laws and holy days (see The church in Rome above).
14.mean: ‘Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions.’ One person’s faith allows him to eat anything; another, ‘weak’, eats only vegetables. One regards one day as more sacred than another; another considers every day alike. Paul’s instruction cuts both ways. The one who eats must not despise the one who does not, and the one who abstains must not judge the one who eats, ‘for God has accepted him’. ‘Who are you to judge someone else’s servant?’ Each should be fully convinced in his own mind, and each does what he does ‘to the Lord’. We will all stand before God’s judgment seat and give an account of ourselves, not of each other.
14.big: On disputable matters, believers must not despise or judge one another, since each answers to the Lord.
14.diff: Christians disagree about which issues count as ‘disputable matters’. Paul’s category covers practices neither commanded nor forbidden by the gospel, such as food, special days and, in 1 Corinthians 8–10, food offered to idols. It does not cover core doctrine (compare Galatians 1:8–9) or clear moral teaching (compare 1 Corinthians 5). The ‘weak’ here are not weaker Christians in general, but believers whose conscience does not yet allow them a freedom that others enjoy.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL
D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

14.ctx: Paul turns from not judging to not causing others to stumble.
14.mean: Resolve not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way. Paul is fully convinced that nothing is unclean in itself, but if someone regards something as unclean, it is unclean to him. If your brother is distressed by what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. ‘Do not by your eating destroy your brother, for whom Christ died.’ ‘For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.’ So pursue what leads to peace and builds others up. Keep your convictions on such matters between yourself and God. ‘everything that is not from faith is sin’: to act against your own conscience is wrong, even if the thing itself is permitted.
14.big: Christian freedom is limited by love for fellow believers whose consciences are more tender.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

15.ctx: Continuing the instruction to ‘the strong’, who felt free to eat anything and ignore special days, and ‘the weak’, who kept food laws and holy days.
15.mean: ‘We who are strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak and not to please ourselves.’ Each should please his neighbour for his good, to build him up, ‘for even Christ did not please himself’. Paul adds that the Scriptures were written to teach us, so that through endurance and encouragement we might have hope. His prayer (verses 5–6) is that God would give them a spirit of unity among themselves as they follow Christ, ‘so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ’. Verses 5–7 are among the passages Community of Brothers returns to.
15.big: Following Christ’s example, believers put others first so that the church glorifies God together.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

15.h: Christ the Servant of Jews and Gentiles
15.ctx: The practical section reaches its theological conclusion, linking the call to welcome one another with Christ’s ministry to Jews and Gentiles alike.
15.mean: ‘Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God.’ Christ became a servant of the circumcised to confirm God’s promises to the patriarchs, and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. Paul quotes four Old Testament passages, from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, showing that Gentiles praising God alongside Israel was always the plan. He ends with a blessing: ‘Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.’
15.big: Christ welcomed Jews and Gentiles alike, so his people must welcome one another.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

15.h: Paul the Minister to the Gentiles
15.ctx: Paul explains why he has written so boldly to a church he did not found.
15.mean: Paul is convinced they are full of goodness and able to instruct one another. He has written boldly as a reminder, because of the grace given him to be ‘a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles’. He describes his ministry in priestly terms: the Gentiles themselves are his offering to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Christ has worked through him ‘by the power of signs and wonders’, so that from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, roughly modern Albania and Croatia, he has fully proclaimed the gospel. His ambition has been to preach where Christ was not known, so as not to build on someone else’s foundation.
15.big: Paul’s ambition is to take the gospel where Christ is not yet known.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

15.ctx: Paul is about to take a collection from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor believers in Jerusalem.
15.mean: Now that there is no more room for him to work in these regions, Paul plans to visit Rome on his way to Spain, the western edge of the known world, and hopes the Romans will help him on his way. First, though, he must take the collection to Jerusalem. The Gentiles have shared in the Jews’ spiritual blessings, so they owe it to them to share material blessings. He asks them to join his struggle by praying that he may be rescued from unbelievers in Judea, that his service will be acceptable to the saints there, and that he may come to them with joy.
15.big: Paul makes bold plans for the gospel and holds them in dependence on prayer.
15.diff: Acts records that Paul did reach Rome, but as a prisoner, after his arrest in Jerusalem (Acts 21–28). Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain. Clement of Rome, writing around AD 96, says Paul reached the far limits of the West, which some take to mean Spain.

src.l: D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

16.ctx: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth, about 10 km from the city. Phoebe very probably carried the letter to Rome.
16.mean: Paul commends ‘our sister Phoebe’, ‘a servant of the church in Cenchrea’. The BSB footnote gives ‘deaconess’. He asks the Romans to welcome her ‘in a manner worthy of the saints’ and help her with anything she needs, ‘for she has been a great help to many people, including me’. The word behind ‘great help’ (prostatis) was used of a patron or benefactor. Phoebe was probably a woman of means who supported Paul’s work and hosted believers. Letters of introduction like this were how travellers in the ancient world found trustworthy hospitality.
16.big: The letter that has shaped the church for two thousand years was entrusted to a faithful woman who served her church.
16.diff: Was Phoebe a deacon in the sense of an office, or a servant of the church more generally? The Greek diakonos can mean either. Many commentators, such as Cranfield and Moo, think a recognised role is in view, though church offices were still developing. Others, such as Hendriksen, think it describes service, such as hospitality. Christians who agree on the meaning of the word still differ over its implications for women’s roles in church leadership today.

src.l: D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

16.ctx: Paul greets around twenty-six people by name, more than in any other letter, though he has never been to Rome. Many had probably met him on his travels.
16.mean: First come Priscilla and Aquila, Paul’s co-workers, who ‘risked their lives for me’ and now host a church in their house. They had been expelled from Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2), and by now they had returned. Then a long list follows: Epenetus, the first convert in Asia; Mary, who worked hard; ‘Andronicus and Junia, my fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners’, who were ‘outstanding among the apostles’ and in Christ before Paul; household groups, slaves and free, Jewish and Gentile names; and several women, including Tryphena, Tryphosa and Persis, who ‘worked hard in the Lord’. ‘Greet one another with a holy kiss.’ The church in Rome was not one congregation but a network of house churches, and Paul knows its people as people.
16.big: The early church was a network of named, valued men and women, slave and free, serving together.
16.diff: Junia (verse 7). The name in the Greek can be accented as the woman’s name Junia or a supposed man’s name Junias. Junia was a common Roman woman’s name, while no example of ‘Junias’ has been found. Early church writers such as Chrysostom took her as a woman, and that is now the consensus. The debated question is the phrase translated ‘outstanding among the apostles’ (BSB). It may mean they were notable apostles, in the broader sense of travelling missionaries (compare Acts 14:14; 2 Corinthians 8:23), as Dunn, Schreiner and many others hold. Or it may mean they were ‘well known to the apostles’, as Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace argued in a much-discussed study (2001). This verse is often cited in debates over women in ministry, and evangelical scholars on both sides of that debate hold each view.

src.l: D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

16.ctx: A brief, sharp warning near the end of the letter.
16.mean: ‘Watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Turn away from them.’ Such people serve their own appetites, not Christ, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the minds of the naive. Paul wants them ‘to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil’. Then a promise: ‘The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet’, an echo of the first promise of the gospel in Genesis 3:15.
16.big: Believers must guard the church’s unity and teaching against divisive people, trusting God’s coming victory over evil.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Romans (Calvin Translation Society), CCEL

16.ctx: Greetings from those with Paul in Corinth.
16.mean: Timothy sends greetings, with several of Paul’s relatives. Then a pleasant surprise: ‘I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.’ Paul dictated his letters to a secretary, as was common. Gaius, who hosts Paul and the whole church, sends greetings, as do Quartus and ‘Erastus, the city treasurer’. The gospel had reached people of every rank, from a secretary to a senior city official.
16.big: The gospel had reached people of every rank, from secretaries to city officials.
16.diff: Verse 24 (‘May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.’) is absent from the oldest manuscripts and is placed in a footnote in the BSB.

b: Excavations at Corinth uncovered a Latin inscription set in a paved square: ‘Erastus laid this pavement at his own expense, in appreciation of his appointment as aedile.’ An aedile was one of the city’s senior officials, responsible for public works and markets. Many scholars accept that this is the Erastus of Romans 16:23. If so, the Corinthian church included a man of real wealth and civic standing.

Others are more cautious. Paul calls Erastus ‘city treasurer’ (oikonomos), which may not be the same office as aedile. The inscription’s exact date is discussed. And Erastus was not a rare name. The identification is possible and attractive, but not certain.

src.l: A. F. Walls, ‘Erastus’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
A. F. Walls, ‘Erastus’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

16.ctx: The closing doxology returns to themes from the opening of the letter: the gospel, promised in the prophets, bringing about the obedience of faith among all nations.
16.mean: ‘Now to him who is able to strengthen you by my gospel and by the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets by the command of the eternal God, in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith: to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.’ The letter ends where it began (1:1–5): the gospel, promised long ago, now made known to all nations, for God’s glory.
16.big: The letter ends where it began: the gospel, promised long ago, now made known to all nations, for God’s glory.
16.diff: The doxology appears in different places in different manuscripts (after chapter 14, 15 or 16), and in a few it is missing. This has led to discussion of how the letter circulated in the early church, perhaps in a shorter form. Most scholars accept the doxology as part of Romans as we have it, and its themes closely match 1:1–5.

src.l: D. R. Brown & D. Mangum, Romans, Logos Research Commentaries (Lexham): surveys Barrett, Byrne, Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Jewett, Kruse, Moo, Schreiner, Witherington and others

1.ctx: Peter writes, probably from Rome ('Babylon', 5:13) in the early 60s, to Christians scattered across five provinces of what is now Turkey. Many were Gentiles facing hostility for their new faith.
1.mean: Peter greets them as elect exiles of the dispersion, chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling with his blood. Father, Spirit and Son are all named in the opening sentence.
1.big: Believers are exiles in this world but chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit and cleansed by the Son.
1.diff: Some scholars think a later follower wrote in Peter's name, pointing to the polished Greek; others note that Silvanus helped write it (5:12), which could explain the style. The traditional view of Petrine authorship remains widely held.

1.ctx: A great opening blessing, one long sentence in the Greek, like Ephesians 1:3–14.
1.mean: Peter says God has caused them to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, to an inheritance that is imperishable, kept in heaven for them, who by God's power are being guarded through faith. For a little while they may be grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of their faith may result in praise at Christ's revelation. Though they have not seen him, they love him and rejoice with joy inexpressible. The prophets searched and enquired about this salvation.
1.big: Suffering believers have a living hope and an inheritance that God himself guards.
1.diff: Reformed interpreters see in verse 5 ('guarded through faith') both God's keeping power and the faith through which he keeps believers — part of the doctrine of perseverance.

1.ctx: The first practical instruction, grounded in the hope just described.
1.mean: Peter says to prepare their minds for action and set their hope fully on the grace coming at Christ's revelation. As obedient children, they must not be conformed to their former passions, but be holy in all their conduct, since it is written: you shall be holy, for I am holy. They were ransomed from their futile ways not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like a lamb without blemish, foreknown before the foundation of the world.
1.big: Believers are to be holy because the holy God ransomed them at the cost of Christ's blood.

1.ctx: Continuing the call to holiness, now focused on love within the church.
1.mean: Peter says having purified their souls by obedience to the truth, they should love one another earnestly from a pure heart, since they have been born again of imperishable seed, through the living and abiding word of God. All flesh is like grass, but the word of the Lord remains for ever (Isaiah 40:6–8).
1.big: New birth through God's enduring word produces sincere love among believers.

2.ctx: Peter draws on Old Testament images of a temple and of Israel as God's people, applying them to a largely Gentile church.
2.mean: Peter says to long for pure spiritual milk. Coming to Christ, a living stone rejected by men but chosen by God, they too are being built as living stones into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood. They are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, to proclaim the excellencies of him who called them out of darkness into his marvellous light.
2.big: The titles once given to Israel now belong to all who belong to Christ, the chosen cornerstone.
2.diff: The phrase 'royal priesthood' underlies the Reformation doctrine of the priesthood of all believers — every Christian has direct access to God through Christ.
2.h: The Living Stone and Chosen People

2.ctx: Instructions for living as exiles within a hostile society, beginning with civil authority.
2.mean: Peter says be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether the emperor or governors. Live as people who are free, not using freedom as a cover-up for evil, but as servants of God. Honour everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the emperor. Servants are to be subject to their masters, even the unjust.
2.big: Believers show their freedom by honourable conduct that silences critics.
2.diff: As at Romans 13, the limits of submission are discussed; Peter himself told the Sanhedrin 'we must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). Instructions to slaves regulate an existing institution rather than approve it.

2.ctx: The instruction to suffering servants leads into one of the richest passages about Christ's death.
2.mean: Peter says Christ suffered for them, leaving an example so they might follow in his steps. He committed no sin; when reviled, he did not revile in return. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed. You were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. Peter draws heavily on Isaiah 53.
2.big: Christ's suffering is both the pattern for believers to follow and the sacrifice that bore their sins.
2.diff: Reformed and evangelical theology reads verse 24 as a clear statement of substitution. 'By his wounds you have been healed' refers in context to spiritual healing from sin; whether it also promises physical healing now is debated, though Peter's own focus is on sin.

3.ctx: The household code continues with marriage. Many of these women had husbands who were not believers.
3.mean: Peter says wives should be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by their conduct. Their beauty should be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit. Husbands should live with their wives in an understanding way, showing honour, since they are heirs together of the grace of life, so that their prayers may not be hindered.
3.big: Christian marriage is marked by respect and honour on both sides, and can itself be a witness.
3.diff: As with Ephesians 5, Christians differ over how the call for wives to submit applies today, and over the phrase 'weaker vessel'. Peter's command that husbands honour their wives as fellow heirs of grace was striking in its setting.

3.ctx: A summary of the whole ethical section from 2:11, addressed now to everyone. Peter's readers were suffering insults and mistreatment from neighbours for their faith.
3.mean: Peter says all of them should have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but bless. He quotes Psalm 34: whoever desires to love life must keep his tongue from evil and seek peace.
3.big: Believers are called to bless even those who treat them badly.

3.ctx: Addressed to believers suffering unjustly. Christians were suspected of disloyalty and immorality because they withdrew from pagan festivals and emperor worship.
3.mean: Peter says even if they suffer for righteousness' sake, they will be blessed. In their hearts they should honour Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope in them — yet with gentleness and respect. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. He went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison. Baptism now saves, not as removing dirt, but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
3.big: Believers can answer for their hope with gentleness because Christ suffered once to bring them to God.
3.diff: Verse 15 is the verse apologetics takes its name from. Verses 18–22 are among the hardest in the New Testament. The 'spirits in prison' have been read as fallen angels, as the dead to whom Christ announced his victory, or as people of Noah's day to whom Christ preached through Noah. Verse 21 on baptism is read by some traditions as baptism conveying salvation, and by most Protestants as baptism signifying the salvation received by faith, as Peter's own clarification suggests.

4.ctx: Peter returns to the example of Christ's suffering from 3:18. Converts from paganism had left behind a social life of feasts, drinking and idol worship, and faced mockery for it.
4.mean: Peter says since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, living no longer for human passions but for the will of God. Former companions are surprised they no longer join in the same flood of debauchery. The end of all things is at hand, so be self-controlled for prayer, love one another earnestly, show hospitality without grumbling, and use every gift to serve one another, so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.
4.big: Living for God's will instead of old passions shows itself in prayer, love, hospitality and service.

4.ctx: Persecution was either happening or expected. Peter writes as it grew under Nero.
4.mean: Peter says do not be surprised at the fiery trial as though something strange were happening, but rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings. If insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed. Let no one suffer as a murderer or thief, but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed. Judgement begins at the household of God. Let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
4.big: Suffering for Christ is not a sign that something has gone wrong, but a share in his sufferings.

5.ctx: Peter addresses church leaders. Elders, also called overseers, led the local churches.
5.mean: Peter writes as a fellow elder and witness of Christ's sufferings. He tells elders to shepherd the flock of God, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly, not domineering but being examples. When the chief Shepherd appears, they will receive the unfading crown of glory.
5.big: Church leaders are under-shepherds who serve willingly and lead by example, answerable to Christ.

5.ctx: Instruction to the younger members, and then to everyone. Verse 5 quotes Proverbs 3:34, the same verse James quotes (James 4:6).
5.mean: Peter says the younger should be subject to the elders, and all should clothe themselves with humility, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves under God's mighty hand, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you. Be sober-minded; your adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion. Resist him, firm in your faith.
5.big: Humble dependence on God, who cares, is the way to face both anxiety and the devil.

5.ctx: The closing blessing and greetings. 'Babylon' is widely understood as a coded name for Rome.
5.mean: Peter says after they have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called them to his eternal glory in Christ, will restore, confirm, strengthen and establish them. He wrote through Silvanus, and sends greetings from the church in Babylon and from Mark, his son.
5.big: The God who called them will himself restore and establish them after their suffering.
5.diff: The mention of Mark supports the early tradition that Mark's Gospel draws on Peter's preaching.

1.ctx: Peter writes what he presents as his final letter, knowing his death is near (1:14). Its authorship has been more widely questioned than any other New Testament book.
1.mean: Peter greets those who have obtained a faith of equal standing by the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
1.big: Peter's greeting calls Jesus Christ both God and Saviour.
1.diff: Many scholars doubt Peter wrote this letter, citing its style and its apparent knowledge of Paul's letters as Scripture (3:16). Others, including many evangelical scholars, defend Petrine authorship, possibly with a different secretary. The church accepted it as Scripture after some hesitation. In verse 1 the Greek construction most naturally reads as one person, 'our God and Saviour', a direct statement of Christ's deity.

1.ctx: The letter's main positive teaching, against false teachers who treated grace as permission to sin.
1.mean: Peter says God's divine power has granted all things for life and godliness, and through his promises believers become partakers of the divine nature. So they must make every effort to add to their faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection and love. Be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election.
1.big: Having been given everything by God, believers must make every effort to grow in godliness.
1.diff: 'Partakers of the divine nature' has been understood very differently: Eastern Orthodox theology builds on it a doctrine of theosis (becoming like God by grace); Reformed and evangelical theology understands it as sharing God's moral character through union with Christ, not becoming divine in essence.

1.ctx: Peter defends the reliability of the apostolic message about Christ's return.
1.mean: Peter says they did not follow cleverly devised myths, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty when he received honour and glory from the Father on the holy mountain. And they have the prophetic word more fully confirmed. No prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation; men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
1.big: The apostles' message rests on eyewitness testimony and on Scripture inspired by the Holy Spirit.
1.diff: Verses 20–21 are a foundational text for the doctrine of the inspiration of Scripture, alongside 2 Timothy 3:16.

2.ctx: A long warning closely parallel to Jude, from which it probably draws. The false teachers claimed Christian freedom meant freedom from moral restraint.
2.mean: Peter says false teachers will arise among them, even denying the Master who bought them. He cites God's judgement on angels who sinned, on the ancient world in the flood, and on Sodom and Gomorrah, while rescuing Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and keep the unrighteous under punishment. The false teachers are bold, greedy and sensual, promising freedom while slaves of corruption. It would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness.
2.big: God will judge false teachers who exploit the church, and will rescue those who belong to him.
2.diff: Verse 1 ('denying the Master who bought them') is discussed in debates about the extent of the atonement, and verses 20–22 in debates about whether true believers can fall away. Reformed interpreters generally read them as describing those who professed faith without genuine conversion.

3.ctx: The false teachers mocked the promise of Christ's return because it had not yet happened.
3.mean: Peter says scoffers will come saying 'Where is the promise of his coming? All things continue as they were.' They deliberately overlook that the world was created by God's word and was once destroyed by water. By the same word the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire, kept until the day of judgement.
3.big: The God who created and once judged the world will certainly judge it again.

3.ctx: Peter answers the scoffers' question about delay. Decades had passed since Jesus' promise to return, and some were concluding it would never happen.
3.mean: Peter says with the Lord one day is as a thousand years. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise, but patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief; the heavens will pass away and the earth be exposed. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought they to be? They wait for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
3.big: The apparent delay in Christ's return is God's patience, giving time for repentance.
3.diff: Verse 9 ('not wishing that any should perish') is often discussed alongside election. Reformed interpreters read it variously as God's genuine desire for all, distinct from his decree, or as referring to his elect ('you'); others see it as showing salvation is open to all. All agree it reveals God's patience and mercy.

3.ctx: The closing exhortations of what Peter presents as his last letter, drawing together the letter's themes of holy living, patience and guarding against error.
3.mean: Peter says to be diligent to be found without spot, at peace. Count the Lord's patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote, whose letters contain some things hard to understand, which the ignorant twist to their destruction, as they do the other Scriptures. Beware of being carried away; grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
3.big: Believers must hold fast against error and keep growing in grace and knowledge of Christ.
3.diff: Verse 16 is notable for placing Paul's letters alongside 'the other Scriptures', showing an early recognition of their authority.

1.ctx: Jude, brother of James and so a brother of Jesus, writes a short urgent letter, probably to Jewish Christians.
1.mean: Jude greets those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ, with mercy, peace and love.
1.big: Believers are called, loved and kept by God.
1.diff: Jude calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ rather than his brother — a mark of humility and of his recognition of who Jesus was.

1.ctx: Jude had intended to write about salvation, but felt compelled to warn instead.
1.mean: Jude urges them to contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints, because ungodly people have crept in, perverting grace into sensuality and denying Jesus Christ. He cites God's judgement on Israel in the wilderness, on angels who sinned, and on Sodom. He quotes a tradition about Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body, and a prophecy from the book of Enoch.
1.big: The faith has been delivered once for all, and must be defended against those who twist grace into licence.
1.diff: Jude quotes the book of 1 Enoch and alludes to a tradition in the Assumption of Moses, neither of which is in the Bible. Most interpreters conclude that quoting a true statement from a non-canonical book does not make the whole book Scripture, as Paul quoted pagan poets.

1.ctx: Having exposed the false teachers, Jude turns to the faithful. The apostles had warned that scoffers would come, as 2 Peter 3:3 also records.
1.mean: Jude says to remember the apostles' predictions that there would be scoffers in the last time. Build yourselves up in your most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, and wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. Have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire.
1.big: Believers keep themselves in God's love, and reach out with mercy to those who are wavering.

1.ctx: One of the great doxologies of the New Testament, often used as a benediction at the close of church services. It balances the letter's stern warnings.
1.mean: Jude gives glory to him who is able to keep them from stumbling and to present them blameless before his glory with great joy — to the only God, our Saviour, through Jesus Christ our Lord.
1.big: The God who warns his people is the same God able to keep them from falling.

1.ctx: A short letter from 'the elder', traditionally John the apostle, to 'the elect lady and her children' — probably a church and its members.
1.mean: The elder writes to those he loves in the truth, because of the truth that abides in them and will be with them for ever.
1.big: Truth and love belong together in the Christian community.
1.diff: Whether 'the elect lady' is an individual woman or a church is debated; most scholars favour a church.

1.ctx: The elder has heard news of the church, perhaps from travelling believers, and finds that some — though apparently not all — are walking in the truth.
1.mean: The elder rejoices to find some walking in the truth, and asks that they love one another — which means walking according to God's commandments.
1.big: Love and obedience to God's commandments are inseparable.

1.ctx: The same false teachers as 1 John, travelling between churches and relying on their hospitality.
1.mean: The elder says many deceivers have gone out who do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Anyone who goes on ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Do not receive such a person into your house or give him any greeting, for that would share in his wicked works.
1.big: Love for the truth means refusing to support those who deny Christ's coming in the flesh.
1.diff: The instruction not to receive false teachers concerns giving them a platform and support in house churches, not general courtesy to unbelievers. How to apply it today is worth discussing.

1.ctx: The closing. Letters in the ancient world were costly and slow, and a visit was the preferred way to settle important matters.
1.mean: The elder has much to write but would rather speak face to face, so that their joy may be complete. The children of their elect sister send greetings.
1.big: Written words serve, but do not replace, face-to-face fellowship.

1.ctx: A short personal letter from the elder to Gaius, a faithful church member.
1.mean: The elder prays that all may go well with Gaius and that he may be in good health, as it goes well with his soul.
1.big: The elder cares for his friend's whole wellbeing, body and soul.
1.diff: Verse 2 is sometimes used to teach that God promises believers prosperity and health. In context it is simply a customary greeting wishing a friend well.

1.ctx: Travelling missionaries relied on the hospitality of local believers.
1.mean: The elder commends Gaius for his faithful hospitality to brothers who were strangers, and asks him to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. We ought to support such people, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
1.big: Supporting those who carry the gospel makes believers partners in their work.

1.ctx: A church power struggle. Diotrephes apparently led a house church and had refused to receive the elder's letter or the travelling teachers the elder sent.
1.mean: The elder says Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge the elder's authority, spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome the brothers, and puts out of the church those who do. Do not imitate evil but good. Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone.
1.big: Love of pre-eminence damages the church; faithful service earns a good name.
1.diff: Whether Diotrephes was a false teacher or simply ambitious and controlling is not stated.

1.ctx: The closing, very similar to 2 John. 'The friends' echoes Jesus' words calling his disciples friends (John 15:14–15).
1.mean: The elder hopes to see Gaius soon and speak face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you; greet the friends, each by name.
1.big: The church is a community of friends known to one another by name.

1.ctx: Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a wealthy believer in Colossae whose house hosted the church. The letter was carried with Colossians by Tychicus and Onesimus.
1.mean: Paul and Timothy greet Philemon, Apphia (probably his wife), Archippus, and the church in his house.
1.big: A private matter is set before the whole church.
1.diff: Paul addresses the church as well as Philemon, which means the request that follows would be heard publicly.

1.ctx: Paul's thanksgiving, as in his other letters. It carefully prepares for his request by praising the very love he will ask Philemon to show.
1.mean: Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, and prays that the sharing of his faith may become effective. He says the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through Philemon.
1.big: Philemon's known love for the saints is the ground of Paul's appeal.

1.ctx: Onesimus was a slave who had run away from Philemon, possibly after stealing, and had met Paul and become a Christian. Runaway slaves faced severe punishment under Roman law.
1.mean: Paul says though he could command, he prefers to appeal on the basis of love, for his child Onesimus, whose name means 'useful' — formerly useless to Philemon but now useful to both. Paul is sending him back, no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother. If he owes anything, charge it to Paul's account; Paul will repay it. He is confident Philemon will do even more than he asks.
1.big: The gospel turns a runaway slave into a brother, and Paul offers to pay his debt himself.
1.diff: Paul does not directly demand Onesimus's freedom, which has troubled readers; many think 'even more than I say' hints at it. Martin Luther and many since have seen in Paul's 'charge it to my account' a picture of Christ taking our debt. The principle of 'no longer a slave but a brother' was one later Christians drew on in opposing slavery.

1.ctx: The closing greetings, overlapping closely with Colossians 4:10–14, which confirms the two letters were written and sent together.
1.mean: Epaphras, a fellow prisoner, sends greetings, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
1.big: The same circle of co-workers stands behind this small, personal letter.

1.ctx: Paul writes to Titus, a Gentile co-worker he left on the island of Crete to organise the churches there. This is one of the three 'Pastoral Letters' with 1 and 2 Timothy.
1.mean: Paul writes as a servant of God and apostle, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, in hope of eternal life promised by God, who never lies, before the ages began.
1.big: Paul's ministry serves the faith and hope of God's chosen people, grounded in God's ancient promise.
