1.diff: The authorship of the Pastoral Letters is debated more than most of Paul's letters, owing to differences in vocabulary and church organisation. Many scholars think a follower of Paul wrote them; many evangelical scholars defend Paul's authorship, perhaps using a secretary.

1.ctx: Crete had several scattered churches needing organised leadership.
1.mean: Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every town. An elder, or overseer, must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, with faithful children, not arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent or greedy, but hospitable, self-controlled, upright, holy and disciplined, holding firm to the trustworthy word so he can give instruction in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it.
1.big: Church leaders are chosen above all for proven character and faithfulness to sound teaching.
1.diff: 'Husband of one wife' is read as requiring marital faithfulness, as excluding the divorced and remarried, as excluding polygamy, or as requiring that elders be married. The most common reading is faithfulness in marriage. The requirements assume male elders, which complementarian churches follow and egalitarian churches read differently.

1.ctx: False teachers, many associated with Jewish myths and circumcision, were upsetting households.
1.mean: Paul says many are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, teaching for shameful gain. He quotes a Cretan poet: 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons', and says the testimony is true. Rebuke them sharply. To the pure all things are pure. They profess to know God but deny him by their works.
1.big: False teaching is exposed by the way its teachers live.
1.diff: Paul quotes the Cretan poet Epimenides. Some readers find the generalisation uncomfortable; Paul is using a well-known local saying to make a point about the false teachers' conduct.

2.ctx: Instruction for different groups within the church, linked throughout to how the gospel is seen by outsiders.
2.mean: Paul tells Titus to teach what accords with sound doctrine: older men to be sober and dignified, older women reverent and to teach what is good, training younger women; younger men to be self-controlled; Titus himself to be a model of good works. Slaves are to be trustworthy, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour.
2.big: Sound doctrine shows itself in ordinary godly living that makes the gospel attractive.

2.ctx: The theological basis for the practical instructions of 2:1–10. 'Grace appeared' refers to Christ's first coming; the 'appearing' of verse 13 to his return.
2.mean: Paul says the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives, waiting for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem us from lawlessness and to purify a people for his own possession.
2.big: God's grace not only saves but trains believers to live godly lives as they wait for Christ's return.
2.diff: As at 2 Peter 1:1, the grammar of verse 13 most naturally reads 'our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ' as one person, a direct statement of Christ's deity. Some translations separate them.

3.ctx: Instruction for believers living among unbelieving neighbours and authorities.
3.mean: Paul says to be submissive to rulers, ready for every good work, speaking evil of no one, gentle and courteous to all. We ourselves were once foolish and disobedient. But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs.
3.big: God saved us by his mercy alone, through the Spirit's renewal, which is why believers treat outsiders with gentleness.
3.diff: 'Washing of regeneration' is read by some traditions as baptism conveying new birth, and by most Protestant interpreters as the inner cleansing of new birth by the Spirit, which baptism signifies. The whole Trinity is named in verses 4–6.

3.ctx: Final practical warnings. The disputes over genealogies and the law seem to have been Jewish speculations the false teachers promoted (compare 1:14).
3.mean: Paul says avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable. As for a divisive person, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him.
3.big: Pointless disputes damage the church, and persistently divisive people must be firmly dealt with.

3.ctx: Closing arrangements. Nicopolis was probably the city on the west coast of Greece, a natural place to spend winter when sea travel stopped.
3.mean: Paul says he will send Artemas or Tychicus, and asks Titus to join him at Nicopolis for the winter. Help Zenas and Apollos on their way. Our people must learn to devote themselves to good works. Grace be with you all.
3.big: The letter closes as it has run throughout: faith expressed in practical good works.

1.ctx: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a major port. Paul founded the church on his second journey, but was forced out after a few weeks by opposition (Acts 17:1–10). This is probably his earliest surviving letter, written from Corinth around AD 50.
1.mean: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet the church and give thanks for their work of faith, labour of love and steadfastness of hope. The gospel came to them not only in word but in power and in the Holy Spirit. They turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
1.big: The Thessalonians' conversion was real: they turned from idols to serve God and wait for his Son.
1.diff: Faith, love and hope appear together here, as in 1 Corinthians 13, and the whole letter is shaped by waiting for Christ's return.

2.ctx: Paul's opponents apparently accused him of being a travelling preacher in it for money and flattery, a common type in the Greek world.
2.mean: Paul reminds them how he came: not with flattery, greed or seeking glory, but gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to be a burden, and exhorting each one like a father with his children. When they received the word of God from him, they accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God. They suffered from their own countrymen as the Judean churches had.
2.big: Paul's conduct shows his message was genuine, and they received it rightly as God's own word.

2.ctx: Paul had been forced to leave Thessalonica suddenly and had been unable to return.
2.mean: Paul says he was torn away from them, but only in person, not in heart. He eagerly wanted to see them again, but Satan hindered him. They are his glory and joy.
2.big: Paul's affection for the church is deep, and separation has not diminished it.

3.ctx: Unable to go himself, Paul had sent Timothy from Athens to strengthen them.
3.mean: Paul says he sent Timothy to establish and exhort them in their faith, so that no one would be moved by these afflictions, for they had been told in advance that they were destined for them.
3.big: Suffering for the faith was expected, not a sign that something had gone wrong.

3.ctx: Timothy has just returned to Paul with news from Thessalonica.
3.mean: Paul says Timothy has brought good news of their faith and love, and that they long to see him. Now he really lives, since they are standing fast in the Lord. He prays night and day to see them, and that the Lord would make them increase and abound in love and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of Jesus.
3.big: The church's steadfastness brings Paul new life, and he prays they will grow in love until Christ comes.

4.ctx: Paul turns to instruction. Sexual morality in the Greco-Roman world was loose by Christian standards, and many of these converts had come from paganism.
4.mean: Paul says this is God's will, their sanctification: that they abstain from sexual immorality and each learn to control his own body in holiness and honour, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God. God has not called them to impurity but in holiness. They are to love one another more and more, live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands.
4.big: God's will for his people is their holiness, shown in sexual purity, love and honest work.

4.ctx: Some believers had died, and the church was grieving, perhaps fearing the dead would miss out when Christ returned.
4.mean: Paul says he does not want them to grieve as others do who have no hope. Since Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep. The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God. The dead in Christ will rise first. Then those who are alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so will always be with the Lord. Encourage one another with these words.
4.big: Christians grieve, but with hope, because believers who have died will rise and all will be with the Lord for ever.
4.diff: Verse 17 ('caught up') is the text behind the idea of a 'rapture'. Some Christians, especially dispensationalists, believe believers will be removed secretly before a period of tribulation. Most historic and Reformed interpreters read the passage as describing Christ's single, public return, with believers going out to meet him as citizens went out to welcome a visiting king — and the scene is anything but secret.

5.ctx: Continuing on Christ's return, now on its timing. 'Peace and security' was a slogan of Roman imperial propaganda, which may be what Paul has in mind.
5.mean: Paul says they know the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When people say 'peace and security', destruction will come suddenly. But they are children of light and of the day, so they should stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. God has not destined them for wrath but to obtain salvation through Jesus, who died for us.
5.big: Believers do not know when Christ will come, so they live ready, as people of the day.

5.ctx: A rapid series of instructions for church life. The church was only months old, with leaders newly appointed after Paul's hurried departure.
5.mean: Paul says respect those who labour among them and are over them in the Lord. Be at peace. Admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all. Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances, for this is God's will. Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good.
5.big: Church life is marked by care for one another, constant prayer and thanksgiving, and discernment.
5.diff: Verses 19–21 bear on the debate about whether prophecy continues today; all agree Paul requires prophecy to be tested.

5.ctx: The closing blessing and instructions. Letters were read aloud in the gathered church, which is why Paul insists this one be read to everyone.
5.mean: Paul prays that the God of peace would sanctify them completely, and that their whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls them is faithful; he will surely do it. He asks for prayer, and charges them to have the letter read to all the brothers.
5.big: God, who is faithful, will complete the work of making his people holy.
5.diff: 'Spirit, soul and body' has been used to argue that humans have three parts. Most interpreters think Paul is simply emphasising the whole person, not giving a technical anatomy.

1.ctx: Written shortly after 1 Thessalonians, probably from Corinth. Persecution had grown, and confusion about Christ's return had increased.
1.mean: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy give thanks that the Thessalonians' faith is growing and their love increasing, and boast of their steadfastness in all their persecutions.
1.big: Faith that grows under persecution is itself a cause for thanksgiving.
1.diff: Some scholars question whether Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians, because its teaching on the end seems different from the first letter. Many others, including most evangelicals, accept it as Paul's, written to correct misunderstanding of the first.

1.ctx: Paul reassures a church suffering growing persecution. The Old Testament language of fire and angels (Isaiah 66:15) is applied here to Christ's return.
1.mean: Paul says their suffering is evidence of God's righteous judgement. God will repay with affliction those who afflict them, and grant relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire. Those who do not obey the gospel will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord.
1.big: God will set things right when Christ returns, bringing relief to his people and judgement on their persecutors.
1.diff: Verse 9 is one of the texts in the debate about the nature of final judgement. The historic view reads 'eternal destruction' as unending punishment; some evangelicals argue for final annihilation. Both take the reality of judgement seriously.

2.ctx: Someone had told the church, perhaps claiming a letter from Paul, that the day of the Lord had already come.
2.mean: Paul says not to be shaken. That day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, who exalts himself against every so-called god and takes his seat in the temple of God. Something is now restraining him. The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth. His coming will be by the activity of Satan with false signs, and those perishing will believe what is false.
2.big: The end has not yet come, and Christ will certainly overthrow every power that sets itself against God.
2.diff: This is among the most obscure passages in Paul, and he says he had already explained it to them in person. The 'man of lawlessness' has been identified with a future antichrist figure, a Roman emperor, or a recurring pattern of opposition; the 'restrainer' with the Roman state, the preaching of the gospel, the Holy Spirit, or an angel. Honest humility is appropriate here.

2.ctx: In contrast to those deceived, Paul gives thanks for the believers.
2.mean: Paul says God chose them as firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, and called them through the gospel to obtain the glory of Christ. So stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught, by spoken word or by letter.
2.big: God chose and called his people to share Christ's glory, so they must hold fast to the apostolic teaching.
2.diff: 'Chose you... to be saved' is read by Reformed theology as God's election of individuals. 'Traditions' here means the apostolic teaching; Protestants understand it as now preserved in Scripture, while Catholic and Orthodox churches see a wider apostolic tradition alongside Scripture.

3.ctx: The closing section. Paul was in Corinth facing opposition from those who rejected the gospel (Acts 18:5–17), which explains his request for deliverance.
3.mean: Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord may spread quickly and that he may be delivered from wicked men. The Lord is faithful; he will establish them and guard them against the evil one.
3.big: The gospel's progress depends on prayer and on the faithfulness of the Lord.

3.ctx: Some in the church had stopped working, perhaps because they thought Christ's return was imminent, and were living off others.
3.mean: Paul says to keep away from any brother walking in idleness. Paul himself worked night and day so as not to be a burden. If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat. Do not grow weary of doing good. Do not regard the disobedient as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
3.big: Expecting Christ's return is no excuse for idleness; believers must work and not burden others.
3.diff: Verse 10 addresses those unwilling to work, not those unable to; it is not a verdict on people who cannot find work or cannot work.

3.ctx: Paul adds his own signature, perhaps because of the forged letter mentioned in 2:2.
3.mean: Paul prays that the Lord of peace himself give them peace at all times. He writes the greeting with his own hand as the mark of every genuine letter. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
3.big: Paul's own signature guards the church against forged teaching.

1.ctx: Paul had left Timothy, a younger co-worker, in Ephesus to deal with false teachers in the church there. This is the first of the 'Pastoral Letters'.
1.mean: Paul, an apostle by command of God our Saviour and Christ Jesus our hope, greets Timothy, his true child in the faith, with grace, mercy and peace.
1.big: Paul writes to his trusted spiritual son as one sent by God.
1.diff: As with Titus, the authorship of the Pastoral Letters is debated; many scholars think a follower of Paul wrote them, while many evangelical scholars defend Paul's authorship.

1.ctx: False teachers in Ephesus were occupied with myths, genealogies and speculative use of the law.
1.mean: Paul tells Timothy to charge certain people not to teach different doctrine or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies. The aim of the charge is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. The law is good if used lawfully, for the lawless and disobedient, in accordance with the gospel.
1.big: Sound teaching aims at love, not speculation.

1.ctx: Paul turns to his own conversion as an example of grace. Before becoming a Christian he had arrested believers and approved the execution of Stephen (Acts 7–9).
1.mean: Paul thanks Christ for appointing him, though he was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent. The saying is trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. He received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe.
1.big: If Christ could save Paul, the worst of sinners, he can save anyone.

2.ctx: Instructions for the church's public worship. The emperor at the time was Nero, which makes Paul's call to pray for 'kings and all in high positions' pointed.
2.mean: Paul urges prayers for all people, for kings and all in high positions, so that we may lead peaceful lives. This pleases God our Saviour, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.
2.big: The church prays for everyone because there is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself for all.
2.diff: 'Desires all people to be saved' and 'ransom for all' feature in debates about election and the extent of the atonement. Reformed interpreters often read 'all' as all kinds of people, including the kings just mentioned; others read it as every individual. 'The man Christ Jesus' stresses his humanity as mediator (see Mark 4:35 on the two natures).

2.ctx: Instructions about women in public worship, one of the most debated passages in the New Testament.
2.mean: Paul says women should adorn themselves modestly, with good works rather than elaborate display. A woman should learn quietly with all submissiveness. He does not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet. He gives reasons from creation — Adam was formed first — and from the fall. She will be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love and holiness.
2.big: Paul grounds instructions about men and women in worship in the order of creation.
2.diff: Complementarian churches, including most Reformed churches and this group, read verse 12 as restricting the church's authoritative teaching office to qualified men, since Paul grounds it in creation. Egalitarian scholars read it as addressing a specific situation in Ephesus, such as false teaching spreading among women. 'Saved through childbearing' is obscure, with readings including Christ's birth, women's ordinary calling, or safe delivery. Nothing here concerns women's worth or standing before God.

3.ctx: The church in Ephesus needed trustworthy leaders to replace or resist the false teachers.
3.mean: Paul says aspiring to be an overseer is a noble task. An overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money. He must manage his own household well, not be a recent convert, and be well thought of by outsiders.
3.big: Church leaders must be men of proven character, able to teach, whose homes show how they would care for God's church.
3.diff: As at Titus 1, 'husband of one wife' is read variously; the most common reading is marital faithfulness. 'Overseer' and 'elder' appear to be the same office in the New Testament.

3.ctx: The second recognised office in the church, serving practical needs.
3.mean: Paul says deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to wine or greedy, holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, and tested first. The women likewise must be dignified and faithful. Deacons must manage their households well.
3.big: Those who serve the church practically must share the same godly character as its leaders.
3.diff: 'The women' in verse 11 may be deacons' wives or women deacons; the Greek allows either. Phoebe is called a deacon in Romans 16:1. Churches differ on whether women may be deacons.

3.ctx: Paul explains why he has written these instructions: he hopes to visit, but may be delayed. The temple of Artemis in Ephesus was renowned for its great pillars.
3.mean: Paul says he writes so that Timothy may know how to behave in the household of God, the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth. Great indeed is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
3.big: The church exists to uphold the truth about Christ, who came in the flesh and was taken up in glory.
3.diff: Verse 16 is probably an early hymn. 'Manifested in the flesh' affirms the incarnation; some later manuscripts read 'God was manifested', but the best manuscripts read 'He who'.

4.ctx: Paul returns to the false teachers, who taught a harsh asceticism.
4.mean: Paul says the Spirit says that in later times some will depart from the faith, devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving. Everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving.
4.big: Rejecting God's good gifts of marriage and food is false teaching, not superior holiness.

4.ctx: Paul instructs Timothy on his own conduct. Timothy was probably in his thirties, young for a leader in a culture that honoured age.
4.mean: Paul says a good servant of Christ Jesus is trained in the words of faith and good doctrine. Have nothing to do with silly myths; train yourself for godliness, which is of value in every way. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Devote yourself to public reading of Scripture, exhortation and teaching. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching.
4.big: A minister's first duty is to guard his own life and his teaching.
4.h: A Good Servant of Jesus Christ

5.ctx: Practical instruction for relating to different members of the church family.
5.mean: Paul says not to rebuke an older man but encourage him as a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
5.big: The church is a family, and its members are to be treated as such.

5.ctx: Widows without family had no social support in the ancient world; the church had taken on their care, which had become complicated.
5.mean: Paul says honour widows who are truly widows. Children and grandchildren should care for their own relatives; anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith. The church should support widows over sixty with a record of good works, while younger widows should remarry. Believers should care for their own widows so the church is not burdened.
5.big: Families must care for their own, and the church for those who have no one else.

5.ctx: Instructions about how the church treats its elders, apparently needed because some elders in Ephesus had fallen into error or faced accusations.
5.mean: Paul says elders who rule well are worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in preaching and teaching; the worker deserves his wages. Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. Those who persist in sin should be rebuked publicly. Do not be hasty in laying on hands.
5.big: Faithful elders should be supported and protected from false accusation, and held accountable when they sin.
5.diff: Verse 17 has been read as distinguishing 'ruling elders' from 'teaching elders', a distinction in Presbyterian church order. Verse 18 quotes Luke 10:7 alongside Deuteronomy as 'Scripture'.

5.ctx: A solemn personal charge, with practical asides. Water in the ancient world was often unsafe, and wine was widely used medicinally.
5.mean: Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ Jesus and the elect angels to keep these rules without prejudice or partiality. He advises him to use a little wine for his stomach. The sins of some are obvious; others appear later. Good works too cannot remain hidden.
5.big: Leaders must act impartially, knowing that the truth about everyone will eventually come out.

6.ctx: Instruction to Christian slaves, including those with believing masters.
6.mean: Paul says slaves should regard their masters as worthy of honour, so that God's name and the teaching may not be reviled. Those with believing masters must not be disrespectful because they are brothers, but serve all the better.
6.big: Believers' conduct in every station of life should adorn the gospel.
6.diff: As elsewhere in the New Testament, the instruction regulates an existing institution rather than approving it.

6.ctx: Paul returns to the false teachers of chapter 1 and exposes their motives. Travelling teachers could make a good living from their followers.
6.mean: Paul says anyone who teaches a different doctrine is puffed up and understands nothing, with an unhealthy craving for controversy, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
6.big: False teaching is often driven by pride and love of money.

6.ctx: Following directly from the warning against treating godliness as gain.
6.mean: Paul says godliness with contentment is great gain; we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out. Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and harmful desires. The love of money is a root of all kinds of evils; some have wandered from the faith through it.
6.big: Contentment with God is true gain, and the love of money leads people away from faith.
6.diff: Verse 10 is often misquoted as 'money is the root of all evil'. Paul says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

6.ctx: Paul turns directly to Timothy. 'Man of God' was a title used of Old Testament prophets such as Moses and Elijah.
6.mean: Paul says flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of eternal life. Keep the commandment until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom God will display — the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light.
6.big: Timothy is to flee greed, pursue godliness and hold fast until Christ appears.

6.ctx: A charge to wealthy believers. Ephesus was one of the richest cities in the Roman world, and the church included people of means.
6.mean: Paul says to charge the rich not to be haughty or set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, who richly provides everything to enjoy. They are to do good, be rich in good works, be generous and ready to share, storing up treasure as a good foundation for the future.
6.big: Wealth is to be enjoyed as God's gift and used generously, not trusted.

6.ctx: The closing charge, returning to the letter's main concern. 'Knowledge' (gnosis) may point to early forms of the teaching later called Gnosticism.
6.mean: Paul says O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge, by which some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
6.big: The apostolic faith is a trust to be guarded, not improved upon.

1.ctx: Paul writes from prison in Rome, expecting execution. This is probably the last letter of his we have, written to Timothy around AD 64–67.
1.mean: Paul, an apostle by the will of God according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, greets Timothy, his beloved child.
1.big: Facing death, Paul writes of the promise of life in Christ.
1.diff: As with the other Pastoral Letters, authorship is debated; the letter's personal detail is often cited in support of Paul's authorship.

1.ctx: Paul remembers Timothy with deep affection, and Timothy's own family background of faith.
1.mean: Paul says he remembers Timothy's tears and longs to see him. He recalls the sincere faith that dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. He tells him to fan into flame the gift of God, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control. Do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel, by the power of God, who saved us and called us, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began.
1.big: Timothy must not be ashamed of the gospel, because God, who saved by his own grace, gives power to endure.
1.diff: Reformed theology draws on verse 9 for God's eternal purpose of grace in salvation, given in Christ before time began.

1.ctx: Paul contrasts those who have deserted him with one who stood by him.
1.mean: Paul says to follow the pattern of sound words and guard the good deposit by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. All in Asia have turned away from him. But Onesiphorus often refreshed him, was not ashamed of his chains, and searched for him in Rome until he found him.
1.big: Faithfulness is shown in guarding the truth and in standing by those who suffer for it.

2.ctx: Paul prepares Timothy to carry on after his death, using several images of endurance.
2.mean: Paul says be strengthened by the grace in Christ Jesus. Entrust what you have heard to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. Share in suffering as a good soldier; an athlete competes by the rules; a farmer works hard. Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead. The saying is trustworthy: if we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will reign with him; if we deny him, he will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.
2.big: The gospel is passed on through faithful endurance, grounded in Christ who remains faithful.
2.diff: Verse 2 describes four generations of teaching — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others — and is often taken as a pattern for training leaders, which fits this group's approach to developing brothers to lead.

2.ctx: Instruction on Timothy's conduct as a teacher amid controversy.
2.mean: Paul says do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. Avoid irreverent babble. The Lord knows those who are his. Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace. The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance.
2.big: A faithful teacher handles God's word rightly and corrects opponents gently, hoping God will bring them to repentance.
2.diff: Verse 25 ('God may perhaps grant them repentance') is one of the texts Reformed theology cites for repentance itself being God's gift.

3.ctx: Paul describes the character of 'the last days', which in the New Testament means the whole period between Christ's first and second comings.
3.mean: Paul says in the last days there will come times of difficulty. People will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. Avoid such people.
3.big: Religion without real godliness is a mark of the age, and must be recognised and avoided.

3.ctx: A contrast between the false teachers and Timothy's own formation.
3.mean: Paul reminds Timothy that he has followed Paul's teaching, conduct, faith, patience, love and sufferings. All who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. Continue in what you have learned, knowing from whom you learned it, and that from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction and training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
3.big: Scripture comes from God himself and fully equips his people for salvation and for every good work.
3.diff: Verse 16 is the foundational text for the doctrine of the inspiration of Scripture. 'Breathed out by God' means Scripture originates from God. Christians differ in how they express its reliability — terms such as 'inerrant' and 'infallible' are used with somewhat different meanings — but this group holds, with the historic evangelical position, that Scripture is fully God's word and our final authority.

4.ctx: Paul's final charge to Timothy, written as he faces death under Nero. The language is formal and solemn, like a legal charge before witnesses.
4.mean: Paul charges Timothy in the presence of God and Christ Jesus: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching. The time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but accumulate teachers to suit their passions. Do the work of an evangelist. As for Paul, he is already being poured out as a drink offering. He has fought the good fight, finished the race, kept the faith. There is laid up for him the crown of righteousness, and not only for him but for all who have loved Christ's appearing.
4.big: Facing death, Paul hands on the charge to preach the word faithfully, whatever the response.

4.ctx: Personal requests from a Roman prison, where prisoners depended on friends for food, clothing and company. Winter in a stone cell would have been cold.
4.mean: Paul asks Timothy to come soon. Demas has deserted him, in love with this present world. Only Luke is with him. Bring Mark, for he is very useful. Bring the cloak left at Troas, and the books, especially the parchments.
4.big: Even the great apostle needed friends, warmth and books in his last days.
4.diff: Paul's request for Mark, whom he once refused to take on a journey (Acts 15:37–39), shows reconciliation.

4.ctx: Paul reflects on his 'first defence', a preliminary hearing in his trial, at which none of his supporters appeared on his behalf.
4.mean: Paul says at his first defence no one came to stand by him; all deserted him — may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by him and strengthened him, so that the message might be fully proclaimed. The Lord will rescue him from every evil deed and bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom.
4.big: When everyone else deserted him, the Lord stood by him.

4.ctx: The final greetings of what is probably Paul's last letter. Prisca and Aquila had worked with Paul in Corinth, Ephesus and Rome.
4.mean: Paul greets Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus. He asks Timothy to come before winter. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
4.big: Paul's last recorded words are grace.

1.ctx: The letter has no greeting. It opens like a sermon, with one of the grandest sentences in the New Testament (verses 1–4). See History & setting of Hebrews above for author and readers.
1.mean: ‘On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son.’ The prophets were real revelation, but partial; the Son is God’s final word. Then seven descriptions of the Son. He is heir of all things and the one ‘through whom He made the universe’. ‘The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature.’ As light is to the sun, and as a seal’s impression is to the seal, so the Son is to the Father: not a copy, but God shown to us. He upholds all things by his word. Having ‘provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high’, a finished work. He is therefore far above the angels, whom some Jews saw as mediators of the law (2:2). Seven Old Testament quotations prove it. God calls him Son (Psalm 2:7); angels worship him (Deuteronomy 32:43); and the Father addresses him: ‘Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever’ (Psalm 45:6). He applies to him words spoken of the LORD as Creator: ‘In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth’ (Psalm 102:25). The angels, by contrast, are ‘ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation’.
1.big: God’s final and fullest word is his Son, who shares God’s very nature, made and sustains all things, and is far above the angels.
1.diff: Verses 8 and 10–12 are among the clearest New Testament texts calling the Son ‘God’ and applying to him Old Testament words about the LORD as Creator. The quotation in verse 6 (‘Let all God’s angels worship Him’) follows the Greek Old Testament, and a Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy found among the Dead Sea Scrolls has the same line (see the BSB footnote), so the writer is not inventing the wording. Some have suggested that verse 8 could be translated ‘God is your throne’, but most translations and commentators reject this as unnatural, and the parallel in verse 10 (‘O Lord’) supports ‘O God’.

2.ctx: The first of five warning passages. Jewish tradition held that angels were present when the law was given at Sinai (compare Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19).
2.mean: ‘We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away.’ The danger is drifting, like a boat slipping its mooring, rather than deliberate rebellion. The argument runs from lesser to greater. If the law spoken through angels was binding and every disobedience was punished, ‘how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?’ This salvation was announced by the Lord himself, confirmed by those who heard him, and affirmed by God ‘through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will’.
2.big: If disobeying the law brought judgment, neglecting the salvation spoken by God’s Son is far more serious.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

2.ctx: The writer turns from Christ’s divine glory (chapter 1) to his true humanity. Together the two chapters are a biblical foundation for the church’s confession that Christ is fully God and fully man in one person.
2.mean: Psalm 8 says God made man ‘a little lower than the angels’ and placed everything under his feet. ‘Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him.’ Humanity has not fulfilled its calling. ‘But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone.’ Jesus is the true man who fulfils Psalm 8. He is the ‘author’ (or pioneer) of salvation, made ‘perfect through suffering’. This does not mean he was ever flawed; he was made fully qualified as Saviour by going through suffering. ‘Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.’ ‘Since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.’ ‘He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest’ and ‘make atonement for the sins of the people’. ‘Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted.’
2.big: The Son became fully human, like his brothers in every way, so that he could die for them, free them from the fear of death, and help them.
2.diff: ‘For everyone’ (verse 9). For whom did Christ die? Arminian (Wesleyan): for every person without exception. Wesley glosses ‘every man’ as everyone ‘That ever was or will be born into the world’, and the Remonstrance (art. 2) says Christ died for all, though only believers enjoy the forgiveness. Reformed: Christ’s death is sufficient for the whole world, but was intended to redeem effectually those the Father gave him (Canons of Dort, Second Head, arts. 3 and 8). Many Reformed readers note that the context speaks of ‘many sons’, ‘brothers’ and ‘the children God has given Me’ (verses 10–13). Others in the Reformed tradition hold a wider view of the atonement’s intent. Both sides agree that the offer of the gospel is to be made to everyone, and that only those who believe are saved. ‘Make atonement’ (verse 17) can also be translated ‘make propitiation’ (BSB footnote): turning away God’s just anger at sin by a sacrifice that God himself provides.

The Five Arminian Articles (1610), art. 2 and 5, in Schaff vol. 3

3.h: Jesus Our Apostle and High Priest
3.ctx: Moses was the most honoured figure in Judaism, the one through whom the law came. God himself called him ‘faithful in all My house’ (Numbers 12:7).
3.mean: ‘Holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling, set your focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest whom we confess.’ He is the ‘apostle’ (the one sent from God to us) and the high priest (the one who represents us to God). The writer honours Moses: both were faithful. But Moses was faithful ‘as a servant in all God’s house’, while ‘Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house’. A servant in a house and the son who owns it are not on the same level. Then a challenge: ‘And we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast.’
3.big: Jesus is greater than Moses as a son is greater than a servant in the household.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

3.ctx: A long quotation of Psalm 95, recalling Israel’s rebellion in the wilderness when they refused to enter the promised land (Numbers 13–14).
3.mean: ‘Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion.”’ The generation that came out of Egypt saw God’s works for forty years, yet their hearts were ‘always going astray’. So God swore, ‘They shall never enter My rest.’ The writer introduces a psalm written by David as what ‘the Holy Spirit says’, in the present tense. Scripture is not just an old record but God speaking now, and the word ‘Today’ is addressed to every new reader.
3.big: Scripture speaks with a present voice, ‘Today’, and warns against the hardness that kept Israel out of the promised land.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

3.ctx: The writer applies Psalm 95 directly to his readers.
3.mean: ‘See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God. But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.’ Sin deceives. It hardens gradually, and the remedy is mutual: every believer has a responsibility to encourage the others, every day. ‘We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first.’ The wilderness generation had all left Egypt and seen the miracles, yet ‘it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter’.
3.big: Believers guard one another against the slow hardening of sin by daily encouragement.
3.diff: Verse 13’s call to ‘exhort one another daily’ sits close to the group’s anchor text in chapter 10. On what verse 14 implies about whether believers can fall away, see the note on 6:1.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL
T. R. Schreiner, Hebrews, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham)

4.ctx: The argument about Israel’s failure to enter the land continues, now applied to the rest God offers.
4.mean: ‘While the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it.’ The writer argues from Scripture. God’s rest has existed since creation, when ‘on the seventh day God rested from all His works’. Israel failed to enter it. Joshua brought them into the land, but that was not the final rest, because centuries later, through David, God still said ‘Today’. So ‘There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.’ Entering it means resting from our own work, as God did from his. ‘Now we who have believed enter that rest.’ Yet it is also still ahead: ‘Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest.’
4.big: God’s true rest, pictured by the Sabbath and the promised land, is entered by faith now and enjoyed fully in the age to come.
4.diff: Christians differ over what this means for a weekly day of rest. The Westminster Confession (21.7–8) teaches that the Sabbath command continues as the ‘Christian Sabbath’, the Lord’s Day, Sunday. Many other Christians see the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ (compare Colossians 2:16–17) while keeping Sunday as the day of worship. Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. Most interpreters read this passage chiefly as being about salvation, rest begun now by faith and completed in the age to come, rather than about which day to keep.

src.l: Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text), ch. 17, 21, 29
Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

4.ctx: A famous passage on God’s word, then the introduction of the letter’s main theme: Christ as high priest.
4.mean: ‘For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.’ The word that warned Israel still exposes us. ‘Nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight.’ That could be terrifying, but the writer immediately turns to comfort. ‘Since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to what we profess. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin. Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.’ The throne of the judge is, for believers, a throne of grace.
4.big: Because our high priest was tempted as we are yet without sin, believers can approach God’s throne with confidence.
4.diff: Verse 15 is central to the church’s teaching on Christ’s true humanity. Theologians have discussed whether Christ could have sinned. Traditionally, many theologians have held that he could not, because he is God the Son, while insisting that his temptations were real and costly. Some evangelical theologians argue that real temptation requires a real possibility of sinning. Either way, the point of the text is that his sympathy is genuine: he knows the full force of temptation, perhaps more than anyone, because he never gave in.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

5.ctx: The writer explains what a high priest is, in terms of the Old Testament priesthood, especially Aaron.
5.mean: ‘Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.’ Two qualifications follow. He must be able to sympathise: ‘He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is subject to weakness.’ And he must be called: ‘No one takes this honor upon himself.’ Christ meets both. He was appointed by God, who said ‘You are My Son’ (Psalm 2:7) and ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’ (Psalm 110:4). And he knows weakness from the inside: ‘During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence.’ This recalls Gethsemane. ‘Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered. And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him.’
5.big: Jesus is a true high priest, appointed by God and made perfect through suffering.
5.diff: ‘Learned obedience’ does not mean he was ever disobedient. He learned by experience what obedience costs, all the way to the cross, which is part of his genuine humanity. ‘He was heard’ does not mean he escaped death. God answered his prayer by raising him from death, and Jesus himself prayed ‘not My will, but Yours’.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

5.ctx: The writer breaks off from Melchizedek to rebuke his readers.
5.mean: ‘We have much to say about this, but it is hard to explain, because you are dull of hearing.’ The problem is not that the subject is too hard but that the readers have become sluggish. ‘Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to reteach you the basic principles of God’s word. You need milk, not solid food!’ Maturity is not just knowing more; it is trained judgment: ‘solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil.’
5.big: Believers are meant to grow up in understanding and discernment, not stay on spiritual milk.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

6.ctx: One of the most difficult and most discussed passages in the New Testament. Read it together with verses 9–12.
6.mean: ‘Let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to maturity.’ The foundations are listed: repentance and faith, ‘instruction about baptisms’, the laying on of hands, the resurrection and eternal judgment. Then the warning. ‘It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age—and then have fallen away—to be restored to repentance, because they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.’ ‘Fallen away’ here means abandoning Christ altogether, not ordinary sins and failures. Calvin calls it ‘a total defection or falling away from the Gospel’. An illustration follows: land that drinks the rain and produces a crop is blessed; land that produces only thorns is cursed. Then the writer’s tone changes: ‘Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case—things that accompany salvation. For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown.’ He wants them to show diligence ‘to the very end, in order to make your hope sure’.
6.big: Turning away from Christ after knowing him is the most serious danger there is, and the writer warns because he is confident of better things for his readers.
6.diff: Christians read this warning in four main ways. (1) Professing but not truly converted: many Reformed interpreters hold that it describes people who experienced much of the church’s life, even the Spirit’s influence, without being born again. Calvin argued that God may give the reprobate ‘some taste of his grace’, while the Spirit of regeneration is given to ‘the elect alone’. (2) A real warning that God uses to keep believers: others in the Reformed tradition, such as Thomas Schreiner, argue that the language describes real Christians. The warning is not about something that will happen to true believers, but is one of the means by which God preserves them. They heed it and so do not fall away. (3) Arminian (Wesleyan): it describes genuine believers who can, and sometimes do, finally fall away. Wesley read the passage as ‘not a supposition, but a plain relation of fact’ about people who ‘were renewed once’. (4) Hypothetical: some read it as an impossible case used for argument (‘if this could happen…’), though most commentators think this weakens the writer’s urgency. Most interpreters agree on three things. The sin in view is deliberate, total rejection of Christ, not ordinary failure. The writer himself is ‘convinced of better things’ for his readers (verse 9). Many pastors add that someone anxious about having committed it shows, by that very concern, that they have not turned their back on Christ.

6.ctx: In the ancient world an oath sworn by a greater authority settled a dispute. God, having no one greater, swore by himself (Genesis 22:16).
6.mean: ‘When God made His promise to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself.’ Abraham waited patiently and obtained the promise. God did not need to swear; he did it for our sake, ‘to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise’. ‘Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie’, his promise and his oath, ‘we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged. We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf.’ The image is striking: an anchor is usually thrown down into the sea, but this one is fixed upward, in heaven, where Jesus has gone ahead.
6.big: Believers’ hope is anchored in God’s unbreakable promise and in Jesus, who has gone before them into God’s presence.
6.diff: Verse 19 is the verse behind the Community of Brothers’ anchor emblem.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

7.ctx: Melchizedek appears briefly in Genesis 14:18–20 as king of Salem (probably Jerusalem) and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham. Psalm 110:4 promises a king who will be ‘a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’.
7.mean: The writer draws out what Genesis says, and what it leaves out. Melchizedek’s name means ‘king of righteousness’, and ‘king of Salem’ means ‘king of peace’. Scripture records him ‘Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God’. For a priest, missing ancestry was remarkable, since Levitical priests had to prove their descent. Then the argument: ‘Consider how great Melchizedek was: Even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the plunder.’ ‘And indisputably, the lesser is blessed by the greater.’ And in a sense Levi, the ancestor of Israel’s priests, ‘paid the tenth through Abraham’. So the order of Melchizedek ranks above the Levitical priesthood.
7.big: Melchizedek, greater than Abraham, foreshadows a priesthood greater than Israel’s.
7.diff: Some have thought Melchizedek was an appearance of Christ himself before the incarnation. Most interpreters, including Calvin, read the writer as saying that Melchizedek resembles the Son because Scripture records no beginning or end for him, not that he literally had none. He was a real king, made by God’s providence into a picture of Christ.

hist.t: Melchizedek in the Dead Sea Scrolls
b: Melchizedek appears only twice in the Old Testament (Genesis 14:18–20; Psalm 110:4), but he fascinated Jewish writers. A fragmentary scroll from Cave 11 at Qumran, known as 11QMelchizedek, pictures him as a heavenly figure appointed by God as judge in the heavenly court, bringing liberation at the end of the age.

This shows that speculation about Melchizedek was alive among Jews in the century before Hebrews. Hebrews takes a different and more restrained line. It builds only on what Scripture says, and on what it does not say: Genesis gives him no genealogy, birth or death, which makes him a fitting picture of the Son of God, who truly has no beginning or end of life (7:3).

7.ctx: The writer argues that a new priesthood means the old system was never meant to be final.
7.mean: ‘If perfection could have been attained through the Levitical priesthood…why was there still need for another priest to appear?’ Psalm 110 shows the old priesthood was temporary, and ‘when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well’. Jesus came from Judah, not Levi. He became a priest ‘not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life’, and with an oath: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind’. ‘Because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood. Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them.’ He is ‘holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners’. ‘Unlike the other high priests, He does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people; He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself.’
7.big: Jesus’ priesthood is permanent and his sacrifice complete, so he saves completely those who come to God through him.
7.diff: ‘The law must be changed’ (verse 12) refers to the law of the priesthood and sacrifices, which Christ fulfils and ends. Most Christian traditions distinguish this from God’s moral will, which the new covenant writes on the heart (8:10).

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

8.ctx: The writer summarises his main point. The tabernacle was built to a pattern Moses was shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), which Hebrews reads as a copy of the heavenly reality.
8.mean: ‘The point of what we are saying is this: We do have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man.’ The earthly priests serve in ‘a copy and shadow of what is in heaven’. That is why Moses was told: ‘See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.’ The earthly tabernacle was real and God-given, but it pointed beyond itself.
8.big: Christ serves in the true sanctuary, of which the earthly one was only a copy.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

8.ctx: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament: Jeremiah 31:31–34, a promise made around the time of the Babylonian exile.
8.mean: ‘Jesus has received a much more excellent ministry, just as the covenant He mediates is better and is founded on better promises.’ The problem with the first covenant lay with the people: ‘God found fault with the people’. So God promised a new covenant that would succeed where the old failed. ‘I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.’ All will know him, ‘from the least of them to the greatest’. ‘For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.’ ‘By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete; and what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear.’
8.big: Christ mediates the new covenant God promised, which writes his law on hearts and fully forgives sin.
8.diff: ‘Will soon disappear’ (verse 13) may hint that the temple was still standing when the letter was written (see When, and to whom? above). Christians differ on how the new covenant relates to Israel. Some see the church as the fulfilment of the promise to ‘the house of Israel’. Dispensationalists expect a future fulfilment for the nation of Israel as well.

9.ctx: The writer describes the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary of Israel’s wilderness years (Exodus 25–40), and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).
9.mean: The tabernacle had two rooms. The first, the Holy Place, held the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread. ‘Behind the second curtain was a room called the Most Holy Place’, with the ark of the covenant, the cherubim and the mercy seat. The priests went into the first room every day. ‘But only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood’, for his own sins and the people’s. The very layout taught something: ‘By this arrangement the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing.’ Its gifts and sacrifices ‘were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper’. They were ‘external regulations imposed until the time of reform’.
9.big: The old system, by its very design, showed that the way to God was not yet fully open.
9.diff: Two details are often raised. (1) Verse 4 links ‘the golden altar of incense’ with the Most Holy Place, but Exodus 30:6 places it in front of the curtain. The altar stood just outside, but it belonged to the inner room in use. 1 Kings 6:22 speaks of the ‘altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary’, and on the Day of Atonement incense from it was taken inside the veil (Leviticus 16:12–13). The Greek word could also mean a golden censer. (2) Verse 4 says the jar of manna and Aaron’s staff were in the ark, but 1 Kings 8:9 says that in Solomon’s day there was nothing in it but the tablets. Exodus 16:33–34 and Numbers 17:10 place the jar and staff ‘in front of the Testimony’. Hebrews describes the wilderness tabernacle as Jewish tradition remembered it, and by Solomon’s time the items may have been lost.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

9.ctx: The heart of the letter’s argument about Christ’s sacrifice, set against the Day of Atonement.
9.mean: ‘He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption.’ If animal blood made people ceremonially clean, ‘how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!’ Christ is the mediator of a new covenant. The writer then plays on a Greek word that means both ‘covenant’ and ‘will’: a will takes effect only when someone dies, and even the first covenant was put into effect with blood (Exodus 24:8). ‘Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.’ Christ entered ‘heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God’, and not repeatedly: ‘now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself. Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment, so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.’
9.big: Christ’s one sacrifice of himself achieves what all the old sacrifices could only picture: eternal redemption.
9.diff: Verse 14 names the Father, the Son and the eternal Spirit together in the one act of Christ’s self-offering. Verse 27 (‘appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment’) is a key text against reincarnation.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

10.ctx: The conclusion of the argument about sacrifice begun in chapter 7. If the temple was still standing, sacrifices were being offered every day as the writer wrote.
10.mean: ‘For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves.’ If its sacrifices could have cleansed, they would have stopped. Instead, ‘those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.’ So Christ came, in the words of Psalm 40: ‘Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me…I have come to do Your will, O God.’ The incarnation was necessary for the atonement: the Son took a body in order to offer it. ‘And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.’ Then a picture. ‘Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices’. There were no chairs in the tabernacle; the work was never done. ‘But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God.’ ‘By a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.’ The Spirit confirms it from Jeremiah: ‘Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.’ ‘And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.’
10.big: Christ’s single sacrifice, once for all, has done what endlessly repeated sacrifices never could.
10.diff: The Lord’s Supper and sacrifice. This passage is central to a historic disagreement. Protestant churches hold that Christ’s sacrifice was offered once and is complete, so the Lord’s Supper is not itself a sacrifice for sin. The Westminster Confession says it is ‘only a commemoration of that one offering up of himself, by himself, upon the cross, once for all’ (29.2), though Reformed believers hold that Christ is truly, spiritually present to faith. Catholic teaching agrees that Christ’s sacrifice cannot be repeated, and does not claim that the Mass repeats it. The Catechism says the Eucharist ‘re-presents (makes present) the sacrifice of the cross’, so that the cross and the Mass are ‘one single sacrifice’, and ‘only the manner of offering is different’ (1366–1367). The question is whether ‘once for all’ and ‘no longer needed’ rule out any ongoing offering (the Protestant view), or are honoured by a sacrament that makes the one offering present (the Catholic view).

10.ctx: The practical application of everything since 4:14, and the passage from which the Community of Brothers takes its name and shape (verses 23–25).
10.mean:
Three invitations (verses 19–25). Because we have ‘confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body’, and a great priest over God’s house: ‘let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith’; ‘Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful’; and ‘let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.’ Faith, hope and love; God, the future, and one another. Meeting together is not optional extra: it is how believers keep each other going.

A warning (verses 26–31). ‘If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains’. In context, the sin is rejecting Christ’s sacrifice, the only one there is: having ‘trampled on the Son of God’ and ‘insulted the Spirit of grace’. ‘It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.’

Encouragement (verses 32–39). ‘Remember the early days’, when they endured ridicule, persecution and the confiscation of property ‘joyfully’. ‘So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward.’ ‘But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.’
10.big: Because Christ has opened the way to God, believers must draw near, hold fast, and keep meeting together to encourage one another.
10.diff: Verses 26–31 raise the same questions as 6:4–6 (see the note there for the four main readings). ‘Deliberately go on sinning’ does not mean any sin committed knowingly. The writer has in mind persistent, settled rejection of Christ, the ‘shrinking back’ of verse 39. The writer again ends with confidence: ‘we are not of those who shrink back’.

b: The readers had suffered public insult, imprisonment of some members, and confiscation of property, but ‘not yet’ to the point of bloodshed (12:4). If the letter was sent to Rome, two known events are candidates.

Claudius, AD 49. The Roman historian Suetonius records that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting ‘at the instigation of Chrestus’. Many historians think this refers to disputes about Christ in the synagogues. Acts 18:2 mentions the same expulsion, which brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth. Expulsion would have meant loss of property, but not martyrdom. That fits these verses well.

Nero, AD 64. After the great fire of Rome, Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians, and that some were torn to death by dogs or burned as torches. Since the readers had ‘not yet’ shed blood, many date the letter before this. Some think the writer is preparing them for exactly such a storm.
The link to Rome is likely but not certain, so these identifications remain suggestions.

11.ctx: Chapter 11 answers 10:38–39 (‘My righteous one will live by faith’) with a gallery of Old Testament examples, often called the ‘hall of faith’.
11.mean: ‘Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended.’ Faith is not wishful thinking. It is confidence in what God has promised (the future) and in what he has revealed (the unseen). It begins with creation: ‘By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.’
11.big: Faith is confident trust in what God has promised but cannot yet be seen.
11.diff: Verse 1 is less a full definition than a description of faith’s character, which the chapter then illustrates. Verse 3 is a key text for creation ‘out of nothing’: the visible world was not made from pre-existing visible material.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.h: The Faith of Abel, Enoch, Noah
11.ctx: The first examples come from Genesis 4–6, before the flood.
11.mean: ‘By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did’, and ‘by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead’. ‘By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death’, because he pleased God. Then a principle for every reader: ‘And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.’ ‘By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family.’ He believed God about a flood no one had seen, and acted on it for years.
11.big: From the beginning, people have pleased God by trusting him and acting on his word.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.h: The Faith of Abraham and Sarah
11.ctx: Abraham, honoured by Jews as father of their nation and by Paul as the father of all who believe (Romans 4), gets the longest treatment.
11.mean: ‘By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going.’ He lived in the promised land in tents, as a foreigner, ‘For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.’ By faith Sarah, though barren and past age, conceived. ‘All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised.’ ‘They acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.’ ‘Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.’ The greatest test came when Abraham offered Isaac, the son of the promise. ‘Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.’
11.big: Faith obeys God’s call and lives as a stranger on earth, looking for the city God is building.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.h: The Faith of Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph
11.ctx: The patriarchs at the end of their lives (Genesis 27–50). Each blessing or instruction looked forward to promises none of them lived to see fulfilled.
11.mean: ‘By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future.’ By faith the dying Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons. ‘By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.’ Joseph was the most powerful man in Egypt, yet he did not want to be buried there. He was sure God would bring his people out, and wanted his bones to go with them (Exodus 13:19).
11.big: Faith looks beyond death to the fulfilment of God’s promises.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.ctx: Moses, the central figure of the old covenant, was raised in Pharaoh’s court with every advantage Egypt could give (Exodus 2; Acts 7:22).
11.mean: By faith Moses’ parents hid him, ‘unafraid of the king’s edict’. ‘By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin. He valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to his reward.’ ‘Disgrace for Christ’ probably means the reproach borne by God’s people and their coming Messiah, which Moses shared by identifying with them. ‘He persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.’ By faith he kept the Passover, and the people crossed the Red Sea.
11.big: Faith chooses suffering with God’s people over the passing pleasures of sin.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

11.ctx: The chapter speeds up, moving from Joshua through the judges, kings and prophets, to the martyrs of the period between the Testaments.
11.mean: ‘By faith the walls of Jericho fell’. ‘By faith the prostitute Rahab…did not perish’. ‘Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets’. Through faith some ‘conquered kingdoms’, ‘shut the mouths of lions, quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword’. But faith did not always lead to rescue. ‘Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection.’ ‘They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword.’ ‘The world was not worthy of them.’ ‘These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised. God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect.’
11.big: Faith sometimes brings deliverance and sometimes brings suffering, and God commends both.
11.diff: The list includes deeply flawed figures such as Samson and Jephthah. The chapter commends their faith, not everything they did.

b: No Old Testament person is said to have been sawn in two. But an ancient Jewish tradition held that the prophet Isaiah was killed in this way under the wicked King Manasseh (compare 2 Kings 21:16). Justin Martyr, writing around AD 155, refers to it in debate with a Jewish teacher: Isaiah, ‘whom you sawed asunder with a wooden saw’. Hebrews probably alludes to it. Verse 35 (‘tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection’) likewise recalls the Jewish martyrs under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC. In 2 Maccabees 7 a mother and her seven sons are tortured to death for refusing to break God’s law, one saying they look for the hope ‘that we will be raised up again by him’.
