12.ctx: The ‘cloud of witnesses’ refers back to the heroes of chapter 11. The picture is a race run in a crowded stadium.
12.mean: ‘Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.’ The witnesses are not so much spectators as examples: they testify that the race can be finished. Jesus is more than an example. He is the pioneer who ran the whole course first and brings faith to completion. ‘Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.’
12.big: Believers run the race of faith by keeping their eyes on Jesus, who ran it first.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

12.ctx: The readers had faced public insult, imprisonment and loss of property (10:32–34), but not yet martyrdom.
12.mean: ‘In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.’ They have forgotten Proverbs 3:11–12: ‘My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. For the Lord disciplines the one He loves.’ Hardship is not a sign that God has abandoned them but that he is treating them as sons. ‘For what son is not disciplined by his father?’ Earthly fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, ‘but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it.’ So, ‘strengthen your limp hands and weak knees’.
12.big: Hardship, received rightly, is the loving training of a Father, not a sign of his absence.
12.diff: ‘Discipline’ here means training more than punishment. Not all suffering is discipline for a particular sin (compare John 9:1–3); the writer presents hardship as something God uses for his children’s good.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

12.ctx: Practical warnings drawn from the argument. The story of Esau selling his birthright for a meal comes from Genesis 25:29–34 and 27:30–40.
12.mean: ‘Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.’ Three dangers. Falling short of God’s grace. A ‘root of bitterness’ that ‘springs up to cause trouble and defile many’ (one bitter person can poison a church). And being ‘godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright’. ‘Afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.’ Esau traded what was eternal for what was immediate, and could not undo it.
12.big: Holiness and perseverance in grace matter; Esau shows the cost of trading eternal things for passing ones.
12.diff: ‘No ground for repentance’ is read in two ways: Esau could not get his father Isaac to change his mind, or Esau himself could not find true repentance. Either way, his tears were for the lost blessing rather than for his sin. ‘Holiness, without which no one will see the Lord’ does not teach that holiness earns salvation. Protestants read it as the holiness that always grows from saving faith; Catholics as the holiness of grace that must be kept to the end.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

12.ctx: A contrast between Mount Sinai, where the law was given in fire and terror (Exodus 19), and Mount Zion, God’s heavenly city.
12.mean: ‘For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm’. At Sinai the sight was so terrifying that even Moses trembled. ‘Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.’ Abel’s blood cried for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks forgiveness. When believers gather to worship, they join this heavenly assembly. Then a final warning: God will shake heaven and earth once more, so that ‘the unshakable may remain’. ‘Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. “For our God is a consuming fire.”’
12.big: Believers have come not to the terror of Sinai but to the joyful assembly of heaven, which calls for grateful, reverent worship.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

13.ctx: Practical instructions for the community’s life together. Travelling believers relied on hospitality, and prisoners in the Roman world often depended on friends for food.
13.mean: ‘Continue in brotherly love. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it’, as Abraham did (Genesis 18). ‘Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them.’ ‘Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.’
13.big: Brotherly love shows itself in hospitality, care for those who suffer, and faithfulness in marriage.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

13.ctx: The instructions rest on Christ’s unchanging faithfulness. Animal sacrifices and food rules were still central to the temple worship the readers had known.
13.mean: ‘Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.”’ Contentment rests on God’s presence. ‘Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.’ So, ‘Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings’. The heart is strengthened ‘by grace and not by foods’. ‘We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.’ On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the sacrificed animals were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). ‘And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate’. ‘Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore. For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.’
13.big: Because Christ never changes and never leaves, believers can be content and bear disgrace for him.
13.diff: ‘We have an altar’ (verse 10) is read differently. Calvin and most Protestant commentators take the altar to be Christ’s sacrifice on the cross, on which believers ‘feed’ by faith. Some interpreters see a reference to the Lord’s Table. Either way, the writer’s point is that clinging to the old system cuts a person off from Christ’s sacrifice.

src.l: Calvin on Hebrews 13:10–15, CCEL

13.ctx: With Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice complete, the writer names the offerings that remain for God’s people.
13.mean: ‘Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.’ The sacrifices are now praise and generosity. ‘Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief.’ Leaders are accountable to God for their people; the people can make that task a joy or a burden. ‘Pray for us’.
13.big: The old sacrifices give way to praise, generosity, and glad support of faithful leaders.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Hebrews (trans. Owen), CCEL

13.ctx: One of the best-loved blessings in Scripture, and the letter’s closing.
13.mean: ‘Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with every good thing to do His will. And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.’ It is the only mention of the resurrection in so many words in the whole letter. God equips us, and God works in us: our obedience is his work. The writer calls his letter a brief ‘word of exhortation’, mentions that ‘our brother Timothy has been released’, and sends greetings from ‘Those from Italy’.
13.big: The God who raised the great Shepherd will equip his people to do his will.
13.diff: The mention of Timothy and ‘those from Italy’ links the letter with Paul’s circle and possibly with Rome (see History & setting of Hebrews above).

1.ctx: Corinth was a wealthy, cosmopolitan port city in Greece, notorious for immorality. Paul founded the church around AD 50 and wrote this letter from Ephesus about AD 54, answering reports and a letter from the church.
1.mean: Paul and Sosthenes greet the church of God in Corinth, those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all who call on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ in every place.
1.big: A church full of problems is still addressed as God's holy people.
1.diff: Calling on 'the name of the Lord' was Old Testament language for worshipping God (Joel 2:32); Paul applies it to Jesus.

1.ctx: Paul's thanksgiving, even for a troubled church, prepares for the issues he will raise.
1.mean: Paul thanks God for the grace given them in Christ, enriched in all speech and knowledge, lacking no gift as they wait for Christ's revealing. God will sustain them to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom they were called into the fellowship of his Son.
1.big: God's faithfulness, not the church's performance, guarantees that he will finish what he began.

1.ctx: The first problem Paul addresses: factions formed around favourite leaders, as Greek philosophers attracted rival followings.
1.mean: Paul appeals for unity and no divisions. Some say 'I follow Paul', others 'Apollos', 'Cephas' or 'Christ'. Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? He is thankful he baptised few of them, for Christ sent him not to baptise but to preach the gospel, not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross be emptied of its power.
1.big: Loyalty to human leaders divides the church, which belongs to Christ alone.

1.ctx: Corinthian believers apparently prized rhetoric and philosophical wisdom, and some felt embarrassed by a crucified Messiah.
1.mean: Paul says the word of the cross is folly to those perishing, but to those being saved it is the power of God. Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. The foolishness of God is wiser than men.
1.big: The cross looks like weakness and foolishness, but it is God's power and wisdom for salvation.

1.ctx: Paul points to the church's own membership as evidence. Corinth's church included a few wealthy people, but most were ordinary workers, freedmen and slaves.
1.mean: Paul says not many of them were wise, powerful or of noble birth. God chose what is foolish, weak, low and despised to shame the wise and strong, so that no one may boast before him. Because of him they are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.
1.big: God chooses the unimpressive so that all glory goes to him and all boasting is in Christ.
1.diff: Reformed theology draws on verses 26–30 for God's sovereign, gracious choice — the church's very existence is 'because of him'.

2.ctx: Paul contrasts his own preaching in Corinth with the polished speakers the Corinthians admired.
2.mean: Paul says he did not come with lofty speech or wisdom, but decided to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified. He came in weakness and fear, and his message was in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that their faith might rest not in human wisdom but in the power of God.
2.big: Faith that rests on God's power, not on persuasive technique, is the kind that lasts.
2.h: Paul's Message by the Spirit's Power

2.ctx: Paul turns to the true wisdom God gives through the Spirit, in contrast to the Greek wisdom the Corinthians prized. 'Mature' may echo the language of mystery religions, reclaimed for the gospel.
2.mean: Paul says there is a wisdom he imparts to the mature, a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which none of the rulers of this age understood, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. What no eye has seen, God has revealed through the Spirit, for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit, for they are folly to him and spiritually discerned. We have the mind of Christ.
2.big: God's wisdom is understood only by the Spirit's revealing work.
2.diff: Verse 14 is cited in Reformed theology for the need of the Spirit's work before anyone can receive the gospel. 'The Lord of glory' in verse 8 is a divine title applied to the crucified Jesus.

3.ctx: Paul returns to the factions of chapter 1. Apollos was an eloquent Jewish preacher from Alexandria who had ministered in Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24–28).
3.mean: Paul says he could not address them as spiritual people but as infants in Christ, since there is jealousy and strife among them. What is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. They are God's field, God's building.
3.big: Leaders are only servants; God alone gives growth.

3.ctx: Paul develops the building image, with a warning for those who build on the foundation.
3.mean: Paul says like a skilled master builder he laid a foundation, and someone else builds on it. No one can lay any other foundation than Jesus Christ. Each one's work will be tested by fire on the Day; if it survives, he will receive a reward; if it is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
3.big: Everything must be built on Christ, and each person's work will be tested by God.
3.diff: Roman Catholic theology has cited verse 15 in connection with purgatory; Protestants read it as testing the quality of ministers' work at the final judgement, not purifying believers' souls. The passage concerns leaders' work first of all.

3.ctx: Paul warns that damaging the church is a serious matter. Corinth had many pagan temples, and destroying a temple was regarded as a grave crime.
3.mean: Paul says do you not know that you (plural) are God's temple and God's Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. The wisdom of this world is folly with God. So let no one boast in men. All things are yours — Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, the present, the future — and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.
3.big: The church is God's temple, and those who divide it answer to God.
3.diff: Here 'you' is plural and refers to the church as a whole; in 6:19 Paul applies the temple image to the individual believer's body.

4.ctx: Paul addresses the Corinthians' tendency to judge and rank their teachers.
4.mean: Paul says to regard apostles as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, and stewards must be found faithful. It is a small thing to be judged by them; he does not even judge himself. The Lord judges; do not pronounce judgement before the time. What do you have that you did not receive? Already you are rich, already kings! — while the apostles are like men condemned to death, fools for Christ's sake, the scum of the world.
4.big: Christian leaders answer to the Lord, and the apostles' suffering exposes the Corinthians' pride.

4.ctx: A change of tone, from the sharp irony of 4:8–13 to fatherly appeal. A 'guide' (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised children, unlike a father who had begotten them.
4.mean: Paul says he writes not to shame them but to admonish them as beloved children. They may have countless guides but not many fathers; he became their father in Christ through the gospel. So be imitators of me. He is sending Timothy to remind them of his ways in Christ, and will come soon.
4.big: Paul corrects the church as a father who brought them to faith.

5.ctx: A case of sexual sin the church was tolerating, perhaps even boasting about as an expression of freedom.
5.mean: Paul says there is sexual immorality among them of a kind not tolerated even among pagans: a man has his father's wife. They are arrogant instead of mourning. When they are assembled, with the power of the Lord Jesus, they are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. A little leaven leavens the whole lump. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
5.big: Tolerating open sin damages the whole church; discipline is meant to lead the sinner to salvation.
5.diff: 'Deliver to Satan' is generally understood as putting the man out of the church's fellowship into the world, with the aim of his repentance. 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 may describe a later restoration. Church discipline is a serious and sensitive matter best handled by a church's own leaders.

5.ctx: Paul clarifies a misunderstanding of an earlier letter he had written, now lost.
5.mean: Paul says he did not mean they should not associate with immoral people of this world, since then they would need to leave the world. He meant not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, reviling, drunkenness or swindling. God judges those outside; purge the evil person from among you.
5.big: The church is to hold its own members to account, not withdraw from unbelievers.

6.ctx: Corinthians were taking fellow believers to pagan courts, where wealthier people had the advantage.
6.mean: Paul asks how any of them dares take a grievance before the unrighteous instead of the saints. The saints will judge the world and even angels. To have lawsuits at all is already a defeat. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? Instead they wrong and defraud their own brothers.
6.big: Believers should settle disputes within the church, even at personal cost, rather than shame Christ publicly.

6.ctx: A warning about the lifestyle some Corinthians thought their freedom permitted.
6.mean: Paul says the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God: neither the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, men who practise homosexuality, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers or swindlers. And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
6.big: The gospel names sin plainly and transforms sinners: 'such were some of you, but you were washed'.
6.diff: The translation of the two Greek words in verse 9 behind 'men who practise homosexuality' is debated; most scholars understand them to refer to both partners in male same-sex sexual acts, which the historic church has consistently taught are outside God's design. Verse 11 makes clear the passage is addressed to a church full of forgiven people.

6.ctx: Some Corinthians argued that what they did with their bodies did not matter spiritually.
6.mean: Paul says flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
6.big: The body matters to God, is the Spirit's temple, and belongs to Christ who bought it.
6.h: The Temple of the Holy Spirit

7.ctx: Paul begins answering questions the Corinthians had written to him about. Some apparently taught that sex, even in marriage, was spiritually inferior.
7.mean: Paul says each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Husband and wife should give each other their conjugal rights, since each has authority over the other's body. He wishes all were single as he is, but each has his own gift. To the married he says, from the Lord, a wife should not separate from her husband. If a believer has an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay, they should not divorce; if the unbeliever leaves, the believer is not enslaved.
7.big: Marriage is good and mutual, and should be preserved wherever possible.
7.diff: Verse 15 is read by many Protestants as permitting divorce and remarriage when an unbelieving spouse deserts. Churches differ on grounds for remarriage, and this is best worked through with a church's own leadership.

7.ctx: A principle Paul applies to circumcision, slavery and marriage alike.
7.mean: Paul says each person should lead the life the Lord has assigned, and remain in the condition in which he was called. Circumcision and uncircumcision count for nothing, but keeping God's commandments. A slave who can gain freedom should take it. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men.
7.big: Christians need not change their outward station to serve God, because their calling in Christ matters more.

7.ctx: Paul turns to the unmarried and the widowed, in light of a 'present distress'.
7.mean: Paul says, as his judgement rather than a command, that it is good to remain as one is, because of the present distress and because the form of this world is passing away. The unmarried person can be anxious about the things of the Lord, the married about how to please their spouse. Marriage is not sin, but singleness allows undivided devotion. A widow may remarry, only in the Lord.
7.big: Both singleness and marriage are good, and singleness has particular freedoms for serving the Lord.
7.diff: The 'present distress' may have been a famine or persecution in Corinth. Paul distinguishes his own advice from the Lord's command, which is worth noticing.

8.ctx: Meat sold in Corinth's markets had often been offered to pagan gods, and social meals were held in temple dining rooms.
8.mean: Paul says knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. We know an idol has no real existence and there is no God but one. For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. But not everyone has this knowledge; some eat as if it were really offered to an idol, and their weak conscience is defiled. Take care that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak.
8.big: Love for a weaker brother matters more than the freedom that knowledge gives.
8.diff: Verse 6 takes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4 ('the LORD our God, the LORD is one') and divides its words between the Father ('God') and Jesus ('Lord'), placing Jesus within the identity of the one God.

9.ctx: Paul uses himself as an example of giving up rights for others, while defending his apostleship.
9.mean: Paul says he is an apostle who has seen the Lord. He has the right to be supported financially, like other apostles, and quotes the law: do not muzzle an ox while it treads the grain. But he has made no use of this right, rather enduring anything than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel. Necessity is laid on him; woe to him if he does not preach the gospel.
9.big: Paul gave up his own rights so that nothing would hinder the gospel.

9.ctx: The famous statement of Paul's missionary principle, set within a chapter about giving up his rights for the sake of others.
9.mean: Paul says though he is free from all, he has made himself a servant to all, that he might win more. To the Jews he became as a Jew, to those outside the law as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ), to the weak weak. He has become all things to all people, that by all means he might save some.
9.big: Paul adapts everything except the gospel itself in order to reach people.
9.diff: 'All things to all people' concerns cultural adaptation, not compromise of truth or morality — Paul immediately notes he remains under the law of Christ.

9.ctx: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics.
9.mean: Paul says in a race all run, but only one receives the prize; so run that you may obtain it. Athletes exercise self-control for a perishable wreath, we for an imperishable one. He disciplines his body and keeps it under control, lest after preaching to others he himself should be disqualified.
9.big: The Christian life demands disciplined, purposeful effort toward a lasting prize.
9.diff: Some read 'disqualified' as losing salvation, others as losing reward or approval for ministry. Reformed interpreters generally take it as the real warning that accompanies genuine perseverance.

10.ctx: Paul returns to the question of idol food, warning against overconfidence.
10.mean: Paul says Israel's fathers were all under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all ate the same spiritual food and drank from the spiritual Rock, and the Rock was Christ. Yet with most of them God was not pleased. These things were written as examples for us. Let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape.
10.big: Privileges do not guarantee faithfulness, but God is faithful to provide a way through every temptation.
10.diff: Verse 13 is often quoted out of context as 'God won't give you more than you can handle'. Its subject is temptation to sin, not suffering in general.

10.ctx: Paul now forbids participating in meals within pagan temples.
10.mean: Paul says flee from idolatry. The cup of blessing is a participation in the blood of Christ, the bread a participation in his body. Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. What pagans sacrifice they offer to demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.
10.big: Believers cannot share both in Christ's table and in pagan worship.
10.diff: Verses 16–17 are central to understanding the Lord's Supper as 'participation' (koinonia). Christian traditions understand this participation differently; all agree it is a real sharing in Christ and makes the church one body.

10.ctx: Paul sums up his principles for disputed matters. 'All things are lawful' seems to have been a Corinthian slogan, which Paul quotes and then qualifies.
10.mean: Paul says all things are lawful, but not all things are helpful or build up. Let no one seek his own good but the good of his neighbour. Eat whatever is sold in the market without raising questions of conscience. But if someone says 'this has been offered in sacrifice', do not eat it, for his conscience's sake. Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
10.big: Christian freedom is used for others' good and God's glory.

11.ctx: Head coverings carried social meaning in Corinth; uncovered women could be seen as immodest or rebellious.
11.mean: Paul says the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God. A man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonours his head; a woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonours hers. He grounds this in creation, yet adds that in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman, for all things are from God.
11.big: Paul wants worship to reflect the created differences between men and women, within their mutual dependence in the Lord.
11.diff: One of the hardest passages in Paul. Christians differ over whether head coverings are a permanent requirement or a cultural expression of a lasting principle; most churches today take the second view. 'Head' is read as authority by complementarians and as source by egalitarians. The passage assumes women pray and prophesy in the gathering.

11.ctx: The Lord's Supper was eaten as part of a real meal. Wealthier members, who could arrive early, apparently ate and drank before poorer members, such as slaves, finished work.
11.mean: Paul says their meetings do more harm than good. When they come together, one goes hungry and another gets drunk. He passes on what he received from the Lord: on the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread and said 'this is my body which is for you; do this in remembrance of me', and the cup: 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood'. As often as you eat and drink, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes. Whoever eats and drinks in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord. Let a person examine himself.
11.big: The Lord's Supper proclaims Christ's death and must be shared in a way that honours all his people.
11.diff: This is the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper, earlier than the Gospels. 'Discerning the body' (verse 29) is read as recognising Christ's presence in the Supper, or as recognising the church as Christ's body — the context of neglecting the poor favours the second. Christian traditions differ on the nature of Christ's presence.

12.ctx: The Corinthians prized spectacular gifts, especially speaking in tongues, as marks of spiritual status.
12.mean: Paul says no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says 'Jesus is accursed', and no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit. There are varieties of gifts but the same Spirit, varieties of service but the same Lord, varieties of activities but the same God. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation. All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.
12.big: Every gift comes from the one Spirit, for the good of the whole church, not for status.
12.diff: Verses 4–6 name Spirit, Lord and God together, one of the Trinitarian patterns in Paul. 'As he wills' presents the Spirit as a person who decides, not an impersonal force. Whether the more spectacular gifts continue today is debated between cessationists and continuationists.

12.ctx: Paul uses the image of a human body, a common image for a community in the ancient world.
12.mean: Paul says just as the body is one and has many members, so it is with Christ. In one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. The foot cannot say it does not belong because it is not a hand; the eye cannot say to the hand 'I have no need of you'. The parts that seem weaker are indispensable. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one is honoured, all rejoice together.
12.big: Every believer is a necessary part of Christ's body, and all share one another's sufferings and joys.
12.diff: 'Baptised in one Spirit' is read by most evangelicals as describing every believer's conversion, and by some Pentecostals as a later experience of empowering.

12.ctx: Paul applies the body image to the different roles and gifts God has given in the church.
12.mean: Paul says they are the body of Christ and individually members of it. God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, gifts of healing, helping, administrating and various kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Do all speak with tongues? Earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.
12.big: God gives different gifts to different people, and no single gift is expected of everyone.
12.diff: The question 'Do all speak with tongues?' expects the answer no, which is cited against the view that tongues is the necessary sign of receiving the Spirit. 'A still more excellent way' introduces chapter 13 on love.

13.ctx: Often read at weddings, this chapter was written to correct a church proud of its gifts but failing in love.
13.mean: Paul says if he speaks in tongues but has not love, he is a noisy gong; if he has prophecy, knowledge and faith to move mountains but not love, he is nothing. Love is patient and kind; it does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude; it does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it rejoices in the truth; it bears, believes, hopes and endures all things. Love never ends. Prophecies, tongues and knowledge will pass away when the perfect comes. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Faith, hope and love abide, and the greatest of these is love.
13.big: Without love, even the greatest gifts are worthless, and love will outlast them all.
13.diff: 'When the perfect comes' is read by most interpreters as Christ's return; some cessationists have read it as the completion of the New Testament, though many cessationists do not rest their case on this verse.

14.ctx: Paul applies the principle of love to the gifts the Corinthians were misusing, especially tongues.
14.mean: Paul says pursue love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy. One who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, but one who prophesies builds up the church. In church he would rather speak five words with his mind to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue. If uninterpreted tongues are spoken when outsiders come in, they will say you are out of your minds; but if all prophesy, the outsider is convicted and worships God.
14.big: Gifts used in the gathered church must build up others and be understandable.
14.diff: What New Testament tongues and prophecy were, and whether they continue, is debated. Most agree tongues in Acts 2 were known languages; whether Corinthian tongues were the same is discussed. All agree Paul's rule is that anything spoken must build up the church.

14.ctx: Practical instructions for orderly gatherings. Early Christians met in homes, where many people could contribute, and where disorder was easy.
14.mean: Paul says when they come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue or an interpretation; let all things be done for building up. Only two or three should speak in tongues, in turn, with interpretation; two or three prophets should speak, and others weigh what is said. God is not a God of confusion but of peace. The women should keep silent in the churches. All things should be done decently and in order.
14.big: Worship should be orderly and edifying, because it reflects the God of peace.
14.diff: Verses 34–35 on women keeping silent are among the hardest in Paul, since in chapter 11 he assumes women pray and prophesy. Readings include a restriction on judging prophecies, on disruptive questioning, or on authoritative teaching; a few scholars think the verses were added later, though they appear in all manuscripts. This is best discussed with a church's own leadership.

15.ctx: Some in Corinth denied the future bodily resurrection, probably influenced by Greek thought that saw the body as worthless.
15.mean: Paul reminds them of the gospel he delivered as of first importance, which he himself received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve, then to more than five hundred at one time, most of whom are still alive, then to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all to Paul.
15.big: The gospel rests on historical events: Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection and appearances to many witnesses.
15.diff: Verses 3–5 are widely recognised by scholars, including sceptical ones, as an early creed Paul received within a few years of the crucifixion — among the earliest evidence for belief in the resurrection. The note that most of the five hundred were still alive invited readers to check.

15.ctx: Paul exposes what denying the resurrection would mean. Some Corinthians believed Jesus rose but denied that believers' bodies would.
15.mean: Paul says if there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised. If Christ has not been raised, our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain; you are still in your sins; those who have died in Christ have perished. If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied.
15.big: Christianity stands or falls on the historical resurrection of Jesus.

15.ctx: Paul affirms the resurrection and sets out its sequence. 'Firstfruits' recalls the first sheaf of the harvest offered to God (Leviticus 23), guaranteeing the rest would follow.
15.mean: Paul says in fact Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive. Each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and power. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. When all things are subjected to him, the Son himself will also be subjected, that God may be all in all.
15.big: Christ's resurrection is the first of the harvest, guaranteeing the resurrection of all who belong to him.
15.diff: Verse 28, the Son being subjected to the Father, is cited by some to deny Christ's equality with God. The historic understanding is that it concerns the Son's role as mediator handing over the completed kingdom, not an inferior nature. Verse 29, 'baptism for the dead', is obscure, with dozens of proposed explanations.

15.ctx: Paul answers the question of what kind of body the resurrected will have.
15.mean: Paul says what you sow does not come to life unless it dies, and what you sow is a bare seed, not the body that is to be. So it is with the resurrection: sown perishable, raised imperishable; sown in dishonour, raised in glory; sown in weakness, raised in power; sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body. As we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
15.big: The resurrection body is continuous with the present one but transformed, as a plant is from its seed.
15.diff: 'Spiritual body' does not mean non-physical, but a body fully animated and governed by the Holy Spirit; the risen Jesus ate and could be touched.

15.ctx: The climax of the resurrection chapter, looking forward to Christ's return.
15.mean: Paul says flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God. He tells a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, at the last trumpet. The dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed. Then shall come to pass the saying: death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labour is not in vain.
15.big: Christ's victory over death means that nothing done for him is ever wasted.
15.diff: 'Flesh and blood' means human nature in its present mortal state, not physical bodies as such — the whole chapter insists on bodily resurrection. Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14.
15.h: Where, O Death, Is Your Victory?

16.ctx: The collection Paul was gathering from Gentile churches for poor believers in Jerusalem, a project he cared about deeply.
16.mean: Paul says on the first day of every week each should put something aside as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when he comes. He will send those they approve to take the gift to Jerusalem.
16.big: Regular, planned giving is part of the church's life, and binds Gentile and Jewish believers together.
16.diff: The mention of 'the first day of every week' is early evidence that Christians met on Sunday.

16.ctx: Paul's travel plans, which later changed (see 2 Corinthians 1).
16.mean: Paul says he will come after passing through Macedonia, perhaps staying the winter. He will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened, and there are many adversaries.
16.big: Paul plans his travels around gospel opportunities, even in the face of opposition.

16.ctx: Instructions about two co-workers. Timothy was young and sometimes timid, and the Corinthians had set Apollos up as a rival to Paul.
16.mean: Paul says if Timothy comes, see that he has nothing to fear, for he is doing the work of the Lord. As for Apollos, Paul urged him to visit, but it was not at all his will to come now.
16.big: Paul and Apollos, whom Corinthians had set up as rivals, are in fact colleagues.

16.ctx: A short summary of the whole letter's appeal, in five commands, written to a church divided, proud and careless in its conduct.
16.mean: Paul says be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love. He commends the household of Stephanas, the first converts in Achaia, who devoted themselves to serving the saints.
16.big: Strength and love belong together in Christian character.
16.diff: 'Act like men' calls for courage and maturity; Paul immediately joins it to love, which suits a men's group well.

16.ctx: The closing greetings. Paul signed the letter himself after a secretary wrote the rest.
16.mean: Paul sends greetings from the churches of Asia, from Aquila and Prisca and the church in their house. He writes the greeting with his own hand: if anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Maranatha — our Lord, come! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus.
16.big: The letter ends with a prayer for the Lord's return and a final word of love.
16.diff: 'Maranatha' is Aramaic, preserved untranslated in a Greek letter to Gentiles — evidence that the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers prayed to Jesus as Lord.

1.ctx: Written from Macedonia around AD 55–56, after a painful visit and a 'severe letter' (now lost). Paul's authority had been attacked by rival teachers in Corinth. It is the most personal and emotional of his letters.
1.mean: Paul, an apostle by the will of God, and Timothy greet the church of God at Corinth, with all the saints throughout Achaia.
1.big: Paul writes as an apostle by God's will, not by human appointment.
1.diff: Many scholars think 2 Corinthians combines more than one letter, noting sharp changes of tone, especially at chapter 10. Others read it as a single letter written over time. Its teaching does not depend on the answer.

1.ctx: Paul had recently come through a crisis in Asia so severe he expected to die (1:8).
1.mean: Paul blesses the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may comfort others with the comfort we receive. He was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired of life itself, but that was to make him rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead.
1.big: God comforts his people in affliction so that they can comfort others, and teaches them to rely on him alone.

1.ctx: Paul had changed his travel plans, and critics accused him of being unreliable and double-minded.
1.mean: Paul says he has behaved with simplicity and godly sincerity. His word is not 'yes and no', for the Son of God, Jesus Christ, was not 'yes and no', but in him it is always yes. All the promises of God find their yes in him. It is God who establishes us in Christ, has anointed us, has put his seal on us and given us his Spirit as a guarantee. He did not come because he wanted to spare them.
1.big: Every promise of God is fulfilled in Christ, and God has sealed his people with the Spirit as a guarantee.

2.ctx: Paul explains why he wrote a painful letter instead of visiting.
2.mean: Paul says he decided not to make another painful visit. He wrote out of much affliction and anguish, with many tears, not to cause pain but to let them know his love. The person who caused pain has been punished enough by the majority; now they should forgive and comfort him, so that he is not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow, and reaffirm their love for him, so that Satan does not outwit them.
2.big: Church discipline aims at restoration, and must be followed by forgiveness and comfort.
2.diff: Some identify the offender with the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5; others think he was someone who had personally opposed Paul during his painful visit.

2.ctx: Paul had been anxious waiting to hear from Titus how the Corinthians received his letter.
2.mean: Paul says thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere. We are the aroma of Christ, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things? We are not peddlers of God's word, but speak as commissioned by God.
2.big: The gospel's messengers spread the knowledge of Christ, which brings life to some and judgement to others.
2.diff: The image is of a Roman triumph, in which a victorious general paraded captives and incense was burned. Paul pictures himself as one of Christ's captives in the procession.

3.ctx: Paul's opponents apparently carried letters of recommendation and questioned Paul's credentials.
3.mean: Paul says he needs no letters of recommendation: the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, on tablets of human hearts. Their sufficiency is from God, who has made them ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
3.big: The changed lives of believers are the proof of a gospel ministry empowered by the Spirit.
3.diff: 'The letter kills' does not mean Scripture's plain meaning is harmful; Paul is contrasting the law written on stone, which exposed sin but could not give life, with the Spirit's work under the new covenant (Jeremiah 31).

3.ctx: Paul compares the ministry of Moses with the ministry of the new covenant, drawing on Exodus 34, where Moses' face shone after meeting God.
3.mean: Paul says if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that Israel could not gaze at Moses' face, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory? When one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another.
3.big: Believers see God's glory in Christ and are progressively transformed into his likeness by the Spirit.
3.diff: 'The Lord is the Spirit' has been discussed in relation to the Trinity. Most interpreters understand Paul to mean that 'the Lord' Moses turned to in Exodus 34 is now encountered through the Spirit — not that the Son and the Spirit are the same person.
3.h: The Glory of the New Covenant

4.ctx: Paul defends the openness of his ministry against accusations of trickery.
4.mean: Paul says having this ministry by God's mercy, they do not lose heart. They have renounced disgraceful underhanded ways and do not tamper with God's word. If the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, whose minds the god of this world has blinded. We proclaim not ourselves but Jesus Christ as Lord. For God, who said 'let light shine out of darkness', has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
4.big: The God who created light shines the knowledge of his glory into hearts through the face of Christ.
4.diff: Reformed theology draws on verses 4–6 for the need of God's direct work to open blinded minds — conversion as an act of new creation.

4.ctx: Paul explains why his own weakness is no argument against his ministry.
4.mean: Paul says we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. We are afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, persecuted but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed, always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that his life may also be manifested. So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. This light momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison, as we look to the things that are unseen and eternal.
4.big: God's power is displayed through human weakness, and present suffering prepares an eternal glory.

5.ctx: Paul continues the theme of wasting away and renewal, turning to death and what follows.
5.mean: Paul says if the earthly tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. In this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling. God has given us the Spirit as a guarantee. We would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. So we make it our aim to please him, for we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ.
5.big: Believers can face death with confidence, knowing they will be at home with the Lord, and live to please him.
5.diff: 'Away from the body and at home with the Lord' is one of the main texts for believers being with Christ immediately after death. The judgement seat of Christ here concerns believers giving account for how they have lived, not the question of their salvation.

5.ctx: The heart of the letter. Paul's opponents questioned his motives and sanity; he answers that Christ's love, shown in his death, is what drives him.
5.mean: Paul says the love of Christ controls us, because one has died for all, therefore all have died, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and was raised. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, the new has come. All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. We are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us: be reconciled to God. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
5.big: In Christ God reconciled the world to himself, and his people are sent as his ambassadors to plead with others to be reconciled.
5.diff: Verse 21 is often called 'the great exchange' and is central to the Reformed doctrine of substitution and imputation: Christ bore our sin, and his righteousness is counted to us. Some scholars understand 'made him to be sin' as 'made him a sin offering'. 'One died for all' features in debates about the extent of the atonement.

6.ctx: Paul appeals to the Corinthians not to waste God's grace, listing his hardships as proof of genuine ministry.
6.mean: Paul says do not receive the grace of God in vain; now is the favourable time, now is the day of salvation. As servants of God they commend themselves by great endurance, in afflictions, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labours, sleepless nights, hunger; by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing yet possessing everything. He opens his heart wide to them and asks them to do the same.
6.big: The marks of true ministry are endurance, love and joy through hardship, not outward success.

6.ctx: A short passage often applied to marriage and business partnerships. Corinth's social life was bound up with pagan temples, feasts and trade guilds dedicated to gods.
6.mean: Paul says do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. What partnership has righteousness with lawlessness, or light with darkness? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? We are the temple of the living God. Therefore go out from their midst and be separate, says the Lord, and I will welcome you, and be a father to you.
6.big: God's people are his temple and must not bind themselves in partnerships that compromise their faith.
6.diff: The image is of yoking two different animals together (Deuteronomy 22:10). Most Christians apply it to marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, though Paul's immediate concern seems to be involvement in pagan worship and with the false teachers. It does not tell believers to end existing marriages (compare 1 Corinthians 7:12–13).

7.ctx: Paul resumes the story of his anxious wait for Titus, broken off at 2:13.
7.mean: Paul says let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God. When he came into Macedonia he was afflicted at every turn, but God, who comforts the downcast, comforted him by the coming of Titus, with news of their longing and zeal for him. His letter grieved them, but only for a while, and he rejoices because their grief led to repentance. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
7.big: Godly sorrow over sin leads to repentance and life; worldly sorrow leads only to despair.

8.ctx: Paul returns to the collection for poor believers in Jerusalem, which the Corinthians had begun but not completed.
8.mean: Paul tells them about the churches of Macedonia, who in extreme poverty overflowed in generosity, giving beyond their means, begging to take part. He asks the Corinthians to excel in this grace too. You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. The goal is fairness: your abundance supplying their need.
8.big: Christian giving flows from the grace of Christ, who became poor to make us rich.
8.diff: Verse 9 is a brief but profound statement of the incarnation: the eternal Son's riches and his becoming poor as a man.

8.ctx: Paul explains the arrangements for handling the collection. Large sums were being carried across the Mediterranean, and suspicion of misuse was easy to arouse.
8.mean: Paul commends Titus and two brothers who will collect the gift. He says they take precautions so that no one should blame them about this generous gift, aiming at what is honourable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man.
8.big: Money given to God's work must be handled transparently and honourably before everyone.

9.ctx: Continuing the appeal about the collection, now with principles of giving.
9.mean: Paul says whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will reap bountifully. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency you may abound in every good work. This service supplies the saints' needs and overflows in thanksgiving to God. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
9.big: God loves cheerful, willing giving, and supplies generously to those who give.
9.diff: The 'sowing and reaping' principle is sometimes used to promise financial return for giving. In context Paul says God enriches givers so that they can be generous in every good work, and the 'harvest' is righteousness and thanksgiving to God.

10.ctx: A sharp change of tone. From here to chapter 13 Paul confronts the rival teachers and defends his apostleship.
10.mean: Paul says by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, he who is humble face to face but bold when away. Though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. The weapons of our warfare have divine power to destroy strongholds. We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ. His opponents say his letters are weighty but his bodily presence weak. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.
10.big: The church's battle is fought with spiritual weapons that bring every thought into obedience to Christ.
10.diff: Verses 4–5 are often applied to spiritual warfare generally; in context the 'strongholds' are arguments and pretensions raised against the knowledge of God, including those of the false teachers.

11.ctx: Paul reluctantly engages in 'foolish' boasting to answer the rival teachers, whom he calls 'super-apostles'.
11.mean: Paul says he feels a divine jealousy for them, having betrothed them to Christ, but fears they are being led astray, accepting another Jesus, a different spirit and a different gospel. He preached to them free of charge. Such men are false apostles, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ; no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
11.big: False teachers can look impressive and spiritual; the test is whether they preach the true Jesus.
11.diff: Paul's warning about 'another Jesus' and 'a different gospel' is often applied today to groups that use Christian language while denying Christ's deity, such as Jehovah's Witnesses and Mormonism.

11.ctx: Paul lists his sufferings as his real credentials, in deliberate contrast to the opponents' boasting.
11.mean: Paul says he speaks as a fool. Are they Hebrews? So is he. Servants of Christ? He is a better one: far greater labours, far more imprisonments, countless beatings, often near death. Five times he received thirty-nine lashes, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and a day adrift at sea; in danger from rivers, robbers, his own people and Gentiles; in toil, hunger, cold and exposure. And daily the pressure of anxiety for all the churches. If he must boast, he will boast of the things that show his weakness — even his escape from Damascus in a basket.
11.big: Paul's credentials as an apostle are his sufferings for Christ, not his achievements.
11.diff: Most of these sufferings are not recorded in Acts, a reminder of how much of Paul's life we do not know.

12.ctx: Paul's opponents apparently boasted of visions and revelations.
12.mean: Paul says he knows a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven — whether in the body or out of the body he does not know — into paradise, and heard things that cannot be told. On behalf of this man he will boast, but on his own behalf only of his weaknesses.
12.big: Paul refuses to build his authority on spiritual experiences, however extraordinary.
12.diff: Most interpreters agree the 'man' is Paul himself, speaking indirectly out of modesty. 'The third heaven' means the highest heaven, the presence of God.

12.ctx: The passage that has comforted countless believers in chronic suffering.
12.mean: Paul says to keep him from becoming conceited, a thorn was given him in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass him. Three times he pleaded with the Lord to remove it. But he said: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Therefore he will boast all the more gladly of his weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon him. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
12.big: God's grace is sufficient in suffering that is not removed, and his power is displayed in human weakness.
12.diff: The thorn is unidentified; suggestions include an eye condition, epilepsy, recurring illness, or persistent opposition. Paul's prayer being answered with 'no' — and the thorn being described both as given and as from Satan — shows how God's purposes and evil can be at work in the same event.

12.ctx: Paul turns from boasting to his pastoral concern for the church.
12.mean: Paul says they forced him to be a fool. He is not inferior to the super-apostles, and the signs of a true apostle were performed among them. He is coming a third time and will not be a burden; he seeks not what is theirs but them. He will most gladly spend and be spent for their souls. He fears he may find quarrelling, jealousy, slander and unrepented sin among them.
12.big: Paul's concern is not for himself but for the church's spiritual health.

13.ctx: Paul prepares for his third visit, when he will deal with unrepentant sin.
13.mean: Paul says every charge must be established by two or three witnesses. He will not spare those who sinned before. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God, and they too are weak in him but will live with him by God's power. Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Do you not realise that Jesus Christ is in you?
13.big: Believers are called to examine themselves honestly to see whether they are truly in the faith.
13.diff: Self-examination is meant to lead to assurance in Christ, not endless anxiety; Paul expects them to find that Christ is in them.

13.ctx: The letter closes with a final appeal and a well-known benediction.
13.mean: Paul says aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
13.big: The letter ends with the whole Trinity: the grace of Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit.
13.diff: Verse 14 is one of the clearest Trinitarian statements in the New Testament and is used as a blessing in churches every week.

1.ctx: Written by John, traditionally the apostle, from exile on the island of Patmos, probably in the 90s under Domitian, to seven real churches in Asia Minor facing pressure to worship the emperor. It belongs to a kind of writing called apocalyptic, which uses vivid symbols to unveil spiritual realities.
1.mean: John says this is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants what must soon take place. Blessed is the one who reads aloud and those who hear and keep what is written, for the time is near.
1.big: The book is an unveiling of Jesus Christ, given to strengthen churches under pressure.
1.diff: Christians read Revelation in four main ways. Preterists see it as chiefly about events in John's own day, especially Rome; historicists as a map of church history; futurists as mostly about a final period before Christ returns; idealists as a symbolic picture of the church's struggle in every age. Many interpreters combine elements. This group would not make any of them a test of fellowship, and the book's central message is clear on all four: Christ reigns and will win.

1.ctx: The greeting, unusual because it comes from the Trinity in vivid terms.
1.mean: John greets the seven churches with grace and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, from the seven spirits before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and freed us from our sins by his blood, and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father — to him be glory for ever. Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him. 'I am the Alpha and the Omega,' says the Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.
1.big: The risen Christ, who freed his people by his blood, is coming visibly as ruler of all earthly kings.
1.diff: 'The seven spirits' is usually understood as the Holy Spirit in his fullness (seven being the number of completeness). The titles Alpha and Omega, first and last, are used both of God and of Jesus across the book (compare 22:13).

1.ctx: John, a fellow sufferer, receives a vision of the risen Christ.
1.mean: John says he was on Patmos on account of the word of God, and on the Lord's day he heard a loud voice. Turning, he saw one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, clothed in a long robe, his hair white like wool, his eyes like flame, his feet like burnished bronze, his voice like many waters, holding seven stars, his face like the sun. John fell at his feet as though dead, and he said: fear not, I am the first and the last, the living one. I died, and behold I am alive for evermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.
1.big: The risen Christ walks among his churches, holding the keys of death itself.
1.diff: John describes him as 'one like a son of man' from Daniel 7:13, then with the white hair Daniel 7:9 gives to the Ancient of Days — a deliberate joining of the two figures. 'The Lord's day' is the earliest clear reference to Sunday as the Christian day of worship.

2.ctx: Ephesus was the leading city of the province, where Paul had ministered for three years. Each of the seven letters follows a pattern: a description of Christ, what he knows, a commendation or rebuke, a command, and a promise to the one who conquers.
2.mean: Christ commends Ephesus for their works, toil and patient endurance, and for testing false apostles. But he has this against them: they have abandoned the love they had at first. Remember, repent and do the works you did at first, or he will remove their lampstand. To the one who conquers he will give to eat of the tree of life.
2.big: Sound doctrine and hard work are not enough if love has been lost.

2.ctx: Smyrna was a wealthy city loyal to Rome, with a significant Jewish population hostile to Christians. Christ says nothing against this church.
2.mean: Christ says he knows their tribulation and poverty — but they are rich. He knows the slander of those who say they are Jews and are not. Do not fear what you are about to suffer; the devil is about to throw some into prison, and they will have tribulation for ten days. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
2.big: Christ does not promise to spare his suffering people, but to keep them through death into life.
2.diff: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was martyred there in the second century, having served Christ for eighty-six years.

2.ctx: Pergamum was the centre of emperor worship in Asia, with a great altar to Zeus — possibly 'Satan's throne'.
2.mean: Christ says he knows where they dwell, where Satan's throne is, and that they held fast even when Antipas was killed. But some hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Israel to eat food sacrificed to idols and practise sexual immorality, and some hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Repent, or he will war against them with the sword of his mouth. To the one who conquers he will give hidden manna and a white stone with a new name.
2.big: Faithfulness under persecution does not excuse tolerating false teaching within the church.

2.ctx: Thyatira was a city of trade guilds, whose feasts involved idol worship and often immorality — hard for Christian tradesmen to avoid.
2.mean: Christ commends their love, faith, service and patient endurance, and that their latter works exceed the first. But he rebukes them for tolerating 'Jezebel', who calls herself a prophetess and teaches his servants to practise sexual immorality and eat food sacrificed to idols. He gave her time to repent. He is the one who searches mind and heart, and will give to each according to their works. To the one who conquers he will give authority over the nations, and the morning star.
2.big: Christ searches hearts, and will not let false teaching inside the church go unjudged.

3.ctx: Sardis was a city with a proud past but in decline, whose citadel had twice been captured because its watchmen slept.
3.mean: Christ says they have the reputation of being alive, but are dead. Wake up and strengthen what remains, for he has not found their works complete. If they will not wake, he will come like a thief. Yet a few have not soiled their garments, and they will walk with him in white. The one who conquers will be clothed in white, and Christ will never blot his name out of the book of life but will confess his name before his Father.
3.big: A reputation for spiritual life is worth nothing if the reality has gone.
3.diff: Verse 5 is discussed in relation to whether names can be removed from the book of life. Reformed interpreters read the promise as assurance rather than as implying that true believers can be blotted out.

3.ctx: Philadelphia was a smaller city, prone to earthquakes, whose Christians faced opposition from the local synagogue.
3.mean: Christ, the holy one, who has the key of David, says he has set before them an open door that no one can shut. They have little power but have kept his word and not denied his name. Because they have kept his word about patient endurance, he will keep them from the hour of trial coming on the whole world. Hold fast what you have. The one who conquers he will make a pillar in God's temple.
3.big: Christ opens doors for weak but faithful churches that no opposition can close.
3.diff: Verse 10 is used by some futurist interpreters to support believers being removed before a tribulation; others read it as God preserving his people through trial, as in John 17:15.

3.ctx: Laodicea was rich in banking, textiles and eye ointment. Its water came by aqueduct and arrived lukewarm — unlike the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis or the cold water of Colossae.
3.mean: Christ, the Amen, the faithful witness, the beginning of God's creation, says he knows their works: neither cold nor hot, and he will spit them out. They say they are rich and need nothing, not knowing they are wretched, poor, blind and naked. He counsels them to buy from him gold refined by fire, white garments and salve for their eyes. Those he loves he reproves and disciplines. Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with him.
3.big: Self-sufficient religion is useless to Christ, who still stands at the door and calls.
3.diff: 'The beginning of God's creation' is cited by Jehovah's Witnesses to argue Christ was created. The Greek word can mean 'origin' or 'ruler', and most scholars read it as source or ruler of creation, consistent with John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16. Verse 20 is addressed to a church, though it is often used as an invitation to individuals.

4.ctx: The vision shifts from earth to heaven. Before any judgement is described, John is shown who sits on the throne.
4.mean: John is called up through an open door in heaven and sees a throne with one seated on it, with the appearance of jasper and carnelian, encircled by a rainbow. Around it are twenty-four elders on thrones, clothed in white with golden crowns.
4.big: Before anything else happens, the reader is shown that God is on his throne.
4.diff: The twenty-four elders are usually understood as representing the whole people of God — twelve tribes and twelve apostles — or as an angelic order.

4.ctx: The worship of heaven, drawing on Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1. The four living creatures resemble the cherubim Ezekiel saw beside God's throne.
4.mean: From the throne come flashes of lightning and peals of thunder. Before it burn seven torches, the seven spirits of God. Four living creatures, full of eyes, never cease to say: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come. The elders cast their crowns before the throne, saying: worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honour and power, for you created all things.
4.big: God is worshipped as holy and worthy because he is the Creator of all things.

5.ctx: The central scene of the book, and the point on which everything turns.
5.mean: John sees a scroll sealed with seven seals, and weeps loudly because no one is found worthy to open it. An elder says: weep no more; the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered. But when John looks, he sees a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and seven eyes. The Lamb takes the scroll, and the living creatures and elders fall down and sing a new song: worthy are you, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and made them a kingdom and priests.
5.big: The Lion conquers as a slain Lamb — the cross is how God wins.
5.diff: John hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb; most interpreters take this as the interpretive key to the whole book. 'Ransomed people from every tribe' is discussed in relation to the extent of the atonement: Reformed interpreters note it says people 'from' every nation rather than all people.

5.ctx: The worship widens from the elders and living creatures to countless angels and then to every creature in existence.
5.mean: John hears thousands upon thousands of angels saying: worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing. Then every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth says: to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and might for ever.
5.big: The Lamb receives the same worship as the one on the throne.
5.diff: That the Lamb is worshipped alongside God, in a book that repeatedly forbids worshipping anyone but God (19:10, 22:9), is a strong statement of Christ's deity.

6.ctx: The Lamb begins to open the seals. The first four bring four horsemen, drawing on Zechariah 1 and 6.
6.mean: The first seal reveals a white horse whose rider has a bow and a crown, going out conquering.
6.big: Conquest is the first of the forces let loose in a fallen world.
6.diff: The rider on the white horse is identified by some as Christ (compare 19:11), and by others — more commonly — as conquest or false messianic power, since he is grouped with war, famine and death.
6.h: The First Seal: The White Horse

6.ctx: The second seal. The four horsemen echo Zechariah 6, where coloured horses patrol the earth as God's agents.
6.mean: A red horse appears, and its rider is permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another; he is given a great sword.
6.big: War is one of the recurring judgements of history.

6.ctx: The third seal. A quart of wheat for a denarius was about a day's wages for a day's food — famine prices for the poor.
6.mean: A black horse appears, its rider holding scales, and a voice announces a day's wages for a quart of wheat, with oil and wine not to be harmed — famine prices for staples while luxuries continue.
6.big: Famine falls hardest on the poor while the wealthy are untouched.

6.ctx: The fourth seal. Sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts are the four judgements listed together in Ezekiel 14:21.
6.mean: A pale horse appears, its rider named Death, with Hades following, given authority over a quarter of the earth to kill with sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts.
6.big: Death follows in the train of war and famine, but its authority is limited and given.

6.ctx: The fifth seal turns from earth to heaven, to believers already killed for their faith. Under the Old Testament altar the blood of sacrifices was poured out.
6.mean: John sees under the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God, crying out: how long before you judge and avenge our blood? They are each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants should be complete.
6.big: The martyrs' cry for justice is heard, and the answer is 'not yet'.
6.diff: The cry 'how long' echoes the psalms of lament. The passage shows that those who have died in Christ are conscious and with him.

6.ctx: The sixth seal brings cosmic upheaval, using language the prophets used for God's decisive interventions in history (Isaiah 13:10, 34:4; Joel 2:31).
6.mean: There is a great earthquake, the sun becomes black, the moon like blood, the stars fall, the sky vanishes. Kings, generals, the rich and the slave alike hide in caves, calling to the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the face of him who is seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?
6.big: No status protects anyone on the day of God's judgement.
6.diff: This language of shaken heavens is drawn from the prophets (Isaiah 34, Joel 2), where it often describes God's decisive intervention in history as well as the end.

7.ctx: An interlude between the sixth and seventh seals, answering the question 'who can stand?'
7.mean: Four angels hold back the winds until the servants of God are sealed on their foreheads. John hears the number: 144,000 from every tribe of Israel, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes.
7.big: God marks and protects his own before judgement falls.
7.diff: The 144,000 are understood by most interpreters as a symbolic number for the whole people of God — twelve tribes multiplied by twelve apostles by a thousand. Some take them as literal Jewish believers. Jehovah's Witnesses teach that only 144,000 go to heaven; the following verses describe a countless multitude in heaven, which tells against that reading.

7.ctx: The scene shifts from the sealed number to what John actually sees.
7.mean: John sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and the Lamb, clothed in white with palm branches, crying: salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb. These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. They will hunger no more, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
7.big: The countless multitude from every nation is the same people God sealed, safe before his throne.

8.ctx: The seventh seal opens, leading into a second sequence of seven. The silence heightens the suspense after six seals of judgement.
8.mean: There is silence in heaven for about half an hour. Seven angels are given trumpets. Another angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints, and then throws the censer filled with fire onto the earth.
8.big: The prayers of God's people are part of what sets God's judgements in motion.

8.ctx: The first four trumpets, which recall the plagues on Egypt in Exodus 7–10, now falling on a world that has enslaved itself rather than God's people.
8.mean: Hail and fire burn a third of the earth; a burning mountain destroys a third of the sea; a star called Wormwood poisons a third of the waters; a third of the sun, moon and stars are struck. An eagle cries 'woe, woe, woe' for those who dwell on the earth.
8.big: God's judgements are partial and warning in nature, striking a third rather than all.

9.ctx: The fifth trumpet, the first of three 'woes'. The imagery draws on the locust plague of Joel 1–2, which darkened the sky like an invading army.
9.mean: A star fallen from heaven opens the shaft of the bottomless pit, and smoke rises. Locusts come out with power like scorpions, told not to harm vegetation but only people without God's seal, tormenting them for five months. Their king is the angel of the bottomless pit, named Abaddon or Apollyon.
9.big: Even the forces of destruction operate only within limits God sets.
9.diff: The imagery draws on the locust plague of Joel. Readings vary widely: demonic forces, invading armies, or symbolic torment.

9.ctx: The sixth trumpet, the second woe. The Euphrates marked the eastern boundary of the Roman empire, from beyond which invasion was most feared.
9.mean: Four angels bound at the Euphrates are released, with an army of two hundred million cavalry. A third of mankind is killed. Yet the rest did not repent of their idolatry, murders, sorceries, immorality or thefts.
