9.big: The point of the passage is not the horrors themselves but that people still would not repent.

10.ctx: An interlude between the sixth and seventh trumpets, as there was between the sixth and seventh seals.
10.mean: A mighty angel comes down with a little scroll open in his hand. Seven thunders sound, but John is told to seal up what they said and not write it. The angel swears that there will be no more delay. John is told to take and eat the scroll; it is sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach, and he must prophesy again about many peoples and nations.
10.big: God's word is sweet to receive and bitter to deliver, because it contains judgement as well as hope.
10.diff: Ezekiel was given a scroll to eat in the same way (Ezekiel 2–3). That John may not write what the thunders said is a reminder that God has not revealed everything.
10.h: The Angel and the Small Scroll

11.ctx: One of the most debated passages in the book. If written before AD 70 the temple still stood; if later, John is using the temple as a symbol of God's people.
11.mean: John is told to measure the temple of God and the altar, but not the outer court, which is given to the nations who will trample the holy city for forty-two months. Two witnesses will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth. They are the two olive trees and lampstands, with power to shut the sky, turn waters to blood and strike the earth — recalling Moses and Elijah.
11.big: God's witnesses are protected and empowered to testify through a limited period of opposition.
11.diff: The two witnesses have been identified as Moses and Elijah, as two future individuals, or — most commonly among interpreters today — as a symbol of the witnessing church. The recurring period (forty-two months, 1,260 days, three and a half years) comes from Daniel and is generally read as a limited time of trial.

11.ctx: The witnesses are killed and then vindicated. 'The great city' is identified as the place where their Lord was crucified, and called Sodom and Egypt.
11.mean: When they have finished their testimony, the beast rises from the pit and kills them. Their bodies lie in the street of the great city for three and a half days while people rejoice. Then the breath of life from God enters them, they stand up, and are called up to heaven. In that hour a great earthquake strikes, and the rest are terrified and give glory to God.
11.big: God's witnesses may be silenced for a time, but God vindicates them publicly.

11.ctx: The seventh trumpet sounds, completing the second sequence of seven and announcing the outcome toward which the whole book moves.
11.mean: Loud voices in heaven say: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever. The elders worship God, saying he has begun to reign; the nations raged, but his wrath has come, the time for judging the dead and rewarding his servants. God's temple in heaven is opened, and the ark of his covenant is seen.
11.big: The decisive announcement of the book: the world's kingdom has become Christ's, and he reigns for ever.
11.diff: Handel set verse 15 in the Hallelujah chorus. The verbs announce the outcome as already accomplished, though the book still has much to describe.

12.ctx: The centre of the book, retelling the whole conflict in symbol. Chapters 12–14 step back from the sequences of seals and trumpets.
12.mean: A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, cries out in labour. A great red dragon with seven heads waits to devour her child. She gives birth to a male child who is to rule all nations with a rod of iron, and he is caught up to God and to his throne. The woman flees into the wilderness, where she is nourished for 1,260 days.
12.big: Satan's attempt to destroy the Messiah failed, and God protects his people.
12.diff: The woman is most often understood as the people of God — Israel giving birth to the Messiah, and then the church. Some see Mary. The child is plainly Christ, described with Psalm 2.

12.ctx: The war in heaven, explaining what lies behind earthly conflict.
12.mean: Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who is thrown down — that ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world, and the accuser of our brothers. A loud voice says salvation has come, for the accuser has been thrown down, and they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.
12.big: Believers overcome Satan not by their own strength but by the blood of the Lamb and faithful testimony.
12.diff: Verse 9 identifies the dragon plainly as Satan. Many interpreters connect this casting down with Christ's death and resurrection (compare John 12:31), rather than with a fall before creation.

12.ctx: Having failed to destroy the Messiah, the dragon turns on his people. The wilderness recalls Israel's protection after the exodus.
12.mean: The dragon pursues the woman, who is given wings to fly to the wilderness. He pours water like a river after her, but the earth helps her. Then the dragon becomes furious and goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring, those who keep God's commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
12.big: Satan's war against God's people is real, but he attacks only because he has already been defeated.

13.ctx: The dragon's agents: two beasts, drawing on Daniel 7. For John's first readers, the imperial power of Rome and its enforced worship would have been the immediate reference.
13.mean: A beast rises from the sea with ten horns and seven heads and blasphemous names. The dragon gives it his power and throne. One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound that was healed, and the whole earth followed it, worshipping the dragon and the beast. It was allowed to make war on the saints and conquer them, and authority was given over every tribe and nation. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
13.big: Political power that demands worship is Satan's instrument, and God's people endure rather than resist it with the same weapons.

13.ctx: The second beast, later called the false prophet (16:13). For John's readers this would have suggested the local priesthood promoting emperor worship.
13.mean: Another beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon. It exercises the first beast's authority and makes the earth worship it, performing great signs, deceiving people, and telling them to make an image of the beast, which it gives breath so that it can speak and cause those who will not worship it to be slain.
13.big: False religion serves worldly power by making its worship look attractive and convincing.

13.ctx: The mark of the beast. Trade guilds and markets in Asia Minor were bound up with civic religion, so refusing to honour the emperor could cost a believer their trade.
13.mean: The second beast causes all, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark. This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
13.big: Refusing to give worldly power the worship due to God may cost believers their livelihood.
13.diff: The most widely held explanation is that 666 encodes 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which matches a variant spelling and supports this. Others see it as symbolic of persistent falling short of seven, the number of completeness. Futurist readings expect a literal future mark. The mark contrasts with the seal of God on his servants' foreheads in chapter 7.

14.ctx: A deliberate contrast with the mark of the beast just described.
14.mean: John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000 who have his name and his Father's name on their foreheads. They sing a new song that no one else can learn. They are described as those who have not defiled themselves, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes, redeemed as firstfruits, in whose mouth no lie was found.
14.big: Those marked as God's own belong to the Lamb and follow him faithfully.
14.diff: The language about not defiling themselves with women is generally understood as symbolic purity — faithfulness rather than spiritual adultery with idolatry — not a claim that marriage defiles.

14.ctx: Three angels announce the gospel, the fall of Babylon and a warning.
14.mean: An angel flies with an eternal gospel to proclaim to every nation, saying: fear God and give him glory, for the hour of his judgement has come. A second says: fallen, fallen is Babylon the great. A third warns that whoever worships the beast will drink the wine of God's wrath. Here is a call for the endurance of the saints. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on; they rest from their labours, and their deeds follow them.
14.big: Even in the middle of judgement, the gospel goes out to every nation as an invitation.
14.h: The Three Angels and Babylon's Fall

14.ctx: Two harvests, drawing on Joel 3:13, where the sickle and winepress picture God's judgement on the nations.
14.mean: One like a son of man sits on a cloud with a golden crown and a sharp sickle, and the earth is reaped. Then another angel gathers the grape harvest and throws it into the great winepress of the wrath of God, which is trodden outside the city.
14.big: History ends in a harvest, gathering some in and treading others out.
14.diff: The two harvests are read by some as the gathering of the saved and the judgement of the wicked, and by others as two images of the same judgement.

15.ctx: A brief scene of worship before the final series of judgements.
15.mean: John sees those who had conquered the beast standing beside a sea of glass, singing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb: great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the nations. All nations will come and worship you.
15.big: The redeemed sing of God's justice, joining the song of the exodus to the song of the Lamb.
15.diff: The song of Moses recalls Exodus 15, sung after passing through the sea — the pattern of rescue through judgement.
15.h: The Song of Moses and the Lamb

15.ctx: The seven angels are given the bowls of God's wrath. The 'tent of witness' recalls the wilderness tabernacle, the place of God's presence and of atonement.
15.mean: The sanctuary in heaven is opened, and seven angels come out with seven plagues, given golden bowls full of the wrath of God. The sanctuary is filled with smoke from the glory of God, and no one can enter until the seven plagues are finished.
15.big: God's final judgements proceed from his own holiness.

16.ctx: The seven bowls, echoing the plagues on Egypt more closely than the trumpets did. Unlike the trumpets, these are complete rather than partial.
16.mean: The bowls bring sores on those with the mark of the beast, the sea and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat, darkness on the beast's kingdom, and the drying up of the Euphrates. Three unclean spirits like frogs go out to assemble the kings for battle at Armageddon. Still people curse God and do not repent. An interruption says: behold, I am coming like a thief; blessed is the one who stays awake.
16.big: God's judgements are just, yet even complete judgement does not by itself produce repentance.
16.diff: 'Armageddon' probably refers to the region of Megiddo, a historic battlefield in Israel. Interpreters differ over whether it names a literal future battle or symbolises the final conflict between God and evil.
16.h: The First Six Bowls of Wrath

16.ctx: The seventh bowl, completing the third and final sequence of seven judgements. 'It is done' echoes the cry from the cross in John 19:30.
16.mean: A loud voice from the throne says 'It is done!' There are lightnings, thunders and the greatest earthquake ever. The great city is split, and Babylon is remembered before God, who gives her the cup of the fury of his wrath. Islands and mountains flee, and great hailstones fall.
16.big: God's judgement on the great city that opposed him is complete.

17.ctx: Chapters 17–18 describe the fall of 'Babylon', the great city opposed to God.
17.mean: An angel shows John a woman seated on a scarlet beast, arrayed in purple and scarlet, holding a golden cup full of abominations, with a name on her forehead: Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes. She is drunk with the blood of the saints.
17.big: The power that seduces the world and persecutes the church is described as a prostitute, not a queen.
17.diff: Most interpreters read Babylon here as Rome for John's first readers, and as a symbol of every seductive, oppressive worldly system since. Some Protestant interpreters historically identified her with the papacy; most today do not.

17.ctx: The angel explains the vision. Rome was known as the city on seven hills, and its emperors were commonly listed by succession.
17.mean: The angel explains that the seven heads are seven hills on which the woman is seated, and also seven kings. The beast that was and is not is an eighth. The ten horns are ten kings who receive authority for one hour and give it to the beast; they will make war on the Lamb.
17.big: Worldly powers unite against Christ, but only for an hour and only by permission.
17.diff: Rome was famously the city on seven hills, which is why most scholars see it in view. Attempts to identify the seven kings with particular emperors have produced many different schemes.

17.ctx: A single verse of triumph set in the middle of the explanation, interrupting the description of the beast's power.
17.mean: The angel says they will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful. The waters are peoples and nations. In the end the beast and the kings will turn on the prostitute and destroy her, for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose.
17.big: The Lamb defeats every power arrayed against him, and even their infighting serves God's purpose.

18.ctx: A long lament over Babylon's fall, echoing the prophets' oracles against Babylon and Tyre.
18.mean: An angel announces: fallen, fallen is Babylon the great. A voice from heaven says: come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins and share her plagues. Her sins are heaped high as heaven.
18.big: God's people must separate themselves from a system built on greed and injustice.

18.ctx: Three groups mourn Babylon's fall — kings, merchants and sailors.
18.mean: The kings who committed immorality with her weep; the merchants weep because no one buys their cargo — gold, silver, jewels, fine cloth, spices, wine, cattle, chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls; the shipmasters cry out at the sight of the smoke.
18.big: Every mourner laments lost trade, not lost people — which is the indictment.
18.diff: The cargo list ends with 'slaves, that is, human souls' (verse 13), placing human beings at the end of a list of merchandise — a pointed judgement on an economy built on people.

18.ctx: The final word on Babylon, echoing Jeremiah 51:63–64, where a scroll weighted with a stone was thrown into the Euphrates as a sign of Babylon's fall.
18.mean: A mighty angel throws a great millstone into the sea, saying Babylon will be thrown down with violence and found no more. The sound of music, craftsmen, mills, lamps and weddings will be heard in her no more. In her was found the blood of prophets and saints.
18.big: The city that shed the blood of God's people is silenced for ever.

19.ctx: Heaven's response to Babylon's fall. After eighteen chapters, this is the first time 'Hallelujah' — 'praise the LORD' — appears in the New Testament.
19.mean: A great multitude cries Hallelujah: salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgements are true and just; he has judged the great prostitute and avenged the blood of his servants. The elders and living creatures worship, and a voice says: praise our God, all you his servants.
19.big: Heaven praises God because his judgements are just and his people are vindicated.
19.diff: 'Hallelujah' appears four times here and nowhere else in the New Testament.

19.ctx: The marriage supper of the Lamb. The Old Testament repeatedly pictures God as the husband of his people (Isaiah 54; Hosea 2), a picture Paul applies to Christ and the church.
19.mean: A great multitude cries: Hallelujah, for the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure — the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. John falls to worship the angel, who says: you must not do that; I am a fellow servant. Worship God.
19.big: History's goal is a wedding: Christ united with his people.
19.diff: The angel's refusal of worship (and again at 22:9) contrasts sharply with the worship of the Lamb in chapter 5 — an argument for Christ's deity.

19.ctx: The return of Christ, in deliberate contrast to the first rider of 6:2. Heaven itself opens, and the rider is named.
19.mean: Heaven opens, and a white horse appears whose rider is called Faithful and True. In righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like flame, on his head are many diadems, and he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood. His name is called The Word of God. The armies of heaven follow him on white horses in fine linen. From his mouth comes a sharp sword to strike the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. On his robe and thigh is written: King of kings and Lord of lords.
19.big: Christ returns openly as the victorious King and Judge.
19.diff: His robe is dipped in blood before any battle begins, which many take as his own blood — he conquers by the cross. His only weapon is the sword from his mouth, his word.
19.h: The Rider on the White Horse

19.ctx: The defeat of the beast and false prophet, described with imagery from Ezekiel 39, where birds are summoned to feast after God's victory.
19.mean: An angel calls the birds to the great supper of God. The beast and the kings gather to make war against the rider and his army. The beast is captured, and with it the false prophet, and both are thrown alive into the lake of fire. The rest are slain by the sword from the rider's mouth.
19.big: The final conflict ends without a struggle: Christ speaks, and it is over.
19.h: Defeat of the Beast and False Prophet

20.ctx: The most debated chapter in the book, and the source of the millennial positions.
20.mean: An angel seizes the dragon, that ancient serpent, binds him for a thousand years and throws him into the pit, so that he might not deceive the nations any longer. John sees thrones, and the souls of those beheaded for their testimony, who came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who shares in it; over them the second death has no power.
20.big: Christ's people reign with him, and death has no power over them.
20.diff: Amillennialists read the thousand years as the present age between Christ's first and second comings, with Satan restrained from deceiving the nations and departed believers reigning with Christ. Postmillennialists expect a coming era of gospel success before Christ returns. Premillennialists expect a literal reign on earth after his return. All three have been held by faithful Christians throughout church history, and this group does not make it a test of fellowship.

20.ctx: Satan's final defeat. Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel 38–39, where they represent the nations gathered against God's people.
20.mean: When the thousand years are ended, Satan is released and deceives the nations, Gog and Magog, gathering them for battle. They surround the camp of the saints, but fire comes down from heaven and consumes them. The devil is thrown into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and false prophet are, and they will be tormented day and night for ever.
20.big: Satan's end is certain, and evil is finally and permanently dealt with.
20.h: Satan Cast into the Lake of Fire

20.ctx: The final judgement, before which there is nowhere left to hide — even earth and sky flee from God's presence.
20.mean: John sees a great white throne, and earth and sky flee away. The dead, great and small, stand before the throne, and books are opened, including the book of life. The dead are judged by what they had done. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire — this is the second death. If anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
20.big: Everyone will stand before God, and judgement will be according to a full and accurate record.
20.diff: The relationship between judgement 'according to works' and salvation by grace is discussed throughout Scripture: the historic Protestant understanding is that works are the evidence brought forward, while the book of life records those redeemed by Christ. Christians differ over whether the lake of fire means unending conscious punishment or final destruction.
20.h: Judgment before the Great White Throne

21.ctx: The goal of the whole Bible, answering the opening chapters of Genesis.
21.mean: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride. A loud voice says: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear, and death shall be no more, nor mourning nor crying nor pain, for the former things have passed away. Behold, I am making all things new. To the thirsty he will give from the spring of the water of life without payment. But the cowardly, faithless, detestable, murderers, immoral, sorcerers, idolaters and liars will have their portion in the lake of fire.
21.big: God's final purpose is not to take people away from earth but to make all things new and dwell with them.
21.diff: The promise is a renewed creation, not escape from the physical world — which is why the Christian hope includes resurrected bodies and a real new earth.
21.h: A New Heaven and a New Earth

21.ctx: The new Jerusalem described. The same angel who showed John the prostitute city in 17:1 now shows him the Bride, setting the two cities against each other.
21.mean: An angel shows John the Bride, the wife of the Lamb: the holy city with God's glory, a great high wall with twelve gates named for the twelve tribes and twelve foundations named for the twelve apostles. The city is a perfect cube of enormous size, of pure gold, with jewelled foundations and gates of single pearls. John saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. It has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. The nations will walk by its light, and nothing unclean will ever enter.
21.big: The city needs no temple because God himself is present with his people.
21.diff: The cube shape matches the Most Holy Place in the temple — the whole city is now the place where God dwells. Old and new covenant people are represented together in its gates and foundations.

22.ctx: Eden restored, and more than restored. The river and the tree of life come from Genesis 2, and the healing leaves from Ezekiel 47.
22.mean: The angel shows John the river of the water of life, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side, bearing fruit each month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. No longer will there be anything accursed. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. Night will be no more, and they will reign for ever.
22.big: The curse of Genesis 3 is reversed, and God's people see his face at last.
22.diff: The single throne 'of God and of the Lamb', with servants rendering worship to 'him' in the singular, is a further indication of the Lamb's full deity.

22.ctx: The epilogue, in which the angel, John and Jesus all speak, with no change of speaker marked between them.
22.mean: The angel says these words are trustworthy and true. 'Behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of this book.' John falls to worship the angel and is told again: worship God. The voice says: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Then: I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things. I am the root and descendant of David, the bright morning star. The Spirit and the Bride say, Come. Let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
22.big: The book ends with Jesus identifying himself and with an open invitation to come and drink.
22.diff: In verses 12–16 the same speaker calls himself the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, and then says 'I, Jesus' — with no change of speaker marked. This is one of the arguments the group's Jehovah's Witness material sets out, since these titles are used of God elsewhere in the book.

22.ctx: The closing warning and blessing, similar in form to Deuteronomy 4:2, which warned against adding to or subtracting from God's commands.
22.mean: John warns that if anyone adds to the words of the prophecy of this book, God will add to him the plagues described; and if anyone takes away, God will take away his share in the tree of life. He who testifies says: surely I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
22.big: The Bible ends with a prayer for Christ's return and a word of grace.
22.diff: The warning concerns this book of prophecy in particular, though similar warnings appear in Deuteronomy 4:2. 'Come, Lord Jesus' is the Greek equivalent of the Aramaic prayer 'Maranatha' in 1 Corinthians 16:22.
22.h: Nothing May Be Added or Removed

1.ctx: Luke's second volume, addressed like his Gospel to Theophilus, probably written in the 60s–80s. It tells how the gospel moved from Jerusalem to Rome in about thirty years.
1.mean: Luke says his first book dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach until he was taken up, after presenting himself alive by many proofs over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. He told them to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Father, for they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit.
1.big: Acts continues what Jesus began, now through his Spirit in his people.
1.diff: 'All that Jesus began to do' suggests Luke sees Acts as the continuing acts of the risen Christ through the church.

1.ctx: The disciples' last recorded question before Pentecost. Many Jews expected the Messiah to restore national independence from Rome, which shapes what they ask.
1.mean: They ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel. Jesus says it is not for them to know times or seasons fixed by the Father, but they will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes, and will be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. Then he is lifted up and a cloud takes him. Two men in white say he will come in the same way.
1.big: Verse 8 is the plan of the whole book, and Christ's return will be as visible and bodily as his departure.
1.diff: Jesus does not deny that God has a future for Israel; he redirects them from calculating dates to their mission.

1.ctx: The eleven return to Jerusalem and wait, together with the women, Mary and Jesus' brothers.
1.mean: Peter says Scripture had to be fulfilled about Judas, and quotes the Psalms. They put forward two who had accompanied them from John's baptism, pray, and cast lots, which fall on Matthias, who is numbered with the eleven.
1.big: The Twelve are restored to full number before the Spirit comes, marking a renewed Israel.
1.diff: This is the last time in Scripture that lots are used for guidance; after Pentecost the Spirit guides directly. Some question whether the choice was premature, since Paul was later called, but Luke reports it without criticism.

2.ctx: Pentecost, fifty days after Passover, a harvest festival that also commemorated the giving of the law at Sinai, when Jerusalem was full of pilgrims.
2.mean: A sound like a mighty rushing wind fills the house, divided tongues as of fire rest on each of them, and they are all filled with the Holy Spirit and begin to speak in other tongues. Devout Jews from every nation hear them telling the mighty works of God in their own languages. Some sneer that they are drunk.
2.big: The Spirit comes on all God's people, and the gospel is heard immediately in every language.
2.diff: Wind and fire are Sinai imagery; what was written on stone is now written on people (Jeremiah 31). The scattering of languages at Babel begins to be reversed. Most interpreters agree the tongues here were real human languages.

2.ctx: Peter's sermon, the first Christian sermon recorded, preached to pilgrims from across the Roman world gathered in Jerusalem for the feast.
2.mean: Peter says this is what was spoken by Joel: God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved. Jesus of Nazareth, attested by mighty works, was delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, and they crucified him — but God raised him, because death could not hold him. He quotes Psalm 16 and Psalm 110, and concludes: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.
2.big: The crucified Jesus has been made Lord and Christ, and the Spirit's outpouring proves it.
2.diff: Verse 23 holds together God's plan and human responsibility in one sentence — a text Reformed theology often cites. Peter applies Joel's 'call on the name of the LORD' to Jesus.

2.ctx: The response to the sermon. These were people in the same city, weeks after the crucifixion, some of whom may have been in the crowd that called for it.
2.mean: Cut to the heart, they ask what they should do. Peter says: repent and be baptised, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself. About three thousand were added that day.
2.big: The response to the gospel is repentance and baptism, with the promise of forgiveness and the Spirit.
2.diff: Whether baptism conveys forgiveness or signifies it is debated; most Protestants take the second, noting that in chapter 10 the Spirit falls before baptism. Verse 39's mention of 'your children' is one text paedobaptists cite. The final clause grounds the call in God's own calling.

2.ctx: Luke's first summary of church life, describing the new community of three thousand believers in Jerusalem.
2.mean: They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers. Awe came on everyone, and many wonders were done. All who believed were together and had all things in common, selling their possessions to give to any who had need. Day by day they attended the temple and broke bread in their homes with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favour with all the people. The Lord added to their number daily.
2.big: The earliest church was marked by teaching, fellowship, the meal and prayer — and by extraordinary generosity.
2.diff: The sharing described was voluntary and occasional, not enforced common ownership: Acts 5:4 says property remained the owner's to dispose of.

3.ctx: The temple at the hour of prayer, three in the afternoon. Begging at temple gates was common, and this man was well known to worshippers.
3.mean: Peter and John meet a man lame from birth, carried daily to the Beautiful Gate. Peter says: I have no silver or gold, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk. He takes his hand, the man's feet are strengthened, and he enters the temple walking and leaping and praising God.
3.big: The apostles have no money but carry the authority of Jesus' name.

3.ctx: Peter's second recorded sermon, preached in Solomon's Colonnade, a covered walkway along the east side of the temple courts where teachers gathered crowds.
3.mean: Peter says it is not their own power or piety. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob glorified his servant Jesus, whom they delivered over and denied before Pilate, killing the Author of life, whom God raised. Faith in his name has made this man strong. He says they acted in ignorance, and urges them to repent and turn back, that their sins may be blotted out, and that God may send Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all things.
3.big: Peter offers repentance and forgiveness to the very people who called for Jesus' death.

4.ctx: The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, controlled the temple and were alarmed by the apostles' preaching.
4.mean: Peter and John are arrested, but many who heard believed — about five thousand men. Before the Sanhedrin, Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, says the man was healed by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised. He is the stone rejected by the builders that has become the cornerstone. There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.
4.big: Salvation is found in Jesus alone — stated by a fisherman to the ruling council that had condemned him.
4.diff: Verse 12's exclusivity is often challenged today. Christians hold it because Jesus alone is God become man and alone bore sin; this does not permit arrogance, since salvation is by grace, not merit.
4.h: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin

4.ctx: The council's response. The Sanhedrin was the supreme Jewish court of seventy-one members, the same body that had condemned Jesus a few months earlier.
4.mean: The council sees Peter and John's boldness and perceives they are uneducated, common men, and recognises that they had been with Jesus. With the healed man standing there, they have nothing to say. They charge them not to speak in Jesus' name, but Peter and John answer: whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge; for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.
4.big: When human authority forbids what God commands, believers must obey God.

4.ctx: The church's response to the first official threats, gathered together after Peter and John are released.
4.mean: They lift their voices together, addressing God as Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth, quoting Psalm 2. They acknowledge that Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and Israel gathered against Jesus to do whatever God's hand and plan had predestined to take place. They do not pray for safety, but for boldness to speak, and for healings in Jesus' name. The place is shaken and they are filled with the Holy Spirit.
4.big: Facing threats, the church prays not for protection but for boldness.
4.diff: Verse 28 is another text holding together God's sovereign plan and the genuine guilt of those who acted.

4.ctx: A second summary of the church's common life, showing how the believers' unity worked out in practice as the community grew.
4.mean: The believers were of one heart and soul, and no one said that anything belonged to him alone. With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection, and there was not a needy person among them, for those who owned land or houses sold them and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, is named as an example.
4.big: Unity of heart showed itself in a generosity that left no one in need.

5.ctx: Immediately after Barnabas's generosity, a contrasting example.
5.mean: Ananias and Sapphira sell property and keep back part of the proceeds while pretending to give all. Peter says Satan filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit; the land was his own, and after it was sold the money was at his disposal. He has not lied to men but to God. Both fall dead, and great fear comes on the whole church.
5.big: The sin was not withholding but lying to God for the appearance of generosity.
5.diff: Peter names the Holy Spirit as the one lied to, then God — one of the clearest indications in Acts of the Spirit's deity. The severity is exceptional rather than a pattern; it occurs at the church's foundation.

5.ctx: A third summary, showing the church's growing influence in Jerusalem. Solomon's Colonnade had become their regular meeting place.
5.mean: Many signs are done through the apostles. The people hold them in high esteem, and more believers are added, so that they carry the sick into the streets hoping Peter's shadow might fall on them. Crowds come from towns around Jerusalem and all are healed.
5.big: The church grows in numbers and in reputation as God works through the apostles.

5.ctx: The second arrest. The Sadducees, who controlled the temple and denied the resurrection, had most to lose from the apostles' preaching.
5.mean: The high priest and the Sadducees, filled with jealousy, arrest the apostles, but during the night an angel opens the prison doors and tells them to go stand in the temple and speak all the words of this Life. At daybreak they are found teaching in the temple.
5.big: God opens the prison not so they can escape but so they can keep preaching.

5.ctx: The apostles are brought back before the Sanhedrin, having been found teaching openly in the temple after their miraculous release.
5.mean: The captain brings them without force, fearing the people. The high priest says they were charged not to teach in this name, yet they have filled Jerusalem with their teaching. Peter and the apostles answer: we must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. We are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit.
5.big: The apostles state the principle that has guided Christians under persecution ever since: we must obey God rather than men.
5.diff: 'God exalted him to give repentance' is one of several texts presenting repentance itself as God's gift.

5.ctx: Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of Paul, intervenes.
5.mean: Gamaliel advises caution, citing failed movements under Theudas and Judas the Galilean: if this plan is of men it will fail, but if it is of God you will not be able to overthrow them — you might even be found opposing God. They beat the apostles, charge them again, and release them. The apostles leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name.
5.big: Wise counsel from an unbeliever spares the apostles, who rejoice at being counted worthy to suffer.
5.diff: Gamaliel's principle — that what is of God will survive — is sound here but not a reliable general test, since false movements have often outlasted a generation.

6.ctx: The church's first internal conflict, along cultural lines: Greek-speaking Jews against Aramaic-speaking Jews.
6.mean: The Hellenists complain that their widows are being neglected in the daily distribution. The Twelve say it is not right for them to give up preaching to serve tables, and tell the church to pick seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom. The word of God continued to increase, and a great many priests became obedient to the faith.
6.big: The church solves a fairness problem by delegating, so that both service and preaching are done well.
6.diff: All seven chosen have Greek names, so the complaining group were given the responsibility — a model of handling grievance. Many see here the origin of the office of deacon.

6.ctx: Stephen, one of the seven chosen in 6:1–7, begins a wider ministry of signs and preaching among Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem.
6.mean: Stephen, full of grace and power, does great signs. Members of a synagogue of freedmen dispute with him but cannot withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he speaks. They secretly instigate men to accuse him of blasphemy against Moses and God, stir up the people, and bring him before the council with false witnesses. His face is like the face of an angel.
6.big: Opposition that cannot answer the truth resorts to false accusation.

7.ctx: Stephen's speech is the longest in Acts, a retelling of Israel's history answering the charge that he spoke against the temple and the law.
7.mean: Stephen begins with the God of glory appearing to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before he lived in the land, and the promise given before Abraham had any inheritance or a child.
7.big: God met Abraham outside the holy land, before the temple existed.
7.diff: Stephen's argument throughout is that God has never been confined to one place or building.
7.h: Stephen's Address: The Call of Abraham

7.ctx: Stephen turns to Joseph, the first of three figures he uses to show that God's chosen deliverers were rejected by their own people.
7.mean: Stephen says the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt, but God was with him and rescued him and gave him favour before Pharaoh, making him ruler over Egypt.
7.big: God's chosen deliverer was rejected by his own brothers — a pattern Stephen is building.

7.ctx: Israel in Egypt, from Jacob's migration to the oppression under a new king, covering four centuries in a few sentences.
7.mean: Jacob goes down to Egypt and dies there with the fathers, who are carried back to Shechem. As the time of the promise drew near, the people multiplied in Egypt until another king arose who oppressed them and forced them to expose their infants.
7.big: God's promise advanced even while his people were enslaved outside the land.

7.ctx: Moses' birth and upbringing during the oppression, when Hebrew infant boys were being killed on Pharaoh's orders.
7.mean: Moses was beautiful in God's sight, hidden three months, then brought up in Pharaoh's household and instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, mighty in words and deeds.
7.big: God's next deliverer was raised in the court of the oppressor.
7.h: The Birth and Adoption of Moses

7.ctx: Moses at forty, in the incident recorded in Exodus 2, when he killed an Egyptian and was rejected by his own people.
7.mean: At forty Moses visited his brothers and killed an Egyptian, supposing they would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not. The next day they rejected him: who made you ruler and judge over us? So Moses fled to Midian.
7.big: Israel rejected their God-sent deliverer the first time, as they had Joseph.
7.diff: The parallel Stephen is drawing is clear: they rejected Joseph, then Moses, and now Jesus.
7.h: The Rejection and Flight of Moses

7.ctx: Forty years later, at the burning bush in Sinai, where God commissioned the man Israel had earlier refused.
7.mean: After forty years an angel appeared to Moses in a flame in a bush in the wilderness of Sinai. God said: I am the God of your fathers. Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. This Moses, whom they rejected, God sent as both ruler and redeemer.
7.big: Holy ground was found in a desert outside the promised land, not in a temple.

7.ctx: Israel's rebellion in the wilderness, at the very time Moses was receiving the law — the golden calf incident of Exodus 32.
7.mean: Stephen says the fathers refused to obey Moses, turned back to Egypt in their hearts, made the golden calf and rejoiced in the works of their hands. God gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as the prophets wrote.
7.big: Israel's history is a pattern of rejecting God's messengers and turning to idols.

7.ctx: Stephen turns to the charge that he spoke against the temple, tracing God's dwelling from the wilderness tent through to Solomon's building.
7.mean: Stephen says the tent of witness was made according to the pattern Moses saw, and was brought in with Joshua and remained until David, who asked to find a dwelling place for God, and Solomon built him a house. Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says: heaven is my throne, and earth my footstool; what house will you build for me?
7.big: God cannot be confined to a building, as Israel's own Scriptures say.

7.ctx: The end of the speech. Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy under the law, though the Sanhedrin's authority to carry out executions was limited under Rome.
7.mean: Stephen calls them stiff-necked, resisting the Holy Spirit as their fathers did, betrayers and murderers of the Righteous One. Enraged, they grind their teeth. Full of the Holy Spirit, Stephen gazes into heaven and sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. They rush at him, drag him out and stone him, with the witnesses laying their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen prays: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and, do not hold this sin against them.
7.big: The first Christian martyr dies praying directly to Jesus and forgiving his killers.
7.diff: Jesus is standing, not seated — often taken as rising to welcome his witness. Stephen's two prayers echo Jesus' own words from the cross, and are addressed to Jesus, which bears on discussions about prayer to Christ.

8.ctx: Saul's approval of Stephen's death leads into the first great persecution.
8.mean: A great persecution breaks out, and all except the apostles are scattered throughout Judea and Samaria. Saul ravages the church, dragging off men and women to prison.
8.big: Persecution scatters the church, which fulfils Jesus' command to go to Judea and Samaria.

8.ctx: The scattered believers preach wherever they go. Samaritans were descendants of mixed marriages after the exile, despised by Jews and worshipping at Mount Gerizim.
8.mean: Philip goes to a city of Samaria and proclaims Christ; crowds pay attention, unclean spirits come out, and there is much joy. When the apostles hear that Samaria has received the word, they send Peter and John, who pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit, and lay hands on them.
8.big: The gospel crosses the deep divide between Jews and Samaritans.
8.diff: The delay between believing and receiving the Spirit here is unusual in Acts. Most interpreters see it as God visibly binding the Samaritan believers to the Jerusalem apostles, preventing a divided church, rather than a pattern for every believer.

8.ctx: Simon, a magician who had amazed the Samaritans and was called 'the Great Power of God'. Magic was widespread in the ancient world.
8.mean: Simon himself believes and is baptised. When he sees the Spirit given through the apostles' hands, he offers money for the power. Peter says: may your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money. Your heart is not right. Repent. Simon asks them to pray for him.
8.big: God's gifts cannot be bought, and a profession of faith is not the same as a right heart.
8.diff: The word 'simony', for buying church office, comes from this episode. Whether Simon was truly converted is debated.

8.ctx: Philip is sent to a desert road, the first individual conversion recorded in detail.
8.mean: An angel sends Philip south, where he meets an Ethiopian court official, treasurer to the queen, reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot. Philip asks if he understands, and beginning with that Scripture tells him the good news about Jesus. The man asks to be baptised, and goes on his way rejoicing.
8.big: The Old Testament read rightly leads to Jesus, and the gospel reaches Africa within a few years.
8.diff: The man was probably a God-fearing Gentile or a Jewish proselyte. Verse 37, a confession of faith before baptism, is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is omitted or footnoted in modern translations.

9.ctx: The conversion of the church's fiercest opponent, told three times in Acts.
9.mean: Saul, breathing threats, is on the road to Damascus when a light from heaven flashes and a voice says: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Blinded, he is led into the city and neither eats nor drinks for three days.
9.big: Jesus identifies himself so closely with his church that persecuting believers is persecuting him.
9.diff: Paul's conversion is not a decision he reaches but an intervention he is subjected to, which shapes everything he later writes about grace.

9.ctx: Ananias, a disciple living in Damascus, is sent to the man who had come to arrest believers like him, carrying letters from the high priest.
9.mean: Ananias objects, having heard how much evil Saul has done. The Lord says: go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel, for I will show him how much he must suffer for my name. Ananias goes, calls him 'Brother Saul', and he regains his sight, is baptised and takes food.
9.big: God's chosen instrument is sent to suffer, and is welcomed as a brother by the man he came to arrest.

9.ctx: Saul begins to preach in the synagogues of Damascus, the very places he had come with authority to arrest Christians.
9.mean: Immediately he proclaims Jesus in the synagogues, saying he is the Son of God. All who hear are amazed, and Saul increases all the more in strength, confounding the Jews in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ.
9.big: The change in Saul is immediate and public.

9.ctx: Saul's first escape. Paul recounts this episode himself in 2 Corinthians 11:32–33, naming the governor under King Aretas.
9.mean: After many days the Jews plot to kill him, watching the gates day and night, but his disciples take him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall in a basket.
9.big: The great apostle's ministry begins with an undignified escape.

9.ctx: Saul in Jerusalem, three years after his conversion according to Galatians 1:18, where the believers had every reason to suspect a trap.
9.mean: The disciples in Jerusalem are afraid of him, but Barnabas takes him and brings him to the apostles, telling how he had seen the Lord and preached boldly. When the Hellenists seek to kill him, the brothers send him to Tarsus. The church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria had peace and was built up.
9.big: Barnabas's willingness to vouch for Saul opens the way for the whole Gentile mission.

9.ctx: Peter's ministry resumes, preparing for the Gentile mission.
9.mean: Peter heals Aeneas, paralysed and bedridden for eight years, at Lydda, saying Jesus Christ heals you. All who lived there turned to the Lord.
9.big: Peter's ministry continues the works of Jesus in Jesus' name.

9.ctx: Joppa, a coastal town. Tabitha (Dorcas in Greek) is the only woman in the New Testament called a disciple using the feminine form of the word.
9.mean: Tabitha, also called Dorcas, full of good works and acts of charity, falls ill and dies. The disciples send for Peter, and the widows show him the garments she made. Peter puts them all outside, kneels and prays, and says: Tabitha, arise. She opens her eyes and sits up. It becomes known throughout Joppa, and many believe. Peter stays with Simon, a tanner.
9.big: God restores life through Peter, and a woman known for practical kindness is greatly missed.
9.diff: Peter's words closely echo Jesus' 'Talitha koum' in Mark 5:41. Staying with a tanner, whose trade involved ritual uncleanness, prepares for what follows in chapter 10.

10.ctx: The turning point of the book: the gospel reaching Gentiles directly.
10.mean: Cornelius, a Roman centurion in Caesarea, a devout God-fearer who gave alms and prayed continually, sees an angel in a vision telling him to send for Simon Peter at Joppa.
10.big: God takes the initiative with a Gentile soldier before Peter knows anything about it.

10.ctx: Peter's vision on the roof of a tanner's house in Joppa, around noon, while he waited for a meal to be prepared.
10.mean: Peter, hungry, falls into a trance and sees a sheet let down with all kinds of animals, and a voice says: rise, kill and eat. Peter refuses, having never eaten anything common or unclean. The voice says: what God has made clean, do not call common. This happens three times.
10.big: God declares clean what the law had separated, preparing Peter for what he is about to do.
10.diff: The vision is about people as much as food, as Peter explains in verse 28. It presupposes what Mark 7:19 states about all foods being clean.

10.ctx: The messengers from Cornelius arrive at the gate just as Peter is puzzling over the vision — the timing is Luke's point.
10.mean: While Peter is perplexed, the men from Cornelius arrive, and the Spirit tells him to go with them without hesitation, for he has sent them. Peter invites them in as guests — already crossing a boundary.
10.big: The Spirit directs Peter to go, removing his hesitation before he understands everything.

10.ctx: Peter arrives at Cornelius's house in Caesarea, the Roman administrative capital, accompanied by six Jewish believers as witnesses (11:12).
10.mean: Cornelius falls at Peter's feet, but Peter lifts him up, saying he too is just a man. He tells them it is unlawful for a Jew to associate with a foreigner, but God has shown him not to call any person common or unclean.
10.big: Peter's own convictions have been changed before he opens his mouth to preach.

10.ctx: Peter's sermon to a Gentile household, the first recorded preaching of the gospel to Gentiles who had not become Jewish proselytes.
10.mean: Peter says: truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. He preaches Jesus of Nazareth, anointed with the Holy Spirit and power, who went about doing good, was put to death on a tree, and whom God raised on the third day and made appear to chosen witnesses. Everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.
10.big: God shows no partiality: forgiveness through Jesus is for people of every nation.
10.diff: Verse 35 does not teach that sincere people of any religion are saved apart from Christ; Peter is sent precisely so that Cornelius may hear the gospel and believe.

10.ctx: The Spirit falls on Gentiles before Peter has even finished speaking, and before any baptism or circumcision — which settles the matter.
10.mean: While Peter is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on all who heard the word. The circumcised believers are amazed, because the gift of the Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles, for they hear them speaking in tongues and praising God. Peter says: can anyone withhold water for baptising these people? And he commands them to be baptised.
10.big: God gives Gentiles the same Spirit, settling the question before the church can debate it.
10.diff: Here the Spirit is received before baptism, which is why most Protestants read Acts 2:38 as baptism signifying rather than conveying the Spirit and forgiveness.
10.h: The Gentiles Receive the Holy Spirit

11.ctx: Peter is criticised on returning to Jerusalem. Eating with Gentiles, not preaching to them, is the charge, since table fellowship implied acceptance.
11.mean: The circumcision party criticises Peter, who explains the whole sequence of events, ending: if God gave the same gift to them as to us, who was I that I could stand in God's way? They fall silent and glorify God, saying: then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.
11.big: The Jerusalem church accepts, on the evidence of God's own action, that Gentiles are included.

11.ctx: The church at Antioch, which becomes the base for the Gentile mission.
11.mean: Those scattered by the persecution over Stephen preach to Jews only, but some from Cyprus and Cyrene speak to Greeks, and a great number believe. Barnabas is sent, and seeing the grace of God he is glad, and exhorts them to remain faithful. He goes to Tarsus to find Saul, and they teach there for a year. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. Agabus predicts a famine, and the disciples send relief to Judea.
11.big: A church of Jews and Gentiles together becomes the springboard for the mission to the world.
11.diff: 'Christian' was probably a nickname coined by outsiders, meaning 'Christ's people'. The relief sent to Judea shows the new churches supporting the mother church.

12.ctx: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, ruled Judea from AD 41 to 44.
12.mean: Herod kills James the brother of John with the sword, and seeing that it pleased the Jews, arrests Peter during Unleavened Bread, guarded by four squads of soldiers.
12.big: One apostle is executed and another delivered; God does not always rescue in the same way.
12.diff: James is the first apostle martyred. Luke reports his death in a single verse and Peter's rescue at length, without explaining why God did one and not the other.

12.ctx: The rescue of Peter, on the night before his trial, while the church gathered at the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, was praying.
12.mean: Earnest prayer is made by the church. The night before his trial, Peter sleeps between two soldiers, bound with chains. An angel wakes him, the chains fall off, and they pass the guards and the iron gate, which opens by itself. Peter comes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where many are praying. The servant Rhoda recognises his voice and in her joy runs back without opening the gate; they tell her she is out of her mind, then that it is his angel. When they open the door, they are amazed.
12.big: God answers the church's prayer while the church struggles to believe he has.
12.diff: Luke's humour is evident: the praying church cannot believe their prayer has been answered.

12.ctx: The death of Herod Agrippa I at Caesarea in AD 44, during games held in honour of the emperor.
12.mean: Herod, in royal robes, delivers an oration, and the people shout that it is the voice of a god and not of a man. Immediately an angel of the Lord strikes him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he is eaten by worms and dies. But the word of God increased and multiplied.
12.big: The king who killed an apostle dies, while the word of God keeps growing.
12.diff: The Jewish historian Josephus independently records Herod Agrippa's sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god, which corroborates Luke's account.

13.ctx: The Antioch church sends out the first deliberate mission to the Gentile world, around AD 46–48.
13.mean: While they were worshipping and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. After fasting and praying they laid hands on them and sent them off.
13.big: The Gentile mission begins not with a strategy meeting but with the Spirit's direct call.
13.diff: The Spirit speaks in the first person and claims both the calling and the workers — language that describes a person, not an impersonal force.

13.ctx: Cyprus, Barnabas's home island, where Sergius Paulus served as Roman proconsul — an educated official of senatorial rank.
13.mean: At Paphos they meet a Jewish false prophet, Bar-Jesus or Elymas, who opposes them before the proconsul Sergius Paulus. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, rebukes him and he is struck blind for a time. The proconsul believes, astonished at the teaching. From here Luke calls him Paul rather than Saul.
13.big: The gospel reaches a Roman official, and Paul emerges as the leader of the mission.
13.diff: 'Saul, who was also called Paul' — he likely had both names from birth, Saul among Jews and Paul among Romans; the change of usage fits his turn to Gentile work.

13.ctx: Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony in the highlands of Asia Minor.
13.mean: In the synagogue Paul preaches, summarising Israel's history from the exodus to David, then announcing that from David's offspring God has brought a Saviour, Jesus. Those in Jerusalem, not recognising him, fulfilled the prophets by condemning him; God raised him, as Psalm 2 and Psalm 16 foretold. Through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which they could not be freed by the law of Moses.
13.big: Paul's first recorded sermon already preaches justification by faith, beyond what the law could do.
13.diff: John Mark leaves them here and returns to Jerusalem, which later causes the split between Paul and Barnabas (15:38).

13.ctx: The response at Pisidian Antioch, and a decisive turn in Paul's ministry, after the synagogue has heard his message once.
13.mean: Many follow them, and the next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers. The Jewish leaders, filled with jealousy, contradict Paul. Paul and Barnabas say boldly that it was necessary for the word to be spoken first to them, but since they reject it, they are turning to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah 49:6: I have made you a light for the Gentiles. The Gentiles rejoice, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
13.big: Rejection by the synagogue turns the mission outward to the Gentiles, in fulfilment of Isaiah.
13.diff: Verse 48, 'as many as were appointed to eternal life believed', is one of the clearest statements in Acts of God's prior appointing, and is frequently cited in Reformed theology.

14.ctx: Iconium, the next city along the Roman road east of Antioch, where Paul and Barnabas again begin in the synagogue.
14.mean: They speak boldly and a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, but unbelieving Jews stir up the Gentiles. They remain a long time speaking boldly, and God bears witness by signs and wonders, until a plot to stone them forces them to flee.
14.big: Opposition and fruitfulness grow together.

14.ctx: Lystra, a rural town where Greek was not the everyday language.
14.mean: Paul heals a man lame from birth. The crowds shout in Lycaonian that the gods have come down, calling Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and the priest of Zeus brings oxen to sacrifice. The apostles tear their garments and rush in, crying: we are men of like nature with you. They preach the living God who made heaven and earth and who did good, giving rains and fruitful seasons. Then Jews from Antioch and Iconium win over the crowds, who stone Paul and drag him out of the city, supposing him dead.
14.big: Paul preaches to pagans from creation rather than Scripture, and the same crowd that worshipped him stones him days later.
14.diff: This is Paul's first recorded sermon to a purely pagan audience, and it starts from God as Creator — a model for speaking with people who do not know the Bible.
14.h: The Visit to Lystra and Derbe

14.ctx: The return journey. Rather than take the short road home over the mountains, they retrace their steps through the cities where they had been attacked.
14.mean: After preaching in Derbe they return through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith, saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. They appoint elders in every church with prayer and fasting, and commit them to the Lord. Back in Antioch they report how God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
14.big: Paul returns to the very cities he was driven from, and appoints elders so the churches can stand.
14.diff: Paul offers no easy gospel: hardship is presented as the road into the kingdom, not a sign of failure.

15.ctx: The crisis that could have split the church permanently, arising as Gentile converts multiplied through the churches Paul had planted.
15.mean: Men come from Judea teaching that unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved. Paul and Barnabas have no small dissension with them, and are sent to Jerusalem to settle the question.
15.big: The question is whether Gentiles must become Jews to be saved — the gospel itself is at stake.

15.ctx: The Jerusalem council, around AD 49, the most consequential meeting in church history.
15.mean: Some believing Pharisees say Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law. After much debate Peter argues that God gave the Gentiles the Holy Spirit just as he did to them, making no distinction, having cleansed their hearts by faith — so why put a yoke on them that neither we nor our fathers could bear? We believe we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will. James cites Amos 9 about God rebuilding David's tent so the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, and proposes not troubling the Gentiles, but asking them to abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled and from blood.
15.big: Salvation is by grace through faith for Jews and Gentiles alike, on exactly the same terms.
15.diff: The four requests are usually understood as concessions to enable Jewish and Gentile believers to eat together, not as conditions of salvation. Some read them as a summary of moral law binding on all.

15.ctx: The council's letter, carried by two respected Jerusalem believers so that it would not be seen as merely Paul's own version of the decision.
15.mean: The apostles and elders with the whole church choose Judas and Silas to carry a letter, which says: it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements.
15.big: The council names the Holy Spirit alongside themselves as party to the decision.
15.diff: 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us' describes a shared decision with a person, not the use of a force.
15.h: The Letter to the Gentile Believers

15.ctx: The reception at Antioch, the church that had sent Paul and Barnabas out and whose Gentile members were most affected by the ruling.
15.mean: The letter is delivered and the church rejoices at its encouragement. Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, encourage and strengthen the brothers.
15.big: A decision that could have divided the church instead brings joy.

15.ctx: The sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas, the two men who had worked together since Barnabas vouched for Saul in Jerusalem.
15.mean: Paul proposes revisiting the churches. Barnabas wants to take John Mark; Paul refuses because Mark had withdrawn in Pamphylia. The disagreement becomes so sharp that they separate: Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus, and Paul takes Silas, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
15.big: Two godly men disagree sharply and part, and God uses both journeys.
15.diff: Luke reports the conflict without taking sides. Mark is later valued by Paul (2 Timothy 4:11) and is traditionally the author of Mark's Gospel — a reminder that a young man's failure need not be final.

16.ctx: Lystra, where Paul had been stoned. Timothy joins the mission.
16.mean: Timothy, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, is well spoken of. Paul circumcises him because of the Jews in those places, since they all knew his father was Greek. The churches are strengthened and increase daily.
16.big: Paul, who refused circumcision for Titus as a matter of principle, accepts it for Timothy as a matter of mission.
16.diff: The difference is that in Galatians circumcision was being demanded as necessary for salvation; here it removes an obstacle to reaching Jews. Paul gives up rights rather than truth.

16.ctx: The Spirit's guidance by closed doors, redirecting the mission away from the populous province of Asia and north-east into Bithynia, and finally to the coast.
16.mean: They are forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak in Asia, and when they try to go into Bithynia the Spirit of Jesus does not allow them. At Troas Paul has a vision of a Macedonian pleading: come over and help us. Immediately they seek to go, concluding that God had called them. Here Luke's narrative shifts to 'we', suggesting he joined the party.
16.big: Guidance came as much through closed doors as through the vision that finally opened one.
16.diff: The 'we' passages are widely taken as evidence that Luke was an eyewitness to parts of the account.

16.ctx: Philippi, a Roman colony, and the first recorded convert in Europe.
16.mean: On the Sabbath they go to a place of prayer by the river and speak to the women gathered. Lydia, a seller of purple goods from Thyatira, a worshipper of God, listens, and the Lord opens her heart to pay attention. She and her household are baptised, and she urges them to stay at her house.
16.big: The Lord opens a heart, and the first church in Europe begins in a businesswoman's home.
16.diff: Luke says plainly that the Lord opened her heart — a text often cited in Reformed discussion of how faith begins. Household baptisms are also cited in debates about baptising children.

16.ctx: Paul and Silas are imprisoned at Philippi, a Roman colony proud of its status, where the charge is framed as introducing customs unlawful for Romans.
16.mean: A slave girl with a spirit of divination, bringing her owners much gain, follows them crying that they proclaim the way of salvation. Paul, annoyed, commands the spirit to come out. When her owners see their hope of gain is gone, they drag Paul and Silas to the authorities, accusing them of disturbing the city. They are beaten with rods and put in the inner prison with their feet in stocks.
16.big: Setting a person free costs her owners money, and that is what leads to the beating.

16.ctx: Around midnight in the inner prison, with Paul and Silas beaten, in stocks, and the other prisoners listening.
16.mean: About midnight Paul and Silas are praying and singing hymns, and the prisoners are listening. An earthquake opens the doors and unfastens the bonds. The jailer, supposing the prisoners have escaped, is about to kill himself, but Paul cries out that they are all there. Trembling, he asks: what must I do to be saved? They say: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household. He washes their wounds and is baptised at once, with all his family, and rejoices that he has believed in God.
16.big: The clearest question and answer about salvation in Acts comes from a jailer at midnight.
16.diff: The promise 'you and your household' means the same offer extends to his family, who then hear the word (verse 32) and believe (verse 34).

16.ctx: The morning after the earthquake, when the magistrates want the matter quietly forgotten.
16.mean: The magistrates send word to release them, but Paul says they have beaten them publicly, uncondemned, though they are Roman citizens, and thrown them into prison — now they want to send them away secretly? Let them come themselves. The magistrates are afraid and apologise.
16.big: Paul uses his legal rights to protect the young church's standing in the city.
16.diff: Beating a Roman citizen without trial was a serious offence; Paul's insistence protects the reputation of the Philippian believers he leaves behind.

17.ctx: Thessalonica, a major city on the main road through Macedonia.
17.mean: Paul reasons with them from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths, explaining that the Christ had to suffer and rise. Some are persuaded, including many devout Greeks and leading women. Jealous opponents form a mob, attack Jason's house and drag believers before the authorities, saying these men who have turned the world upside down have come here, acting against Caesar's decrees, saying there is another king, Jesus.
17.big: Preaching that Jesus is king is heard as a political challenge to Caesar.

17.ctx: Berea, a quieter town off the main road, where Paul's companions send him by night to escape the Thessalonian mob.
17.mean: The Bereans are more noble than those in Thessalonica: they receive the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many believe. When the Thessalonian opponents follow, Paul is sent away to the coast.
17.big: The mark of a noble hearer is eager reception combined with careful checking against Scripture.
17.diff: The Berean Standard Bible used on this website takes its name from this passage.

17.ctx: Athens, the intellectual centre of the Greek world, though past its political peak.
17.mean: Paul's spirit is provoked as he sees the city full of idols. He reasons in the synagogue and daily in the marketplace. Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debate with him, calling him a babbler and a preacher of foreign divinities, because he preached Jesus and the resurrection, and bring him to the Areopagus.
17.big: Paul engages the philosophers of Athens on their own ground.

17.ctx: Paul's address at the Areopagus, a model of preaching to those with no Bible.
17.mean: Paul says he perceives they are very religious, having seen an altar 'to the unknown god', and proclaims what they worship as unknown. God made the world and everything in it, does not live in temples or need anything, and made every nation from one man so that they might seek him, though he is not far from each one of us. He quotes their own poets: in him we live and move and have our being, and we are his offspring. Since we are God's offspring, we should not think the divine being is like gold or stone. God now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world by a man whom he has appointed, giving assurance by raising him from the dead. Some mock, some want to hear again, and some believe, including Dionysius and Damaris.
17.big: Paul starts from creation and their own poets, but ends where he always ends: repentance, judgement and the resurrection.
17.diff: Paul adapts his starting point without softening his message. The mixed response — mockery, curiosity and faith — is typical.

18.ctx: Corinth, a wealthy and immoral port city, where Paul stays eighteen months.
18.mean: Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, recently expelled from Rome by Claudius, and works with them as a tentmaker. When Silas and Timothy arrive he devotes himself fully to preaching. Opposed, he shakes out his garments and turns to the Gentiles. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes with his household. The Lord tells Paul in a vision: do not be afraid, go on speaking, for I am with you, and I have many in this city who are my people.
18.big: God encourages a fearful Paul by telling him he already has people in the city.
18.diff: Verse 10, 'I have many in this city who are my people', speaks of people not yet converted, and is often cited in Reformed discussion of election as the ground of confidence in evangelism.

18.ctx: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia and brother of the philosopher Seneca, held office around AD 51–52, giving one of the firmest dates in New Testament chronology.
18.mean: The Jews bring Paul before Gallio, charging him with persuading people to worship contrary to the law. Before Paul can speak, Gallio dismisses the case as a matter of their own law, and drives them from the tribunal.
18.big: A Roman ruling effectively protects the church's freedom to preach.
18.diff: An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's proconsulship to around AD 51–52, providing one of the firmest dates in New Testament chronology.

18.ctx: Paul returns toward Antioch by way of Ephesus, leaving Priscilla and Aquila there, at the end of the second missionary journey.
18.mean: Paul sails with Priscilla and Aquila, having cut his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow. He leaves them at Ephesus and returns to Antioch. Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian Jew who knew only John's baptism, speaks boldly, and Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.
18.big: A gifted preacher is corrected privately by a married couple, and goes on to great usefulness.
18.diff: Priscilla is usually named first, which many take to indicate her prominence. Their private correction of Apollos is often cited as a model of handling a teacher's error.

18.ctx: Paul's third journey begins, around AD 53, from Antioch. He revisits the churches of Galatia and Phrygia before settling at Ephesus for nearly three years.
18.mean: Luke says Paul spent some time in Antioch, then departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
18.big: Paul's pattern is not only to plant churches but to return and strengthen them.

19.ctx: Ephesus, where Paul spends about three years, his longest recorded stay.
19.mean: Paul finds disciples who had received only John's baptism and had not heard of the Holy Spirit. He explains that John told people to believe in the one coming after him, and they are baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul lays hands on them the Holy Spirit comes, and they speak in tongues and prophesy.
19.big: Followers of John's preparatory message are brought into the full Christian gospel.
19.diff: This is a transitional situation, not a pattern for every believer; these men belonged to the era before Pentecost had reached them.
19.h: The Holy Spirit Received at Ephesus

19.ctx: Paul's extended ministry in Ephesus, the leading city of the province of Asia and centre of the cult of Artemis, whose temple was one of the wonders of the world.
19.mean: Paul speaks boldly in the synagogue for three months, then withdraws to the hall of Tyrannus, reasoning daily for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word. God does extraordinary miracles through him.
19.big: Sustained daily teaching in one city reaches a whole province.

19.ctx: The seven sons of Sceva. Ephesus was famous for magical practices, and 'Ephesian writings' were well-known collections of spells.
19.mean: Itinerant Jewish exorcists try to use the name of Jesus whom Paul proclaims. The evil spirit says: Jesus I know, and Paul I recognise, but who are you? The man overpowers them, and they flee wounded. Fear falls on all, the name of the Lord Jesus is magnified, and many who practised magic bring their books and burn them publicly, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver.
19.big: Jesus' name is not a formula, and real repentance costs the Ephesian converts a fortune.
19.diff: Fifty thousand drachmas was roughly fifty thousand days' wages — a striking measure of genuine repentance.

19.ctx: The riot in Ephesus, stirred up by tradesmen whose income depended on pilgrims buying silver shrines of Artemis.
19.mean: Demetrius, a silversmith making shrines of Artemis, warns fellow craftsmen that Paul's preaching threatens their trade and the temple's reputation. The city fills with confusion, and for two hours the crowd shouts: great is Artemis of the Ephesians. The town clerk finally quiets them, pointing out the men are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers, and that there are courts.
19.big: The opposition is commercial first and religious second, and Luke lets Demetrius say so himself.

20.ctx: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, gathering the collection for Jerusalem.
20.mean: Paul encourages the believers, spends three months in Greece, and, when a plot is made against him, returns through Macedonia. Luke lists seven companions, representatives of the churches carrying the gift.
20.big: Paul's travel is shaped by care for the churches and by opposition.

20.ctx: Troas, on the first day of the week, when the believers gathered to break bread — one of the earliest references to Christians meeting on Sunday.
20.mean: On the first day of the week they gather to break bread, and Paul talks until midnight. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in a window, sinks into sleep and falls from the third storey and is taken up dead.
