22.mean: Jesus asks whose son the Christ is. They say David's. He asks how David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord: the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand. No one can answer him a word, and from that day no one dares ask him any more questions.
22.big: The Messiah is David's descendant and also David's Lord — a puzzle answered by the incarnation.
22.diff: Psalm 110:1 is the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament.

23.ctx: A sustained denunciation of the religious leadership, delivered publicly in the temple during Jesus' final week.
23.mean: Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach but not what they do, for they tie up heavy burdens and love places of honour and titles. He pronounces seven woes: shutting the kingdom in people's faces, making converts twice as much sons of hell, blind guides who tithe herbs while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness, cleaning the outside of the cup, whitewashed tombs, and building the tombs of the prophets their fathers killed.
23.big: Religion that is all display and no justice draws Jesus' sharpest words.
23.diff: These verses have been misused to justify hostility toward Jewish people. Jesus speaks as a Jew to Jewish leaders, in the tradition of Israel's own prophets, and the next passage shows his grief rather than hatred.

23.ctx: The lament that closes the denunciation, and shows what lies behind it.
23.mean: Jesus says: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killing the prophets and stoning those sent to you! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you desolate.
23.big: The anger of the woes is the grief of a rejected saviour.

24.ctx: The fifth and final teaching block. A disciple admires the temple's stones, some of which weighed many tonnes.
24.mean: Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask when this will be, and what will be the sign of his coming and of the end of the age. Jesus warns of false messiahs, wars, famines and earthquakes: these are the beginning of birth pains.
24.big: Jesus prepares his followers both for the fall of Jerusalem and for a long wait before his return.
24.diff: The disciples ask two questions at once, which is why the discourse moves between AD 70 and the final coming. Interpreters divide over where the line falls: many read verses 4–35 as chiefly about Jerusalem and 36–51 as the return; others see a double reference throughout. All agree on the repeated command to stay alert.

24.ctx: Warnings of persecution and false teaching within the church.
24.mean: Jesus says they will be delivered up, hated by all nations, and many will fall away and betray one another. Lawlessness will increase and love grow cold, but the one who endures to the end will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.
24.big: Endurance under pressure marks genuine faith, and the gospel will reach all nations first.

24.ctx: The 'abomination of desolation' comes from Daniel, first applied to Antiochus IV desecrating the temple in 167 BC.
24.mean: When they see it standing in the holy place, those in Judea must flee to the mountains without going back for anything. Pray that flight not be in winter or on a Sabbath, for there will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning. If those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved; but for the elect's sake they will be cut short.
24.big: Jesus gives practical warning to escape a coming catastrophe in Judea.
24.diff: Proposed identifications include Roman standards in the temple and the Zealot occupation before the siege; the Judea-specific instructions fit AD 70 closely. Eusebius records that Jerusalem's Christians fled before the city fell.

24.ctx: The coming of the Son of Man, described with prophetic imagery from Isaiah and Daniel.
24.mean: Jesus says do not believe reports that he is in the wilderness or inner rooms, for as lightning flashes from east to west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be. The sun will be darkened, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and great glory, and he will gather his elect from the four winds.
24.big: Christ's return will be unmistakable and universal, needing no announcement.
24.diff: Interpreters differ over whether these verses describe the second coming or use prophetic imagery for God's judgement in AD 70; most evangelical and Reformed interpreters take the first.
24.h: The Return of the Son of Man

24.ctx: Still on the Mount of Olives. Fig trees in Judea lose their leaves in winter, so new leaves were a reliable sign that summer was near.
24.mean: When the fig tree's branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, summer is near. So when they see all these things, they know he is near. This generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
24.big: The generation that heard Jesus saw the temple fall, exactly as he said.
24.diff: 'This generation' is most naturally the generation alive at the time, which saw AD 70; some take it as the Jewish people or the generation alive at the end.
24.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree

24.ctx: The hinge of the discourse, turning from signs to the unknown timing of the end.
24.mean: Jesus says concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels, nor the Son, but the Father only. As in the days of Noah they were eating and drinking until the flood came and swept them away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Two will be in a field; one is taken and one left. Stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
24.big: Because no one knows the day, the only right response is constant readiness.
24.diff: That the Son does not know is understood in historic Christian teaching as spoken according to his human nature, having genuinely taken on human limitation (see Mark 4:35). 'One taken, one left' is read by some as the rapture and by others as judgement sweeping people away, as in Noah's flood.

25.ctx: Three parables about readiness, given as the final teaching block closes.
25.mean: Ten virgins take lamps to meet the bridegroom; five bring oil and five do not. While he is delayed all sleep, but at midnight the cry comes. The foolish ask for oil and are sent to buy it, and while they are away the door is shut. Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
25.big: Readiness cannot be borrowed at the last moment.
25.h: The Parable of the Ten Virgins

25.ctx: A parable about faithfulness during the master's absence. A talent was an enormous sum, around twenty years' wages.
25.mean: A man entrusts five, two and one talents to three servants. The first two trade and double them and are commended: well done, good and faithful servant. The third hides his in the ground, saying he knew the master was hard, and is condemned as wicked and slothful.
25.big: Those who belong to Christ are trusted with something and expected to use it.

25.ctx: The final judgement scene, unique to Matthew, closing the whole teaching block.
25.mean: The Son of Man sits on his throne and separates all nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. To those on his right: I was hungry and you gave me food, thirsty and you gave me drink, a stranger and you welcomed me, naked and you clothed me, sick and in prison and you visited me — as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me. Those on his left are sent away to eternal punishment, the righteous into eternal life.
25.big: Christ identifies himself with the hungry and imprisoned, and judges by how people treated them.
25.diff: Whether 'the least of these my brothers' means all the poor, or Christ's persecuted messengers, is debated. Either way the passage rules out a professed faith indifferent to need. The parallel of 'eternal punishment' with 'eternal life' is central to discussions of the nature of final judgement.

26.ctx: Two days before Passover, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims.
26.mean: Jesus tells the disciples he will be delivered up to be crucified. The chief priests and elders plot to arrest him by stealth, but not during the feast, lest there be an uproar.
26.big: Jesus announces his death before his enemies have even settled their plan.

26.ctx: Bethany, at the house of Simon the leper, two miles from Jerusalem.
26.mean: A woman pours very expensive ointment on his head. The disciples are indignant at the waste, but Jesus says she has done a beautiful thing, preparing him for burial, and that wherever the gospel is proclaimed, what she has done will be told.
26.big: Extravagant devotion to Jesus is honoured, and his burial is acknowledged in advance.

26.ctx: Immediately after the anointing at Bethany, in deliberate contrast to the woman who had just poured out a year's wages.
26.mean: Judas goes to the chief priests and asks what they will give him; they pay him thirty pieces of silver — the price of a slave in Exodus 21:32.
26.big: One person pours out a year's wages; another sells him for the price of a slave.

26.ctx: The first day of Unleavened Bread, when Passover lambs were sacrificed.
26.mean: Jesus sends disciples into the city to a certain man, saying: my time is at hand; I will keep the Passover at your house.
26.big: Jesus directs the arrangements rather than being overtaken by events.

26.ctx: The Passover meal, which recalled the exodus through a set order of food and cups.
26.mean: Jesus says one of them will betray him, and each asks: is it I, Lord? Then he takes bread, blesses and breaks it: take, eat; this is my body. And the cup: this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. He will not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drinks it new with them in his Father's kingdom.
26.big: Jesus interprets his own death in advance as the covenant sacrifice for the forgiveness of sins.
26.diff: Christian traditions differ over what happens at the Lord's Supper. All accept that Jesus himself gave this meaning to his death and commanded the meal. Matthew alone adds 'for the forgiveness of sins'.

26.ctx: On the way to the Mount of Olives, after singing the Passover psalms.
26.mean: Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7 — I will strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered — and promises to go before them to Galilee after he is raised. Peter insists he will never fall away, and Jesus tells him that this night, before the rooster crows, he will deny him three times.
26.big: Jesus foresees his followers' failure and promises to meet them beyond it.

26.ctx: Gethsemane, meaning oil press, an olive grove on the Mount of Olives.
26.mean: Jesus becomes sorrowful and troubled, saying his soul is very sorrowful, even to death. He falls on his face and prays: my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will. Three times he prays, and three times finds the disciples sleeping: the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.
26.big: Jesus' human will genuinely recoils and genuinely submits to the Father.
26.diff: This is one of the clearest windows in the Gospels onto Christ's full humanity (see Mark 4:35). That he asked and was not spared says something important about unanswered prayer.

26.ctx: Judas arrives with a crowd from the chief priests and elders.
26.mean: Judas identifies Jesus with a kiss. A disciple draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant; Jesus says: put your sword back, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Do you think I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will send more than twelve legions of angels? But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled? All the disciples forsake him and flee.
26.big: Jesus goes to his death by choice, refusing the force available to him.
26.diff: Matthew alone records the saying about the sword and the twelve legions, and it has featured in Christian discussion of violence ever since.

26.ctx: A night hearing before Caiaphas and the council, irregular under later Jewish law.
26.mean: False witnesses come forward but do not agree. Jesus is silent until the high priest puts him under oath: tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus says: you have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. The high priest tears his robes and charges blasphemy, and they judge him deserving death.
26.big: Jesus claims the place beside God from Psalm 110 and Daniel 7, and is condemned for it.

26.ctx: In the courtyard, while the trial goes on inside. Matthew interweaves the two scenes.
26.mean: A servant girl says Peter was with Jesus; he denies it. Another accuses him; he denies with an oath. Bystanders say his accent betrays him; he begins to invoke a curse and swear that he does not know the man. Immediately the rooster crows, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.
26.big: While Jesus confesses who he is, his leading disciple denies knowing him.

27.ctx: Early morning, after the night hearing before Caiaphas. Under Roman rule the Sanhedrin could not carry out a death sentence, so they take him to the governor.
27.mean: Matthew says that when morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death, and they bound him, led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor.
27.big: A religious verdict must be turned into a political charge to be carried out.

27.ctx: Matthew alone records Judas's end here, placing it between the council's verdict and Jesus' appearance before Pilate.
27.mean: Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, returns the thirty pieces of silver saying he has sinned in betraying innocent blood. They refuse it, and he throws it down, departs and hangs himself. The priests buy the potter's field with it, which Matthew links to a prophecy associated with Jeremiah.
27.big: Remorse without repentance ends in despair.
27.diff: Acts 1:18 describes Judas's death differently; common explanations combine hanging with a subsequent fall. Matthew's citation blends Zechariah 11 with Jeremiah 19 and 32, a known difficulty.

27.ctx: Pilate's questioning, with the charge now framed as claiming kingship.
27.mean: Pilate asks: are you the King of the Jews? Jesus says: you have said so. To the accusations of the chief priests he gives no answer, so that the governor is greatly amazed.
27.big: Jesus is silent before his accusers, fulfilling Isaiah 53:7.

27.ctx: A Passover custom of releasing a prisoner, not attested outside the Gospels.
27.mean: Pilate offers Barabbas or Jesus. His wife sends word about a dream, warning him to have nothing to do with this righteous man. The chief priests persuade the crowd to ask for Barabbas, and they cry: let him be crucified.
27.big: The guilty man goes free and the innocent one is condemned in his place.

27.ctx: Pilate's attempt to clear himself, in a province he governed badly enough to be recalled to Rome a few years later.
27.mean: Seeing a riot beginning, Pilate washes his hands, saying he is innocent of this man's blood. The people answer: his blood be on us and on our children. He releases Barabbas and delivers Jesus to be crucified.
27.big: Pilate performs innocence while doing the thing he knows is unjust.
27.diff: Verse 25 has been terribly misused through history to justify violence against Jewish people. Matthew records the crowd in Jerusalem on one day, not a verdict on a whole people for all time; the New Testament lays responsibility for Jesus' death on human sin generally and on God's purpose (Acts 2:23).

27.ctx: Inside the governor's headquarters, before the whole battalion.
27.mean: The soldiers strip him, put a scarlet robe on him, twist a crown of thorns, put a reed in his right hand, kneel and mock him as King of the Jews, spit on him and strike him.
27.big: The soldiers' mockery states the truth they cannot see.

27.ctx: Golgotha, outside the city walls. Simon of Cyrene, in North Africa, is compelled to carry the cross.
27.mean: Jesus refuses wine mixed with gall. They crucify him and divide his garments by lot, and put the charge above his head: this is Jesus, the King of the Jews. Two robbers are crucified with him. Passers-by, chief priests and the robbers mock him: he saved others; he cannot save himself.
27.big: The mockers speak more truly than they know: to save others, he would not save himself.

27.ctx: From noon to three in the afternoon, near the end of some six hours on the cross.
27.mean: Darkness covers the land. Jesus cries: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani — my God, my God, why have you forsaken me — the opening of Psalm 22. He cries out again and yields up his spirit. The temple curtain is torn from top to bottom, the earth shakes, tombs are opened, and the centurion and those with him say: truly this was the Son of God.
27.big: At the moment of his death a Roman officer confesses what the leaders denied.
27.diff: Matthew alone records the opened tombs, a passage much discussed. How to understand Jesus' forsakenness is a theological question Christians answer differently: Reformed and much evangelical theology holds that he bore the judgement due to sinners in his human nature, without division in the Trinity. Psalm 22 ends in vindication, not despair.

27.ctx: Late Friday afternoon. Jewish law required burial before nightfall, and the Sabbath began at sunset, which made haste necessary.
27.mean: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man and a disciple, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in a clean linen shroud and lays it in his own new tomb, rolling a great stone to the entrance. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite the tomb.
27.big: The burial is witnessed, and the tomb is known.

27.ctx: Matthew alone records the guard at the tomb, which matters for the accusation in 28:11–15.
27.mean: The chief priests ask Pilate for a guard, recalling that Jesus said he would rise after three days, lest the disciples steal the body. Pilate grants it, and they seal the stone and set a guard.
27.big: Jesus' enemies remember his prediction better than his disciples do.

28.ctx: Early on the first day of the week. Women's testimony carried little legal weight, which makes them unlikely invented witnesses.
28.mean: There is a great earthquake, and an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it. The guards tremble and become like dead men. The angel tells the women: he is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place, then go quickly and tell his disciples. As they run, Jesus meets them and says: greetings. They take hold of his feet and worship him.
28.big: The tomb is empty, and the risen Jesus is worshipped by the first witnesses.

28.ctx: The counter-story, which Matthew says was still circulating when he wrote.
28.mean: Some of the guard report to the chief priests, who give the soldiers a sum of money to say the disciples stole the body while they slept. This story has been spread among the Jews to this day.
28.big: The earliest explanation offered against the resurrection still conceded that the tomb was empty.

28.ctx: The closing scene, on a mountain in Galilee where Jesus had directed them.
28.mean: They see him and worship, but some doubt. Jesus says: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
28.big: The risen Christ sends his people to all nations with all authority and his abiding presence.
28.diff: The singular 'name' shared by Father, Son and Spirit is a key text for the doctrine of the Trinity. The promise 'I am with you' answers the name Immanuel in 1:23, closing the Gospel where it began.

1.ctx: Luke, a doctor and Paul's travelling companion, is the only Gentile author in the New Testament. He writes to Theophilus, probably a patron, and his Gospel is the first of two volumes with Acts.
1.mean: Luke says many have undertaken to compile a narrative, and that he too, having followed all things closely from the beginning, decided to write an orderly account, so that Theophilus may have certainty concerning the things he has been taught.
1.big: Luke states his method openly: careful investigation of eyewitness testimony, written so the reader can be sure.
1.diff: This is the only Gospel that begins by explaining how it was researched, and it is often cited in discussions of the Gospels' historical reliability.

1.ctx: Zechariah, a priest of the division of Abijah (1 Chronicles 24:10), serves in the temple; burning incense was a once-in-a-lifetime privilege chosen by lot.
1.mean: Gabriel appears and says Elizabeth will bear a son named John, who will be great, filled with the Holy Spirit from birth, and go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Zechariah doubts because of their age and is struck mute until the birth.
1.big: God begins his great work with an elderly childless couple and a priest who struggles to believe.

1.ctx: Nazareth, an obscure Galilean village. Mary is betrothed, a legally binding arrangement before the couple lived together.
1.mean: Gabriel tells Mary she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who will be great, called the Son of the Most High, and given the throne of his father David, reigning for ever. She asks how, since she is a virgin. The angel says the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the child will be called holy, the Son of God. Nothing will be impossible with God. Mary says: behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.
1.big: The eternal Son enters the world through the willing obedience of an ordinary young woman.
1.diff: Mary's question is about means rather than doubt, and she is not rebuked as Zechariah was. The virgin conception is affirmed in the historic creeds and underlies Christ being truly God and truly man (see Mark 4:35).

1.ctx: Mary travels to the Judean hill country, a journey of several days, to visit her relative Elizabeth.
1.mean: When Mary greets her, the baby leaps in Elizabeth's womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries: blessed are you among women, and why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? Blessed is she who believed.
1.big: Elizabeth recognises Mary's unborn child as her Lord.

1.ctx: Mary's song, traditionally called the Magnificat, draws heavily on Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2.
1.mean: Mary says her soul magnifies the Lord and her spirit rejoices in God her Saviour, for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. He has scattered the proud, brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble, filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty, in remembrance of his mercy to Abraham and his offspring.
1.big: God's salvation overturns the world's order, lifting the lowly and humbling the powerful.
1.diff: Mary calls God 'my Saviour', which Christians have long noted as her own acknowledgement of need.

1.ctx: The birth of John, and the naming ceremony on the eighth day at his circumcision.
1.mean: Neighbours assume he will be named after his father, but Elizabeth insists on John. Zechariah writes: his name is John. Immediately his mouth is opened and he blesses God, and fear comes on all their neighbours.
1.big: Obedience to God's word restores the voice doubt had silenced.
1.h: The Birth of John the Baptist

1.ctx: Zechariah's song, traditionally called the Benedictus, the first prophecy after centuries of silence.
1.mean: Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, blesses God for visiting and redeeming his people, raising a horn of salvation in the house of David, remembering his holy covenant and the oath to Abraham, so that they might serve him without fear. His child will be called the prophet of the Most High, going before the Lord to give knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of sins, because of the tender mercy of our God, the sunrise visiting us from on high.
1.big: God is keeping promises made to Abraham and David, and the dawn is breaking.

2.ctx: Luke anchors the birth in datable imperial history. The census under Quirinius has been much discussed by historians.
2.mean: Joseph goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David, with Mary. While they are there she gives birth to her firstborn son, wraps him in swaddling cloths and lays him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
2.big: The Saviour of the world is born in the town of David and laid in a feeding trough.
2.diff: Josephus dates a census under Quirinius to AD 6, later than Herod's death, which is a recognised difficulty. Proposed solutions include an earlier registration, a different translation of 'first', or an earlier term of office for Quirinius. The word rendered 'inn' more probably means the guest room of a family house.

2.ctx: Shepherds were a disreputable trade, often unable to keep ceremonial law and not accepted as witnesses in court.
2.mean: An angel announces good news of great joy for all the people: a Saviour, Christ the Lord, born in the city of David. A multitude of the heavenly host praises God: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased. The shepherds go and find it as they were told, and make it known.
2.big: The first people told are shepherds, and the first evangelists are men whose word no court would take.

2.ctx: Jewish law required circumcision on the eighth day and presentation of the firstborn, with a sacrifice.
2.mean: He is circumcised and named Jesus, and they bring him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, offering a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.
2.big: Jesus is born under the law, and his family's offering is the one allowed for the poor.
2.diff: Leviticus 12:8 permits birds instead of a lamb for those who cannot afford one — quiet evidence that the family was poor.

2.ctx: Simeon, a righteous and devout man, had been told he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ.
2.mean: Simeon takes the child in his arms and blesses God: Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel. He tells Mary the child is appointed for the fall and rising of many, and a sword will pierce her own soul.
2.big: An old man sees in an infant the salvation prepared for Gentiles as well as Israel.

2.ctx: Anna, a prophetess of great age, had worshipped in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day.
2.mean: Anna comes up at that very hour, gives thanks to God, and speaks of the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
2.big: A widow of eighty-four is among the first to proclaim the Messiah.

2.ctx: The family returns to Galilee after fulfilling the law's requirements.
2.mean: Luke says the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.
2.big: Jesus grew as a real child, in wisdom as well as body (see Mark 4:35 on his full humanity).

2.ctx: The only glimpse of Jesus between infancy and adulthood. Families travelled to Passover in large groups, which explains how he was missed.
2.mean: At twelve Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem. After three days his parents find him in the temple among the teachers, listening and asking questions, and all are amazed at his understanding. He says: did you not know that I must be in my Father's house? They do not understand. He goes down with them and is submissive, and Mary treasures these things in her heart. Jesus increases in wisdom and stature and in favour with God and man.
2.big: Even as a boy Jesus knows God as his Father, yet grows and submits like any son.
2.h: The Boy Jesus at the Temple

3.ctx: Luke dates John's ministry against six named rulers, around AD 28–29 — the most precise dating in the Gospels.
3.mean: John proclaims a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, as Isaiah 40 foretold: all flesh shall see the salvation of God. He tells the crowds to bear fruit in keeping with repentance and not rely on descent from Abraham. Asked what to do, he tells the crowds to share clothes and food, tax collectors to collect no more than authorised, and soldiers to be content with their wages. He announces one mightier, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire.
3.big: Real repentance shows itself in ordinary honesty and generosity.
3.diff: Only Luke records John's specific instructions to different groups, which fits his consistent interest in wealth and justice.
3.h: The Mission of John the Baptist

3.ctx: Luke mentions the baptism briefly, and notes something the other Gospels do not.
3.mean: When all the people were baptised, and Jesus also had been baptised and was praying, the heavens opened, the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.
3.big: Luke alone notes that Jesus was praying — one of many such notes in this Gospel.

3.ctx: Luke's genealogy runs backwards from Jesus to Adam and then to God, unlike Matthew's, which starts at Abraham.
3.mean: Jesus, about thirty years old, was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, and the list runs back through David and Abraham to Adam, the son of God.
3.big: Luke traces Jesus to the first man, because his Gospel is for the whole human race.
3.diff: The differences from Matthew are usually explained by one giving Joseph's legal royal line and the other Mary's descent, or by legal versus biological lines.

4.ctx: Immediately after the baptism, in the wilderness for forty days. Luke gives the temptations in a different order from Matthew, ending at the temple.
4.mean: The devil tempts Jesus to turn stone to bread, to gain all the kingdoms of the world by worshipping him, and to throw himself from the temple. Jesus answers each with Deuteronomy. The devil departs from him until an opportune time.
4.big: Jesus resists by Scripture what Israel failed, and the conflict is only postponed.

4.ctx: A summary of Jesus' return to Galilee in the power of the Spirit.
4.mean: He teaches in their synagogues, being glorified by all, and a report about him goes out through all the surrounding country.
4.big: Jesus' ministry begins with wide acclaim, which will not last.

4.ctx: Nazareth, his home town. Luke places this rejection at the start of the ministry, as a programme for the whole Gospel.
4.mean: Jesus reads Isaiah 61 — the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, to proclaim good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, to set at liberty those oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favour — stopping before the day of vengeance. He says: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing. When he points out that Elijah was sent to a Sidonian widow and Elisha healed a Syrian, they are filled with wrath and try to throw him off a cliff.
4.big: Jesus announces his mission to the poor and outcast, and is nearly killed for saying God's mercy reaches Gentiles.

4.ctx: Capernaum, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, becomes Jesus' base after Nazareth rejects him. Synagogue teaching on the Sabbath was open to visiting rabbis.
4.mean: In the synagogue a man with an unclean demon cries: what have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? I know who you are, the Holy One of God. Jesus rebukes him and the demon comes out without harming him. All are amazed at the authority and power of his word.
4.big: Jesus' word alone commands the spirit world.

4.ctx: Simon's house in Capernaum, before Simon has been called to follow in chapter 5. Malaria and fevers were common around the lake.
4.mean: Jesus rebukes a high fever in Simon's mother-in-law and she rises and serves them. At sunset all who had sick friends bring them, and he lays hands on each one and heals them. Demons come out crying that he is the Son of God, but he rebukes them.
4.big: Jesus heals individually, laying hands on each one who comes.

4.ctx: At daybreak Jesus withdraws to a desolate place, and the crowds seek him out.
4.mean: The people try to keep him from leaving, but he says he must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, for that is why he was sent.
4.big: Jesus refuses to let popularity in one place limit his mission.

5.ctx: The Lake of Gennesaret, another name for the Sea of Galilee. Luke gives fuller detail of the disciples' call than Matthew or Mark.
5.mean: Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, then tells him to let down the nets. Simon objects that they toiled all night and caught nothing, but at his word does it, and the catch nearly sinks two boats. Simon falls at Jesus' knees: depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. Jesus says: do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men. They leave everything and follow him.
5.big: The first response to seeing who Jesus is, is to feel one's own sinfulness.

5.ctx: Leprosy covered several skin conditions and brought ritual uncleanness and exclusion under Leviticus 13–14.
5.mean: A man full of leprosy falls on his face: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. Jesus stretches out his hand and touches him. Immediately the leprosy leaves. He charges him to tell no one but show himself to the priest. Yet the report goes abroad, and Jesus withdraws to desolate places to pray.
5.big: Jesus touches the untouchable, and cleanness passes from him to the man.

5.ctx: Pharisees and teachers of the law have come from every village of Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem.
5.mean: Friends lower a paralysed man through the tiles because of the crowd. Jesus says: man, your sins are forgiven. The scribes ask who can forgive sins but God alone. Jesus asks which is easier to say, then tells him to rise and go home, so they may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. Amazement seizes them all.
5.big: Jesus proves an invisible claim to a divine right by a visible healing.

5.ctx: Levi, also called Matthew, collected tax for Rome, making him a collaborator in popular view.
5.mean: Jesus says 'follow me' and Levi leaves everything and rises and follows, then holds a great feast with many tax collectors. The Pharisees grumble, and Jesus says those who are well have no need of a physician: I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.
5.big: Jesus deliberately seeks those the religious had written off.

5.ctx: John's disciples and the Pharisees fasted often; Jesus' disciples did not.
5.mean: Jesus asks whether wedding guests can fast while the bridegroom is with them. The days will come when he is taken away, and then they will fast.
5.big: Jesus' presence is a wedding, and his removal is foretold from early on.

5.ctx: Two short images continuing the answer about fasting, with a third saying that Luke alone adds about preferring old wine.
5.mean: Jesus speaks of a patch from a new garment tearing an old one, and new wine bursting old skins. Then he adds: no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says the old is good.
5.big: What Jesus brings needs new forms, and people naturally prefer what they are used to.

6.ctx: Plucking grain while passing was permitted, but the Pharisees classed it as reaping, forbidden on the Sabbath.
6.mean: Jesus cites David eating the consecrated bread and says the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.
6.big: Jesus claims authority over an institution God himself established.

6.ctx: Another Sabbath, in the synagogue, with scribes and Pharisees watching to find grounds to accuse him.
6.mean: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus tells the man with the withered hand to stand in the middle, and asks whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or harm, to save life or destroy it. He heals the man, and they are filled with fury and discuss what they might do to him.
6.big: Doing good on the Sabbath is lawful, and saying so provokes fury.

6.ctx: Luke alone says Jesus spent the whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve.
6.mean: Jesus goes out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continues in prayer to God. When day comes he calls his disciples and chooses twelve, whom he named apostles, including Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
6.big: The most consequential choice of Jesus' ministry follows a night of prayer.

6.ctx: Jesus comes down and stands on a level place, which is why this is often called the Sermon on the Plain.
6.mean: A great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon comes to hear and be healed, and power comes out from him and heals them all.
6.big: People come from Jewish and Gentile regions alike, and all are healed.

6.ctx: Luke's version of the Beatitudes is shorter and blunter than Matthew's, addressed directly as 'you'.
6.mean: Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God; you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied; you who weep now, for you shall laugh; you when people hate and exclude you on account of the Son of Man — rejoice, for your reward is great in heaven.
6.big: God's blessing rests on the poor and hungry, not on the comfortable.
6.diff: Matthew's 'poor in spirit' draws out the inner dependence; Luke's blunter form fits his consistent concern for the materially poor. Both are Jesus' teaching.

6.ctx: Four woes matching the four blessings, found only in Luke, and fitting his sustained concern about wealth and comfort.
6.mean: Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation; woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry; woe to you who laugh now; woe to you when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
6.big: Present comfort and popularity can be the whole of a person's reward.

6.ctx: The hardest instruction in the Gospels, given to people under real oppression.
6.mean: Jesus says love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you. To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other. Give to everyone who begs from you. As you wish that others would do to you, do so to them. Love your enemies and do good, expecting nothing in return, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
6.big: God's children are to imitate his kindness toward those who do not deserve it.
6.diff: Where Matthew says 'be perfect', Luke says 'be merciful' — the same call expressed in terms of God's character.

6.ctx: Practical instruction on how disciples treat one another, continuing the sermon on the plain after the command to love enemies.
6.mean: Jesus says judge not, and you will not be judged; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you, good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over. Can a blind man lead a blind man? Take the log out of your own eye first.
6.big: Generous, non-condemning treatment of others is met with generosity from God.

6.ctx: A short parable about trees and fruit, which Jesus applies to speech and then to the foundations of a life.
6.mean: Jesus says no good tree bears bad fruit; each tree is known by its own fruit. The good person produces good out of the good treasure of his heart, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
6.big: What comes out in speech reveals what is stored in the heart.

6.ctx: The closing challenge of the sermon, in a land where dry riverbeds flooded suddenly.
6.mean: Jesus asks why they call him Lord, Lord, and do not do what he tells them. The one who hears and does is like a man who dug deep and laid a foundation on rock; the one who hears and does not do is like a man who built without a foundation, and the ruin of that house was great.
6.big: Calling Jesus Lord without obeying him leaves a life with no foundation.

7.ctx: A Roman centurion in Capernaum, evidently respected, who had built the local synagogue.
7.mean: Jewish elders plead his case. As Jesus approaches, the centurion sends friends to say he is not worthy, and that Jesus need only say the word, since he himself understands authority. Jesus marvels and says: not even in Israel have I found such faith.
7.big: A Gentile soldier's grasp of Jesus' authority exceeds anything Jesus has found in Israel.

7.ctx: Nain, a village in Galilee. A widow who had lost her only son had lost her livelihood and protection as well.
7.mean: Jesus sees the funeral procession and has compassion, saying: do not weep. He touches the bier and says: young man, I say to you, arise. The dead man sits up and begins to speak, and Jesus gives him to his mother. Fear seizes them all and they glorify God, saying a great prophet has arisen among us.
7.big: Jesus raises the dead out of compassion for a woman nobody else could help.
7.diff: Found only in Luke, and one of three raisings in the Gospels. It closely echoes Elijah and Elisha raising widows' sons.

7.ctx: John is in prison, and what he hears of Jesus does not match his expectation of a Messiah bringing judgement.
7.mean: John sends to ask: are you the one who is to come? Jesus heals many in that hour and says: go and tell John what you have seen and heard — the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.
7.big: Jesus answers doubt with evidence from Isaiah rather than rebuke.

7.ctx: Jesus speaks about John after his messengers leave, to crowds who had themselves gone out into the wilderness to be baptised.
7.mean: Jesus says John is more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3, and that none born of women is greater — yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater. Luke adds that the people and tax collectors declared God just, having been baptised by John, but the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God's purpose for themselves.
7.big: The religious experts rejected God's purpose while tax collectors accepted it.

7.ctx: A dinner at a Pharisee's house, where guests reclined at low tables with their feet behind them.
7.mean: A woman of the city, a sinner, wets his feet with her tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them. Simon thinks that if Jesus were a prophet he would know what sort of woman she is. Jesus tells of two debtors forgiven different amounts, and asks which will love more. Simon has given no water, kiss or oil; she has not ceased. Her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. Your faith has saved you; go in peace.
7.big: Great forgiveness produces great love, and the respectable host understands neither.
7.diff: This is a different occasion from the anointing at Bethany in the other Gospels; the woman is not named, and identifying her with Mary Magdalene is a later tradition with no basis in the text.

8.ctx: Luke alone records the women who travelled with Jesus and funded the mission.
8.mean: Jesus goes through cities and villages preaching, with the twelve and some women who had been healed: Mary called Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Herod's household manager, Susanna and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
8.big: Women were among Jesus' followers and paid for the ministry out of their own resources.

8.ctx: The parable of the sower, told to a great crowd gathered from town after town.
8.mean: Seed falls on the path, the rock, among thorns and into good soil, yielding a hundredfold. Asked what it means, Jesus quotes Isaiah 6, then explains: the seed is the word of God, snatched away by the devil, received with joy but withering in time of testing, choked by cares, riches and pleasures, or held fast in an honest and good heart, bearing fruit with patience.
8.big: The word meets different hearts, and fruitfulness comes with patience.

8.ctx: Short sayings on light and on hearing, following the explanation of the sower and applying it to how the disciples listen.
8.mean: No one lights a lamp and covers it; nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest. Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given.
8.big: How a person listens to God's word determines what they receive.

8.ctx: Jesus' mother and brothers arrive while he is teaching, and cannot reach him because of the crowd.
8.mean: Unable to reach him for the crowd, they send word. Jesus says: my mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.
8.big: The closest family bond is hearing and doing God's word.

8.ctx: The Sea of Galilee lies in a basin surrounded by hills and is prone to sudden violent squalls.
8.mean: Jesus falls asleep as they sail. A windstorm fills the boat, and they wake him: Master, Master, we are perishing. He rebukes the wind and the raging waves, and there is a calm. He asks: where is your faith? They are afraid and marvel: who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?
8.big: Jesus sleeps from exhaustion and commands the sea as only God does (see Mark 4:35).

8.ctx: The country of the Gerasenes, Gentile territory opposite Galilee, hence the pigs.
8.mean: A man with many demons, living among the tombs, falls before him. The demons, named Legion, beg not to be sent into the abyss, and enter a herd of pigs which rushes into the lake. The people find the man clothed and in his right mind, and are afraid and ask Jesus to leave. The man begs to go with him, but Jesus sends him home to declare how much God has done for him.
8.big: A man beyond all human help is restored and sent as the first missionary to the Gentiles.

8.ctx: Luke, like Mark, interweaves two healings linked by the number twelve.
8.mean: Jairus, a synagogue ruler, begs Jesus to come to his dying only daughter. On the way a woman with a discharge of blood for twelve years, who had spent all her living on physicians, touches the fringe of his garment and is healed. Jesus says power has gone out from him, and tells her: daughter, your faith has made you well. Word comes that the girl is dead, but Jesus says: do not fear; only believe. He takes her hand: child, arise. Her spirit returns and he tells them to give her something to eat.
8.big: Jesus' power reaches long illness, ritual uncleanness and death itself.
8.diff: Luke, a doctor, is the only one who does not say the woman had grown worse under physicians' care.

9.ctx: Jesus sends out the Twelve, the first time his ministry is extended through others.
9.mean: He gives them power and authority over demons and to cure diseases, and sends them to proclaim the kingdom, taking nothing for the journey.
9.big: The mission extends through those Jesus has called and equipped.

9.ctx: Herod Antipas, who had executed John, hears reports and is perplexed.
9.mean: Some say John has been raised, some Elijah, some that one of the prophets has risen. Herod says he beheaded John, so who is this? And he sought to see him.
9.big: Even the ruler who killed John is left asking who Jesus is.

9.ctx: The apostles return, and Jesus withdraws with them to Bethsaida, but the crowds follow.
9.mean: Jesus welcomes them, speaks of the kingdom and heals. As the day wears away the Twelve want the crowds sent off, but Jesus says: you give them something to eat. With five loaves and two fish he feeds about five thousand men, and twelve baskets are left over.
9.big: Jesus provides abundantly for the crowd his disciples wanted to send away.
9.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand

9.ctx: Luke alone notes that Jesus was praying alone before asking the question.
9.mean: Jesus asks who the crowds say he is, then who they say. Peter answers: the Christ of God.
9.big: The turning point of the Gospel comes after Jesus has been praying.

9.ctx: Immediately after the confession, Jesus redefines what Messiah means.
9.mean: He strictly charges them to tell no one, saying the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised.
9.big: The Messiah must suffer — a necessity, not an accident.

9.ctx: Jesus turns from his own path to the path of everyone who follows him.
9.mean: If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. Whoever would save his life will lose it. What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose himself?
9.big: Following Jesus means a daily cross, and only the life given away is kept.
9.diff: Only Luke adds 'daily', turning a single decision into a continuing pattern.

9.ctx: About eight days later, on a mountain. Luke alone says Jesus went up to pray and that the transfiguration happened as he prayed.
9.mean: As he prays his appearance is altered and his clothing becomes dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak of his departure, which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter, heavy with sleep, offers to make three tents. A cloud overshadows them and a voice says: this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him.
9.big: The glory of the one who must die is revealed, and the Father commands them to listen to him.
9.diff: Luke alone records the subject of the conversation: his 'departure' — literally his exodus — to be accomplished at Jerusalem.

9.ctx: The next day, coming down from the mountain of transfiguration to a crowd where the other disciples have failed to help a boy.
9.mean: A man begs Jesus to look at his only son, seized by a spirit. The disciples could not cast it out. Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit, heals the boy and gives him back to his father, and all are astonished at the majesty of God.
9.big: The glory on the mountain and the misery below belong to the same story.
9.h: The Boy with an Evil Spirit

9.ctx: While everyone is marvelling, Jesus tells them something they cannot hear.
9.mean: Jesus says: let these words sink into your ears; the Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. But they did not understand, and it was concealed from them, and they were afraid to ask.
9.big: At the height of the crowd's wonder, Jesus speaks of betrayal.
9.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion

9.ctx: An argument among the disciples, immediately after the passion prediction.
9.mean: An argument arises about which of them is the greatest. Jesus takes a child and puts him by his side, saying whoever receives this child in my name receives me; the one who is least among you all is the one who is great. John objects that someone outside their group was casting out demons; Jesus says do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.
9.big: Greatness is receiving the insignificant, and Jesus' work is wider than his disciples' circle.

9.ctx: The turning point of Luke's Gospel: a long journey section to Jerusalem runs from here to chapter 19.
9.mean: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. A Samaritan village does not receive him because of it. James and John ask whether to call down fire from heaven; he turns and rebukes them.
9.big: Jesus sets his face toward the cross, and rebukes disciples who want to punish rejection.

9.ctx: Three would-be followers meet Jesus on the road as he travels toward Jerusalem, having just set his face to go there.
9.mean: One offers to follow anywhere; Jesus says foxes have holes but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Another asks first to bury his father; Jesus says: leave the dead to bury their own dead; you go and proclaim the kingdom. A third asks to say farewell at home; Jesus says no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom.
9.big: Following Jesus takes priority over comfort, family duty and unfinished business.
9.diff: These sayings are deliberately shocking. They are not a general rule against family obligation but a statement of Christ's absolute claim.

10.ctx: Only Luke records this second, larger sending, in pairs ahead of Jesus into the towns he intends to visit.
10.mean: Jesus appoints seventy-two others and says the harvest is plentiful but the labourers few; pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers. He sends them as lambs among wolves, to carry no moneybag, and to say 'the kingdom of God has come near to you' in any town that receives them.
10.big: The mission widens beyond the Twelve, and prayer for workers comes first.
10.diff: Manuscripts divide between seventy and seventy-two; the number may echo the nations of Genesis 10, suggesting a mission to the world.

10.ctx: Woes on the Galilean towns where most of Jesus' miracles were done.
10.mean: Jesus says it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgement than for Chorazin and Bethsaida, and that Capernaum will be brought down to Hades. The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and him who sent me.
10.big: Greater exposure to Christ brings greater accountability.

10.ctx: The seventy-two return from the mission Jesus sent them on, full of excitement at what happened in his name.
10.mean: They return with joy: even the demons are subject to us in your name. Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven, and that he has given them authority over the enemy, but tells them not to rejoice in this so much as that their names are written in heaven.
10.big: Spiritual power is real, but belonging to God is the greater cause for joy.

10.ctx: One of the few places where Luke records Jesus' own prayer of rejoicing.
10.mean: Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and says: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.
10.big: The Son alone reveals the Father, and does so to the childlike rather than the clever.
10.diff: Luke notes that Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit — Father, Son and Spirit all appear in one verse.

10.ctx: A lawyer tests Jesus, then tries to limit the definition of neighbour. The road from Jerusalem to Jericho was a notorious descent through wilderness.
10.mean: Asked what to do to inherit eternal life, the lawyer cites loving God and neighbour. Wanting to justify himself, he asks who his neighbour is. Jesus tells of a man beaten by robbers, passed by a priest and a Levite, and helped by a Samaritan who bandaged his wounds, took him to an inn and paid for his care. Which proved neighbour? Jesus says: you go, and do likewise.
10.big: Jesus reverses the question: not who qualifies as my neighbour, but who acts like one.
10.diff: Samaritans and Jews were bitterly hostile, which is the point of the story; the priest and Levite may have feared ritual defilement from a body.
10.h: The Parable of the Good Samaritan

10.ctx: A village, probably Bethany. Luke alone records this incident, immediately after the good Samaritan.
10.mean: Martha welcomes Jesus and is distracted with much serving, while Mary sits at the Lord's feet and listens. Martha complains; Jesus says: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.
10.big: Sitting as a disciple at Jesus' feet is not a luxury but the one necessary thing.
10.diff: Sitting at a teacher's feet was the posture of a disciple, which in that culture was not a woman's place.

11.ctx: Luke places the Lord's Prayer in response to a disciple's request, after seeing Jesus praying.
11.mean: Jesus gives a shorter form than Matthew's: Father, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come; give us each day our daily bread; forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us; and lead us not into temptation.
11.big: Jesus teaches his disciples to address God simply as Father.

11.ctx: Two parables about persistence in prayer, found here in Luke.
11.mean: Jesus tells of a friend who gets up at midnight because of his neighbour's persistence, then says: ask and it will be given, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened. If you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.
11.big: God gives generously to those who keep asking, and his greatest gift is the Spirit.
11.diff: Where Matthew says 'good things', Luke says 'the Holy Spirit' — the gift that matters most in Luke and Acts.

11.ctx: Jesus casts out a mute demon, and the crowd divides over the explanation.
11.mean: Some say he casts out demons by Beelzebul; others seek a sign. Jesus says a kingdom divided against itself falls, and if he casts out demons by the finger of God, the kingdom of God has come upon them. When a stronger man attacks and overcomes the strong man, he takes away his armour. Whoever is not with me is against me.
11.big: Jesus' power over demons shows God's kingdom has arrived and the strong man is being overpowered.

11.ctx: A short, unsettling parable about reformation without genuine change.
11.mean: An unclean spirit leaves a person, finds the house swept and put in order, and returns with seven others, so the last state is worse than the first.
11.big: Moral tidying without Christ leaves a person more vulnerable, not less.

11.ctx: A brief exchange found only in Luke, interrupting the dispute about whether Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul.
11.mean: A woman in the crowd calls out: blessed is the womb that bore you. Jesus says: blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it.
11.big: Jesus redirects praise of his mother to obedience to God's word.

11.ctx: The crowds increase as Jesus travels, and some ask for a sign from heaven to authenticate him.
11.mean: Jesus says this generation is evil and seeks a sign, but none will be given except the sign of Jonah. The queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgement and condemn this generation, for something greater than Solomon and Jonah is here.
11.big: Gentiles who responded to lesser messengers will condemn those who reject Christ.

11.ctx: A short saying about light and the eye, applied to inner receptiveness.
11.mean: No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar. Your eye is the lamp of your body; if it is healthy your whole body is full of light. Be careful, then, that the light in you is not darkness.
11.big: What a person lets in determines whether they live in light or darkness.

11.ctx: A Pharisee invites Jesus to dine, and is astonished that he does not wash before the meal.
11.mean: Jesus pronounces woes: they clean the outside of the cup while inside they are full of greed; they tithe herbs and neglect justice and the love of God; they love the best seats and greetings. Woe to the lawyers, who load people with burdens they will not touch, who build the tombs of the prophets their fathers killed, and who have taken away the key of knowledge. From then on the scribes and Pharisees press him hard, lying in wait to catch him.
11.big: Religious expertise that burdens others and neglects justice draws Jesus' sharpest words.
11.h: Woes to Pharisees and Experts in the Law

12.ctx: Thousands gather, trampling one another, and Jesus speaks first to his disciples.
12.mean: Jesus says beware the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered that will not be revealed; what you have said in the dark will be heard in the light.
12.big: Hypocrisy is futile because everything will finally be made public.

12.ctx: A word to disciples facing real danger, since Jesus' opponents were already plotting.
12.mean: Jesus says do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do; fear him who has authority to cast into hell. Five sparrows sell for two pennies, yet not one is forgotten by God; even the hairs of your head are numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.
12.big: Fear of God displaces fear of people, and the Father's care reaches the smallest detail.

12.ctx: A word about public allegiance, given to disciples who would be dragged before synagogues and rulers, followed by a hard saying about the Spirit.
12.mean: Everyone who acknowledges Jesus before others, the Son of Man will acknowledge before the angels of God. Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. When brought before authorities, do not be anxious, for the Holy Spirit will teach you what to say.
12.big: Public confession of Christ matters, and the Spirit helps those put on trial for it.
12.diff: As in Matthew 12 and Mark 3, blasphemy against the Spirit describes a settled, hardened rejection; anyone anxious about having committed it has shown by that anxiety that they have not.

12.ctx: A man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute, and Jesus refuses and warns instead.
12.mean: Jesus says: take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. He tells of a rich man whose land produced plentifully, who planned bigger barns and said to his soul: take your ease, eat, drink, be merry. But God said: fool! This night your soul is required of you. So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.
12.big: A life built on accumulation ends with everything going to someone else.
12.diff: Found only in Luke, and characteristic of his sustained concern about wealth.
12.h: The Parable of the Rich Fool

12.ctx: Addressed to disciples, immediately after the parable of the rich fool.
12.mean: Jesus says do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or wear. Consider the ravens and the lilies; how much more valuable are you. Seek his kingdom, and these things will be added. Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
12.big: Anxiety is answered by the Father's pleasure in giving his children the kingdom.

12.ctx: Luke's version of treasures in heaven is more direct about possessions.
12.mean: Jesus says sell your possessions and give to the needy; provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, a treasure in the heavens that does not fail. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
12.big: Giving away what cannot be kept secures what cannot be lost.

12.ctx: Three short parables about readiness, using images of servants awaiting a master.
12.mean: Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, like men waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast. Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake; he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and come and serve them. Be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. To whom much was given, of him much will be required.
12.big: The returning master serves his watchful servants, and greater privilege brings greater responsibility.

12.ctx: One of Jesus' most difficult sayings, spoken as he travels toward Jerusalem.
12.mean: Jesus says he came to cast fire on the earth, and has a baptism to undergo, and is under great distress until it is accomplished. He came not to give peace but division: households will be divided, father against son and mother against daughter.
12.big: Allegiance to Jesus divides even the closest households.
12.diff: His 'baptism' is his death. This describes the effect of following Christ, not an endorsement of conflict.

12.ctx: Addressed to the crowds, using their skill at forecasting weather.
12.mean: Jesus says they know how to interpret a cloud rising in the west or a south wind, but do not know how to interpret the present time.
12.big: People skilled at reading the weather are blind to what God is doing in front of them.

12.ctx: A short warning drawn from the law courts, where a debtor could be imprisoned until the debt was paid in full.
12.mean: Jesus says why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him, lest he drag you to the judge and you be put in prison until you have paid the last penny.
12.big: There is still time to settle accounts with God, but not indefinitely.

13.ctx: Two recent disasters, one caused by Pilate and one an accident, raise the question of whether victims were worse sinners.
13.mean: Jesus asks whether the Galileans Pilate killed, or the eighteen crushed by the tower of Siloam, were worse offenders. No, he says, but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
13.big: Jesus refuses to treat suffering as proof of particular guilt, and turns the question into a call to repent.
13.diff: This is one of the clearest places Scripture addresses the assumption that disaster indicates God's specific judgement on victims.

13.ctx: A parable following directly from the call to repent. The fig tree was a common image for Israel in the prophets.
13.mean: A man finds no fruit on his fig tree for three years and tells the vinedresser to cut it down. The vinedresser asks for one more year to dig round it and fertilise it, and if it bears fruit next year, well; if not, cut it down.
13.big: God's patience is real and generous, and it is not endless.
13.h: The Parable of the Barren Fig Tree

13.ctx: A Sabbath in a synagogue, with a woman bent over for eighteen years.
13.mean: Jesus calls her, lays hands on her, and she is made straight and glorifies God. The synagogue ruler objects that there are six days for work. Jesus calls them hypocrites: each of them unties an ox on the Sabbath, so should not this daughter of Abraham, bound by Satan for eighteen years, be loosed? His adversaries are put to shame and the people rejoice.
13.big: Jesus values a suffering woman above a rule his opponents already bent for livestock.

13.ctx: Two short parables of growth, told after the Sabbath healing.
13.mean: The kingdom is like a mustard seed a man sowed, which grew and became a tree in whose branches the birds made nests.
13.big: Small and unpromising beginnings do not limit what God will grow.
13.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed

13.ctx: The second of a pair of growth parables, using an image from a woman's daily work of baking bread.
13.mean: The kingdom is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.
13.big: The kingdom works unseen until everything is changed.

13.ctx: Jesus continues toward Jerusalem, teaching through towns and villages.
13.mean: Someone asks whether those who are saved will be few. Jesus says: strive to enter through the narrow door, for many will seek to enter and will not be able. Once the master has shut the door, those outside will say they ate and drank in his presence, and he will say: I do not know where you come from. People will come from east and west and recline at table in the kingdom, and some who are last will be first.
13.big: Jesus answers a question about numbers with a command to make sure you enter.

13.ctx: Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod Antipas, who had executed John the Baptist, wants to kill him too.
13.mean: Jesus says: go and tell that fox, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course. Then: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killing the prophets — how often would I have gathered your children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
13.big: Jesus' journey cannot be stopped by a king, and his warning is soaked in grief.

14.ctx: A Sabbath meal at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, where Jesus is being watched carefully.
14.mean: A man with dropsy is before him. Jesus asks the lawyers and Pharisees whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath; they are silent. He heals the man and asks which of them, having a son or an ox fall into a well, would not immediately pull him out on a Sabbath day.
14.big: Jesus exposes the inconsistency of rules that make room for livestock but not for people.
14.h: Jesus Heals a Man with Dropsy

14.ctx: Observing how guests choose places of honour at the Sabbath meal, where seating openly displayed a person's status.
14.mean: Jesus says do not sit in the place of honour, lest a more distinguished person come; sit in the lowest place, and be invited higher. Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. To his host he says: when you give a feast, do not invite friends or rich neighbours who can repay you, but the poor, crippled, lame and blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you.
14.big: Kingdom hospitality is directed at those who cannot return the favour.

14.ctx: A guest's pious remark prompts a parable about refusing God's invitation.
14.mean: A man gives a great banquet, and those invited make excuses — a field, oxen, a new wife. The master sends his servant to bring in the poor, crippled, blind and lame, and then to the highways and hedges to compel people to come in, that his house may be filled. None of those first invited will taste his banquet.
14.big: God's invitation is refused by the respectable and accepted by the desperate.
14.diff: 'Compel them to come in' was tragically used in later centuries to justify forced conversion; in the parable it describes urgent persuasion of people who would not presume they were welcome.

14.ctx: Great crowds are travelling with Jesus, and he deliberately thins them.
14.mean: Jesus says whoever does not hate his own father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, cannot be his disciple. Whoever does not bear his own cross cannot be his disciple. Count the cost, like a man building a tower or a king going to war. Any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
14.big: Jesus tells prospective followers to count the cost before they start.
14.diff: 'Hate' here is a Semitic way of expressing comparative preference, as in Genesis 29:31; Jesus commands love for family elsewhere. The point is that nothing may rival allegiance to him.

14.ctx: A short saying closing the section on counting the cost of discipleship. Salt from the Dead Sea region could become contaminated and useless.
14.mean: Salt is good, but if it has lost its taste it is fit neither for the soil nor the manure heap. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.
14.big: A disciple who has lost what makes him distinct is of no use at all.

15.ctx: Tax collectors and sinners draw near, and the Pharisees grumble that Jesus receives them and eats with them. All three parables answer that complaint.
15.mean: A man with a hundred sheep who loses one leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the lost one until he finds it, lays it on his shoulders rejoicing, and calls friends to rejoice with him. There is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous who need no repentance.
15.big: God searches for the lost and celebrates when they are found.
15.h: The Parable of the Lost Sheep

15.ctx: The second of three parables, with a woman as the central figure.
15.mean: A woman with ten silver coins who loses one lights a lamp, sweeps the house and seeks diligently until she finds it, then calls her friends to rejoice. So there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
15.big: God's search is thorough, and heaven's joy is over repentance.
15.h: The Parable of the Lost Coin

15.ctx: The longest and best known of Jesus' parables, often called the prodigal son though it is equally about the elder brother.
15.mean: A younger son demands his inheritance, squanders it in a far country, and ends up feeding pigs. Coming to himself, he returns rehearsing a confession, but while he is still a long way off his father sees him, feels compassion, runs, embraces and kisses him, and calls for the best robe, a ring, sandals and the fattened calf. The elder son is angry and will not go in, saying he has served for years and never been given a young goat. The father says: son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours; it was fitting to celebrate, for your brother was dead and is alive; he was lost and is found.
15.big: God runs to welcome returning sinners, and pleads with the respectable to come in too.
15.diff: A father running was undignified in that culture. The parable ends without saying whether the elder brother went in, leaving the Pharisees who prompted it to answer for themselves.
15.h: The Parable of the Prodigal Son

16.ctx: One of Jesus' most puzzling parables, told to the disciples but with the Pharisees listening.
16.mean: A manager about to be dismissed reduces his master's debtors' bills to secure friends for the future, and the master commends his shrewdness. Jesus says the sons of this world are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light, and tells them to make friends by means of unrighteous wealth. One who is faithful in little is faithful in much. No servant can serve two masters: you cannot serve God and money.
16.big: Money is a trust to be used with foresight for eternal purposes, never a master.
16.diff: The master commends shrewdness, not dishonesty. Interpreters differ over whether the manager forgave his own commission or reduced illegitimate interest.
16.h: The Parable of the Shrewd Manager

16.ctx: The Pharisees, who loved money, ridicule him, and Jesus answers.
16.mean: Jesus says they justify themselves before men, but God knows their hearts; what is exalted among men is an abomination before God. The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom is preached. Not a dot of the Law will fail. Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery.
16.big: God sees past self-justification, and his law is not set aside by the kingdom's arrival.

16.ctx: A parable unique to Luke, and the only one in which Jesus gives one of his own characters a name.
16.mean: A rich man in purple and fine linen feasts daily while Lazarus, covered with sores, lies at his gate. Both die; Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side and the rich man is in torment. He asks for water, then that Lazarus be sent to warn his brothers. Abraham says a great chasm has been fixed, and: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.
16.big: How wealth is used in this life has consequences in the next, and Scripture is sufficient warning.
16.diff: Christians differ over how far the parable describes the afterlife in detail or uses familiar imagery to make its point. Its closing line is pointed, given the resurrection that follows.

17.ctx: Teaching for the disciples about sin within the community, following the parable of the rich man and Lazarus.
17.mean: Jesus says temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come. If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him — even seven times in a day.
17.big: Correction and ready forgiveness belong together in the church.

17.ctx: The apostles ask for more faith, apparently daunted by the command to forgive a brother seven times in a day.
17.mean: They ask: increase our faith. Jesus says if you had faith like a grain of mustard seed you could uproot a mulberry tree. He tells of a servant who, after working in the field, is not thanked for doing what was commanded: so you also, when you have done all, say we are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.
17.big: The issue is not more faith but the greatness of its object, and service earns no claim on God.

17.ctx: On the border between Samaria and Galilee, where leprosy forced people to live apart.
17.mean: Ten lepers stand at a distance and cry for mercy. Jesus tells them to show themselves to the priests, and as they go they are cleansed. One, a Samaritan, turns back praising God and falls at Jesus' feet giving thanks. Jesus asks: were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?
17.big: The only one who returns to thank Jesus is the outsider.

17.ctx: The Pharisees ask when the kingdom of God will come, expecting an observable political event.
17.mean: Jesus says the kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say 'look, here it is', for the kingdom of God is in the midst of you. He then tells the disciples that the days of the Son of Man will be like the days of Noah and of Lot — ordinary life continuing until judgement falls suddenly. Remember Lot's wife. Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it.
17.big: The kingdom is already present in Jesus, and the day of his revealing will come suddenly.
17.diff: The phrase can be translated 'within you' or 'among you'; since Jesus is addressing Pharisees, 'among you' — in the person of Jesus himself — is the more natural reading.

18.ctx: Luke states the parable's purpose before telling it. Widows in that society had no legal standing and depended on a judge's goodwill.
18.mean: Jesus tells them always to pray and not lose heart. A widow keeps coming to an unjust judge who neither fears God nor respects man, until he gives her justice to be rid of her. If even he will act, will not God give justice to his elect who cry to him day and night? Yet when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?
18.big: God is not like the unjust judge, so his people should keep praying and not give up.
18.h: The Parable of the Persistent Widow

18.ctx: Addressed to those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and treated others with contempt.
18.mean: A Pharisee stands and thanks God that he is not like other men, fasting twice a week and tithing all he gets. A tax collector, standing far off, will not lift his eyes but beats his breast: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Jesus says this man went down to his house justified rather than the other, for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.
18.big: Justification comes to the man who asks for mercy, not the one who lists his record.
18.diff: This is the clearest picture of justification in the Gospels, and matches what Paul teaches in Romans.
18.h: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector

18.ctx: Parents bring even infants for Jesus to touch, and the disciples rebuke them for wasting his time.
18.mean: Jesus calls them to him and says: let the children come to me, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.
18.big: The kingdom is received by those who come with nothing but need.

18.ctx: A wealthy ruler, in a culture where wealth was widely seen as a mark of God's favour.
18.mean: He asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, calling Jesus good. Jesus asks why he calls him good, since no one is good but God alone, and lists commandments. The man says he has kept them all from youth. Jesus says: one thing you still lack; sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and come, follow me. He becomes very sad, for he was extremely rich. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. Those who hear ask who then can be saved; Jesus says what is impossible with man is possible with God.
18.big: Salvation is humanly impossible and possible only as God's gift.
18.diff: Jesus' question about 'good' is not a denial of his own goodness but an invitation to think about what calling him good implies.

18.ctx: The third and fullest passion prediction, as they approach Jerusalem.
