18.mean: Jesus takes the Twelve and says everything written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished: he will be delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, shamefully treated, spat upon, flogged and killed, and on the third day rise. They understood none of these things; the saying was hidden from them.
18.big: Jesus goes to his death knowingly, and his closest followers cannot take it in.
18.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion

18.ctx: Near Jericho, the last town before the steep climb to Jerusalem, on the road crowded with Passover pilgrims.
18.mean: A blind beggar hears the crowd and cries: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me. Those in front rebuke him, but he cries out all the more. Jesus stops and asks what he wants. Recover your sight; your faith has made you well. Immediately he recovers his sight and follows him, glorifying God, and all the people give praise to God.
18.big: A blind beggar names Jesus as Messiah and follows him toward Jerusalem.

19.ctx: Jericho. Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector, which made him rich and, in popular view, a traitor and a thief.
19.mean: Being short, Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree. Jesus looks up and says: Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today. He receives him joyfully, while all grumble that Jesus has gone to be the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus says he will give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold anything he has defrauded. Jesus says: today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
19.big: Luke's summary of Jesus' whole mission comes at a tax collector's house.
19.diff: Fourfold restitution exceeds what the law required (Leviticus 6:5), showing genuine repentance rather than a purchase of favour.

19.ctx: Told because they supposed the kingdom of God was to appear immediately as they neared Jerusalem.
19.mean: A nobleman goes to receive a kingdom, leaving ten servants a mina each. His citizens hate him and send a delegation. On his return the first has made ten minas more, the second five, and each is given cities. A third hides his in a handkerchief, calling the master severe, and is condemned by his own words. The enemies who would not have him reign are brought and slain.
19.big: The kingdom is not appearing immediately; meanwhile the king's servants are to be at work.
19.diff: The detail of the nobleman travelling for a kingdom would have recalled Archelaus, who went to Rome to be confirmed as ruler while a Jewish delegation opposed him.
19.h: The Parable of the Ten Minas

19.ctx: The entry into Jerusalem, arranged deliberately by Jesus, at the end of the long journey section that began in 9:51.
19.mean: Jesus sends for a colt, and the disciples set him on it and spread their cloaks. The whole multitude praises God: blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest! Pharisees tell him to rebuke his disciples; he answers that if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.
19.big: Jesus is openly hailed as King, and refuses to silence the praise.

19.ctx: Luke alone records Jesus weeping over the city as it comes into view.
19.mean: Jesus weeps, saying: would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. Your enemies will set up a barricade and tear you down, because you did not know the time of your visitation.
19.big: Jesus weeps over the judgement he announces.
19.diff: The description matches the Roman siege of AD 70 closely, including the earthwork ramps Josephus records.

19.ctx: The temple's outer court was used for trade in sacrificial animals and currency exchange.
19.mean: Jesus drives out those who sold, saying: my house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers. He teaches daily in the temple, while the chief priests, scribes and principal men seek to destroy him but cannot find a way, for all the people hang on his words.
19.big: Jesus takes authority over the temple, and his popularity holds his enemies back.

20.ctx: Chief priests, scribes and elders confront Jesus as he teaches in the temple.
20.mean: They demand to know his authority. He asks whether John's baptism was from heaven or from man. They reason that either answer traps them, and say they do not know; so he declines to tell them.
20.big: Those unwilling to face the truth about God's messenger forfeit an answer.

20.ctx: The vineyard image comes from Isaiah 5, and the leaders understand it.
20.mean: Tenants beat the owner's servants and finally kill his beloved son to seize the inheritance. Jesus asks what the owner will do, and the people say: surely not! He quotes Psalm 118 on the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone. The scribes and chief priests seek to lay hands on him, for they perceived he had told the parable against them.
20.big: Jesus is the beloved son whose rejection brings judgement and vindication.
20.h: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants

20.ctx: Spies pretending sincerity try to trap Jesus over the Roman poll tax.
20.mean: They ask whether it is lawful to give tribute to Caesar. Jesus asks whose likeness is on the denarius and says: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. They marvel and fall silent.
20.big: The coin bears Caesar's image, and people bear God's.

20.ctx: The Sadducees accepted only the books of Moses and denied the resurrection.
20.mean: They pose the case of a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus says those considered worthy of that age neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die any more and are equal to angels, being sons of God and of the resurrection. He argues from the burning bush that God is not God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him. Some scribes say: Teacher, you have spoken well.
20.big: Jesus proves the resurrection from the books his opponents accepted.

20.ctx: Jesus now takes the initiative and poses his own question from Psalm 110.
20.mean: How can they say the Christ is David's son, when David himself says: the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand?
20.big: The Messiah is David's descendant and also David's Lord.

20.ctx: A warning to the disciples in the hearing of all the people.
20.mean: Beware of the scribes, who like to walk in long robes and love greetings and the best seats, who devour widows' houses and for a pretence make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.
20.big: Religious display combined with exploiting the vulnerable brings greater judgement.

21.ctx: The temple treasury had trumpet-shaped receptacles in the court of the women.
21.mean: Jesus sees rich people putting in their gifts, and a poor widow putting in two small copper coins. He says she has put in more than all of them, for they contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.
21.big: God measures giving by what is kept back, not by the amount given.
21.diff: Luke places this immediately before the prediction of the temple's destruction, as Mark does.

21.ctx: Someone admires the temple's fine stones and votive offerings. Herod's rebuilding was still unfinished, and some stones weighed many tonnes.
21.mean: Jesus says the days will come when not one stone will be left on another. Asked when, he warns against being led astray by those claiming 'I am he' and 'the time is at hand', and says wars and tumults must first take place, with earthquakes, famines and terrors.
21.big: Jesus warns against both deception and panic as the temple's end approaches.
21.diff: As in Matthew and Mark, the discourse addresses both the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and Christ's final coming; interpreters differ over where the emphasis falls in each section.

21.ctx: A warning of persecution placed before the events just described, so the disciples would know what to expect first.
21.mean: Before all this they will lay hands on you and persecute you, delivering you to synagogues and prisons, brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness. Do not meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom. You will be betrayed even by parents and relatives, and hated by all, but not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.
21.big: Persecution becomes an opportunity to bear witness, and Christ himself supplies the words.

21.ctx: Luke states plainly what Matthew and Mark describe in Daniel's imagery.
21.mean: When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, know that its desolation has come near. Let those in Judea flee to the mountains. These are days of vengeance, to fulfil all that is written. They will fall by the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
21.big: The fall of Jerusalem is described plainly, with practical instructions to escape it.
21.diff: Luke's wording, naming armies rather than the 'abomination of desolation', is often noted as making the AD 70 reference explicit.

21.ctx: The scene widens from Jerusalem to the coming of the Son of Man.
21.mean: There will be signs in sun, moon and stars, distress of nations, people fainting with fear, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. When these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.
21.big: For God's people, the signs that terrify the world are grounds to lift their heads.
21.h: The Return of the Son of Man

21.ctx: A short parable drawn from the seasons. Fig trees in Judea lose their leaves in winter, so new leaves reliably signalled summer.
21.mean: Look at the fig tree and all the trees: when they put out leaves you know summer is near. So when you see these things, know the kingdom of God is near. This generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
21.big: Jesus' words will outlast creation itself.
21.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree

21.ctx: The closing exhortation of the discourse, given to disciples who would live through the long wait he has just described.
21.mean: Watch yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. Stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape and to stand before the Son of Man. Each day he taught in the temple, and at night he lodged on the Mount of Olives.
21.big: Readiness is a matter of daily watchfulness and prayer, not calculation.

22.ctx: The Feast of Unleavened Bread, called the Passover, draws near, and the leaders fear the people.
22.mean: The chief priests and scribes seek how to put him to death, for they feared the people.
22.big: The plot is already formed; only the method is missing.

22.ctx: Luke, like John, names the power behind Judas's decision, at the point where the plot needed someone on the inside.
22.mean: Satan enters into Judas called Iscariot, one of the Twelve. He goes to the chief priests and officers to betray him, and they are glad and agree to give him money. He consents and seeks an opportunity to betray him in the absence of a crowd.
22.big: The betrayal comes from within the Twelve, and Luke names the power behind it.

22.ctx: The day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed.
22.mean: Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare, telling them to follow a man carrying a jar of water — unusual, as women normally carried water — to a large upper room.
22.big: Jesus has arranged everything in advance.

22.ctx: Luke's account of the Last Supper, with details the others do not include.
22.mean: Jesus says he has earnestly desired to eat this Passover with them before he suffers, and will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it: this is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me. And the cup after supper: this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. But the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table.
22.big: Jesus gives his coming death the meaning of a new covenant, and commands the meal as remembrance.
22.diff: Luke alone records 'do this in remembrance of me' alongside Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11. Some manuscripts shorten verses 19–20; most modern translations include the longer text. Christian traditions differ over what happens at the Supper.

22.ctx: A dispute among the disciples, at the table, moments after the bread and cup.
22.mean: An argument arises about which of them is the greatest. Jesus says the kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship, but not so with you: let the greatest become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? But I am among you as the one who serves. You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you a kingdom.
22.big: At the table where he gives himself, Jesus redefines greatness as service.

22.ctx: A word to Peter that names both his failure and his restoration in advance.
22.mean: Jesus says Satan demanded to have them, to sift them like wheat, but he has prayed for Simon that his faith may not fail, and when he has turned again, to strengthen his brothers. Peter says he is ready to go to prison and death; Jesus says the rooster will not crow this day until he denies three times that he knows him.
22.big: Jesus prays for Peter before he falls, and promises his restoration before he denies.

22.ctx: The Mount of Olives, where Jesus had been lodging each night that week, which is why Judas knew where to find him.
22.mean: He tells them to pray that they may not enter into temptation. Withdrawing about a stone's throw, he kneels and prays: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done. Being in agony he prays more earnestly, and his sweat becomes like great drops of blood falling to the ground. Rising, he finds them sleeping for sorrow.
22.big: Jesus' human will genuinely recoils and genuinely submits to the Father.
22.diff: Verses 43–44, about the angel and the sweat like blood, are absent from some early manuscripts and footnoted in many Bibles; Luke the doctor is the only Gospel writer to describe the physical distress in this way.
22.h: Jesus Prays on the Mount of Olives

22.ctx: Judas arrives with a crowd while Jesus is still speaking, and greets him with the customary kiss of a disciple to his teacher.
22.mean: Jesus asks: would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? A disciple strikes the high priest's servant and cuts off his right ear, but Jesus says: no more of this, and touches his ear and heals him. To the chief priests and officers he says: this is your hour, and the power of darkness.
22.big: Jesus' last recorded miracle before the cross heals an enemy who came to arrest him.
22.diff: Only Luke, the doctor, records the healing of the ear.

22.ctx: The high priest's house, where Peter follows at a distance and sits by the fire.
22.mean: A servant girl says he was with him; Peter denies it. Another says he is one of them; he denies it. An hour later another insists, since he is a Galilean. While he is still speaking the rooster crows. The Lord turns and looks at Peter, and Peter remembers and goes out and weeps bitterly.
22.big: Luke alone records the look of Jesus that broke Peter.

22.ctx: The men holding Jesus mock him through the night while he waits for the council to assemble at daybreak.
22.mean: They beat him, blindfold him and ask him to prophesy who struck him, and say many other things against him, blaspheming.
22.big: The one who will judge the world is mocked as a false prophet.

22.ctx: At daybreak, before the council of elders, chief priests and scribes.
22.mean: They ask whether he is the Christ. He says: if I tell you, you will not believe; but from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God. They all ask: are you the Son of God, then? He says: you say that I am. They say they need no further testimony.
22.big: Jesus claims the place beside God from Psalm 110 and Daniel 7, and is condemned for it.

23.ctx: The council brings Jesus to Pilate, needing a charge Rome will act on.
23.mean: They accuse him of misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar and saying he is Christ, a king. Pilate asks if he is King of the Jews; Jesus says: you have said so. Pilate finds no guilt in him, but they insist he stirs up the people from Galilee to here.
23.big: The religious charge is repackaged as sedition, and Pilate finds no case.

23.ctx: Learning Jesus is a Galilean, Pilate sends him to Herod Antipas, who is in Jerusalem for the feast.
23.mean: Herod is glad, hoping to see a sign, and questions him at length, but Jesus makes no answer. Herod and his soldiers treat him with contempt, array him in splendid clothing and send him back. That day Herod and Pilate became friends.
23.big: Jesus is silent before a king seeking entertainment.
23.diff: Found only in Luke, and one of several places where he notes that Jesus was examined and found guilty of nothing.

23.ctx: Pilate calls together the chief priests, rulers and people, having now had Jesus examined by Herod as well as himself.
23.mean: Pilate says neither he nor Herod found any guilt; he will punish and release him. They shout for Barabbas, imprisoned for insurrection and murder. Pilate appeals a third time — what evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death — but their voices prevail, and he delivers Jesus over to their will.
23.big: Three times a Roman governor declares Jesus innocent and three times he gives way.

23.ctx: Simon of Cyrene, in North Africa, is seized to carry the cross behind Jesus, who had already been flogged.
23.mean: A great multitude follows, including women mourning. Jesus says: daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but for yourselves and your children. At the place called The Skull they crucify him with two criminals. Jesus says: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. The rulers and soldiers mock him. One criminal rails at him, but the other rebukes him and says: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Jesus says: truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.
23.big: From the cross Jesus forgives his executioners and promises paradise to a dying criminal.
23.diff: Both sayings are found only in Luke. The prayer of forgiveness is absent from some early manuscripts but is widely regarded as authentic. The criminal's salvation, with nothing to offer, has comforted countless dying believers.

23.ctx: From noon until three in the afternoon, after Jesus has been on the cross for some hours.
23.mean: Darkness comes over the whole land and the curtain of the temple is torn in two. Jesus calls out: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit — quoting Psalm 31 — and breathes his last. The centurion praises God, saying: certainly this man was innocent. The crowds return home beating their breasts, and those who knew him stand at a distance.
23.big: Luke records Jesus dying with a psalm of trust on his lips.
23.diff: Where Matthew and Mark record the cry of Psalm 22, Luke gives Psalm 31:5 — the prayer Jewish children were taught at bedtime.

23.ctx: Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council who had not consented to their decision.
23.mean: Joseph, a good and righteous man looking for the kingdom of God, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen and lays it in a rock-hewn tomb where no one had yet been laid. The women from Galilee see the tomb and how the body was laid, then return and prepare spices, and rest on the Sabbath according to the commandment.
23.big: The burial is witnessed and the tomb's location known, which matters for what follows.

24.ctx: At early dawn on the first day of the week, the women come with the spices they prepared.
24.mean: They find the stone rolled away and the body gone. Two men in dazzling apparel say: why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you while he was still in Galilee. They remember his words and tell the eleven, but these words seem to them an idle tale, and they do not believe them. Peter runs to the tomb and sees the linen cloths by themselves.
24.big: The first witnesses to the resurrection are women whose testimony the apostles dismiss.
24.diff: Luke's admission that the apostles disbelieved, and that women were the first witnesses, is often noted as evidence the account was not invented to persuade.

24.ctx: Two disciples walk to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, that same day.
24.mean: Jesus draws near but their eyes are kept from recognising him. They explain their sorrow: they had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel. He says: O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interprets to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. At table he takes bread, blesses and breaks it, their eyes are opened, and he vanishes. They say: did not our hearts burn within us while he opened to us the Scriptures?
24.big: The risen Jesus teaches that the whole Old Testament is about him.
24.diff: This is the clearest statement in the Gospels of how Christians are to read the Old Testament — as pointing to Christ throughout.

24.ctx: That same evening, while the two are reporting to the eleven.
24.mean: Jesus stands among them: peace to you. They are startled, thinking they see a spirit. He says: see my hands and my feet; touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. He eats a piece of broiled fish before them. Then he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures, saying that the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses; stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.
24.big: The resurrection is bodily — he eats — and the mission to all nations follows from it.
24.diff: Luke insists on the physical reality of the resurrection body against any idea of a ghost or vision.

24.ctx: Bethany, on the Mount of Olives, where Luke's Gospel ends and Acts begins.
24.mean: Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses them, and while he blesses them he parts from them and is carried up into heaven. They worship him and return to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God.
24.big: The Gospel ends with Jesus blessing his people, and with joy rather than loss.

18.ctx: About 715 BC. Hezekiah, son of the faithless Ahaz, becomes king of Judah. The northern kingdom of Israel has already fallen to Assyria (722 BC, recalled in verses 9–12), and Judah is an Assyrian vassal paying tribute.
18.mean: Hezekiah is given one of the highest ratings of any king in Kings: he ‘did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done’, and ‘no king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him’. He removed the high places, the local shrines where worship had drifted into Canaanite practice. He smashed the sacred pillars and Asherah poles. He even broke up Nehushtan, the bronze snake Moses made (Numbers 21:4–9), because people were burning incense to it. A genuine relic of God’s past saving work had become an idol. Hezekiah ‘trusted in the LORD’, held fast to him, and kept his commands, and the LORD was with him. So he rebelled against the king of Assyria and defeated the Philistines. Then the writer pauses to recall the fall of Samaria. Israel was exiled ‘because they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God’. The two kingdoms stand side by side: one destroyed for unfaithfulness, one led by a king who trusts.
18.big: Hezekiah is the model of a king who trusts the LORD, even to the point of destroying a sacred object that had become an idol.
18.diff: The dates in this chapter are hard to fit together. Verse 1 places Hezekiah’s accession in Hoshea’s third year (before 722 BC), but verse 13 puts Sennacherib’s invasion of 701 BC in Hezekiah’s fourteenth year, which implies an accession around 715 BC. Many scholars explain this through a period of co-regency with Ahaz, or different ways of counting reigns. Others think one of the figures has been miscopied. The overall setting is not in doubt.

b: In 2015 Eilat Mazar’s Hebrew University excavation on the Ophel, at the foot of the Temple Mount, found a small clay seal impression (a bulla) reading ‘Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz king of Judah’. It was found in a refuse dump from Hezekiah’s time or shortly after.

The seal shows a two-winged sun flanked by Egyptian-style ankh symbols. Royal symbols of this kind were common across the region; the excavators suggest the design dates from late in Hezekiah’s reign.

src.l: Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs: ‘Impression of King Hezekiah’s royal seal discovered’ (Ophel excavations, Hebrew University, Dec 2015)
John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)
Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs: ‘Impression of King Hezekiah’s royal seal discovered’ (Ophel excavations, Hebrew University, Dec 2015)

18.ctx: 701 BC. Hezekiah has joined a revolt against Assyria with Egyptian backing (compare Isaiah 30:1–5). The new Assyrian king, Sennacherib, sweeps down the coast to crush it.
18.mean: ‘Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah.’ After the glowing introduction, this comes as a shock. The king who trusted the LORD loses almost his whole kingdom. Hezekiah sends to Sennacherib at Lachish: ‘I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand.’ The price is 300 talents of silver and 30 talents of gold, about ten tonnes of silver and one of gold. To pay it, Hezekiah empties the temple and palace treasuries and strips the gold from the temple doors he had himself overlaid. The writer does not comment, but the contrast with verses 5–7 is deliberate. Hezekiah’s first move under pressure is the old political one of buying off the enemy, and it does not work.
18.big: Faithfulness does not exempt God’s people from crisis, and buying peace from the world does not bring it.

b: Sennacherib’s campaign is one of the best documented events in the Old Testament. His annals survive on clay prisms (the Taylor Prism in the British Museum, and others in Chicago and Jerusalem). In them he says he took 46 of Hezekiah’s walled cities and countless villages, deported 200,150 people, and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem ‘like a caged bird’.

Where the records agree. Both sides record Judah’s fortified cities falling (18:13), Hezekiah sending tribute (18:14–16) and Jerusalem surrounded (18:17). Both give the gold as 30 talents. The silver differs: 300 talents in the Bible, 800 in the Assyrian record. Exaggeration in royal propaganda, a different way of counting, or extra payments sent later have all been suggested.

What the annals leave out. The annals never claim that Jerusalem fell. Hezekiah was the leader of the revolt, yet he stayed on his throne, and the tribute was sent on to Nineveh afterwards. Other rebels on this campaign were not so fortunate. Sennacherib replaced Luli, king of Sidon, who fled and died in exile, and he executed the nobles of Ekron. An Assyrian king who had taken the rebel leader’s capital would have said so. The silence fits the Bible’s account that the siege of Jerusalem ended without the city being taken.

src.l: D. J. Wiseman, ‘Sennacherib’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)

hist.t: Lachish: the siege in stone and in the ground
b: Lachish, one of Judah’s most important fortified cities, about 40 km south-west of Jerusalem, was Sennacherib’s headquarters (18:14, 17; 19:8). In his palace at Nineveh he had the siege carved in a continuous series of reliefs lining a central room. They show slingers and archers attacking, battering rams pushed up ramps, defenders throwing torches, captives led away, rebels impaled, and Sennacherib on his throne receiving the plunder. The reliefs are now in the British Museum, displayed in a room of about the same size as the original.

The ground confirms the stone. Excavations (Starkey 1932–38, Aharoni 1966–68, Ussishkin 1973–87) found the Assyrian siege ramp at the south-west corner, a counter-ramp the defenders built inside the walls, hundreds of arrowheads, sling stones and pieces of armour, and mass burials of about 1,500 people in nearby caves.

A point of honesty: Lachish was a major victory, not a minor one. It was a great fortress, and the reliefs show the siege accurately. But it is striking that the king chose Lachish, not Jerusalem, as the centrepiece of his palace. As Tyndale House puts it, Sennacherib ‘was not able to take the crown jewel’. The reliefs celebrate the victory he did win.

b: The king’s jars. Large numbers of storage-jar handles stamped lmlk, ‘belonging to the king’, together with one of four place names, have been found across Judah. The excavations at Lachish showed that these jars belonged to a royal supply system set up before Sennacherib’s invasion, which most archaeologists attribute to Hezekiah (compare 2 Chronicles 32:27–29).

Hezekiah’s tunnel. 2 Kings 20:20 and 2 Chronicles 32:30 say Hezekiah brought the water of the Gihon spring into the city. A tunnel over 500 metres long, cut through solid rock, still carries it under the City of David. An inscription found inside it in 1880 (now in Istanbul) describes the two teams of diggers cutting towards each other until they met ‘axe to axe’. Some scholars once dated the tunnel centuries later. In 2003, though, radiocarbon dating of plant material in the plaster and uranium–thorium dating of cave deposits, published in Nature, placed it around 700 BC. That is Hezekiah’s time, as the Bible says.

18.ctx: Despite the tribute, Sennacherib sends three senior officials with a large army from Lachish to Jerusalem. Their titles, Tartan (commander-in-chief), Rabsaris (chief official) and Rabshakeh (chief cupbearer, here the spokesman), are known from Assyrian records.
18.mean: The Rabshakeh stands at the very spot where Isaiah had once challenged Hezekiah’s father to trust God (Isaiah 7:3), and makes a masterful propaganda speech. He attacks every source of hope in turn. Egypt is ‘that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it’. The LORD? Hezekiah has removed his high places and altars, so surely God is offended. That is a clever misreading of Hezekiah’s reform. Besides, he claims, ‘The LORD himself said to me, “Go up against this land and destroy it.”’ When the officials ask him to speak Aramaic, the diplomatic language, rather than Hebrew in the people’s hearing, he deliberately turns to the people on the wall. Do not let Hezekiah deceive you. Make peace and you will each eat from your own vine until I take you to a land like your own. Then comes the climax: ‘Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?’ Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Samaria: their gods failed. The people stay silent, as Hezekiah commanded, and the officials bring the speech to the king with their clothes torn.
18.big: The enemy’s strongest weapon is the argument that God cannot or will not save; the question of the chapter is whether the LORD is just another national god.

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)
D. J. Wiseman, ‘Sennacherib’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

19.ctx: Hezekiah’s response to the Rabshakeh’s speech. Isaiah the prophet, whose ministry spans the reigns of Uzziah to Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1), enters the story.
19.mean: This time Hezekiah’s first move is the right one. He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and goes into the house of the LORD. He sends his officials to Isaiah with a picture of helplessness: ‘Children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.’ His hope rests on one thing: the Assyrian has mocked ‘the living God’. Perhaps the LORD will hear and rebuke him. Isaiah’s answer is brief and calm: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard… I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.’ The whole rest of the story is the fulfilment of these two sentences.
19.big: When God’s name is mocked, his people can bring the matter to him and leave the defence of his honour in his hands.

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)

19.ctx: Sennacherib has moved on from Lachish to Libnah, nearby. News comes that an Egyptian and Nubian army is advancing.
19.mean: The Rabshakeh returns to find his king fighting at Libnah, and Sennacherib hears that Tirhakah king of Cush is marching against him. This is the first stage of Isaiah’s ‘rumour’. Rather than withdraw, Sennacherib sends a letter to Hezekiah that sharpens the earlier speech. Do not let ‘your God in whom you trust’ deceive you. Look at the list of kingdoms and their gods that Assyria has destroyed. The challenge is now aimed directly at the LORD’s trustworthiness.
19.big: The conflict is no longer between two kings but between the king of Assyria and the God of Israel.

b: The problem. Tirhakah (Egyptian Taharqa) of Egypt’s Nubian 25th Dynasty reigned c. 690–664 BC. But the campaign of 2 Kings 18–19 happened in 701 BC, when he was not yet king.

Where the majority of scholars stand. The New Bible Dictionary notes that most scholars regard the mention of Tirhakah as an anachronism. Many therefore suggest the biblical account merges Sennacherib’s campaign of 701 BC with a second, later campaign against Jerusalem during Tirhakah’s reign. That would also explain why Sennacherib’s murder (19:37) seems to follow soon after.

The case for the biblical account as it stands. Egyptologist K. A. Kitchen argues that Tirhakah, a royal prince, could well have commanded the Egyptian and Nubian force in 701 BC. He was called ‘king’ because that is what he was by the time the account was written down, much as we might say ‘Queen Elizabeth was born in 1926’. An argument once used against this, that Tirhakah was too young in 701, has been answered by specialists. On the other side, the two-campaign theory has a serious weakness: neither the surviving Assyrian annals nor the Babylonian chronicles mention any second campaign against Judah. And the Bible does not say how long after his return Sennacherib died. ‘He returned to Nineveh and stayed there’ covers twenty years. A single campaign in 701 BC, as the text presents it, remains a reasonable reading of the evidence.

19.ctx: Hezekiah takes the letter into the temple. This prayer is one of the great prayers of the Old Testament, repeated in Isaiah 37.
19.mean: Hezekiah spreads the letter out before the LORD and prays. He begins with who God is: ‘O LORD, God of Israel, enthroned between the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.’ Then he faces the facts honestly. It is true that the Assyrian kings have destroyed these nations and thrown their gods into the fire, ‘for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands’. Sennacherib’s list proves less than he thinks: of course idols could not save. Last comes the request, and its purpose: ‘Save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone, O LORD, are God.’ Hezekiah’s chief concern is God’s glory among the nations, not just his own survival.
19.big: Faithful prayer starts with who God is, tells him the truth about the situation, and asks for help so that his name will be known.

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)

19.ctx: Isaiah’s reply to Hezekiah’s prayer: a poem addressed to Sennacherib, then a sign for Hezekiah, then a direct promise.
19.mean: ‘I have heard your prayer concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria.’ The poem turns the tables. ‘The Virgin Daughter of Zion’, apparently defenceless, despises and mocks the invader and shakes her head as he leaves. Sennacherib boasted of his own achievements, crossing mountains and drying up rivers. But God says he planned it all ‘long ago’. Assyria was only ever the tool of God’s purposes (compare Isaiah 10:5–19). Because of his arrogance God will put ‘my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth’, the way a captive or a beast is led (compare Amos 4:2), and lead him back the way he came. Then comes a sign for Hezekiah. For two years the people will eat what grows by itself, because the fields have been ravaged, and in the third year they will sow and reap again. A remnant will take root. Finally the promise: the king of Assyria ‘will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it… or build up a siege ramp against it’. ‘I will defend this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.’
19.big: The proud empire that thinks it controls history is only an instrument in God’s hand, and he will defend his people for his own name’s sake.
19.diff: Some find a tension between ‘he will not… build up a siege ramp against it’ (19:32) and Sennacherib’s claim to have hemmed Jerusalem in with earthworks. The prophecy concerns a full assault on the city, which never happened. The Assyrian claim describes a blockade, which both sides agree happened (18:17).

src.l: John W. Olley, The Message of Kings, The Bible Speaks Today (IVP, 2011)
D. J. Wiseman, ‘Sennacherib’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

19.ctx: The fulfilment, told in three short verses.
19.mean: ‘That very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians.’ The writer gives no details, only the result: in the morning the camp was full of dead bodies. Sennacherib broke camp, returned to Nineveh and stayed there. Every part of Isaiah’s word is fulfilled. Not an arrow was shot at the city. The king went home by the way he came. And one day, worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch, he was killed by his own sons, who escaped to Ararat, while Esarhaddon reigned in his place. The writer passes over the twenty years between his return and his death (see the drop-down), because the point is not the timing but the outcome. The king who asked which god could save from his hand was not saved by his own.
19.big: God delivers his people by his own power, and those who mock him come to nothing.

hist.t: What happened to the Assyrian army?
b: What is agreed. Sennacherib’s campaign ended without the capture of Jerusalem, and he went home with Hezekiah still on the throne. His own annals agree with the Bible on this (see the note on 18:13).

The Bible’s account. ‘That very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians.’ The Bible gives the cause as God’s direct action and does not describe the means.

Herodotus. Writing in the fifth century BC, the Greek historian Herodotus records a story he heard from Egyptian priests (2.141). When ‘Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians’ marched against Egypt, its priest-king Sethos prayed in his god’s temple. That night, near Pelusium on Egypt’s border, field mice swarmed the Assyrian camp and ‘gnawed quivers and bows and the handles of shields’, so the army fled and many were killed. It is a different location and a different explanation. But it is an independent, non-Israelite memory of a sudden disaster striking Sennacherib’s army through divine action after prayer.

Plague? Herodotus does not mention disease. The link many scholars have suggested is an inference, but a reasonable one. In the ancient world, swarms of rodents went together with epidemics. The Bible itself pairs rats with a plague of tumours (1 Samuel 6:4–5). And elsewhere in Scripture ‘the angel of the LORD’ is the agent of plague: in 2 Samuel 24:15–16 and 1 Chronicles 21:12, a plague sent on Israel is carried out by ‘the angel of the LORD ravaging every part of Israel’. The Jewish historian Josephus (first century AD) describes the disaster as ‘a pestilential distemper’ sent by God, and presents this as the account of the Babylonian historian Berossus. How much of that passage really comes from Berossus is uncertain.

The critical view. Many scholars treat the Herodotus story as Egyptian legend with little historical value. Many also regard the figure of 185,000 as impossibly large, or as a later exaggeration. Some suggest that numbers using the Hebrew elef (‘thousand’) could originally mean military units. Those who read the account as a later composition also see the swift death of Sennacherib in 19:37 as compressing twenty years.

The strongest case for the biblical account. Three independent kinds of evidence point the same way. Assyrian records are silent where a victory would be expected. Hezekiah was left on his throne. And a separate Egyptian tradition remembers Sennacherib’s army suffering a sudden, divinely sent catastrophe. A plague in a crowded military camp is entirely plausible, and Scripture elsewhere uses this very language for one. The Bible does not need Herodotus to be right in detail. The point is that the outside evidence is consistent with Jerusalem’s deliverance being sudden and decisive, exactly as the Bible says.

b: Sennacherib was assassinated in 681 BC, twenty years after the campaign. The Babylonian Chronicle records that he was killed by his son in a rebellion. His younger son Esarhaddon, already named crown prince, describes in his own inscription the turmoil with his brothers that followed, and he succeeded to the throne, just as verse 37 says. The Bible names the assassins as Adrammelech and Sharezer; versions of these names also appear in later Greek writers quoted by Josephus and others.
The irony the writer intends is plain. Sennacherib mocked the God of Israel as unable to save. He died at the hands of his own sons in the temple of a god who could not save him.

1.ctx: 605 BC. Nebuchadnezzar has just defeated Egypt at Carchemish and is bringing the small kingdoms of Syria and Palestine under his control. Judah’s king Jehoiakim submits.
1.mean: The book opens with what looks like a defeat for God. Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem and carries temple articles to ‘the house of his god’ in Shinar, the old name for Babylonia, recalling Babel (Genesis 11). But the writer adds one phrase that changes everything: ‘the Lord delivered’ Jehoiakim into his hand. Babylon wins only because God hands Judah over, as the prophets had warned. Then the king’s official selects young men of royal and noble families, ‘without blemish’, gifted and educated, to be trained for three years in the language and literature of the Chaldeans. Their Hebrew names honour Israel’s God: Daniel means God is my judge. They are given Babylonian names, some of which honour Babylon’s gods. The empire’s strategy is to remake them as Babylonians.
1.big: Even when God’s people lose, it is because God has handed them over, and he has not let go of them.

b: Daniel dates Nebuchadnezzar’s move against Jerusalem to Jehoiakim’s third year; Jeremiah 25:1 and 46:2 link Nebuchadnezzar’s first year and the battle of Carchemish (605 BC) with Jehoiakim’s fourth year. Critical scholars such as Davies regard Daniel 1:1 as historically confused, noting that 2 Kings 24 records no capture of Jerusalem at this time.

The case for Daniel’s accuracy. Babylonian records (the Babylonian Chronicle) show Nebuchadnezzar campaigning in ‘Hatti’, which means Syria and Palestine, in 605 BC, immediately after Carchemish. Judeans and Babylonians counted reign-years differently. Babylon did not count the part-year in which a king came to the throne (the ‘accession year’), while Jeremiah follows a Judean method that did. Chronologists such as Edwin Thiele and Rodger Young have shown that the two figures then describe the same year. Daniel 1:2 also does not claim Jerusalem was destroyed. It says Jehoiakim was ‘delivered into his hand’ and some temple articles were taken, consistent with a city submitting as a vassal.

1.ctx: The young men are assigned food and wine from the king’s table.
1.mean: ‘Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself.’ He accepts the education, the job and even the new name, but draws a line at the king’s food. The reason is not stated. Possibly the food was not prepared according to the law of Moses, or had been offered to idols, or eating from the king’s table bound a man to the king. Daniel does not rebel or lecture. He asks politely, then proposes a ten-day test of vegetables and water. God gives him favour with the official, and at the end of the test the four look healthier than the rest. Faithfulness here is quiet, wise and specific.
1.big: God’s people can serve inside a pagan system while drawing clear lines where obedience to God is at stake.
1.diff: Why Daniel refused the food is debated. Explanations include the food laws (Leviticus 11), food offered to idols, or refusing the obligation that came with eating the king’s food. The text does not say, and the point is the resolve, not the menu. The passage does not teach that vegetarian food is holier.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

1.ctx: The end of the three years of training.
1.mean: ‘God gave knowledge and understanding in every kind of literature and wisdom.’ Their wisdom is God’s gift, not simply the fruit of Babylon’s schooling, and Daniel is given understanding of visions and dreams. That sets up the rest of the book. Examined by the king, they are ‘ten times better’ than all his magicians and enchanters. The chapter closes noting that Daniel remained ‘until the first year of King Cyrus’, 539 BC. He outlasted the whole Babylonian empire that had captured him.
1.big: God, not Babylon, is the source of true wisdom, and his servant outlasts the empire that took him captive.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

2.ctx: From 2:4 the book switches from Hebrew to Aramaic, the international language of the empire, and stays in Aramaic until the end of chapter 7.
2.mean: Nebuchadnezzar has a dream that troubles him, and he demands that his experts tell him not only its meaning but the dream itself. Otherwise they will be torn limb from limb. Behind this may be suspicion: anyone can invent an interpretation, but only real insight could know the dream. The wise men protest that no one on earth could do this, ‘except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals’. Without realising it, they have stated the point of the chapter. Furious, the king orders the execution of all the wise men of Babylon, Daniel and his friends included.
2.big: Human wisdom reaches its limit exactly where God’s revelation begins.
2.diff: Verse 1 places this in Nebuchadnezzar’s ‘second year’, which seems early if Daniel had a three-year training (1:5). Babylonian accession-year counting, where a king’s first part-year did not count, removes most of the difficulty.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

2.ctx: The executioner is already at work when Daniel hears the decree.
2.mean: Daniel responds ‘with discretion and tact’, asks for time, and goes home to his three friends to pray for mercy from ‘the God of heaven’. In the night the mystery is revealed. Before he does anything else, Daniel worships. ‘He changes the times and seasons; he removes kings and establishes them.’ This doxology states the theme of the whole book. The God who reveals the secret is also the one who controls the history the dream will describe.
2.big: Daniel’s first response to answered prayer is praise, and his praise declares that God rules the times and the kings.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

2.ctx: Daniel is brought before the king.
2.mean: Daniel takes no credit: ‘There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.’ The dream was a huge statue: head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with clay. A stone cut out ‘not by human hands’ struck the feet and the whole statue crumbled like chaff, while the stone became a mountain filling the earth. The interpretation: ‘You are that head of gold.’ After Nebuchadnezzar come three lesser kingdoms, the fourth strong as iron yet divided and brittle. ‘In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.’ The stone is God’s kingdom, not built by human hands. It does not reform the empires; it replaces them all.
2.big: Every human empire, however glorious, is temporary; God’s kingdom, coming from outside human history, will fill the earth and last for ever.
2.diff: The four kingdoms are identified in two main ways: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome (the traditional view), or Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece (the majority critical view). See the drop-down at 7:15. Christians have generally seen the stone as Christ and his kingdom, inaugurated at his first coming and completed at his return. Some (premillennial interpreters) place its full arrival at a future reign of Christ on earth.

2.ctx: The king’s reaction.
2.mean: The most powerful man in the world falls on his face before a Jewish exile. He confesses, ‘Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries.’ Daniel is made ruler over the province of Babylon and chief over its wise men. At his request his three friends are given administrative posts. The confession is real but incomplete. Nebuchadnezzar’s understanding of God will be tested in the next chapters.
2.big: God honours those who honour him, and makes even pagan kings acknowledge his power.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

3.ctx: Some time after chapter 2. The statue is sixty cubits high and six wide (about 27 by 2.7 metres) and stands on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.
3.mean: Having been told he is the golden head of a statue, Nebuchadnezzar builds a statue entirely of gold, as if to say his kingdom will not pass. He summons every official of the empire to its dedication. When the music sounds, all must fall down and worship it; anyone who refuses will be thrown into a blazing furnace. The repeated lists of officials and instruments are deliberate, almost comic. The whole machinery of the empire bows on cue. The test is a loyalty test as much as a religious one, and that has been the shape of persecution in many ages.
3.big: Empires demand worship; God’s people must decide in advance whom they will bow to.

b: Three of the instruments in 3:5 have Greek names (lyre qitharos, harp pesanterin, and possibly sumponyah). Critical scholars take this as a sign of the Hellenistic period after Alexander. In reply: these are only instrument names; Greek mercenaries and traders were active in the Near East from the seventh century BC; Assyrian inscriptions mention Greek captives; and Noonan argues the forms are non-Attic, pointing to borrowing before Alexander. Over twenty Persian loanwords appear in the same chapters, and they suit the Persian period. This is a real argument on both sides, and neither is decisive by itself.

3.ctx: Some ‘Chaldeans’, here meaning members of the class of court experts, report the three Jews.
3.mean: The accusers stress that these are Jews the king himself appointed, and that they have ‘ignored you, O king’ and refused to serve his gods or worship the statue. Given one more chance, the three answer with famous calm. ‘We have no need to answer you in this matter. If the God whom we serve exists, then he is able to deliver us… But even if he does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.’ Their faith does not depend on rescue. They believe God can save them, they do not presume he will, and they will obey either way.
3.big: Real faith says ‘he is able’ and ‘even if he does not’ in the same breath.
3.diff: Verse 17 can be translated ‘If the God whom we serve exists, then he is able’ (BSB) or ‘If this be so, then the God whom we serve is able’ (BSB footnote, and most older versions). The difference is in the Aramaic. Neither expresses doubt about God; the point is that the outcome is in his hands.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

3.ctx: The furnace is heated seven times hotter. The men who throw the three in are killed by the heat.
3.mean: The king looks into the fire and sees four men walking about, unbound and unharmed, ‘and the fourth looks like a son of the gods’. He calls them out as ‘servants of the Most High God’. Not a hair is singed, their clothes are untouched, and there is not even the smell of fire on them. Nebuchadnezzar blesses their God, who ‘has sent his angel and delivered his servants who trusted in him’, and decrees that no one may speak against him. God did not keep them out of the fire. He met them in it.
3.big: God does not always keep his people out of the fire, but he is with them in it.
3.diff: Who was the fourth figure? Nebuchadnezzar himself calls him an angel (verse 28). Many Christian interpreters, from early times, have seen a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son of God. The text leaves the king’s description as he gave it, and both readings agree that God was present with them.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

4.ctx: Chapter 4 is written as a royal proclamation by Nebuchadnezzar himself, in the first person. It begins and ends with praise.
4.mean: The king opens by declaring what he has learned: ‘His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; his dominion endures from generation to generation.’ The rest of the chapter tells how he learned it the hard way. A pagan emperor proclaiming the God of Israel to ‘the people of every nation and language who dwell in all the earth’ is the climax of the stories about Nebuchadnezzar.
4.big: The most powerful king of his age publicly confesses that God’s kingdom, not his, is everlasting.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

4.h: Nebuchadnezzar’s Dream of a Great Tree
4.ctx: At the height of his prosperity, ‘at ease in my house’, the king has another dream.
4.mean: He sees an enormous tree at the centre of the earth, reaching the sky, sheltering animals and birds and feeding all creatures. Then a ‘watcher, a holy one’ comes down from heaven and orders it cut down, leaving only the stump bound with iron and bronze. Then the image shifts from tree to man: ‘Let his mind be changed from that of a man, and let him be given the mind of a beast, till seven times pass.’ The purpose is stated: ‘so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom he wishes, setting over it the lowliest of men’. Again the wise men fail, and Daniel is called.
4.big: God sets kings up and brings them down, so that everyone may know who really rules.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

4.ctx: Daniel is shaken by what he must say.
4.mean: Daniel is appalled and wishes the dream applied to the king’s enemies. He tells it straight, though: the tree is the king himself. Nebuchadnezzar will be driven from human society to live like a wild animal ‘until you acknowledge that the Most High rules’. The stump means the kingdom will be restored when he does. Then Daniel adds pastoral counsel: ‘Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity.’ Even a word of judgment comes with a call to repent.
4.big: A faithful servant speaks hard truth with compassion, and calls even the powerful to repent.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

4.ctx: Twelve months later, walking on the roof of his palace.
4.mean: ‘Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?’ The boast is barely finished when a voice from heaven pronounces sentence. That same hour he is driven away, eats grass like cattle, and is drenched with dew, his hair like eagles’ feathers and his nails like birds’ claws. Babylon really was magnificent; Nebuchadnezzar’s own inscriptions boast of his building works. His sin was not building but taking the glory for himself.
4.big: Pride that takes God’s glory for itself is brought low.
4.diff: The illness has been compared to rare conditions in which a person believes they are an animal (sometimes called boanthropy), but the text does not give a diagnosis, and the cause is presented as God’s judgment. On the lack of Babylonian records, see the drop-down.

hist.t: Nebuchadnezzar’s madness and the ‘Prayer of Nabonidus’
b: No Babylonian record mentions Nebuchadnezzar’s illness. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a fragmentary ‘Prayer of Nabonidus’ (4Q242), in which Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, is struck with an illness for seven years at Teima in Arabia and is helped by a Jewish exile. Many critical scholars think the Daniel story is a reworking of this tradition, transferred from Nabonidus to the more famous Nebuchadnezzar.

The case for Daniel’s account. The two stories differ considerably: the illness, the place, the setting and the role of the Jew. That fits two separate traditions better than one story copied from the other. Royal annals were written to glorify the king and routinely omitted humiliations. And Tanner notes a tradition preserved by the Babylonian priest Berossus that Nebuchadnezzar fell suddenly ill late in his reign. The fact that Nabonidus really did spend ten years at Teima, leaving Belshazzar in charge, is well established.

4.ctx: ‘At the end of those days’.
4.mean: ‘I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me.’ Looking up is the turning point. He praises the God whose dominion is everlasting, who ‘does as he pleases with the army of heaven and the peoples of the earth’. No one can hold back his hand or ask him, ‘What have you done?’ His kingdom is restored and even increased, and he ends: ‘All his works are true and all his ways are just, and he is able to humble those who walk in pride.’
4.big: Sanity begins with looking up to God; the humbled king ends by praising the King of heaven.
4.diff: Whether Nebuchadnezzar was truly converted is debated. Some see genuine faith, others an acknowledgment of the God of Israel as supreme without abandoning other gods. The text records his confession without further comment.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

5.ctx: October 539 BC, the last night of the Babylonian empire. Cyrus’s Persian army is at the gates, and King Nabonidus is away.
5.mean: Belshazzar holds a great banquet for a thousand of his nobles. Drunk, he orders the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar took from the Jerusalem temple to be brought, so that he, his nobles, his wives and his concubines can drink from them. They praise the gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone. It is calculated contempt: the vessels of the God of Israel used to toast idols. With the city under threat, the feast is also defiance, a show that Babylon cannot fall.
5.big: Treating holy things with contempt is a sign of a heart and a kingdom ripe for judgment.

b: Until the nineteenth century, Belshazzar was known almost only from Daniel and writings that drew on it; ancient historians named Nabonidus as Babylon’s last king, and critics treated ‘King Belshazzar’ as an error. Cuneiform texts have since shown that Bel-shar-usur (Belshazzar) was Nabonidus’s son and crown prince. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that while Nabonidus stayed at Teima in Arabia, ‘the crown prince, the officials and the army’ were in Babylonia. A text known as the Verse Account says Nabonidus ‘entrusted the kingship’ to him. Legal documents include oaths in the names of both Nabonidus and Belshazzar.

This explains two details in chapter 5. Belshazzar offers Daniel ‘third’ place in the kingdom (5:7, 16, 29) because he himself was second, under his absent father. And Nebuchadnezzar can be called his ‘father’ because Aramaic and Hebrew use ‘father’ for an ancestor or predecessor; Belshazzar may in fact have been Nebuchadnezzar’s grandson through his mother. Critical scholars still note that Belshazzar was never formally ‘king’. Daniel, though, describes what he actually was in Babylon: the man in charge.

5.ctx: ‘At that moment’.
5.mean: The fingers of a human hand appear and write on the plaster wall by the lampstand. The king turns pale and his knees knock together. He offers purple robes, a gold chain and the rank of ‘third highest ruler in the kingdom’ to anyone who can read it. Again the wise men fail. The queen, probably the queen mother, remembers Daniel, now an old man forgotten by the court, who had ‘the spirit of the holy gods’ under Nebuchadnezzar.
5.big: The arrogant feast is interrupted by a message no human wisdom can read.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

5.ctx: Daniel is brought in, now in his eighties.
5.mean: Daniel waves away the rewards and first preaches. God gave Nebuchadnezzar his greatness and humbled him when he became proud. ‘But you, his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this.’ Belshazzar’s sin was not ignorance but defiance. Then the reading: mene, mene, tekel, parsin. These are weights or coins, which Daniel reads as verbs. Mene, ‘numbered’: God has numbered the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end. Tekel, ‘weighed’: you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting. Peres, ‘divided’: your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians, with a play on Paras, Persia. ‘That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom.’
5.big: Those who know the truth and still defy God are weighed and found wanting, and his judgment comes on time.

hist.t: ‘That very night’: the fall of Babylon, 539 BC
b: Babylon fell to the Persians in October 539 BC. Herodotus (5th century BC) records that Cyrus diverted the Euphrates so his troops could enter along the riverbed, and that the Babylonians in the centre of the city ‘went on dancing and rejoicing’ at a festival, unaware. Xenophon also describes the city being taken during a festival and the king being killed, though he gives no name. The New Bible Dictionary concludes that the ‘king’ who died was Belshazzar, while Nabonidus was captured on his return. The details of the Greek accounts are debated, but the setting fits Daniel 5 strikingly: a feast, a sudden fall, the ruler killed that night.

6.ctx: The new regime after the fall of Babylon. Darius organises the kingdom under 120 satraps, with three administrators over them, Daniel among them.
6.mean: Daniel so outshines the others that the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom. His jealous colleagues look for grounds to accuse him and find none, because ‘he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him’. Their conclusion is a remarkable tribute: the only way to catch him is ‘concerning the law of his God’. They persuade the king to sign a decree that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king, on pain of the lions’ den. Under ‘the law of the Medes and Persians’, it cannot be revoked.
6.big: A life so blameless that enemies can attack it only through its faithfulness to God is the best witness.

b: No inscription found so far names ‘Darius the Mede’, and the records make clear that Babylon fell to the forces of Cyrus the Persian. Many critical scholars therefore regard him as a literary figure, perhaps confused with the later Persian king Darius I.

Several identifications have been proposed by scholars who take Daniel as history. None has won general agreement. (1) Gubaru (or Ugbaru), the general or governor who took Babylon for Cyrus and governed it. (2) Cyrus himself: D. J. Wiseman pointed out that 6:28 can be translated ‘the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus’ (the BSB footnote gives this reading). Cyrus was of partly Median descent and was about sixty-two in 539 BC. (3) Cyaxares II, son of the Median king Astyages, described by the Greek writer Xenophon. Josephus says that the Darius who took Babylon with ‘his kinsman Cyrus’ was ‘the son of Astyages, and had another name among the Greeks’. Tanner favours this view.
Honest summary: the absence of outside evidence is a genuine difficulty. But Belshazzar was also once missing from the records, and an argument from silence is not proof of error.

6.ctx: Daniel learns the decree has been signed.
6.mean: He goes home, opens his windows towards Jerusalem, and prays three times a day, giving thanks, ‘just as he had done before’. He does not flaunt it and he does not hide it. He simply refuses to stop. The king, trapped by his own law, tries all day to save him, then has him thrown to the lions with the words, ‘May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!’ At dawn he hurries to the den. ‘My God sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions,’ Daniel answers. ‘They have not hurt me, for I was found innocent in his sight.’ His accusers and their families are thrown in instead, a severe Persian punishment the writer reports without approving.
6.big: Daniel’s courage lies in quiet, unchanged faithfulness, and God vindicates him.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

6.ctx: The king’s decree after Daniel’s rescue.
6.mean: Darius writes to ‘the people of every nation and language’ that everyone must tremble before the God of Daniel: ‘For he is the living God, and he endures forever; his kingdom will never be destroyed.’ As with Nebuchadnezzar in chapter 4, a foreign king ends up proclaiming the everlasting kingdom of Israel’s God. The stories end with Daniel prospering ‘during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian’.
6.big: The stories end where the visions will begin: God’s kingdom outlasts every empire.
6.diff: Verse 28 can be read ‘the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus’ (BSB footnote). This is the basis of one proposed identification of Darius the Mede (see the drop-down at 6:1).

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

7.h: Daniel’s Vision of the Four Beasts
7.ctx: The first year of Belshazzar, before the events of chapter 5. The visions now begin, and they cover the same ground as chapter 2 from a different angle.
7.mean: Daniel sees the four winds of heaven stirring up the great sea, a picture of the chaotic world of nations, and four beasts rising from it. A lion with eagle’s wings, made to stand like a man and given a human heart, recalls Nebuchadnezzar’s story in chapter 4. Next a bear raised on one side with three ribs in its mouth, then a leopard with four wings and four heads, and finally a fourth beast, ‘terrifying—dreadful and extremely strong’, with iron teeth and ten horns. Among the horns a little horn comes up, with eyes like a man’s and ‘a mouth that spoke words of arrogance’. In chapter 2 the empires looked like a glorious statue; here God shows what they are really like: beasts.
7.big: From heaven’s point of view, the great empires of the world are beasts.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

7.h: Daniel’s Vision of the Ancient of Days
7.ctx: The scene moves from the sea to heaven’s courtroom.
7.mean: Thrones are set up and ‘the Ancient of Days’ takes his seat. His clothing is white as snow and his hair like pure wool. His throne is flaming fire with wheels of fire, a river of fire flows from him, and myriads serve him. ‘The court was convened, and the books were opened.’ While the little horn is still boasting, the fourth beast is slain and destroyed. The other beasts lose their power, though they are allowed to live for a time. The beasts make a great deal of noise, but the outcome is decided in a courtroom they cannot see.
7.big: Above the noise of the beasts, God sits enthroned as judge, and the outcome is decided in his court.

src.l: J. Paul Tanner, Daniel, Evangelical Exegetical Commentary (Lexham, 2020): defends the traditional date

7.h: Daniel’s Vision of the Son of Man
7.ctx: The climax of the vision, and one of the most important passages in the Old Testament for understanding Jesus.
7.mean: ‘I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven.’ After four beasts comes one who is human: the footnote gives the literal ‘one like a son of man’, and in Aramaic ‘son of man’ simply means a human being. Yet he comes ‘with the clouds’, which in the Old Testament is the way God himself travels (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1). He is led to the Ancient of Days and given ‘dominion, glory and kingship’, so that every nation and language should serve him, and his kingdom will never be destroyed. Jesus took ‘the Son of Man’ as his favourite title for himself. At his trial he joined it to this verse: ‘you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven’ (Mark 14:62). The high priest understood the claim at once and called it blasphemy. The figure is truly human, yet shares God’s throne and receives the worship due to God. Christians see here both natures of Christ, fully God and fully man.
7.big: God’s kingdom is given to one like a son of man, and Jesus claimed to be him.
7.diff: Who is the ‘one like a son of man’? The traditional Jewish and Christian reading is an individual heavenly Messiah-figure, as in the Gospels, and some later Jewish writings (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra) also read it of a heavenly individual. Many critical scholars take him as a symbol of ‘the people, the saints of the Most High’ (7:18, 27), just as the beasts symbolise kingdoms. Some identify him with an angel such as Michael. Christian interpreters reply that the king and his people belong together, so the Son of Man receives the kingdom on behalf of his people and shares it with them (compare 7:27).

7.ctx: Daniel, troubled, asks one of those standing by to explain.
7.mean: The four beasts are four kings or kingdoms that will arise from the earth, ‘but the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever’. Daniel asks especially about the fourth beast and the little horn. The horn will speak against the Most High, wear down the saints, and try to change the set times and the law. The saints will be given into his hand ‘for a time, and times, and half a time’, usually understood as three and a half years. That is a limited period: the persecution has a fixed end. Then the court sits, his dominion is taken away, and the kingdom is given to ‘the people, the saints of the Most High’. Daniel is left pale and keeps the matter in his heart.
7.big: God’s people may be persecuted for a limited time, but the kingdom will be theirs for ever.
7.diff: The identity of the fourth kingdom and the little horn is disputed (see the drop-down). Traditional Christian interpretation reads the little horn of chapter 7 as a final Antichrist figure (compare 2 Thessalonians 2; Revelation 13). Critical scholarship sees Antiochus IV here as in chapter 8.

hist.t: The four kingdoms: does the fourth mean Greece or Rome?
b: Chapters 2 and 7 describe four kingdoms, then God’s everlasting kingdom. Everyone agrees the first is Babylon.

The critical reading (the majority in academic scholarship): Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece. On this view the fourth is Alexander’s empire and its successors, and the ‘little horn’ is Antiochus IV. Davies argues that 8:21 names the ‘king of Greece’, from whose kingdom the wicked ruler of chapter 8 comes. He also notes that Isaiah 13:17 and Jeremiah 51:11 speak of the Medes overthrowing Babylon.

The traditional reading: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome. Its arguments: Daniel himself treats Media and Persia as one, as a single ram with two horns (8:20) and ‘the law of the Medes and Persians’ (6:8). The writing on the wall gives Babylon directly to ‘the Medes and Persians’ (5:28). The third beast of chapter 7, with four heads, matches Greece divided four ways after Alexander, as does the goat of chapter 8. This reading was held by first-century Jews: Josephus says Daniel ‘also wrote concerning the Roman government’. The Gospels apply Daniel’s kingdom and Son of Man to Jesus. The little horn of chapter 8 (Antiochus) is then a forerunner of a greater end-time enemy pictured by the little horn of chapter 7.

8.h: Daniel’s Vision of the Ram and the Goat
8.ctx: The third year of Belshazzar. From here to the end the book is in Hebrew again. Daniel is in Susa, later a Persian capital.
8.mean: A ram with two horns, one longer than the other and the longer coming up last, charges west, north and south, and no one can stand against it. Then a goat with one prominent horn races from the west without touching the ground, smashes the ram and tramples it. At the height of its power the goat’s great horn is broken, and four horns grow in its place. From one of them comes a small horn that grows great towards the south, the east and ‘the Beautiful Land’. It even reaches the host of heaven, takes away the daily sacrifice, throws down the sanctuary and casts truth to the ground. A holy one asks, ‘How long?’ The answer: ‘2,300 evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be properly restored.’
8.big: Even the desecration of God’s sanctuary has a set limit, after which it will be restored.

8.ctx: The angel Gabriel, named here for the first time in Scripture, explains the vision.
8.mean: The vision concerns ‘the time of the end’. The ram is the kings of Media and Persia; the goat is the king of Greece, and its great horn the first king. The four horns are four kingdoms that will arise from his nation, but without his power. In their latter time ‘an insolent king, skilled in intrigue’ will arise. He will destroy mighty men and the holy people, magnify himself, and even stand against ‘the Prince of princes’. ‘Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands.’ Daniel is told to seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future. He is left exhausted and ill, and does not understand it.
8.big: God names the empires before they appear, and the most arrogant persecutor will be broken without a human hand.
8.diff: Almost all interpreters identify this ‘insolent king’ with Antiochus IV (see the drop-down). Many traditional interpreters also see him as a pattern, or ‘type’, of a final Antichrist, since the vision concerns ‘the time of the end’ (8:17, 19). On the 2,300 evenings and mornings, see the drop-down.

hist.t: The goat, the broken horn and Antiochus IV
b: Chapter 8 names its own symbols: the ram is ‘the kings of Media and Persia’ and the goat is ‘the king of Greece’ (8:20–21). The great horn broken at the height of its power is Alexander, who died in 323 BC aged 32. The four horns are the kingdoms his generals carved out. Interpreters of every school identify the small horn that grows from one of them with Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC). He stopped the daily sacrifice and set up a pagan altar in the temple in December 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54–59).

The ‘2,300 evenings and mornings’ (8:14) is read either as 2,300 days (about six years, from the start of the trouble around 171 BC) or as 1,150 days, counting the evening and morning sacrifices separately (about three years). Either way it ends with the sanctuary restored. Judas Maccabeus rededicated the temple in December 164 BC, three years after its defilement. Because the identification is so clear, chapter 8 is central to both sides of the dating debate. Critics see a writer describing his own time; traditional interpreters see detailed prediction.

9.ctx: The first year of Darius the Mede (539/538 BC). Daniel has been reading Jeremiah’s prophecy that Jerusalem’s desolation would last seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11–12; 29:10), and the seventy years are nearly up.
9.mean: Scripture drives Daniel to prayer, not to calculation. With fasting, sackcloth and ashes he confesses the sins of his people as his own: ‘We have sinned and done wrong… we have not listened to your servants the prophets.’ He makes no excuses. Righteousness belongs to God; open shame belongs to us. The exile is exactly what the law of Moses warned of. Then he pleads, not on the basis of Israel’s merit, but of God’s character and name: ‘We are not presenting our petitions before you because of our righteous acts, but because of your great compassion.’ It ends urgently: ‘O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act! For your sake, O my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your name.’
9.big: True prayer takes God’s promises seriously, confesses sin honestly, and pleads God’s mercy and name rather than our merit.
